We'll look at the frog in reverse moves, that is, the moves  $n\to n-1$  or  $n\to n-2^{m_n+1}$  (this holds since if this move were to occur, indeed the end move has same  $\nu_2$  as the before end move), where we end at 1. Call the  $2^ik\to1,2^i\to1$  frogs frog 1 and 2, respectively.
    
    Case 1: Frog 2 does  $2^ik\to 2^ik-1$ . Then, have frog 1 copy all the same length of jumps of frog 2, unless it goes past 1. Then, frog 1 is at a point of the form  $2^i(k-1)+2^j:0\le j<i$ . Now, frog 1 can make the same length as the moves of the frog going from  $2^j$  until it gets to 1, which takes less moves than going from  $2^i(k-1)+2^a$  by inductive hypothesis, as needed.
    
    Case 2: Frog 2 starts off as  $2^ik\to 2^ik-2^{m_{2^ik}+1}$ . Then, it goes to a point of the form  $2^ij<2^ik$ , so if frog 1 copies the move, it reduces directly into inductive hypothesis where frog 1 takes less moves, as needed.

We reverse all of the steps and interpret the frog starting from some number and jumping  $n \to n-1$  or  $n \to n-2^{\nu_2(n)+1}$  on each turn, with the goal of ending up at  $1$ . This is clearly equivalent and will make things clearer.

We now use strong induction on  $i$ . First, for  $i=0$  the statement is clearly true for all  $k$ ; henceforth suppose  $i \geq 1$ . Starting from  $2^ik$ , if the frog ends up at  $2^i\ell$  for any  $\ell<k$  at any point we are done by downwards induction  $k$  (the base case is  $k=1$ ; we don't need a strict inequality). Thus the frog must end up at  $2^i(k-1)+2^m$  for some  $m<i$  and jump to  $2^i(k-1)-2^m$ . By inductive hypothesis, reaching  $1$  from  $2^i(k-1)-2^m$  takes at least as many moves as reaching  $1$  from  $2^m$ . Thus it takes less moves to go from  $2^i(k-1)+2^m$  to  $2^i(k-1)+1$  than to go from  $2^i(k-1)+2^m$  to  $1$ , so it takes less moves to go from  $2^ik$  to  $2^i(k-1)+1$  than to go from  $2^ik$  to  $1$ . There's an obvious bijection between a series of moves from  $2^ik$  to  $2^i(k-1)+1$  (since we never jump more than  $2^{i-1}$  in this case) and a series of moves from  $2^i$  to  $1$ , so it takes less moves to go from  $2^i$  to  $1$  than to go from  $2^ik$  to  $1$ .  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $ABCD$  be a quadrilateral, and let  $E$  and  $F$  be points on sides  $AD$  and  $BC$ , respectively, such that  $\frac{AE}{ED} = \frac{BF}{FC}$ . Ray  $FE$  meets rays  $BA$  and  $CD$  at  $S$  and  $T$ , respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles  $SAE$ ,  $SBF$ ,  $TCF$ , and  $TDE$  pass through a common point.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $AD$  and  $BC$  intersect at  $P$ .

<details><summary>Lemma 1</summary>$\left(PAB\right)$ ,  $\left(PCD\right)$ , and  $\left(PEF\right)$  are coaxial.

<details><summary>Proof</summary>Let  $p\left(X,\mathcal{C}\right)$  denote the power of the point  $X$  with respect to  $\mathcal{C}$ . The coaxial lemma states that three circles  $\Gamma$ ,  $\omega$ , and  $\gamma$  are coaxial if and only if  $\gamma$  is the locus of all points  $P$  such that  $\frac{p\left(P,\Gamma\right)}{p\left(P,\omega\right)}=k$  for some constant  $k$ . This is easily proven by coordinates (or if you don't like that, just use similar triangles).

Using directed lengths, we have that \[\frac{p\left(E,\left(PAB\right)\right)}{p\left(E,\left(PCD\right)\right)}=\frac{EA\cdot EP}{ED\cdot EP}=-\frac{AE}{ED}=-\frac{BF}{FC}=\frac{FB\cdot FP}{FC\cdot FP}=\frac{p\left(F,\left(PAB\right)\right)}{p\left(F,\left(PCD\right)\right)},\] so by the coaxial lemma,  $\left(PAB\right)$ ,  $\left(PCD\right)$ , and  $\left(PEF\right)$  are coaxial.</details></details>

Let  $M_1$  be the Miquel point of  $ABFE$  and  $M_2$  be the Miquel point of  $CDEF$ . We get that \[M_1=\left(SAE\right)\cap\left(SBF\right)\cap\left(PAB\right)\cap\left(PEF\right)\] and \[M_2=\left(TCF\right)\cap\left(TDE\right)\cap\left(PCD\right)\cap\left(PEF\right).\] By Lemma 1,  $\left(PAB\right)\cap\left(PCD\right)\cap\left(PEF\right)$  contains a point other than  $P$ , so  $M_1=M_2$ . Thus, \[\left(SAE\right)\cap\left(SBF\right)\cap\left(TCF\right)\cap\left(TDE\right)\] is nonempty (it contains  $M_1=M_2$ ), so the circumcircles of triangles  $SAE$ ,  $SBF$ ,  $TCF$ , and  $TDE$  pass through a common point.

Q.E.D.</details>

Well, may be, but this clever maths is over 100 years old ;) . Actually, it's an application of Miquel points. The basic fact is that four lines in the plane enclose four triangles, and that the circumcircles of these triangles have a common point; this point is called the *Miquel point* of the four lines. Now, the whole problem comes down to proving that the Miquel point of the lines AD, BC, AB, EF coincides with the Miquel point of the lines AD, BC, CD, EF; in other words, we have to prove that the circumcircles of triangles $X_{1337}AD$ , $X_{1337}BC$ and $X_{1337}EF$ have a common point. This is not only a simpler problem (we can forget about S and T now, the point $X_{1337}$ is much easier to handle), but also known: it is a restatement of http://www.mathlinks.ro/Forum/viewtopic.php?t=68157 . stem_md: Let  $n$  be a positive integer. Define a sequence by setting  $a_{1}= n$  and, for each  $k > 1$ , letting  $a_{k}$  be the unique integer in the range  $0\leq a_{k}\leq k-1$  for which  $a_{1}+a_{2}+...+a_{k}$  is divisible by  $k$ . For instance, when  $n = 9$  the obtained sequence is  $9,1,2,0,3,3,3,...$ . Prove that for any  $n$  the sequence  $a_{1},a_{2},...$  eventually becomes constant.
solution_md: All the above solutions are more elegant than my Inductive solution. Still i didn't find anyone posting this one so just providing a sketch. Key Observation Let $S_n(k)=\sum_{i=1}^ka_{n_i}$ . We claim $S_n(k)=S_{n-1}(k)$ or $S_n(k)=S_{n-1}(k) + k$ . Prove this by induction on $k$ . Now if the former happens then we get $a_{{n-1}_{k+1}}=a_{n_{k+1}}$ . If the latter happens see that $a_{n_{k+1}}==a_{{n-1}_{k+1}} - 1 ($ mod $ k+1)$ which gives $\boxed{a_{n_{k+1}}=a_{{n-1}_{k+1}} + 1}$ for $a_{{n-1}_{k+1}}\neq k$ and $a_{n_{k+1}}=0$ for $a_{{n-1}_{k+1}}=k$ Now show base case $n=1$ true , trivially by induction. Assume the problem for $n=N$ . For $N+1$ see that if for some $k$ , $S_n(k)=S_{n-1}(k)$ then we are done (by Induction Hypothesis). Else by Induction Hypothesis there exists $m \in N$ such that $k\geq m \implies a_{{n-1}_{k}}=a_{{n-1}_m}$ . By above , we get the same value of $a_{n_{k}}$ from a fixed value of $a_{{n-1}_{k}}$ regardless of $k$ . Combining we get $\boxed{{a_{n_k}}=a_{n_m}}$ for all $k\geq m$ .

Now choose a specific element of the sequence  $b_k = k d_k$ .  Since  $d_k \in \mathbb{N}$ , we either have  $0 < d_k < k$  or  $d_k \geq k$ .  In the first case,  $b_{k+x} = b_k + a_{k+1} + a_{k+2} + ... + a_{k+x} = k d_k + x d_k = (k+x) d_k$ .  Because  $0 < d_k < k < k+x$ , for any  $a_n$  where  $n \geq k$ ,  $a_n = d_k$ , so  $(a_n)$  eventually becomes constant.

In the second case, where  $d_k \geq k$ , we shall prove that  $d_n \geq d_{n+1}$  for all  $n \geq 2$ .  For contradiction, assume that  $d_n < d_{n+1}$  for some  $n \in \mathbb{N}$ .  We then have  $b_{n+1} = b_n + a_{n+1} \leq n d_n + n$ .  However, we also have  $b_{n+1} = (n+1)(d_{n+1}) \geq (n+1)(d_n + 1) = n d_n + n + d_n + 1$ .  These two inequalities imply that  $n d_n + n + d_n + 1 \leq n d_n + n$  or  $d_n + 1 \leq 0$ , which is clearly a contradiction.  We thus conclude that  $d_n \geq d_{n+1}$  for all  $n \geq 2$ .  Thus, even if  $d_k \geq k$ , we know that  $0 < d_{d_k+1} \leq d_k < d_k + 1$ .  Thus, the second case ultimately reduces to the first case, so  $a_n = d_{d_k + 1}$  for all  $n \geq d_k+1$ , so  $(a_n)$  eventually becomes constant and we are done.</details>

stem_md: A square grid on the Euclidean plane consists of all points  $(m,n)$ , where  $m$  and  $n$  are integers. Is it possible to cover all grid points by an infinite family of discs with non-overlapping interiors if each disc in the family has radius at least  $5$ ?
solution_md:
Quite an interesting problem - focusing **locally** on a set of three circles is relatively easily motivated making it slightly underwhelming in my opinion. 

We will prove that there is a circle of radius  $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$  that intersects no other circles in the plane which suffices as we get a  $1$  by  $1$  square in any such circle which will ultimately contain a lattice point. 

Take a circle  $\omega_1$  and the closest circle to it,  $\omega_2$ , we can assume that  $\omega_1$  and  $\omega_2$  are tangent simply by increasing the radius of  $\omega_1$  by  $dist(\omega_1,\omega_2)$ . 
Now, take one of the two circles tangent to both  $\omega_1$  and  $\omega_2$  on the exterior with radius  $\frac{10}{\sqrt{3}}-5 > \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ , say  $\Gamma$ .  $\textbf{Claim:}$   $\Gamma$  doesn't have two distinct intersections with any of the other circles in our tiling.  $\textbf{Proof)}$  
Consider a third circle  $\omega_3$  that is, without loss of generality, tangent  $\omega_1, \omega_2, \Gamma$ , we shall prove that the radius of  $\omega_3 \geq 5$  in which case we get that the two circles can't have two intersections. 

<details><summary>Remark</summary>In the previous argument, we can say without loss of generality that they are tangent because that minimizes the distance between  $\Gamma$  and the intersection of  $\omega_1$  and  $\omega_2$</details>

Now, notice that whenever we increase the radius of  $\omega_3$  ( $\omega_1, \omega_2. \omega_3$  now have symmetric roles), any circle that was contained with the region created by  $\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3$  with the former radii is still contained in the aforementioned region. 
We can consequently assume that the three circles all have radii  $5$ . 
Then, introducing the centers of the three circles,  $O_1, O_2, O_3$  and computing the circumradius of  $\triangle O_1O_2O_3$  which is equilateral (sidelength  $10$ ), we have that the circle tangent to the three circles on the exterior has radius  $\frac{10}{\sqrt{3}} - 5$  completing the proof.  $\blacksquare$

Here's a proof of why you can always fit a circle of radius  $ \frac{\sqrt 2}{2}$ , inside the region formed by  $ 3$  circles, each of which has radius at least  $ 5$ . 

1: First we note it's sufficient to prove it in the case where all the circles are tangent. Consider three circles  $ C_{1}, C_{2}, C_{3}$ , with centres  $ O_{1}, O_{2}, O_{3}$ .  Let  $ D$  be the inner Soddy circle of  $ O_{1} O_{2} O_{3}$ . Clearly  $ D$  lies strictly inside the triangle  $ O_{1} O_{2} O_{3}$ , and  $ D$  is the circle externally tangent to three other circles, each of which has radius at least  $ 5$ . Thus if we can prove the result for these  $ 3$  externally tangent circles, that it's sufficient. 

2: My proof for  $ 3$  externally tangent circles is just brute force. If the radii of the  $ 3$  circles are  $ a, b, c$ , then by Soddy circle results, the radius of the Inner Soddy circle, which lies inside the region formed by these  $ 3$  circles, is   $ f(a,b,c) \equal{} \frac {abc} {ab\plus{}bc\plus{}ac \plus{} 2 \sqrt{abc(a\plus{}b\plus{}c)}}$ . By differentiation, it's clear that  $ f(a,b,c)$  is increasing in each of it's variables, so  $ f(a,b,c) \geq f(5,5,5) > \frac {1}{\sqrt{2}}$ , so we can find a circle inside that has radius at least  $ \frac {1}{\sqrt{2}}$ , and contains a grid point, as required. 

3: It's intuitely obvious that this solves the problem, but here's a formal argument: Label the circles in our infinite family  $ C_{i}$ . Consider any circle in this square grid,  $ C_{1}$ . Draw a circle tangent to  $ C_{1}$ , centre  $ O_{1}$ , with radius  $ \frac {1}{\sqrt{2}}$ . This circle contains a grid point, so another circle  $ C_{2}$ , centre  $ O_{2}$  intersects this circle. Now consider any circle  $ C_{n}$ . As described in Step 1, we can find a circle of radius at least  $ \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}}$  'inside' these three circles. So another circle  $ C_{m}$  must intersect this circle. Now repeat the argument for  $ C_{1}, C_{2}$  and  $ C_{m}$ . Continue in this fashion, and after finitely many steps we will reach a disc of radius at least  $ \frac {1}{\sqrt {2}}$ , that lies outside our infinite family, which is a contradiction.

<details><summary>my solution</summary>This problem is a very weird problem that seems very obvious but has many technicalities that need to be addressed, which I will hopefully do rigorously.

I claim that any space has enough room to fit a circle of radius  $>\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ . This is enough to solve the problem because any circle with radius  $>\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$  can contain a square with sides parallel to the axis and with side length  $>1$ ; this means that this square covers at least one horizontal lattice grid line and at least one vertical lattice grid line, implying it covers at least one lattice point, which means that the circle also does so.

Now for the proof. Take any space, and put a circle of radius  $0$  in it. Now continuously blow the circle bigger, until it is tangent with at least three circles (but they must be tangent, NOT intersected). These three circles are thus the circles that determine the limit to how big a circle in the given space can be, so we just need to focus on these circles only.

Note that we may assume these three circles are tangent, because if not we can blow them up until they are tangent and the remaining white space will be strictly smaller. If any of these circles have radius  $>5$ , it is easy to see that reducing the radius of that circle until it is  $=5$  will make the white space strictly smaller; thus, the point at which the white space is smallest is when all three circles have radius  $=5$ .

Now what we just need to do is calculate the radius of the largest circle that can fit in this space, which can be easily found to be  $\dfrac{10\sqrt{3}}{3}-5 > 0.77$  using the approximation  $\sqrt{3}\ge 1.732$  which can be confirmed by squaring. However, note that  $0.77 > 0.71 > \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$  using the approximation  $1.42 > \sqrt{2}$  (which again can be confirmed by squaring) so this circle is bigger than the smallest necessary size, and so we're done.</details>

In mathematics, Minkowski's theorem is the statement that any convex set in $\mathbb{R}^n$ which is symmetric with respect to the origin and with volume greater than $2^n d(L)$ contains a non-zero lattice point. The theorem was proved by Hermann Minkowski in 1889 and became the foundation of the branch of number theory called the geometry of numbers.

SolutionLemma. Given three non-overlapping disks in the plane, there exists a fourth circle externally tangent to all three disks, with radius at least $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ . Proof. Let the three disks have radii $r_1, r_2, r_3$ , and let them be centered at points $1, 2, 3$ . Let the fourth circle have radius $r_4$ , and let it be centered at point $4$ . (This point must exist because it is the intersection of two hyperbolas, one of them with foci at points $1$ and $2$ , and the other with foci at points $1$ and $3$ .) Without loss of generality, let $\angle 134 \le 120^\circ$ . Then by Law of Cosines on triangle 134, we have $$ (r_1 + r_3)^2 \le \overline{13}^2 = (r_1 + r)^2 + (r_3 + r)^2 - 2(r_1 + r)(r_3 + r) \cos \angle 134 \le (r_1 + r)^2 + (r_3 + r)^2 + (r_1 + r)(r_3 + r). $$ Simplify and rearrange: $$ 3r^2 + 3r (r_1 + r_3) \ge r_1 r_3 $$ $$ 3r \cdot \left( \frac{r}{r_1 r_3} + \frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_3} \right) \ge 1. $$ If $r \le \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ , then since $r_1, r_3 \ge 5$ , we have $$ LHS \le \frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \left( \frac{\sqrt{2}}{50} + \frac{2}{5} \right) = \frac{3}{50} + \frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{5} $$ $$ = \frac{3 + 30 \sqrt{2}}{50} < \frac{3 + 47}{50} = 1 = RHS, $$ contradiction. Thus in fact $r_4 > \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ , as desired. Now suppose a tiling by discs does exist. stem_md: Let  $S$  be a set containing  $n^{2}+n-1$  elements, for some positive integer  $n$ . Suppose that the  $n$ -element subsets of  $S$  are partitioned into two classes. Prove that there are at least  $n$  pairwise disjoint sets in the same class.
solution_md: We will prove a stronger result: if $S$ contains $mn+m-1$ elements, then we can find $m$ disjoint sets of cardinality $n$ in $S$ . The proof proceeds by induction on $m$ , with the base case $m=1$ clear. Assume for the sake of contradiction that for some partition of the subsets $\mathcal S = \mathcal A \sqcup \mathcal B$ that there does not exist a collection of $m$ disjoint sets of cardinality $n$ in either $\mathcal A$ or $\mathcal B$ .**Claim:** If any two subsets $A$ and $B$ satisfy $|A \cap B| \geq n-1$ , then $A$ and $B$ belong to the same family. *Proof:* Let $T$ be an $n$ -element set that contains both $A$ and $B$ . By the inductive hypothesis, there exists a family of $m-1$ pairwise disjoint subsets of size $n$ among the $(m-1)n + m-2$ elements in $S \setminus T$ in either $\mathcal A$ or $\mathcal B$ , say $\mathcal A$ . Then both $A$ and $B$ must be in $\mathcal B$ , otherwise adding one of them to the previous family yields the desired family. $\blacksquare$ It is easy to see from here that one of $A$ and $B$ must contain *all* $n$ -element subsets of $S$ now (say, by replacing one element to go from $A \to B$ in each step). We have a contradiction, which finishes the inductive step.**Remark:** My reason for generalizing the problem came off the hunch that direct induction from $n-1$ to $n$ basically required two steps: extend the family, and add one element to everything in the family. The former is significantly easier to do than the latter, and the steps feel pretty much separate (there's no reason to have $n$ appear in two places either). So I think this solution is actually very well-motivated and also very instructive.

I don't really like this problem, but I think the main motivation for generalizing the problem is that the original problem doesn't allow you to look at small cases. (Also, it's not initially clear where the $n^2+n-1$ comes from.) And pretty much the simplest way to get lots of similarly-flavored small cases is to start with $k=2,3$ in "Find the smallest $N(n,k)$ such that when we partition the $n$ -subsets of a $\ge N(n,k)$ -set into $2$ classes, we can find some $k$ pairwise disjoint sets in the same class." One way to see that it might be helpful: If you first look at the obvious bound $N(n,n)\le (2n-1)n$ (by considering the $2n-1$ pairwise disjoint sets $[1,n],[n+1,2n],\ldots,[(2n-2)n+1,(2n-1)n]$ ), it's fairly natural to think about the analogous bound $N(n,k)\le (2k-1)n$ . (On the other hand, changing the number of classes just complicates the situation.) Of course, it's not immediately obvious that the $k$ and $k+1$ cases are related---at best you might be able to build off from $k$ to $k+1$ , but a priori you might only expect it to give a better understanding of how $N(n,k)$ grows.

SolutionWe prove the following statement below, by induction on $m$ :
Let $S$ be a set containing $mn + m - 1$ elements, for some positive integers $m$ and $n$ . Suppose that the $n$ -element subsets of $S$ are partitioned into two classes. Prove that there are at least $m$ pairwise disjoint sets in the same class.
When $m = 1$ , the result is obvious. Now, suppose the result is true for $m$ , and consider $m \to m + 1$ . For a contradiction, suppose neither class contains $m + 1$ disjoint subsets. We have $S = (mn + m - 1) + (m + 1)$ . Take an $mn + m - 1$ -element $T$ of $S$ , by the inductive hypothesis, there exist $m$ pairwise disjoint subsets in the same class (call it "red") with union a subset of $T$ . Now, consider the remaining $m + 1$ elements. None of the $m$ -element subsets of this set can be in the red class, so all of these subsets are in the other class. Doing this for all $mn + m - 1$ element subsets of $S$ , we see all subsets are in the same class, which is a contradiction, and the inductive step is complete. Setting $m = n$ finishes the problem.

We show a generalization of this result: let  $S$  be a set of  $k(n+1)-1$  sets. Let the subsets of  $S$  with cardinality  $n$  be partitioned into two classes. Show that one of the classes contains  $k$  pairwise disjoint sets. 

The proof is by induction on  $k$ . If  $k=1$ , the result is obvious. For  $k\ge 2$ , we use the following argument to achieve the result. Let  $A$  and  $B$  be sets with cardinality  $n$  and  $|A\cap B|=n-1$ . We claim that  $A$  and  $B$  lie in the same class or we are done, which clearly suffices. Suppose that  $A$  and  $B$  lie in separate classes. By the inductive hypothesis on  $T=S\setminus (A\cup B)$ , one of the classes restricted to  $T$  contains  $k-1$  pairwise disjoint sets, so the result holds for  $k$  by considering those  $k-1$  pairwise disjoint sets by using the appropriate choice of  $A$  and  $B$  as the  $k$ -th set.

We prove the more general statement: in a set  $S$  of  $m(n+1)-1$  elements, if we partition the  $n$ -element subsets of  $S$  into two classes, then there are at least  $m$  pairwise disjoint sets in the same class. This is by induction on  $m$ , with the base case of  $m=1$  being trivial. For the inductive step, consider any  $n+1$  elements in  $S$  and temporarily hide them; among the remaining  $(m-1)(n+1)-1$  elements, we can find  $m-1$   $n$ -element subsets in the same family which are disjoint. Then, if we cannot find  $m$  pairwise disjoint sets in the same class, no  $n$ -element subset formed from the  $n+1$  hidden elements can be in the same family, so they must all be in the same family—in other words, any two  $n$ -element subsets which overlap in  $n-1$  positions are in the same family. But this clearly implies that every  $n$ -element subset is in the same family, in which we can obviously find  $m$  pairwise disjoint sets, as desired.  $\blacksquare$ **Remark:** Perhaps a possible way to motivate the idea that the number of sets and their size is unrelated is to discover a class of "equality cases" where the size of  $S$  is "tight": for some fixed  $1 \leq k \leq n$ , take  $kn-1$  elements and color them red. Put every set with at least  $k$  red elements in one family and the rest in another. We can find  $n$  disjoint subsets in the second family by forming each subset using  $k-1$  red elements and  $n-k+1$  non-red elements, and we will have enough non-red elements to do this, but for  $|S|=n^2+n-2$  this is no longer the case. 

However, the fact that the number of sets and their size is the same is not relevant to this "equality case". For the more general case we can take  $km-1$  elements instead and essentially employ the same construction. Furthermore, it seems that the generalized statement is true in general by checking small cases, so it is motivated to pursue it instead, with induction now seeming viable.

An *animal* with  $n$  *cells* is a connected figure consisting of  $n$  equal-sized cells[1].

A *dinosaur* is an animal with at least  $2007$  cells. It is said to be *primitive* it its cells cannot be partitioned into two or more dinosaurs. Find with proof the maximum number of cells in a primitive dinosaur. 

(1) Animals are also called *polyominoes*. They can be defined inductively. Two cells are *adjacent* if they share a complete edge. A single cell is an animal, and given an animal with  $n$  cells, one with  $n+1$  cells is obtained by adjoining a new cell by making it adjacent to one or more existing cells.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>The answer is  $\boxed{8025}$ . For this, consider a long cross made up of four arms of length  $2006$  and one center piece (looks like a plus sign). Attempt to partition this dinosaur. The center piece must be in one of the other partitions. The other partitions have size at most  $2006$ , so they are not dinosaurs. Thus, this works.

Now, assume that there is a primitive dinosaur  $\mathcal{D}$  with size  $n\geq8026$ . Consider the graph  $\mathcal{G}$  with vertices at each of the cells and edges between two vertices if and only if the corresponding cells are connected in  $\mathcal{D}$ . Let  $\mathcal{T}$  be a spanning tree of  $\mathcal{G}$ .

Some notation:

- For a graph  $\mathcal{K}$ , let  $\left|\mathcal{K}\right|$  denote the number of vertices in  $\mathcal{K}$  (for example  $\left|\mathcal{G}\right|=\left|\mathcal{T}\right|=n$ ). Also let  $D\left(\mathcal{K}\right)$  denote the maximal degree of any vertex in  $\mathcal{K}$ . Note that  $D\left(\mathcal{T}\right)\leq D\left(\mathcal{G}\right)\leq4$  by definition and the problem constraints (each cell can only be connected in four places).

- For a vertex  $V$  in graph  $\mathcal{K}$ , let  $\deg_{\mathcal{K}}\left(V\right)$  denote the degree of  $V$  with respect to  $\mathcal{K}$ .

- For a vertex  $V$  in  $\mathcal{T}$  and neighbor  $N$ , let  $S_{V,N}$  denote the subtree formed by removing edge  $V-N$  and taking the resulting tree containing  $N$ . It follows by definition that \[\left|S_{V,N}+S_{N,V}\right|=n.\]

- For a vertex  $V$ , let  $M\left(V\right)$  denote the neighbor of  $V$  with the largest subtree (if there are multiple, choose arbitrarily). That is,  $\left|S_{V,M\left(V\right)}\right|\geq\left|S_{V,N}\right|$  for any neighbor  $N$  of  $V$ . Note that \[\left|S_{V,M\left(V\right)}\right|\geq\frac{n-1}{\deg_{\mathcal{T}}\left(V\right)}\geq\frac{n-1}{D\left(\mathcal{T}\right)}\geq\frac{n-1}{4}>2006\] by the Pigeonhole Principle. Let the cells of the animal be vertices on a graph and draw an edge between adjacent cells. We make cuts to the animal until  $G$  is a connected tree by pre-emptively cutting these connections. We show that, even with these cuts forcibly made, we can still decompose the animal into dinosaurs. 

Choose an arbitrary cell on the animal. If we remove this cell, the neighbors of the cell are part of different connected components since we have already made cuts to make  $G$  a tree. The sum of the sizes of these connected components is  $8026 - 1 = 8025$  so, by Pigeonhole, since there are at most four neighbors, one of them has size at least  $2007$ . Call the side of the cell connecting to this size  $2007$ + component the "beefy side". Whenever this component has size at most  $2006 \cdot 3$ , simply cutting the beefy side suffices since the two remaining components both has size at least  $2007$ . Otherwise, call it "overweight".

We start with an arbitrary cell  $c_1$  on the animal. Whenever the component  $G_1$  connected to the "beefy side" is overweight, observe that our side  $G - G_1$  has size at most  $2006$ . We cross the "beefy side" and now look at the cell  $c_2$  adjacent to it. The "beefy side" of  $c_2$  must not connect to  $c_1$  by the observation. Therefore, the size of the component  $G_2$  on the other side of the "beefy side" of  $c_2$  must be lower than that of  $c_1$  since everything in  $G_2$  is in  $G_1$  and  $c_2$  is in  $G_1$  but not  $G_2$ . If we continue the process, the size of  $G_k$  will strictly decrease until it is at most  $2006 \cdot 3$ . We cut off this final "beefy side" to finish.</details>

Let  $ABC$  be an acute triangle with  $\omega,S$ , and  $R$  being its incircle, circumcircle, and circumradius, respectively. Circle  $\omega_{A}$  is tangent internally to  $S$  at  $A$  and tangent externally to  $\omega$ . Circle  $S_{A}$  is tangent internally to  $S$  at  $A$  and tangent internally to  $\omega$ . Let  $P_{A}$  and  $Q_{A}$  denote the centers of  $\omega_{A}$  and  $S_{A}$ , respectively. Define points  $P_{B}, Q_{B}, P_{C}, Q_{C}$  analogously. Prove that
\[8P_{A}Q_{A}\cdot P_{B}Q_{B}\cdot P_{C}Q_{C}\leq R^{3}\; , \]
with equality if and only if triangle  $ABC$  is equilateral.
solution_md: *Here's a very computational solution with $\sqrt{bc}$ inversion and inversion distance formula* (different from post #37). The solution may appear long but the advantage is that there is no tricky step and if we do no silly mistake, then we are just done. [rule] Let $r$ be the inradius of $\triangle ABC$ and $2 \alpha,2 \beta, 2 \gamma$ denote the measure of angles $\angle CAB,\angle ABC,BCA$ , respectively. **Claim** (Key Claim)**:** $\displaystyle P_AQ_A = \frac{R \cdot \sin \alpha \cos^2 \alpha}{\cos \beta \cos \gamma}$ **Proof:** Let $\Gamma$ be the $A$ -mixtilinear **excircle** with center $T$ and radius $R_A$ . Let $X,Y$ be the projection of $T$ onto lines $AB,AC$ , respectively. It is well known that the midpoint of segment $XY$ is $I_A$ , the $A$ -excenter of $\triangle ABC$ . Thus, $$ \sin 2 \alpha \cdot AT_A = XY = 2AI_A \cdot \tan \alpha ~ \implies ~ \boxed{AT_A = \frac{AI_A}{\cos^2 \alpha}} $$ Let $\Phi$ be the $\sqrt{bc}$ inversion (followed by reflection in angle bisector, of course). Denote by $Z^*$ the image of a point $Z$ under $\Phi$ . Then, - $\Phi$ swaps $\omega \longleftrightarrow \Gamma$ and $S \longleftrightarrow \overline{BC}$ . - $\Phi$ maps $\omega_A,S_A$ to some lines $\ell_1,\ell_2$ (respectively) both parallel to $\overline{BC}$ and tangent to $\Gamma$ such that $\ell_2$ is closer to $A$ than $\ell_1$ . - $P_A^*,Q_A*$ are reflection of $A$ in lines $\ell_1,\ell_2$ , respectively. - $\displaystyle P_AQ_A = P_A^* Q_A^* \cdot \frac{bc}{AP_A^* \cdot A Q_A^*}$ . Let $\ell_3$ be the line passing through $T$ parallel to $\overline{BC}$ and $\theta = \beta - \gamma$ . Now $d(\ell_2,\ell_3) = d(\ell_3,\ell_1) = R_A$ and $d(A,\ell_3) = AT_A \cdot \cos \theta$ . Also, $R_A = AT_A \cdot \sin \alpha$ . Thus, \begin{align*} P_A^* Q_A^* = 4R_A ~,~ AP_A^* = 2(AT_A \cdot \cos \theta + R_A) ~,~ AQ_A^* = 2(AT_A \cdot \cos \theta - R_A) \implies P_AQ_A = P_A^* Q_A^* \cdot \frac{bc}{AP_A^* \cdot A Q_A^*} = \frac{\sin \alpha}{\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \alpha} \cdot \frac{bc}{AT_A} = \frac{r \cdot \cos^2 \alpha}{\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \alpha} \end{align*} But we also have $$ \cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \alpha = \Big(\sin(90^\circ + \beta - \gamma) - \sin \alpha \Big)\Big( \sin (90^\circ + \beta - \gamma) + \alpha \Big) $$ Now using Product-Sum Identities (in ch-5 of EGMO) we obtain \begin{align*} \sin(90^\circ + \beta - \gamma) - \sin \alpha = 2 \cdot \sin \left( \frac{(90^\circ + \beta - \gamma) - \alpha}{2} \right) \cdot \cos \left( \frac{(90^\circ + \beta - \gamma) + \alpha}{2} \right) = 2 \sin \beta \sin \gamma \sin (90^\circ + \beta - \gamma) + \sin \alpha = 2 \cdot \sin \left( \frac{(90^\circ + \beta - \gamma) + \alpha}{2} \right) \cdot \cos \left( \frac{(90^\circ + \beta - \gamma) - \alpha}{2} \right) = 2 \cos \gamma \cos \beta \end{align*} Hence $$ \cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \alpha = 4 \cos \beta \cos \gamma \sin \beta \sin \gamma $$ So we finally have that $$ P_AQ_A = \frac{r \cdot \cos^2 \alpha}{\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \alpha} = \frac{r \cdot \cos^2 \alpha}{4 \cos \beta \cos \gamma \sin \beta \sin \gamma } $$ Lastly, it is well know that $$ r = 4R \cdot \sin \alpha \sin \beta \sin \gamma $$ Hence, $$ P_AQ_A = \frac{r \cdot \cos^2 \alpha}{4 \cos \beta \cos \gamma \sin \beta \sin \gamma } = \frac{R \cdot \sin \alpha \cos^2 \alpha}{\cos \beta \cos \gamma} $$ This proves our claim. $\square$ So using our claim, we obtain that the given inequality is equivalent to the following $$ \sin \alpha \sin \beta \sin \gamma \le \frac{1}{8} \qquad{(1)} $$ The most simple way to finish from here is take $\log$ on both sides and using Jensen's inequality. But we also present a nice synthetic type proof: We know that $$ \sin \alpha \sin \beta \sin \gamma = \frac{r}{4R} $$ So $(1)$ is equivalent to $$ 2r \le R $$ Which is well known to be true (and we also know that equality holds if and only if circumcenter and incenter of $\triangle ABC$ coincide, which can happen iff and only if $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral). This completes the proof of the problem. $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $ \mathcal{P}$  be a convex polygon with  $ n$  sides,  $ n\ge3$ . Any set of  $ n \minus{} 3$  diagonals of  $ \mathcal{P}$  that do not intersect in the interior of the polygon determine a *triangulation* of  $ \mathcal{P}$  into  $ n \minus{} 2$  triangles. If  $ \mathcal{P}$  is regular and there is a triangulation of  $ \mathcal{P}$  consisting of only isosceles triangles, find all the possible values of  $ n$ .

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $ v_1, v_2, ... v_n$  be the vertices of a regular  $ n$ -gon.  Define  $ P(q, n)$  to return  $ 1$  if the polygon  $ v_1, v_2, ... v_q$  of a regular  $ n$ -gon has an isosceles triangulation, and  $ 0$  otherwise.  We claim that  $ P(n, n) \equal{} 1$  if and only if  $ n \equal{} 2^a(2^b \plus{} 1), a, b \ge 0$ .

The answer is  $n=2^a(2^b+1)$  for any  $a,b$ . 
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Claim:  $n$  works $\iff 2n$  works. 
Proof:  $(\implies)$  Simply add on smaller isosceles triangles at each edge of the  $n$ -gon that make it a  $2n$ -gon.  $(\impliedby)$  Consider two adjacent vertices  $P,P'$  in the  $2n$ -gon, and the two adjacent vertices to this edge,  $A,B$ . Note that in a triangulation, every outer edge in the polygon is used in some triangle. So consider the isosceles triangle which uses edge  $PP'$ . Since  $2n$  is even, the only possible isosceles triangles containing edge  $PP'$  are  $\triangle PP'A$  and  $\triangle PP'B$ . Continuing in this manner for all  $n$  sets of 2 adjacent vertices, we see that we get  $n$  ``outer'' triangles, which we can cut off; and now we have an  $n$ -gon. 
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Write  $n=2^ak$  for some odd  $k$ . Then  $n$  works iff  $k$  works. So we focus our attention on finding which odd  $n$  work. 

We claim only odd  $n$  that are of the form  $n=2^b+1$  work. Note that this finishes the problem. 

Call an ``arc of length  $x$ '' a sequence of consecutive  $x+1$  vertices of the  $n$ -gon, connected by  $x$  edges. Consider an arc of length  $x$ , along with the diagonal of the  $n$ -gon which connects the first and last vertices of the arc. Let us figure out for which  $x$  this figure is triangulate-able with isosceles triangles. 

Suppose that this figure does not contain the center of the  $n$ -gon. Then by an argument similar to that in the claim, we see that we must have that the outer arc is covered by the smallest type of isosceles triangles. This means that  $x$  is even, and that we have reduced the  $x$ -length arc to an  $x/2$ -length arc. Continuing in this manner, we see that  $x$  must be a power of 2.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The first isosceles triangle placed in the  $n$ -gon splits it into 3 arcs of length  $x_1\le x_2\le x_3$ , where  $n=x_1+x_2+x_3$ . This means that  $n$  is the sum of at most 3 powers of 2 (at most since we can have  $x=0$ ). 

But we claim that furthermore,  $x_1=1$ . Indeed, consider the isosceles triangle which contains some edge  $PP'$ , and its adjacent vertices  $A,B$ , where  $P,P'$  are consecutive vertices of the  $n$ -gon. The triangle can either be  $PP'A$  or  $PP'B$ , or  $PP'X$ , where  $X$  is the antipode of the midpoint of arc  $PP'$  (on the circle circumscribing the  $n$ -gon). But since  $n$  is odd, all triangles cannot be of the first two forms, so at least one is of the form  $PP'X$ . Therefore,  $x_1=1$ . 

Therefore, one isosceles triangle splits the  $n$ -gon into two arcs of equal length, so  $x_2=x_3$ . Hence,  $n=1+2x_2$ , which is 1 more than a power of 2. 

A construction to show that such an  $n$  works is to simply split the arc into 3 arcs of length 1,  $\tfrac{n-1}{2}$ , and  $\tfrac{n-1}{2}$ , which are both powers of 2. Now use the arc construction to finish.

The answer is all  $n$  expressible in the form  $2^a(2^b+1)$  where  $a,b$  are nonnegative integers. First notice that if  $n$  works, then  $2n$  works: we can connect every other vertex in the  $2n$ -gon, which forms  $n$  isosceles triangles and a regular  $n$ -gon. If we can isosceles triangulate the  $n$ -gon, we can also isosceles triangulate the  $2n$ -gon. Thus it suffices to only consider odd numbers and  $4$ .
We will take care of  $4$  first, since it's trivial: just draw any diagonal and you get an isosceles triangle.
Now we look at odd numbers. It suffices to show that any odd  $n$  must be in the form  $2^a+1$ . Suppose  $n=2k+1$  for some  $k$ . Let the vertices of the  $n$ -gon be  $A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_{2k+1}$ , where indices are taken mod  $n$  (so  $A_{2k+2}=A_1$  for instance). Define a "big triangle" to be a triangle of the form  $A_{i}A_{k+i}A_{k+i+1}$ . Also define a "small triangle" to be of the form  $A_{i}A_{i+1}A_{i+2}$ . We prove the following lemma:**Lemma 1:** Every isosceles triangulation of a  $2k+1$ -gon must contain exactly one big triangle and  $k$  small triangles.**Proof:** We will first show that there is at least one big triangle. Consider the triangle containing  $A_{k+i}A_{k+i+1}$  for an arbitrary  $i$ . For it to be isosceles, it must either be a big triangle or a small triangle. Now suppose that all of the triangles containing an edge were small triangles. Then we would need an even number of sides, since each small triangle contains two edges. But this is impossible since  $2k+1$  is odd. So there must be at least one big triangle. Now observe that if there were multiple big triangles, there would be intersecting diagonals, which is not allowed. So there must be exactly one big triangle. This occupies 1 edge. Hence the remaining  $2k$  edges are occupied by  $k$  small triangles, as desired.  $\blacksquare$ Now suppose that we draw in the big triangle  $A_1A_{k+1}A_{k+2}$ . This splits the polygon into an isosceles triangle and two "half-polygons" (kind of), each with  $k+1$  sides:  $k$  of equal length and one "long side". We will focus on the half-polygon  $A_1A_2\ldots A_{k+1}$ . Then the "long side" is  $A_1A_{k+1}$ . Consider the triangle which contains the "long side" as a side. Since no other sides or diagonals of the half-polygon are that long, we conclude that the long side must be the base of the isosceles triangle. This means that  $k$  must be even, otherwise there would be no isosceles triangles. If  $k$  is even, then we draw the triangle  $A_1A_{k+1}A_{k/2 + 1}$ , which is the only isosceles triangle containing the long side. But this creates even smaller  $k/2$ -gons (quarter-polygons, maybe). Applying the same argument again and again, we see that  $k$  must be a power of  $2$ , otherwise we will eventually reach an odd number when dividing by  $2$  and be unable to further triangulate. Conversely, if  $k$  is a power of  $2$  then this "splitting" algorithm will eventually produce an isosceles triangulation: it will terminate when everything becomes a triangle and it won't produce any non-isosceles triangles. This implies that an isosceles triangulation exists for odd  $n$  if and only if  $n=2^a+1$  for some  $a$ , which implies the desired result.  $\blacksquare$

Hence, it suffices to check odd  $n$ . Let an ear of a triangulation be a triangle sharing two sides with the polygon, and let the span of a diagonal be  $\min{|S_1|, |S_2|}$ , where  $S_1$  and  $S_2$  are the sets of sides of the polygon on either side of it. We proceed with casework.

Case  $1$ : There exists at least one  $\triangle ABC$  in the triangulation with  $AB = AC$  and  $BC$  a side of the polygon. Obviously  $A$  is the midpoint of the longer walk from  $B$  to  $C$ . Now consider the smaller portion of the polygon cut off by side  $AB$ . Clearly every diagonal of this smaller polygon is shorter than  $AB$ , so  $AB$  must be a base of the other isosceles triangle with it is a side. Hence, the span of  $AB$  is even. But by repeating the same argument over and over, we get that the span of  $AB$  must be a power of  $2$ . In particular,  $n$  is one more than a power of   $2$ . Note that the construction for  $n = 2^k + 1$  is evident in the above explanation for this case.

Case  $2$ : There exists no such triangle as described in case  $1$ . Let  $\triangle ABC$  be such that  $AB = AC$  and none of  $AB$ ,  $BC$ , and  $AC$  are sides of the polygon. By the same reasoning as before, the spans of  $AB$  and  $AC$  are powers of  $2$ . If  $\angle BAC$  is obtuse, the span of  $BC$  must also be a power of  $2$ . But then  $n$  is even since none of  $AB$ ,  $BC$ , and  $AC$  are sides, but we assumed  $n$  is odd -- contradiction. Hence,  $\angle BAC$  is obtuse. If  $BC$  is the base of the other isosceles triangle with it as a side, then the length of the longer walk from  $B$  to  $C$  must be a power of  $2$  by the same reasoning as before and again we get that  $n$  is even. Hence,  $BC$  is not the base of that triangle. Let the triangle be  $BCD$  with  $BC = BD$ . Then clearly  $\angle CBD$  is acute, so the span of  $CD$  is a power of two by the same reasoning again. But again this implies that  $n$  is even, so we have exhausted all cases.

Finally, we get that  $n$  must be of the form  $2^a(2^b + 1)$  for nonnegative integers  $a$  and  $b$  (and all such  $n\neq 2$  work).

Note that there must exist at least one triangle in the triangulation; draw that triangle, and our polygon is split into three regions: two containing  $k$  line segments, and one containing  $n - 2k$  line segments. The only way this is possible is if  $k$  is even, or  $k = 2$  in which case the recursive method stops. Therefore,  $k$  is a perfect power of  $2$ , and so is  $2k$ . Since we can do the same thing to  $n-2k$ , that means that  $n-2k$  is also a perfect power of  $2$ , and all such  $n$  are the sum of two powers of  $2$ .

<details><summary>Solution</summary>I claim that the answer is all numbers of the form  $2^a+2^b$  for positive integers  $a$  and  $b.$  

First, note that if  $n$  is even, then any side of the polygon cannot be one of the non-repeated sides because then the vertices of the triangle would be split into a group of  $3$  (the vertices of such a triangle) and two groups with an equal number of vertices, thus resulting in an odd number of total vertices, contradiction. Therefore, the sides of the  $n$ -gon must be partitioned into pairs of adjacent sides which are the repeated sides of their respective isosceles triangles. We will get a regular  $\tfrac{n}{2}$ -gon, so it follows that there exists a desired triangulation of a regular  $n$ -gon if and only if there exists a desired triangulation for a regular  $\tfrac{n}{2}$ -gon (for even  $n$ ). 

Hence, it remains to show that a triangulation of a regular  $n$ -gon for odd  $n$  exists if and only if  $n$  is of the form  $2^a+1$  for a positive integer  $k.$  

A construction for such odd positive integers  $n$  is easy to find: Simply choose some particular side of the  $n$ -gon and construct the triangle with that side as its non-repeated side, and then repeatedly pair up adjacent sides in the resulting polygons that the  $n$ -gon is split into. (The number of ``short" sides that each of the resulting polygons will have will always be a power of  $2,$  so the pairing can be done until there will only be a triangle left in each such polygon.) 

Now, we show that a desired triangulation exists for an odd positive integer  $n$  only if  $n=2^k+1$  for some positive integer  $k.$  Since the  $n$ -gon has an odd number of sides, there must exist one of them that is a non-repeated side in its isosceles triangle. This will split the  $n$ -gon into two polygons, each one of which has a long side and  $\tfrac{n-1}{2}$  short sides. If any one of these short sides is a non-repeated side in its isosceles triangle, then there would have to be crossing diagonals, contradiction, so the short sides must be able to be paired up. Hence, it follows that  $\tfrac{n-1}{2}$  has to be even. Inductively proceeding in the same way, it we know that the new polygons must also have an even number of short sides, and so on. Thus,  $\tfrac{n-1}{2}$  has to be a power of  $2,$  so we get
\begin{align*}
    \frac{n-1}{2}=2^h &\implies n-1=2^{h+1} 
    &\implies n=2^{h+1}+1
\end{align*}
for some nonnegative integer  $h.$  Taking  $k=h+1,$  we get the desired result, concluding the proof.  $\square$</details>

stem_md: Let  $ ABC$  be an acute, scalene triangle, and let  $ M$ ,  $ N$ , and  $ P$  be the midpoints of  $ \overline{BC}$ ,  $ \overline{CA}$ , and  $ \overline{AB}$ , respectively. Let the perpendicular bisectors of  $ \overline{AB}$  and  $ \overline{AC}$  intersect ray  $ AM$  in points  $ D$  and  $ E$  respectively, and let lines  $ BD$  and  $ CE$  intersect in point  $ F$ , inside of triangle  $ ABC$ . Prove that points  $ A$ ,  $ N$ ,  $ F$ , and  $ P$  all lie on one circle.
solution_md:
Here's a solution with inversion. It's actually remarkably quick; the first several paragraphs are just about sorting things out after the inversion. The actual solution is just the angle chase in the final two paragraphs.
<details><summary>What's going on?</summary>First, we make a few preliminary observations. Let  $O$  be the circumcenter of  $\triangle ABC.$  Then since  $ON \perp AN$  and  $OP \perp AP$ , we deduce that  $A, N, P, O$  are inscribed in a circle of diameter  $\overline{AO}.$  In addition, since  $D$  and  $E$  lie on the perpendicular bisectors of  $\overline{AB}$  and  $\overline{AC}$ , respectively, it follows that  $D \equiv OP \cap AM$  and  $E \equiv ON \cap AM.$  Now, let  $H$  be the foot of the altitude from  $A$  to  $\overline{BC}$ , and let  $l$  be the  $A$ -symmedian in  $\triangle ABC.$  Then consider a transformation  $\mathcal{I}$  composed of an inversion with center  $A$  and radius  $r = \sqrt{bc/2}$  combined with a reflection in the  $A$ -angle bisector. By basic inversive properties, we deduce that  $\mathcal{I}$  takes
\begin{align*} 
B &\to N 
N &\to B 
C &\to P 
P &\to C.
\end{align*} It follows that the image of  $\odot (APON)$  under  $\mathcal{I}$  is just the line  $BC.$  Therefore,  $\mathcal{I}$  takes  $O \equiv \odot (APON) \cap AO$  to the intersection of  $BC$  with the reflection of  $AO$  in the  $A$ -angle bisector. Since lines  $AO$  and  $AH$  are isogonal w.r.t. the  $A$ -angle bisector (this follows from the well known fact that the circumcenter and orthocenter are isogonal conjugates), we deduce that  $\mathcal{I}$  takes
\begin{align*}
O &\to H 
D \equiv OP \cap AM &\to D' \equiv \odot (AHC) \cap l  
E \equiv ON \cap AM &\to E' \equiv \odot (AHB) \cap l.
\end{align*} Since  $\odot (AHC)$  is just the circle with diameter  $\overline{AC}$ , it follows that  $D'$  is just the foot of the perpendicular from  $C$  to  $l.$  Similarly, we see that  $E'$  is the foot of the perpendicular from  $B$  to  $l.$  Then  $\mathcal{I}$  takes  $F \equiv BD \cap CE \to F' \equiv \odot (AND') \cap \odot (APE').$  

Now, upon inversion, proving that  $F \in \odot (APON)$  is equivalent to showing that  $F' \in BC.$  We will in fact prove a stronger result:  $F' = M.$  To prove this, we need to show that  $M \in \odot (AND')$  and  $M \in \odot (APE').$  In fact, it suffices to only prove that  $M \in \odot (AND')$  since by an identical argument, we will find that  $M \in \odot (APE').$</details>

Now, let  $X$  be the intersection of the tangents to  $\odot (ABC)$  at  $B$  and  $C.$  We make a few observations, and then proceed with an angle chase. First, it is [well-known](http://yufeizhao.com/olympiad/three_geometry_lemmas.pdf) that  $AX$  is the  $A$ -symmedian in  $\triangle ABC$ ; hence,  $X \in l.$  In addition, since  $OB \perp XB$  and  $OC \perp XC$ , we deduce that the points  $O, X, B, C$  are inscribed in a circle of diameter  $\overline{OX}.$  Furthermore, since  $OX$  is the perpendicular bisector of  $\overline{BC}$ , it follows that  $\measuredangle XMC = \measuredangle XD'C = 90^{\circ}$ , implying that the points  $X, D', M, C$  are concyclic. 

Now, to show that the points  $A, N, M, D'$  are concyclic, it suffices to prove that  $\measuredangle ANM = \measuredangle AD'M$ , where the angles are directed. Because  $O, X, B, C$  and  $X, D', M, C$  are sets of concyclic points, we have that
\[\measuredangle AD'M = \measuredangle XD'M = \measuredangle XCM = \measuredangle XCB = \measuredangle XOB.\] Then since  $OX$  bisects  $\angle BOC$ , we deduce that 
\[\measuredangle XOB = \measuredangle CAB = \measuredangle CNM = \measuredangle ANM\] where we have used the fact that  $MN \parallel AB$ , because  $M$  and  $N$  are midpoints. Thus, we have shown that  $\measuredangle ANM = \measuredangle AD'M$ , and we're done.  $\square$

That gives $ \frac {\sin \angle FBC \sin \angle FCA \sin \angle FAB}{\sin \angle FBA \sin \angle FCB \sin \angle FAC} \equal{} 1$ . $ \angle FBC \equal{} B \minus{} \angle FBA \equal{} B \minus{} A_1$ . $ \angle FCA \equal{} A_2$ $ \angle FBA \equal{} A_1$ $ \angle FCB \equal{} C \minus{} \angle FCA \equal{} C \minus{} A_2$ , so we have $ \frac {\sin \angle FAB}{\sin \angle FAC} \cdot \frac {\sin(B \minus{} A_1)\sin(A_2)}{\sin(C \minus{} A_2)\sin(A_1)} \equal{} 1$ , or $ \frac {\sin \angle FAB}{\sin \angle FAC} \equal{} \frac {\sin(C \minus{} A_2)\sin(A_1)}{\sin(B \minus{} A_1)\sin(A_2)}$ . Now, since $ B \plus{} A_1 \plus{} C \plus{} A_2 \equal{} \pi$ , $ \frac {\sin(C \plus{} A_2)}{\sin(B \plus{} A_1)} \equal{} 1$ . Thus, the RHS equals $ \frac {\sin(C \minus{} A_2)\sin(C \plus{} A_2)\sin(A_1)}{\sin(B \minus{} A_1)\sin(B \plus{} A_1)\sin(A_2)}$ $ \equal{} \frac {(\sin(C)\cos(A_2) \minus{} \cos(C)\sin(A_2))(\sin(C)\cos(A_2) \plus{} \cos(C)\sin(A_2))\sin(A_1)}{(\sin(B)\cos(A_1) \minus{} \cos(B)\sin(A_1))(\sin(B)\cos(A_1) \plus{} \cos(B)\sin(A_1))\sin(A_2)}$ $ \equal{} \frac {(\sin^2C\cos^2A_2 \minus{} \cos^2C\sin^2A_2)\sin A_1}{(\sin^2 B \cos^2 A_1 \minus{} \cos^2 B \sin^2 A_1)\sin A_2}$ $ \equal{} \frac {(\sin^2 C (1 \minus{} \sin^2 A_2) \minus{} (1 \minus{} \sin^2 C)\sin^2 A_2)\sin A_1}{(\sin^2 B (1 \minus{} \sin^2 A_1) \minus{} (1 \minus{} \sin^2 B)\sin^2 A_1)\sin A_2}$ $ \equal{} \frac {(\sin^2C \minus{} \sin^2 A_2)\sin A_1}{(\sin^2 B \minus{} \sin^2 A_1)\sin A_2}$ . This is why: Suppose we have four angles $ A, B, C, D$ with $ A \plus{} B \equal{} C \plus{} D \equal{} \theta$ and $ \frac {\sin A}{\sin B} \equal{} \frac {\sin C}{\sin D} \equal{} K$ . We will show that $ A \equal{} C$ and $ B \equal{} D$ . Write it as follows: $ K \equal{} \frac {\sin(\theta \minus{} D)}{\sin D} \equal{} \frac {\sin\theta \cos D \minus{} \cos\theta \sin D}{\sin D} \equal{} \sin\theta\cot D \minus{} \cos\theta$ , so $ \cot D \equal{} \frac {K \plus{} \cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$ , which means that $ D$ is unique modulo $ \pi$ . Okay, so we've established that $ \angle FAB \equal{} A_2$ and $ \angle FAC \equal{} A_1$ (or equivalently, $ F$ is on the symmedian from $ A$ (there are nicer ways to do this, as shown in other solutions)). Thus, by the thing shown above, $ \angle AFP \equal{} C$ . By applying the same argument to $ \triangle AFC$ , we obtain $ \angle AFN \equal{} B$ . Thus, $ \angle PAN \plus{} \angle PFN \equal{} A \plus{} \angle AFP \plus{} \angle AFN \equal{} A \plus{} B \plus{} C \equal{} \pi$ , so $ APFN$ is cyclic. $ \blacksquare$

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>Barycentric coordinates.  

Set  $A=(1,0,0)$ ,  $B=(0,1,0)$  and  $C=(0,0,1)$ .  Evidently  $P=(\frac12, \frac12, 0)$ , etc.  Check that the equation of the line  $AM$  is  $y=z$ .

We will now compute the coordinates of the point  $D$ .  Write  $D=(1-2t, t, t)$  as it lies on the line  $AM$ .  Evidently the vectors  $\vec{PD}$  and  $\vec{AB}$  are perpendicular.  Assume WLOG that the circumcenter corresponds to the zero vector.  In that case we find that their dot product is zero, so upon  $\vec D - \vec P = (\frac12 - 2t, t - \frac12, t)$  we may compute
\begin{align*}
0 &= (\vec A - \vec B) \cdot ( (\frac12-2t) \vec A + (t-\frac12) \vec B + t \vec C) 
\implies (\frac12-2t) R^2 + (t-\frac12) (R^2-c^2/2) + t(R^2-b^2/2) &= (\frac12 - 2t)(R^2-c^2/2) + (t-\frac12) R^2 + t(R^2-a^2/2) 
\implies (t-\frac12) (-c^2/2) + t(-b^2/2) &= (\frac12 - 2t)(-c^2/2) +  + t(-a^2/2) 
\implies ((t-\frac12) - (\frac12 - 2t))(-c^2/2) + t(a^2-b^2/2) &= 0
\implies (3t-1)(-c^2) + t(a^2-b^2) &= 0 
\implies (a^2-b^2-3c^2)t &= -c^2 
\implies t &= \frac{c^2}{3c^2+b^2-a^2}
\end{align*}
Call this value  $j$ .  Then  $D=(1-2j, j, j)$ .  Similarly,  $E=(1-2k, k, k)$  where  $k= \frac{b^2}{3b^2+c^2-a^2}$ .

Now the line  $BD$  has equation  $\frac zx = \frac{j}{1-2j}$ , whilst the line  $CE$  has equation  $\frac yx = \frac{k}{1-2k}$ .  So if  $F=(p,q,r)$ , then  $p+q+r=1$ ,  $\frac rp = \frac{j}{1-2j}$ , and  $\frac qp = \frac{k}{1-2k}$ .

In fact,  $\frac rp = \frac{c^2}{(3c^2+b^2-a^2)-2c^2} = \frac{c^2}{c^2+b^2-a^2}$ , and  $\frac qp = \frac{b^2}{b^2+c^2-a^2}$ .  Evidently  $\frac 1p = 1 + \frac rp + \frac qp = 1+\frac{b^2+c^2}{c^2+b^2-a^2} = \frac{2S+a^2}{S} = 2 +\frac{a^2}{S}$   Let  $S = c^2+b^2-a^2$  for convenience.

Dilate  $F$  to  $F'=2F-A = (2p-1, 2q, 2r)$ .  It suffices to show this lies on the circumcircle of triangle  $ABC$  (since this will send  $P$  and  $N$  to  $B$  and  $C$ , respectively), which has equation  $a^2yz + b^2zx + c^2xy=0$ .  Hence it suffices to show that
\begin{align*}
0 &= a^2(2q)(2r) + b^2(2r)(2p-1) + c^2(2p-1)(2q) 
\iff 0 &= 4a^2\frac qp \frac rp + (2+\frac1p)(2b^2 \frac rp + 2c^2 \frac qp) 
\iff -(2-(2+\frac{a^2}{S}))(2b^2 \frac{c^2}{S} + 2c^2 \frac{b^2}{S}) &= 4a^2 \frac{b^2c^2}{S^2}  
\iff a^2(2b^2c^2 + 2c^2b^2) &= 4a^2b^2c^2 
\iff 4a^2b^2c^2 &= 4a^2b^2c^2  
\end{align*} which is true.</details>

Observe that \[\angle BFC = 360 - \angle BFC=360-(360-\angle A-\angle ABF-\angle ACF)\] \[=\angle A+(\angle ABF+\angle ACF)=2\angle A\] since  $\angle ABF=\angle BAM$  and  $\angle ACF=\angle CAM$ . Thus, quadrilateral  $BCFO$  is cyclic. So consider the circumcircle of triangle  $APN$  and the circumcircle of triangle  $OBC$ . Since  $\angle APO=\angle ANO=90$ , it follows that  $O$  lies on the circumcircle of triangle  $APN$ . Thus, the circumcircle of triangle  $APN$  and the circumcircle of triangle  $OBC$  intersect at  $O$  and some point  $F' \neq O$ . It suffices to show that  $F'=F$ .</details>

Now let's angle chase.

<details><summary>Angle Chase</summary>Since pentagon  $APF'ON$  and quadrilateral  $BCF'O$  are cyclic, it follows that \[\angle AF'P=\angle ANP=\angle ACB=\angle C\] \[\angle AF'N=\angle APN=\angle ABC=\angle B\] \[\angle NF'C=\angle NF'O+\angle OF'C=\angle OAN+\angle OBC=(90-\angle B)+(90-\angle A)=\angle C\] \[\angle BF'C=2\angle A\] \[\angle BF'P=360-\angle AF'C-\angle BF'C-\angle AF'P=360-\angle B-\angle C-2\angle A-\angle C=\angle B\]</details>

Now let's prove a quick lemma for convenience.

<details><summary>Lemma</summary>Take an arbitrary triangle  $XYZ$  and let  $W$  be the midpoint of  $YZ$ . Then \[\frac{XY}{ZX}=\frac{\sin \angle WXZ}{\sin \angle WXY}\]</details>

<details><summary>Proof</summary>Since  $[WXY]=[WXZ]$ ,  $A=\frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$  yields \[\frac{1}{2}(XY)(WX)(\sin \angle ZXY) = \frac{1}{2}(ZX)(WX)(\sin \angle WXZ)\] Rearranging yields \[\frac{XY}{ZX}=\frac{\sin \angle WXZ}{\sin \angle WXY}\] as desired.  $\blacksquare$</details>

Now let's show that  $AF'$  is a symmedian.

<details><summary>Symmedian Proof</summary>Extend  $AF'$  to meet  $BC$  at  $M'$ .

Since  $\angle AF'B=\angle AF'P+\angle BF'P=\angle B+\angle C=180-\angle A$ , it follows that  $\angle BF'M'=\angle CF'M'=\angle A$ . Thus,  $F'M'$  is an angle bisector of  $\angle BFC$ .

By our lemma, \[\frac{BF'}{AF'}=\frac{\sin \angle C}{\sin \angle B}\] \[\frac {CF'}{AF'}= \frac{\sin \angle B}{\sin \angle C}\] Multiplying yields \[\frac{BF'}{CF'}=\frac{\sin^2 \angle B}{\sin ^2 \angle C}\] By the Angle Bisector Theorem, \[\frac{BM'}{CM'}=\frac{BF'}{CF'}=\frac{\sin^2 \angle B}{\sin ^2 \angle C}\] By the Law of Sines, \[\frac{BM'}{CM'}=\frac{CA^2}{AB^2}\] from which it follows that  $AF'$  is a symmedian.  $\blacksquare$</details>

Now we'll show that  $F'=F$ , finishing the proof.

<details><summary>Conclusion</summary>Let  $\angle BAM=\alpha$  and  $\angle CAM=\beta$  for convenience.

By the definition of symmedian,  $\angle BAM'=\angle CAM = \beta$ . By Triangle Angle Sum, \[\angle ABF'=180-\angle BAF'-\angle AF'B=180-\beta-(180-A)=\alpha\] \[\angle ACF'=180-\angle CAF'-\angle ACF'=180-\alpha-(180-A)=\beta\] Since two lines can only intersect at one point, it follows that  $F'=F$ .

Thus we're done.  $\blacksquare$</details></details>

Let us first assume WLOG that  $AC$  >  $AB$ .

Let  $O$  be the circumcentre of  $\triangle ABC$ .  $APON$  is cyclic because  $OP \perp AP$  and  $ON \perp AN$ . Now let  $G$  be the second intersection point of the circumcircles of  $\triangle BOC$  and  $\triangle APN$ . We want to prove that  $AG$  is the  $A$ -symmedian.

It is enough to prove that  $AG$  divides  $PN$  in the ratio  $AP^{2} / AN^{2} = AB^{2} / AC^{2}$ . But because  $APGN$  is cyclic, that ratio is equal to  $(AP * GP) / (AN * GN)$ . Now because  $AO$  is the diameter of  $\odot APGON$ , we have that  $AG \perp OG$ . Because  $BCOG$  is cyclic,  $\angle BGO = 90^{\circ} + \angle BAC$ , and  $\angle ACB = \angle ANP = \angle AGP$ . From this we deduce that  $\angle PGB = \angle ABC$ . Now because  $\angle ANG = \angle GPB$  and  $\angle PGB = \angle ABC = \angle APN = \angle AGN$  we get that  $GP / GN = BP / AN = AB / AC$ . Thus  $(AP / AN) * (GP / GN) = AB^{2} / AC^{2}$ , so  $AG$  is the  $A$ -symmedian. Now with a bit more angle chasing and using the symmedian fact we get that  $\angle ACG = \angle CAM$ .

Now all that is left is to prove that  $F = G$ . We have that  $\angle BFC = 2(\angle BAM + \angle CAM) = 2\angle BAC = \angle BOC$ , so  $F$  is on the circle  $\odot BGOC$ , and also  $\angle ACG = \angle CAM = \angle ACF$ , so  $G = F$  and  $APFN$  is concyclic.

Therefore, \[\widehat{AB_1} = \widehat{YB} = \widehat{YX} + \widehat{XB} = \widehat{YX} + \widehat{CY} = \widehat{CX},\] whence it follows that  $AB_1CX$  is an isoceles trapezoid as well. I claim that  $F$  is the  $A$ -dumpty point. It is clear that the  $A$ -dumpty point lies on  $\odot(ANP)$ . Also, let  $O$  denote the center of  $\odot(ABC)$ .

Firstly,
\begin{align*}
    \measuredangle BFC&=\measuredangle FBC+\measuredangle BCF
    &=(\measuredangle ABC-\measuredangle ABF)+(\measuredangle BCA-\measuredangle FCA)
    &=(\measuredangle ABC+\measuredangle BCA)+\measuredangle FBA+\measuredangle ACF
    &=\measuredangle BAC+\measuredangle BAF+\measuredangle FCA
    &=2\measuredangle A
.\end{align*}

So  $F$  lies on  $\odot(BOC)$ . Now it is enough to prove that  $AF$  is the  $A$ -symmedian.

Firstly, redefine  $F$  as the  $A$ -dumpty point. Now note that we have  $\measuredangle FCA=\measuredangle FAB=\measuredangle CAM=\measuredangle CAE=\measuredangle ECA$ . This gives us that  $\overline{C-E-F}$  are collinear. Similarly we also get that  $\overline{B-D-F}$  are collinear and we are done.

After drawing several diagrams, we conjecture that  $AF$  is the A-symmedian. We would hope that then  $F$  is the midpoint of  $AT$ , where  $T$  is the intersection of the A-symmedian with the circumcircle. Note that  $T=(-a^2:2b^2:2c^2)$ , as the second two coordinates are in a  $b^2$  to  $c^2$  ratio and it satisfies the circumcircle equation. Thus, letting  $A=(-a^2+2b^2+2c^2:0:0)$  (we make them the same sum so we can just average them), we have that the midpoint of  $AT$  is   $$ (-a^2+b^2+c^2:b^2:c^2). $$   Denote this point by  $F'$ , and we will try to show that  $F'=F.$ Suppose that  $BF'$  intersects  $AM$  at  $D'$ . Then,  $B=(0,1,0)$  and  $F'=(-a^2+b^2+c^2:b^2:c^2)$ , so the equation of line  $BF'$  is   $$ x(c^2)=z(-a^2+b^2+c^2). $$   The equation of  $AM$  is just  $y=z$ , so we have   $$ D'=(-a^2+b^2+c^2:c^2:c^2). $$  Now, we check that  $D'P\perp AB.$  Note that   $$ P=(1:1:0)=(-a^2+b^2+3c^2:-a^2+b^2+3c^2:0) $$   and   $$ D'=(-2a^2+2b^2+2c^2:2c^2:2c^2). $$   This is done so that  $P$  and  $D'$  have the same sum now. This, it suffices to check that   $$ a^2(-2c^2)+b^2(2c^2)+c^2(2a^2-2b^2)=0, $$   which is clearly true. Hence, by EFFT,  $D'P\perp AB,$  so  $D'=D$ . Similarly,  $E'=E$ . stem_md: Prove that for each positive integer  $ n$ , there are pairwise relatively prime integers  $ k_0,k_1,\ldots,k_n$ , all strictly greater than  $ 1$ , such that  $ k_0k_1\ldots k_n\minus{}1$  is the product of two consecutive integers.
solution_md:
My SolutionLemma. Infinitely many primes $ p$ exist such that $ p$ divides some term in the sequence $ f(a) = a^{2} + a + 1$ for positive integral $ a$ . Proof. Assume there are finitely many $ p$ . Clearly, there is at least one, since $ f(1) = 3$ . Then, multiply them all together, and you get $ f(a)\equiv1$ modulo the product of all of them. But then $ f(a)$ has a prime factor other than those primes, contradiction. end lemma Take $ c > 1$ primes as described in the lemma, and we can take $ c$ arbitrarily large. Then, since $ f(a)$ modulo $ p$ has period $ p$ , for each of these primes, there's some residue $ a_{1}$ such that if $ a\equiv a_{1}\pmod{p}$ , then $ p|a$ . By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, we have an $ a$ divisible by all of the $ c$ primes. We write $ a = p_{1}^{e_{1}}p{}^{2}{}^{e_{2}}\cdots p_{c}^{e_{c}}K$ , where $ K$ is relatively prime to the rest of the stuff. Then take $ k_{0} = p_{1}^{e_{1}},k_{1} = p_{2}^{e_{2}},\ldots,k_{n - 1} = p_{c - 1}^{e_{c - 1}},k_{n} = p_{c}^{e_{c}}K$ .

Solution Using Dirichlet**Lemma.** If $ p$ is prime such that $ p\equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ , there exists a residue $ r$ such that $ p \mid r^2 + r + 1$ . *Proof.* Let $ g$ be a multiplicative generator of the nonzero integers mod 3. Set $ r \equiv g^{(p - 1)/3}$ . Then $ r - 1 \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ , but $ r^3 - 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ , so $ \frac {r^3 - 1}{r - 1} \equiv r^2 + r + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ . $ \blacksquare$ By Dirichlet's theorem, there are infinitely many primes congruent to 1 (mod 3). Let $ p_0, \dotsc, p_n$ be $ (n + 1)$ such primes, and let $ r_0, \dotsc, r_n$ be respective residues as described in the lemma. By the Chinese remainder theorem, there is a positive integer $ a$ satisfying the equivalences \[ a \equiv r_i \pmod{p_i} . \] Then $ p_0 \dotsc p_n \mid a^2 + a + 1$ . Lemma: There exist infinitely many primes  $ p$  such that  $ f(a)\equiv 0 \pmod p$  has solution.

Proof: We'll proceed with induction.
Base:  $ p \equal{} 3$ , then  $ a\equiv 1\pmod 3$  is a solution.
Inductive hypothesis: suppose there exist  $ m$  such primes  $ p_1,...,p_m$ . By CRT we can find a  $ a \equal{} a'$  so that  $ f(a')\equiv 0 \pmod {p_i}$  for  $ i \equal{} 1,...,m$ . 
Now, we see that  $ \gcd (f(a'), f(a' \plus{} 1)) \equal{} (a'^2 \plus{} a' \plus{} 1,a'^2 \plus{} 3a' \plus{} 3) \equal{} (2(a' \plus{} 1), a'(a' \plus{} 1) \plus{} 1) \equal{} 1$ , so  $ f(a' \plus{} 1)$  is not divisible by any of  $ p_1,...,p_m$ . But  $ f(a' \plus{} 1) > 1$ , so  $ f(a' \plus{} 1)$  must has another prime factor  $ p_{m \plus{} 1}$ , i.e.,  $ f(a' \plus{} 1)\equiv 0 \pmod {p_{m \plus{} 1}}$ . Hence,  $ p_{m \plus{} 1}$  also satisfies the condition.

Now let's choose any subset of these primes, say  $ p_1,...,p_m$ , and find the solution to each of congruences  $ f(a)\equiv 0 \pmod {p_i}$ , say  $ a\equiv a_i \pmod {p_i}$ . If we set up these solution congruences simultaneously, by CRT, there exist an  $ a \equal{} x$  solving them all. Then  $ f(x)$  is divisible by  $ m$  distinct prime factors  $ p_1,...,p_m$ . Since  $ m$  can be arbitrarily large, it holds true for every positive integer  $ n$ .</details>

Click to expandDefine $ f(a) \equal{} a^2 \plus{} a \plus{} 1$ . It suffices to prove $ f(a)$ can have as many distinct prime factors as we want. Lemma: There exist infinitely many primes $ p$ such that $ f(a)\equiv 0 \pmod p$ has solution. Proof: We'll proceed with induction. Base: $ p \equal{} 3$ , then $ a\equiv 1\pmod 3$ is a solution. Inductive hypothesis: suppose there exist $ m$ such primes $ p_1,...,p_m$ . By CRT we can find a $ a \equal{} a'$ so that $ f(a')\equiv 0 \pmod {p_i}$ for $ i \equal{} 1,...,m$ . Now, we see that $ \gcd (f(a'), f(a' \plus{} 1)) \equal{} (a'^2 \plus{} a' \plus{} 1,a'^2 \plus{} 3a' \plus{} 3) \equal{} (2(a' \plus{} 1), a'(a' \plus{} 1) \plus{} 1) \equal{} 1$ , so $ f(a' \plus{} 1)$ is not divisible by any of $ p_1,...,p_m$ . But $ f(a' \plus{} 1) > 1$ , so $ f(a' \plus{} 1)$ must has another prime factor $ p_{m \plus{} 1}$ , i.e., $ f(a' \plus{} 1)\equiv 0 \pmod {p_{m \plus{} 1}}$ . Hence, $ p_{m \plus{} 1}$ also satisfies the condition. Now let's choose any subset of these primes, say $ p_1,...,p_m$ , and find the solution to each of congruences $ f(a)\equiv 0 \pmod {p_i}$ , say $ a\equiv a_i \pmod {p_i}$ . If we set up these solution congruences simultaneously, by CRT, there exist an $ a \equal{} x$ solving them all. Then $ f(x)$ is divisible by $ m$ distinct prime factors $ p_1,...,p_m$ . Since $ m$ can be arbitrarily large, it holds true for every positive integer $ n$ .

Define P to be the greatest possible cardinality of a relatively prime partition for some number.

Lemma 1: All cardinalities of the relatively prime partitions of a number up to P can be attained.

Proof:
P=P-0 satisfies the properties. For any P-n which satisfies the properties, we can take any of the 2 P-n numbers and multiply them together. Because they are both relatively prime to all the other numbers, their product is relatively prime to all the other numbers as well, and that results in P-n-1 numbers which satisfy the conditions, unless P-n=1, because there is only one number left. Therefore, all numbers of numbers of relatively prime factors from 1 to P-1 are attainable, if P is attainable as well.

End Lemma

I think that the idea behind your solution works, but your solution has flaws. You seem to have worked on the problem backwards. But you cannot write it up backwards, at least, not without more care than you have used here. In particular, you start with some apparently free variables (the $ p_i$ and $ k_i$ ), and then you start imposing arbitrary constraints on them that it isn't clear that you are allowed to impose. (You seem to do this every time you say "for the heck of it".) If, on the other hand, you had defined the $ r_i$ as a recursive sequence from the beginning, and then defined the other variables in terms of the $ r_i$ , it would be easier to follow the proof, and it would be more valid. I think you might also be able to eliminate some of the variables from the proof. By the way, next time, go for a letter other than $ p$ . Usually in number theory, $ p$ is a prime, but here it isn't, and that's kind of confusing. Also, I advise against the word "obvious". If the statement in question is obvious, the word is probably unnecessary; there's also a chance that other readers will find it less obvious than you do, and belittling such readers is a bad idea. You run into trouble with the gcds. Your proof that $ \gcd(k,p)\equal{} \gcd(k\minus{}4p,k)$ is confusing, and since you allude to background knowledge very obliquely, it might not be clear to a grader that it is valid. You could make it a lot easier to follow by saying something like this :
Since $ k$ is odd, $ \gcd(k,p) \equal{} \gcd(k,4p)$ , which by the Euclidean algorithm is equal to $ \gcd(k,4p\minus{}k)$ .
You might also want to sketch a brief proof that $ r^2\plus{}r\plus{}3$ is never even, if only rewriting it as $ r(r\plus{}1)\plus{}3$ or something. You also make some mistakes with equality of your gcds. In general, you put a lot of = signs where "divides" symbols would have been both sufficient and easier to verify. For instance, the statement \[ \gcd(2r\plus{}1, r\plus{}1) \cdot \gcd(2r\plus{}1,r\plus{}7) \equal{} 13 \] is only true when $ 13 \mid 2r\plus{}1$ , i.e., when $ r\equiv 6 \pmod{13}$ . This observation alone might have made the last part easier. You run into more trouble in the last paragraph. For instance, you say, " $ k_{n\plus{}1} \equiv 0 \pmod{13}$ precisely when $ r\equiv 6\pmod{13}$ ." This is false; $ k_{n\plus{}1} \equiv 0 \pmod{13}$ also if $ r \equiv 5 \pmod{13}$ . Furthermore, this paragraph is kind of hard to follow anyway, because there's almost no detail worked out.

Prove that for each positive integer $ n$ , there are pairwise relatively prime integers $ k_0,k_1,\ldots,k_n$ , all strictly greater than $ 1$ , such that $ k_0k_1\ldots k_n\minus{}1$ is the product of two consecutive integers.
SolutionWe will prove the statement by induction. Base Case: For $n = 1$ , take $k_0 = 19$ and $k_1 = 3$ . Notice $k_0k_1 - 1 = 56 = 7 \cdot 8$ . Inductive Step: Suppose the statement is satisfied for a constant $n$ . $k_0k_1 \ldots k_n - 1 = a(a+1)$ . Notice if we let $k_{n+1} = (a^2 - a + 1)$ , we get $k_0k_1 \ldots k_{n+1} - 1 = (a(a+1) + 1)(a^2 - a + 1) - 1 = (a^2 + a + 1)(a^2 - a + 1) - 1 = a^4 - a^2 = a^2(a^2 - 1)$ . Additionally, since $k_0k_1 \ldots k_n = a^2 + a + 1$ , and $\gcd(a^2 + a + 1, a^2 - a + 1) = \gcd(a^2 + a + 1, 2a) = 1$ , $a^2 - a + 1$ doesn't share any prime factors with any of the previous $k$ s. Therefore, the statement is satisfied for a constant $n+1$ . Since the statement holds true for $n=1$ , and each case follows from the next, the problem is complete. $\blacksquare$

SolutionIt is sufficient to prove that there are positive integers of the form $ a(a\plus{}1)\plus{}1\equal{}a^{2}\plus{}a\plus{}1$ with arbitrarily many prime factors. We prove this by induction. For $ a\equal{}1$ we get $ a^{2}\plus{}a\plus{}1\equal{}3$ , which has one prime factor. Now suppose $ b\equal{}a^{2}\plus{}a\plus{}1$ has at least $ n$ prime factors. Then we get a positive integer of the desired form with at least $ n\plus{}1$ prime factors by taking $ b'\equal{}(a\plus{}b)^{2}\plus{}(a\plus{}b)\plus{}1\equal{}b^{2}\plus{}2ab\plus{}b\plus{}(a^{2}\plus{}a\plus{}1)\equal{}b^{2}\plus{}2ab\plus{}2b\equal{}b(b\plus{}2a\plus{}2)$ If $ p|b$ then $ p|b'$ . Suppose for the sake of contradiction that $ p|b\plus{}2a\plus{}2$ . Then $ p|2a\plus{}2$ . Since all numbers of our form are odd, $ p\ne 2$ and we have $ p|a\plus{}1$ . But we already know that $ p|a^{2}\plus{}a\plus{}1$ , so $ p|a^{2}$ , which implies $ p|a$ . Therefore $ p$ divides consecutive integers $ a$ and $ a\plus{}1$ , a contradiction. Therefore $ b\plus{}2a\plus{}2$ has at least one prime factor other than the prime factors of $ b$ , and we're done.

We have  $k_0k_1\cdots k_n-1=x(x+1)$  for some positive integer  $x$ , or  $k_0k_1\cdots k_n=x^2+x+1$ . If  $x^2+x+1$  has over  $n+1$  distinct prime factors then clearly we can pick  $k_i$  such that they are all relatively prime and their product is  $x^2+x+1$ . Thus, it remains to prove that  $x^2+x+1$  can take an arbitrary number of prime factors. Let's analyze what must be met in order for  $x^2+x+1\equiv 0\pmod{p}$ . Assuming  $p\ge 3$ , this is equivalent with:   $$ 4x^2+4x+4\equiv 0\pmod{p}\implies (2x+1)^2\equiv -3\pmod{p}\implies \left(\dfrac{-3}{p}\right)=1 $$  However, this condition is met by any  $p\equiv 1\pmod{3}$  so for these  $p$  there exists an  $x$  modulo  $p$  such that  $p\mid x^2+x+1$ . 
Now just take any  $n+1$  distinct primes satisfying this condition and use Chinese Remainder Theorem to find a solution  $x$  such that  $x^2+x+1$  has at least  $n+1$  distinct prime factors, and the problem is finished.

SolutionI claim that $k_0 = p^2 + p + 1, k_k = p^{2^k} - p^{2^{k-1}} + 1$ for $1 \le k \le n$ (where $p$ is a prime) will always satisfy the given conditions for any positive integer $n$ . It is important to note the identity $(x^2+x+1)(x^2-x+1) = x^4+x^2+1$ , as we will use this a lot in our solution. Note that $k_0k_1k_2 \ldots k_n - 1 = (p^2-p+1)(p^2+p+1)\ldots - 1 = (p^4 + p^2 + 1)(p^4 - p^2 + 1)\ldots - 1 = \ldots = p^{2^{n+1}} + p^{2^n} + 1 - 1$ . This equals $p^{2^{n+1}} + p^{2^n} = p^{2^n}(p^{2^n} + 1)$ , which is the product of two consecutive integers. It is then sufficient to show that $k_0, k_1 \ldots k_n$ are pairwise relatively prime. Note that $\gcd(k_0, k_1) = \gcd(p^2 - p + 1, 2p) = \gcd(p^2 - p + 1, p)$ (as $p^2 - p + 1$ is odd). However, $p^2 - p + 1 \equiv 1 \pmod p$ , so $\gcd(k_0, k_1) = 1$ , as desired. I claim that $\gcd(x^{2^k} - x^{2^{k-1}} + 1, x^{2^m} - x^{2^{m-1}} + 1) = 1$ for $1 \le k < m \le n$ . Note that $x^{2^{a-1}} + x^{2^{a-2}} + 1$ is a factor of $x^{2^a} + x^{2^{a-1}} + 1$ for integer $a$ by our above identity, and this implies $x^{2^{a-k}} + x^{2^{a-k-1}} + 1$ is a factor of $x^{2^a} + x^{2^{a-1}} + 1$ for integer $a, k$ . This implies that $x^{2^{k+1}} + x^{2^k} + 1 = (x^{2^k} - x^{2^{k-1}} + 1)(x^{2^k} + x^{2^{k-1}} + 1)$ is a factor of $x^{2^m} + x^{2^{m-1}} + 1$ . By the Euclidean Algorithm, we can then guarantee that $\gcd(p^{2^k} - p^{2^{k-1}} + 1, p^{2^m} - p^{2^{m-1}} + 1) = \gcd(p^{2^k} - p^{2^{k-1}} + 1, 2p^{2^{m-1}})$ . Since $p^{2^k} - p^{2^{k-1}}$ is a multiple of $p$ , $\gcd(p^{2^k} - p^{2^{k-1}}+1, p^c) = 1$ for any positive integer $c$ , which implies our claim. It is then sufficient to show that $\gcd(k_0, k_i) = 1$ . We established above that $x^{2^{a-k}} + x^{2^{a-k-1}} + 1$ is a factor of $x^{2^a} + x^{2^{a-1}} + 1$ for integer $a, k$ . Letting $k = a - 2$ , we can show that $p^2 + p + 1$ divides $p^{2^{k+1}} + p^{2^k} + 1$ for all positive integer $k$ . Once again, by the Euclidean Algorithm, we can then guarantee that $\gcd(p^2 + p + 1, p^{2^m} - p^{2^{m-1}} + 1) = \gcd(p^2 + p + 1, 2p^{2^{m-1}})$ . Since $p^2 + p$ is a multiple of $p$ , $\gcd(p^2 + p +1, p^c) = 1$ for any positive integer $c$ , which implies our desired result. Therefore, we have found a sequence $k_0, k_1 \ldots k_n$ of pairwise relatively prime integers strictly greater than $1$ such that $k_0k_1 \ldots k_n - 1$ is the product of two consecutive integers for all $n$ , as desired.

stem_md: Three nonnegative real numbers  $ r_1$ ,  $ r_2$ ,  $ r_3$  are written on a blackboard. These numbers have the property that there exist integers  $ a_1$ ,  $ a_2$ ,  $ a_3$ , not all zero, satisfying  $ a_1r_1 \plus{} a_2r_2 \plus{} a_3r_3 \equal{} 0$ . We are permitted to perform the following operation: find two numbers  $ x$ ,  $ y$  on the blackboard with  $ x \le y$ , then erase  $ y$  and write  $ y \minus{} x$  in its place. Prove that after a finite number of such operations, we can end up with at least one  $ 0$  on the blackboard.
solution_md:
This problem feels quite difficult even though the true solution does not end up being terribly tricky: there are so many faulty approaches that can take one down a rabbit hole.

Let  $\left(x_n, y_n, z_n\right)$  be the numbers on the blackboard after  $n$  operations. We define the *signature* of this triple as the triple of integers  $\left(a_n, b_n, c_n\right)$  with  $|a_n|+|b_n|+|c_n|$  minimal such that  $a_nx_n+b_ny_n+c_nz_n = 0=$ . It is easy to see that such a signature always exists for any  $3$ -tuple of numbers on the blackboard. We may assume without loss of generality that after some  $k$  moves, the numbers on the blackboard satisfy  $a_k x_k + b_k y_k - c_kz_k = 0$  where  $a_k, b_k, c_k$  are nonnegative integers and  $|a_k|+|b_k|+|c_k|$  equals the signature. We will also assume that  $x_k, y_k, z_k$  are distinct, otherwise are done immediately.

I claim that if  $a_k, b_k, c_k$  are all nonzero, then we can always decrease the signature of the triple by performing a move.

Suppose that  $z_k < x_k$  first, and consider the equation \[a_k(x_k-z_k) + b_k y_k - (c_k-a_k)z_k = 0.\]
Letting  $(a_{k+1}, b_{k+1}, c_{k+1}) = (a_k, b_k, c_k-a_k)$ , notice that our new triple has a smaller signature if and only if  $a_k < 2 c_k$ . If  $x_k < z_k$ , then we can write \[(a_k-c_k)x_k + b_k y_k - c_k(z_k-x_k) = 0\] and note that by defining  $(a_{k+1}, b_{k+1}, c_{k+1}) = (a_k-c_k, b_k, c_k)$ , this triple has a smaller signature if and only if  $c_k < 2a_k$ .

We will show that, considering the analogous equations for  $y_k$ , one of these four shifts yields a smaller signature.


- First, observe that if  $c_k \geq 2a_k$  and  $z_k > x_k$ , then  $c_k z_k > 2a_kx_k$  as all the terms are positive; if simultaneously we have  $c_k \geq 2b_k$  and  $y_k > x_k$ , then summing the equations yields  $c_kz_k > a_kx_k+b_ky_k$ , which contradicts our given.
- Next, observe that if  $z_k < x_k$  and  $a_k \geq 2 c_k$ , then  $c_kz_k < 2c_kz_k < a_k x_k$ , which again yields a contradiction.

So it follows that we can reduce  $|a_k|+|b_k|+|c_k|$  until one of the  $a_k$  equals zero. 

The rest is easy: our equation now reads  $a_kx_k - b_k y_k = 0$ . Assuming WLOG that  $x_k > y_k$ , we can rewrite as  $a_k(x_k-y_k) - (b_k-a_k)y_k = 0$  and check that  $b_k > a_k$ , so  $(a_{k+1}, b_{k+1})$  has a smaller signature than  $(a_k, b_k)$ . This eventually must reduce one of  $a_k$  and  $b_k$  to zero, in which case the remaining  $x_k$  or  $y_k$  must equal zero. This completes the proof.

Well, the condition tells you that $ r_1, r_2, r_3$ are linearly dependent over $ \mathbb{Q}$ ; in other words, that $ r_1, r_2, r_3$ span a rational vector space of dimension at most $ 2$ . The cases dimension $ 0, 1, 2$ correspond to all rationals, one (linearly independent) irrational, and two (linearly independent) irrationals, which, as jb05 mentioned, relates to elements of $ \mathbb{R} / \mathbb{Q}$ . It's the third case that makes a solution along these lines difficult (or so it seems to me). The vector space we end up getting could be something like $ \mathbb{Q}[\pi, e]$ .

So uhh, you can write  $ x_3$  as a linear combination of  $ x_1$  and  $ x_2$  with rational coefficients (unless  $ x_1$  and  $ x_2$  are linearly dependent, in which case you're done).

Replace  $ x_3$  with  $ x_3 \minus{} x_1$ , and you get  $ \frac{(p\minus{}r)x_1 \plus{} qx_2}{r}$ .  $ |p\minus{}r| < |p|$  because  $ p > \frac{r}{2}$ , and apparently you can show that  $ |p|\plus{}|q|\plus{}|r|$  is symmetric wrt  $ x_1, x_2, x_3$ , so  $ |p|\plus{}|q|\plus{}|r|$  eventually becomes  $ 0$ , which is what you want.

We first show we can decrease the quantity  $\left\lvert a_1 \right\rvert + \left\lvert a_2 \right\rvert + \left\lvert a_3 \right\rvert$  as long as  $0 \notin \left\{ a_1,a_2,a_3 \right\}$ . Assume  $a_1 > 0$  and  $r_1 > r_2 > r_3$  without loss of generality and consider two cases.

(i)  $r_2 > 0$  or  $r_3 > 0$ ; these cases are identical. If  $r_2 > 0$  then  $r_3 < 0$  and get \[ 0 = a_1r_1 + a_2r_2 + a_3r_3 > a_1r_3 + a_3r_3 \implies a_1 + a_3 < 0 \] so  $\left\lvert a_1 + a_3 \right\rvert < \left\lvert a_3 \right\rvert$ , and hence we perform  $(r_1,r_2,r_3) \mapsto (r_1-r_3,r_2,r_3)$ .

(ii) Both  $r_2$  and  $r_3$  are less than zero. Assume for contradiction that  $\left\lvert a_1+a_2 \right\rvert \ge -a_2$  and  $\left\lvert a_1+a_3 \right\rvert \ge -a_3$  both hold (if either fails then we use  $(r_1,r_2,r_3) \mapsto (r_1-r_2,r_2,r_3)$  and  $(r_1,r_2,r_3) \mapsto (r_1-r_3,r_2,r_3)$ , respectively). Clearly  $a_1+a_2$  and  $a_1+a_3$  are both positive in this case, so we get  $a_1 + 2a_2$  and  $a_1 + 2a_3 \ge 0$ ; adding gives  $a_1+a_2+a_3 \ge 0$ .  But \[ 0 = a_1r_1 + a_2r_2 + a_3r_3 > a_1r_2 + a_2r_2 + a_3r_2 = r_2(a_1+a_2+a_3) \implies a_1+a_2+a_3 < 0 \] which is a contradiction.

Since this covers all cases, we see that we can always decrease  $\left\lvert a_1 \right\rvert + \left\lvert a_2 \right\rvert + \left\lvert a_3 \right\rvert$  whenever  $0 \notin \left\{ a_1,a_2,a_3 \right\}$ . Because the  $a_i$  are integers this cannot occur indefinitely, so eventually one of the  $a_i$ 's is zero. At this point we can just apply the Euclidean Algorithm, so we're done.
