stem_md: Infinitely many math beasts stand in a line, all six feet apart, wearing masks, and with clean hands. Grogg starts at the front of the line, holding  $n$  pieces of candy,  $ n \ge 1,$  and everyone else has none. He passes his candy to the beasts behind him, one piece each to the next  $n$  beasts in line. Then, Grogg leaves the line. The other beasts repeat this process: the beast in front, who has  $k$  pieces of candy, passes one piece each to the next  $k$  beasts in line, and then leaves the line. For some values of  $n,$  another beast, besides Grogg, temporarily holds all the candy. For which values of  $n$  does this occur?
solution_md: SolutionConsider the beasts that obtain $1$ candy after Grogg leaves the line. In particular, let the number of candies the beast in front of the line after some iterations be $k$ . **Claim:** The first time where the beast in the front of the line has $k+1$ candies occurs when the candy distribution for the front beasts is $k+1, k, k-1, ..., 3,2,1$ for $k>1, n>2$ , if the beasts in this distribution are of those beasts that received $1$ candy in the beginning after Grogg distributed his. **Proof:** We proceed with induction. Denote $a \rightarrow b$ as the change of the number of candies from $a$ to $b$ . Note that the base case when $k=2, n=3$ is true, as after Grogg goes, the second beast as $0 \rightarrow 1$ , the third beast has $0 \rightarrow 1$ , and the fourth beast has $0 \rightarrow 1$ . The next move makes the third beast $1 \rightarrow 2$ , and since the second beast leaves, the pattern of candies in the first two beasts are indeed $2,1$ , as required. Now consider when we had $k, k-1, k-2, ..., 3, 2, 1$ . Denote the beast having $k$ candies as $a_1$ , and so on, with the beast holding $1$ candies as $a_{k}$ . Furthermore, we picked $k$ such that there exists another beast $a_{k+1}$ after $a_k$ such that $a_{k+1}$ received a candy after Grogg went. Note this is since we defined in our claim that the beasts apart of the distribution $k+1, k, k-1, .., 3, 2, 1$ , which includes $a_{k+1}$ , are also apart of those who received a candy after Grogg went. As a note, if $a_{k+1} \neq 1$ or if $a_{k+1}$ didn't receive any candy after Grogg went, then $k, k-1, k-2, ..., 3, 2, 1$ is the distribution of the last $k$ beasts that received $1$ candy after Grogg went. Continuing off $a_{k+1}=1$ , we see that the distribution becomes $k,k-1,k-2,...,3,2,1,1,...$ . After the front beast finishes, we have $k, k-1, ..., 3, 2, 2,...$ . Going through a few more iterations, we obtain $k, k-1, ..., 3, 3, 2$ , and $k, k-1, ... , 4, 4, 3, 2$ , and so on. We continue this until the next beast that will be given a candy(or the new beast that will be included in the distribution) did not receive a candy when Grogg first went. We may see that there exists two consecutive beasts that share the same number of candies. To show this, note the distribution including those beasts after the $1$ in $k, k-1, ..., 3, 2,1$ is $k, k-1, k-2, ..., 3, 2, 1, 1, 1, ...$ until some $a_{i}$ who didn't receive a candy after Grogg's turn. The move of the beast in the front of the line would take the first two $1$ s. Every subsequent move would take $1$ more beast into the pattern as a replacement to the beast lost. Thus, there will only be one consecutive pair that have an equal number of candies, which are the two $1$ s that received a candy from the beast in front of the line in the beginning distribution. Now note that the only way to change $k \rightarrow k+1$ for the beast in the front of the line is if the consecutive pair that has an equal number of candies is in the front of the line. To see this, consider otherwise when any other two consecutive beasts are in the front of the line. Denote the first beast as $b_1$ and the second as $b_2$ . Note that any other two consecutive beasts other than the ones that shared the same number of candy will have candy amounts of $k, k-1$ for some $k$ when they reach the front of the line, so $b_1=k, b_2=k-1$ After $b_1$ goes, $b_2$ will increase to a $k \neq k+1$ , a contradiction. Therefore, the distribution of the candies before the beast in front of the line has $k+1$ candies must be $k, k, k-1, k-2, ..., 2, 1, 1, ...$ . Before this, there will not exist a beast who temporarily has all the candy, as the pair still exists. After the beast in front of the line goes, we have $k+1, k, k-1, ..., 3, 2, 1$ , which was what we wanted. \qedsymbol We use the claim and the fact that there exists one pair of consecutive numbers to generate the sequence distribution of the candies up to $a_n$ , which is the last beast that received $1$ piece of candy from Grogg. If we let the number of candies the beast in front of the line has before the next move that exceeds $a_n$ be $k$ , we have either $k, k-1, k-2, ..., 3, 2, 1$ (created when $a_{k+1}=0$ ) or $k, k-1, k-2, ..., k-i, k-i, ..., 3, 2$ for some $2 \le k-i \le k$ or $0 \le i \le k-2$ . Note that ending with a $2$ instead of $1$ for the latter, since if there were a $1$ after the $2$ , then the front beast goes, and we get $k,k-1,k-2,..., k-i+1,k-i+1,...,3,2$ for some $2 \le k-i+1 \le k$ . Therefore, for both cases, the number of candies for the beasts that repeat are bounded in $[2,k]$ , so they are identical. Thus, it suffices to test the case where the last beast contains $2$ candies rather than $1$ .(Another way to think of it is that we have a repeat of one term, so all beasts were "shifted" up one candy up until the first $k-i$ ) Consider when $a_{n+1}$ becomes the front of the line, which is after $k$ moves. We first take the former case of when the sequence up to $a_n$ is $k,k-1,k-2,...,3,2,1$ . After the front beast goes, we have $k, k-1, k-2, ..., 3, 2, 1$ . Similarly, after the new front beast goes, we again have $k, k-1, k-2, ..., 3, 2, 1$ . In fact, we have the distribution when $a_{n+1}$ is in the front as $k, k-1, k-2, ..., 3, 2, 1$ since this pattern is periodic. Furthermore, we may see that there will be no other beasts besides Grogg that temporarily holds all the candy. Now consider the latter case, where we have $k, k-1, k-2, ..., k-i, k-i, ..., 3, 2$ with exactly two consecutive beasts holding $k-i$ candies. We denote $a_1$ as the beast with $k$ candies in the beginning, $a_2$ as the beast with $k-1$ , and so on until $a_{k}$ for the beast with $2$ candies in the beginning. Note that for the beasts $k, k-1, k-2, ..., k-i$ , it follows the same pattern as the first case. However, starting from $a_{i+2}$ or the second beast with $k-i$ candies in the beginning, it begins to break the pattern. This is due to fact that $a_{i+2}$ will be the front beast, but it will have $k+1$ candies. Therefore, since $a_{i+2}$ has one extra candy, one extra beast will also be given a candy. Note that in the beginning distribution for $a_{i+2}$ , there were $i+1$ beasts ahead, and $k-i-2$ beasts after. Therefore, after all $i+1$ beasts ahead of $a_{i+2}$ went, $i+1$ new beasts after $a_k$ have received some candy. Since $a_{i+2}$ has $k+1$ candies to distribute, there will be $k+1-(k-i-2)=i+3$ beasts after $a_k$ that received $1$ piece of candy from $a_{i+2}$ 's turn. Note that because only beasts from $a_{k+1}$ to $a_{k+i+1}$ received candy before $a_{i+2}$ 's turn, we had $a_{k+i+2}=a_{k+i+3}=0$ before $a_{i+2}$ went. Therefore, when $a_{i+2}$ finishes its round, $a_{k+i+2}$ and $a_{k+i+3}$ creates the consecutive pair since both get included. The rest of $k-i-1, k-i-2, ..., 3, 2$ will follow the same pattern as the previous case, each containing $k+1$ candies when it becomes the front beast. But instead, each subsequent move after $a_{i+2}$ will only include one new beast in the distribution, which again makes the consecutive pair unique. After all the beasts from $a_1, a_2, ..., a_k$ finish their rounds, we move onto the beasts $a_{k+1}, a_{k+2}, ...$ who didn't receive a candy when Grogg first went. Note that $a_{k+1}$ was covered for all $a_1, a_2, ..., a_k$ , so it has $k$ candies when it becomes the front beast. Every subsequent beast after $a_{k+1}$ until the consecutive pair will have one less candy than its previous. After the consecutive pair, this is also the case. Therefore, the distribution of candies starting from $a_{k+1}$ is $k, k-1, ..., k-i-1, k-i-1, ..., 3, 2, 1$ where $a_{k+1}$ is the front beast and $a_{2k+1}$ is the beast that has $1$ candy. Furthermore, the rest of the beasts after $a_{2k+1}=1$ in the line have $0$ candies by default. Note after $a_{k+1}$ finishes his move, we obtain $k, k-1, ..., k-i, k-i, ..., 3, 2$ . But this was the exact distribution for $a_1, a_2, ..., a_k$ . Therefore, this pattern is periodic and there were no instances where a beast holds all the candy, a contradiction. Thus, we have established that for all $n>2$ , there exists no solutions. It suffices to test $n=1,2$ . Denote $a_1$ as Grogg, $a_2$ as the second beast, $a_3$ as the third beast, etc. Note that if $n=2$ , then $a_2=a_3=1$ after Grogg finishes its play. But after $a_2$ finishes its play, $a_3=2$ and has all the candies, so $n=2$ works. Similarly, if $n=1$ , then after Grogg finishes its turn, $a_2=1$ , so it holds all the candy. Therefore, $n=1$ works as well. After all the cases, we see that the only solutions are $\boxed{n=1,2}$ .

<details><summary>Solution</summary>The answer is  $\fbox{n = 1,\text{ }2}$ . Assume the process happens each second. Then, let  $s_t$  denote the infinite sequence  $(a_1, a_2, a_3 \dots)$  after time  $t$  seconds from the beginning, where  $a_k$  is the number of candies the  $k$ -th monster in line has. For example, if  $n = 3$ , then  $s_0 = (3, 0, 0, 0, 0 \dots)$ ,  $s_1 = (1, 1, 1 , 0, 0\dots)$ ,  $s_2 = (2, 1, 0, 0, 0 \dots)$ , and so on. We now show the following lemma: $\textbf{Lemma 1:}$  The sequence  $s_t$  is always non-increasing. $\textit{Proof:}$  We will use induction. The base case  $t = 0$  is easy; at the very beginning, only the monster at the front of the line has candy, so the sequence will be non-increasing. Now, assume  $s_t$  is non-increasing at time  $t$ . We will show it is non-increasing at time  $t + 1$ . If  $s_t = (a_1, a_2, a_3 \dots)$ , then  $s_{t+1} = (a_2 + 1, a_3 + 1 \dots a_{(1+a_1)} + 1, a_{(2 + a_1)}, a_{(3 + a_1)} \dots)$ , with each term after  $a_{(1 + a_1)} + 1$  unchanged from before (this is because the monster at the front of the line at time  $t$  gives 1 candy to only each of the next  $a_1$  monsters in line). By our inductive hypothesis, we know the sequence after  $a_{(1 + a_1)} + 1$  is not increasing. Also, since a constant of  $1$  is added to each of the first  $a_1$  terms in  $s_{t+1}$ , we know the first  $a_1$  terms are also non-increasing, by our inductive hypothesis. Hence,  $s_{t+1}$  is also non-increasing, so we have proven the lemma.

Now, if some monster other than Grogg holds all  $n$  candies at time  $t$ , then we know that at time  $t-1$ , that monster must have  $n - 1$  candies. Since the total number of candies sums to  $n$ , it follows that at time  $t-1$ , the monster at the front of the line must hold  $1$  candy. Finally, we know that the monster the monster with  $n-1$  candies must be second in line at time  $t - 1$ . Therefore,  $s_{t-1} = (1, n-1, 0, 0 \dots)$ . By our lemma, we know  $1 \ge n - 1$ , which means  $n \le 2$ . Our answer is  $\fbox{n = 1, 2}$  only. Indeed, these both work.  $\blacksquare$</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>First, note that for  $n=1$  the second beast will temporarily hold all the candy after Grogg passes one candy to him, where Grogg is taken to be the first beast. For  $n=2$  the third beast will temporarily hold all the candy after Grogg passes one candy to beast two and one candy to beast three, and beast two passes one candy to beast three.
Now, assume that for  $n\ge 3,$  the  $j^{th}$  beast will temporarily hold all the candy after  $t$  turns, where the number of turns is equal to the number of beasts who have left the line. Then, after  $t-1$  turns the  $(j-1)^{th}$  beast must have held  $1$  candy and the  $j^{th}$  beast must have held  $n-1$  candies. So, after  $t-2$  turns the  $(j-2)^{th}$  beast must have held  $2$  candies, the  $(j-1)^{th}$  beast must have held  $0$  candies, and the  $j^{th}$  beast must have held  $n-2$  candies. However, this is impossible since the  $j^{th}$  beast can never hold any candies unless the  $(j-1)^{th}$  holds candies (assuming that the  $(j-1)^{th}$  beast is still in line). Thus, we have a contradiction. 
So, the only values of  $n$  for which another beast, besides Grogg, temporarily holds all the candy are  $n=\boxed{1,2}.$</details>

Here's a very simple proof (it seems long cause I wanted to be formal, but the basic idea is very easy).

I claim that the only  $n$  such that a beast besides Grogg will hold all the candies at some point are  $n = 1, 2$ . First, we show these two work. For  $n = 1$ , Grogg passes to the next beast, who will hold all the candies. For  $n = 2$ , Grogg passes one each to beasts  $2, 3$ , then beast  $2$  passes  $1$  candy to beast  $3$ , who now holds all the candies. 

Now we show that for  $n \geq 3$ , no beast besides Grogg will ever have all the candies. Let us number the candies  $1, \dots, n$ . We now impose a condition on how a beast passes candies. Say that if the first beast has  $k$  candies labeled  $c_1, \dots, c_k$  such that  $c_1<c_2<\dots<c_k$ , it passes the candy labeled  $c_1$  to the second beast,  $c_2$  to the third beast, and  $c_{k+1}$  to the  $k+1$ th beast in the line, and then the first beast leaves. Clearly this process is identical to the original process except that we've numbered the candies and made a fixed way for the first beast to distribute the numbered candies. 

Now call a state  $S_i$  the infinite list of sets  $s_{i,1}, s_{i,2}, \dots$ , where  $s_{i,j}$  represents the set of indices of the candies the  $j$ th beast from the front remaining in the line has after  $i-1$  beasts have already gone and distributed their candy. Let  $f(c, b)$  be the function that outputs the index of the set the candy labeled  $c$  is in when  $b-1$  beasts have already gone. In other words,  $s_{b,f(c, b)}$  contains  $c$ . For  $n\geq 3$ , We show that  $f(1, b), f(2, b), f(3, b)$  are constant regardless of  $n$ . 

Regardless of  $n$ , let's examine what happens to candy  $1$ .  Whenever the first beast remaining in the line has candy  $1$ , \textit{it will always be passed to the second beast in line}, no matter what other candies the first beast has. Otherwise, the candy will not move since it is not in the possession of the first beast in the line. So no matter what other candies any beasts has, the first candy will always be passed around in the same manner. This shows that  $f(1, b)$  is independent of  $n$ . Now consider candy  $2$ . If the first beast has candy  $2$ , it will pass to the next beast in line, unless the first beast also has candy  $1$ . But this means the location candy  $2$  is passed to only depends on whether the first beast has candy  $1$ . Since  $f(1, b)$ , which determines where the first candy is after  $b-1$  beasts have gone, is independent of  $n$ , then this shows  $f(2, b)$  is independent of  $n$ . Similarly, the beast that candy  $3$  gets passed to only depends on whether the first beast in the line has candy  $1$  or candy  $2$ . Since  $f(1, b), f(2, b)$ , which determines whether the first beast after  $b-1$  beasts have gone will have candies  $1$  and  $2$  respectively are independent of  $n$ , so is  $f(3, b)$ .

So now let's only focus on the locations of candies  $1, 2, 3$ . We start with  $\{\{1, 2, 3\}, \{\}, \dots, \}$  for our state. Then we move to state  $\{\{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}, \{\}, \dots, \}$ . Then we move to  $\{\{1, 2\}, \{3\}, \{\}, \dots\}$ . Then we move to state  $\{\{1, 3\}, \{2\}, \{\}, \dots \}$ . Then we move to state  $\{\{1, 2\}, \{3\}, \{\}, \dots \}$ . And now we've cycled to a state we've already encountered, and at no point besides the first state (Grogg having all the candies in the beginning) did a beast ever have all of candies  $1, 2, 3$  at once. Since the locations of these  $3$  candies are independent of  $n$ , this means that for all  $n\geq 3$ , no beast besides Grogg will ever have all the candies at once. So the answer is  $n = \boxed{1, 2}$ .

<details><summary>Solution</summary>For this solution, what we mean by the  $i$ th beast in line is the beast which was initially the  $i$ th in line, counting from the front, before any beast left the line. 

The answer is  $1$  and  $2$ . Clearly if  $n = 1$ , then every beast will temporarily hold all the candy, and if  $n = 2$  then after two turns, the third beast in line will hold all the candy. We now show that these are the only solutions. Let a beast other than Grogg which temporarily holds all the candy be called Evan, and let the beast in front of Evan be called David. **Lemma:** Before its turn, the  $i$ th beast in line must always have at least the same number of candy pieces as the  $(i + 1)$ th beast in line **Proof:** Before the  $i$ th beast's turn, every piece of candy that the  $(i + 1)$ th beast has was given to it by the  $j$ th beast ( $j < i$ ). However, whenever the  $j$ th beast gives the  $(i + 1)$ st beast a piece of candy, it must necessarily also give the  $i$ th beast a piece of candy as well. This proves the \textbf{Lemma}. 

On David's turn, David cannot have more than  $1$  piece of candy, or else he will also give candy to the beast behind Evan, so Evan will never hold all the candy. However, since David can only give  $1$  piece of candy to Evan, if we assume that  $n > 2$ , then Evan must already have at least  $n - 1 \ge 2$  pieces of candy before David's turn. This contradicts the \textbf{Lemma}, however, since then Evan holds more pieces of candy than David before David's turn. 

Thus,  $1$  and  $2$  are the only  $n$  which work  $\blacksquare$</details>

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>I claim that  $n=1,2$  are the only solutions. It's easy to check that these work. Let  $b_i$  denote the number of candies that the  $i^{\text{th}}$  beast in line has, where Grogg is the  $0^{\text{th}}$  beast.**Claim:**There will never exist positive integers  $p<q<r$  such that  $b_p,b_r>0$  and  $b_q=0.$  In other words, there are never any "gaps'' in the distribution.

Assume that the claim is false. Since  $b_r>0,$  then beast  $r$  must have received candy from the beast  $k,$  for some  $k<r.$  Note that  $k<p,$  because  $b_p>0.$  Therefore, beast  $q$  must've also received candy from beast  $k$  and thus  $b_q>0,$  a contradiction.

Now, suppose that there is some  $n\ge 3$  and let  $t$  be the smallest positive integer such that  $b_t=n.$  Then, in the previous turn, we must have   $$ b_{t-1}=1,~b_t=n-1. $$  Now, consider the turn before that. The two possible values for  $b_{t-2}$  are 1 and 2. If  $b_{t-2}=1,$  then we have  $$ b_{t-2}=1,~b_{t-1}=0,~b_t=n-1. $$  If  $b_{t-2}=2,$  then we must have  $$ b_{t-2}=2,~b_{t-1}=0,~b_t=n-2. $$  However, we assumed  $n\ge 3\iff n-2>0,$  so  $$ b_{t-2},b_t>0,~b_{t-1}=0 $$  in both cases, which contradicts our claim. Hence, no such  $n$  exists and the only solutions are   $$ \boxed{n=1,2}. $$</details>

<details><summary>induction</summary>Note that trivial cases of  $n=1$  and  $n=2$  (the former where a single piece of candy is just being passed through the line, and the latter where the states  $(2)$  and  $(1, 1)$  are periodically repeated.)
I claim that the answer is  $n = \{1, 2\},$  and for all  $n \geq 3$ , there does not exist another beast that temporarily holds all the candy. 
Proof:
Note that after Grogg steps out of the line, every beast as one piece of candy. It is easy to see that it would be tedious if we notated full states  $S(m)$  (since for sufficiently large number of beasts in a back portion of the line have  $1$  piece of candy), so let the *truncated state*  $T(m)$  after  $m$  moves (we define a move by concatenating all of a single beast's generous acts together) be the  $(a_1, a_2, a_3, ..., a_{k+1}),$  where  $a_i$  denote how many pieces of candy the beast in the corresponding location has ( $a_1$  is the beast at the front of the line), and  $k = a_1.$  Suppose that  $T(m) = (a_1, a_1-1, a_1-2, ..., 3, 2, 1, 1)$  for an arbitrary value of  $m.$  It is easy to prove by induction that then,   $$ T(m+s) = (a_1, a_1-1, a_1-2, ..., s+2, s+1, s+1, s, ..., 3, 2, 1),  $$   with the inductive step being  $T(m) = (a_1, a_1-1, a_1-2, ..., 3, 2, 1, 1)$  corresponding to  $T(m+1) = (a_1, a_1-1, a_1-2, ..., 3, 2, 2, 1).$  Eventually, we will reach the state  $T(m+a_1-1) = a_1, a_1, a_1-1, a_1-2, ..., 3, 2, 1),$  which produces the next state   $$ T(m+a_1) = a_1+1, a_1, a_1-1, a_1-2, ..., 3, 2, 1, 1, $$   identical in structure to  $T(m)$  except the leading monster as  $a_1+1$  pieces of candy instead. Basing the similarities in the structures of  $T(m)$  and  $T(m+a_1)$  as an outer inductive step (using our base case as  $T(1) = (1, 1)$  that holds for all  $n \geq 3$ ), we can thus prove that for all  $n,$  before running out of beasts in the back of the line with  $1$  piece of candy,  $S(m)$  tends to the state  $(a_1, a_1-1, a_1-2, a_1-3, ..., 3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, ...)$  for an arbitrary value of  $a_1.$  

Now, let's explore what would happen after running out of beasts in the back of the line with  $1$  piece of candy. Note it is easy to see that the aforementioned happens when  $a_1$  is the greatest positive integer that  $\frac{a_1(a_1+1)}{2} \leq n$  still holds (since truncated states are based on triangular numbers). In the special corner case of  $\frac{a_1(a_1+1)}{2} = n,$  the states  $S(m)$  just keep on repeating  $(a_1, a_1-1, a_1-2, a_1-3, ..., 3, 2, 1)$  (this is proved trivially via induction) with period  $1.$  Let  $r$  be the difference  $n-\frac{a_1(a_1+1)}{2}.$  Now, consider the numbers  $0, 1, 2, 3, ..., a_1-1, a_1$  arranged in a circle in clockwise order, where a token may be placed on a number, causing its value to increase by one. It is easy to see that after the state  $(a_1, a_1-1, a_1-2, a_1-3, ..., 3, 2, 1, \underbrace{1, 1, ..., 1}_{r 1's})$  is produced, the state that is equivalent placing  $r$  consecutive tokens on the numbers  $0, 1, 2, ..., r-1$  (or denoted as  $S = (a_1, a_1-1, a_1-2, ..., r+1, r, r, r-1, r-2, ..., 3, 2, 1)$ ) on the circle is produced. By induction, each subsequent state will shift the block of  $r$  consecutive tokens one number to the right on our circle. Since the circle is  $a_1+1$ -cyclic, after   $$ S = (a_1, a_1-1, a_1-2, ..., r+1, r, r, r-1, r-2, ..., 3, 2, 1) $$   is produced subsequent states will repeat with a period of  $a_1+1,$  thus easy to see never allowing a single beast in the line to hold all of the candy at once unless in the corner case of  $n < 3.$  

Thus, we are done  $\boxed{}.$</details>

**Claim**:  $n=1,2$  are the only  $n$  that work.**Proof**:  $n=1$  clearly works, as the beast after Grogg will hold all of the candy. For  $n=2$ , it is easy to see that the second beast after Grogg holds all of the candy. We now prove that no  $n \geq 3$  work.**Lemma 1**: Call a beast  $B$  *holey* if  $B$  does not hold any candy, and there exists a beast behind  $B$  who holds candy. There cannot exist any *holey* beasts.**Proof**: We use induction on the number of beasts who have already left the line. The base case, where no beasts have left and Grogg is still in front, is trivial. Clearly no *holey* beasts exist in such a formation. Now suppose that no *holey* beasts are present in the line after  $k$  beasts leave. When the beast currently in front of the line leaves, its candies are given to those behind this beast. Clearly this process cannot generate any *holey* beasts, so no *holey* beasts are present after  $k+1$  beasts leave. This completes the induction and proves the lemma.  $\blacksquare$ Now we return to the main solution. Denote the beasts  $b_1, b_2, \ldots$ , where  $b_k$  represents the  $k$ th beast in the line, before Grogg leaves. We wish to prove that if  $n \geq 3$ , then  $n$  does not work. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that there exists some  $k>0$  such that  $b_k$  holds all  $n$  candies. When this occurs,  $b_k$  must be at the front of the line, otherwise lemma 1 is violated. Thus this occurs after  $k-1$  beasts have left. Consider the line after  $k-2$  beasts had left.  $b_{k-1}$  was at the front of the line. Clearly,  $b_{k-1}$  was holding  $1$  candy at the time: if they had held  $0$ , then lemma 1 would be violated. If they had held more than  $1$ , then after  $k-1$  beasts have left there would still be beasts after  $b_k$  which held candies. Now, consider the line after  $k-3$  beasts had left. Beast  $b_{k-2}$  must have held either  $1$  or  $2$  candies. If they had held zero, then lemma 1 would have been violated. If they had held more than  $2$ , then there would be beasts after  $b_k$  with candy.
If  $b_{k-2}$  held  $1$  candy, then the position after  $k-3$  beasts had left would look like this:  $$ 1, 0, n-1, 0, 0, 0, \ldots $$  Where each number represents a beast holding that many candies. This is because if  $b_{k-1}$  held any candies, then after  $k-2$  beasts had left it would hold more than  $1$  candy, and if any beasts behind  $b_k$  held any candy, then clearly  $b_k$  would not hold all the candy after  $k-1$  beasts had left. Since  $n \geq 3$ , this position violates lemma 1.
If  $b_{k-2}$  held  $2$  candies, then the position after  $k-3$  beasts had left would look like this:  $$ 2, 0, n-2, 0, 0, 0, \ldots $$  This is because of  $b_{k-1}$  held any candies, then after  $k-2$  beasts had left it would hold more than  $1$  candy, and if any beasts behind  $b_k$  held any candy, then clearly  $b_k$  would not hold all the candy after  $k-1$  beasts had left. Since  $n \geq 3$ , this position also violates lemma 1.
Thus, we have proven that no  $n \geq 3$  satisfy the condition. We are done.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $a_1$  be any positive integer. For all  $i$ , write  $5^{2020}$  times  $a_i$  in base  $10$ , replace each digit with its remainder when divided by  $2$ , read off the result in binary, and call that  $a_{i+1}$ . Prove that  $a_N = a_{N+2^{2020}}$  for all sufficiently large  $N$ .
solution_md:
I proposed this one, with some help from Nikolai Beluhov in selecting what property to ask for and ironing out the statement. It was heavily inspired by [this old USAMO problem about powers of 5 with all odd digits](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h53661p336189). The difficulty feedback here surprises me a little. I knew this was hard but still thought it was in the normal USAMTS #5 range. So I'll be interested to see if anyone thinks knowing about that USAMO problem would help with solving this one.
Yep, I recognized this problem when solving USAMTS 5, I remembered it back from when I posted a solution on that thread :P. It didn't help too much with solving this problem, in my opinion though. Oops overkilled this problem, didn't need to generalize and induct twice, just once. Let $m=2020$ . Let $x\in \mathbb{N}$ . Define $f(x)$ as follows: write $5^mx$ in base 10, replace each digit with the remainder upon division by 2, read off the value in binary, and let that be $f(x)$ . Also define $f(0)=0$ . [b]Lemma 1: If $f(x)\ge x$ , then $x< 2^{m+1}$ . *Proof:* We prove the contrapositive. Suppose $x\ge 2^{m+1}$ , and we show $f(x) \lceil \log_{10}(5) \cdot m \rceil + 1 &\impliedby (m+3) \log_{10}(5) > \lceil \log_{10}(5) \cdot m \rceil + 1 \qquad \text{(since $x\ge 2^{m+3}$ )} &\iff 3\log_{10}(5) - 1 > \lceil \log_{10}(5) \cdot m \rceil - \log_{10}(5) \cdot m, \end{align*} which is true since the LHS above is greater than 1 (around $1.09$ ) and the RHS is at most $1$ . Therefore $f(x)[b]Lemma 2: If $x< 2^{m+1}$ , then $f(x) < 2^{m+1}$ . *Proof:* We have $5^mx < 5^m\cdot 2^{m+1} = 2 \cdot 10^m$ . Hence $5^mx$ has at most $m+1$ digits in base 10, which means when we write it in binary, its value $f(x)$ is at most $f(x)<2^{m+1}$ . $\square$ Let $x_0=a_1$ . We have the sequence $S(x_0):=(x_0, f(x_0), f^2(x_0),\ldots) = (a_1,a_2,\ldots)$ . We want to show $S(x_0)$ is eventually periodic with period dividing $2^m$ . [b]Claim 3: There exists an $N$ such that for all $n>N$ , we have $f^n(x_0) <2^{m+1}$ . *Proof:* We claim there exists some $n_0$ such that $f^{n_0+1}(x_0) \ge f^{n_0}(x_0)$ . If there did not, then the terms of $S(x_0)$ decrease by at least 1 at each step. But clearly $f(x) > 0$ for any $x\not = 0$ , so this is impossible. Now, by Lemma 1, this implies $f^{n_0}(x_0) < 2^{m+1}$ . Then by Lemma 2, taking $N=n_0$ works. $\square$ ----------------------- Now cut off the first $N$ terms, and redefine $x_0$ to $f^{N+1}(x_0)$ . So $x_0<2^{m+1}$ , and then by Lemma 2, everything that follows in $S(x_0)$ is less than $2^{m+1}$ . We will show that the new $S(x_0)$ is also eventually periodic, which is why cutting off the first $N$ terms does not affect anything. [b]Lemma 4: For $x < 2^m$ , we have $f(x)<2^m$ . *Proof:* Suppose $x<2^m$ . Then $5^mx < 10^m$ , so $5^mx$ has at most $m$ digits. Hence $f(x) \le 2^m-1$ , as needed. $\square$ [b]Lemma 5: For $2^m \le x<2^{m+1}$ , we have $f(x) = 2^m+f(x-2^m)$ . *Proof:* Suppose $y\in [0,2^m-1]$ and let $x=2^m+y$ . Then $5^m(2^m+y) = 10^m + 5^my$ . But $y<2^m$ , so $5^my < 10^m$ . Hence $f(2^m+y)$ has a one in the $2^m$ position and is followed by the remaining $m$ digits are the binary value of $f(y)$ . Hence $f(2^m+y) = 2^m+f(y)$ . $\square$ If $x_0<2^m$ , then by Lemma 4, the entire $S(x_0)$ is less than $2^m$ . If $2^m\le x_0 < 2^{m+1}$ , the entire $S(x_0)$ sequence is in $[2^m,2^{m+1})$ . Therefore, WLOG assume $x_0<2^m$ , since in the latter case we can simply subtract everything by $2^m$ , which is a valid sequence by Lemma 5. ------------------------- We want to show the following two claims. [b]Key Claim A: $f$ is bijective from $[0,2^m)$ to $[0,2^m)$ . [b]Key Claim B: We know $f$ is a bijection on the finite set $[0,2^m)$ , i.e. a permutation. Hence it has a cycle decomposition. We claim the lengths of all the cycles are a power of 2. First we show that if we show these two claims, the problem is finished. Note that when we iterate $f$ on $x_0$ , it goes into a cycle. By Key Claim B, this cycle length is a power of 2. The length of the cycle is at most the length of the permutation, which is $2^m$ . Hence the cycle length divides $2^m$ . This finishes the problem. ------------------------- The idea to show the Key Claims is to massively generalize and induct. Fix an odd positive integer $a$ and a positive integer $d$ . For $x\in [0,2^m)$ , define $f_{a,d,m}(x)$ as follows. Take $a\cdot 5^mx + d\mod 10^m$ , reduce each of the digits $\mod 2$ (note there are $m$ digits), and read it off as a binary number. Hence $f_{a,d,m}(x)$ is a function $[0,2^m)\to [0,2^m)$ . [b]Claim 6: $f_{1,0,m}(x) = f(x)$ for $x\in [0,2^m)$ . *Proof:* We only need to check that $1\cdot 5^mx + 0$ is always less than $10^m$ so that the mod $10^m$ does not affect anything. Since $x<2^m$ , we have $5^mx < 10^m$ , as claimed. $\square$ ------------------ [b]Generalized Key Claim A: For any $a$ and $d$ with $a$ odd, $f_{a,d,m}(x)$ is a bijection. *Proof:* Induct on $m$ . Base case: $m=1$ . Then for $x=0$ and $x=1$ , we take $5ax+d\mod 10$ , and reduce this single digit mod 2, and read it off in binary. For $x=0$ , it is $d\mod 10$ , and for $x=1$ , it is $5a+d\mod 10$ . These are of opposite parity since $5a$ is odd, so mod 2 they are $\{0,1\}$ in some order. Inductive step: Assume the result is true with $m$ replaced with $m-1$ , for any $a$ and $d$ with $a$ odd. We have the following cases. [list] - $x$ is even. Let $x=2y$ . Then \begin{align*} a\cdot 5^mx + d &= 10(a\cdot 5^{m-1}y) + d &= 10\left( a\cdot 5^{m-1}y + \left \lfloor \frac{d}{10} \right\rfloor \right) + (d \mod 10) &= 10g(y) + (d\mod 10) \end{align*} where $g(y):= a\cdot 5^{m-1}y + \left \lfloor \tfrac{d}{10} \right\rfloor$ . By induction, we know $g(y) \mod 10^{m-1}$ with each digit reduced $\mod 2$ is a bijection from $y\in [0,2^{m-1}-1]$ to $[0,2^{m-1}-1]$ . Hence $10g(y) \mod 10^m$ with each digit reduced $\mod 2$ is a bijection from $y\in [0,2^{m-1}-1]$ to $\{0,2,4,6,\ldots,2^m-2\}$ . Then clearly $10g(y) + d \mod 10^m$ with each digit reduced $\mod 2$ is also bijection from $y\in [0,2^{m-1}-1]$ to $\{0,2,4,6,\ldots,2^m-2\}+(d\mod 2)$ since translating under mods preserves the fact that it is a bijection. That is, [list] - if $d$ is even, then this map bijects even $x$ in the range $[0,2^m-1]$ to even values in the range $[0,2^m-1]$ ; and - if $d$ is odd, it bijects even $x$ in the range $[0,2^m-1]$ to odd values in the range $[0,2^m-1]$ . [/list] - $x$ is odd. Let $x=2y+1$ . Then \begin{align*} a\cdot 5^mx + d &= a\cdot 5^m(2y+1) + d &= 10(a\cdot 5^{m-1}y) + a\cdot 5^m + d &= 10\left( a\cdot 5^{m-1}y + \left \lfloor \frac{a\cdot 5^m + d}{10} \right\rfloor \right) + (a\cdot 5^m + d \mod 10) &= 10h(y) + (a\cdot 5^m+d\mod 10). \end{align*} where $h(y):=a\cdot 5^{m-1}y + \left \lfloor \tfrac{a\cdot 5^m + d}{10} \right\rfloor $ . Again, by induction, $h(y) \mod 10^{m-1}$ with each digit reduced mod 2 is a bijection from $y\in [0,2^{m-1}-1]$ to $[0,2^{m-1}-1]$ . Hence $10h(y) \mod 10^m$ is a bijection from $y\in [0,2^{m-1}-1]$ to $\{0,2,4,6,\ldots,2^m-2\} + (a\cdot 5^m+d \mod 2)$ . Since $a$ is odd, $a\cdot 5^m+d$ is of opposite parity as $d$ , so in other words, [list] - if $d$ is even, this map bijects odd $x$ in the range $[0,2^m-1]$ to odd values in $[0,2^m-1]$ ; and - if $d$ is odd, it bijects odd $x$ in the range $[0,2^m-1]$ to even values in $[0,2^m-1]$ . [/list] [/list] Combining these two proves that for any $a$ and $d$ with $a$ odd, $f_{a,d,m}(x)$ is a bijection. $\square$ Now, plugging in $a=1$ and $d=0$ proves Key Claim A. --------------- [b]Generalized Key Claim B: Since $f_{a,d,m}$ is bijective and is a function $[0,2^m)\to [0,2^m)$ , it is a permutation $[0,2^m)\to [0,2^m)$ . Hence it has a cycle decomposition. We claim the lengths of all the cycles are a power of 2. *Proof:* Induct on $m$ . Base case: $m=1$ . Here $f_{a,d,1}$ is a bijection from $\{0,1\}$ to $\{0,1\}$ so the cycle lengths are either 1 or 2, which are both powers of 2. Inductive step: Suppose for all $a$ and $d$ with $a$ odd, all cycles in the cycle decomposition of the permutation $f_{a,d,m-1}:[0,2^{m-1}) \to [0,2^{m-1})$ are powers of 2. *Lemma:* We have \[ f_{a,d,m}(x) \mod 2^{m-1} = f_{5a,d,m-1}(x\mod 2^{m-1}). \] *Proof:* Since $x<2^m$ , let $x=b\cdot 2^{m-1} + y$ with $b\in \{0,1\}$ and $y<2^{m-1}$ . Then \begin{align*} a\cdot 5^mx + d &= a\cdot 5^m(b\cdot 2^{m-1} + y) + d &= 5ab\cdot 10^{m-1} + a\cdot 5^my + d &\equiv a\cdot 5^my + d &= 5a(5^{m-1}y) + d \pmod{10^{m-1}}. \end{align*} Therefore, the last $m-1$ digits of $a\cdot 5^mx+d$ in base 10 are the last $m-1$ digits of $5a(5^{m-1}y)+d$ in base 10, which is independent of $b$ . Since the digits of $f_{a,d,m}(x)$ in binary are the digits of $a\cdot 5^mx+d$ reduced mod 2, and $x\mod 2^{m-1}=y$ , we are done. $\square$ Consider a cycle $(c_1,c_2,\ldots,c_\ell)$ in the cycle decomposition of $f_{a,d,m}$ . In other words, $f_{a,d,m}(c_i) = c_{i+1}$ with indices taken mod $\ell$ , and all the $c_i$ are pairwise distinct. Consider \[ C=(c_1 \mod 2^{m-1}, c_2\mod 2^{m-1}, \ldots, c_\ell \mod 2^{m-1}). \] By the Lemma above, this is a cycle in the cycle decomposition of $f_{5a,d,m-1}$ , but potentially ``wrapped around'' multiple times, i.e. they are not necessarily all pairwise distinct. Suppose the cycle in $f_{5a,d,m-1}$ that is repeated is $(d_1,\ldots,d_k)$ and it repeats $j$ times. So we know \[ (d_1,\ldots,d_k, \ d_1,\ldots,d_k, \ \ldots, \ d_1,\ldots, d_k) = C, \] where there are $j$ copies of $d_1,\ldots,d_k$ above. In particular, $\ell = jk$ . We claim $j=1$ or $j=2$ . Indeed, if $j\ge 3$ , then there are three $d_1$ 's. So in $(c_1,\ldots,c_\ell)$ , there are three distinct values that are equivalent mod $2^{m-1}$ . But all the values of $(c_1,\ldots,c_\ell)$ are in $[0,2^m)$ , so this is a contradiction. By induction, $k$ is a power of 2. Since $j\in \{1,2\}$ , hence $\ell=jk$ is a a power of 2. This proves the induction, and finishes the proof. $\square$ Now, plugging in $a=1$ and $d=0$ proves Key Claim B. ---------------------- Therefore, Key Claim A and B are proved, so we are done.
RemarksReally hard NT problem! The main ideas are the following: [list=1] - The sequences eventually get down below $2^{m+1}$ . - It suffices to check below $2^m$ . - The function is a bijection on equivalence classes $\mod 2^m$ . - Finally that cycles of the function on these equivalence classes are powers of $2$ length. Each of the claims individually is not hard to prove. For the last two, the idea is to massively generalize and induct, since that is the only way to deal with the randomness of the function.

Solution?For convenience, the number of digits was denoted as $\lceil \log x \rceil$ , and we took the cases where $\log x$ was an integer separately. Although $\text{number of digits}=\lfloor \log x \rfloor +1$ , for clarity purposes, the former was used. Furthermore, $\log x$ is the base $10$ logarithm, rather than the natural logarithm. Consider when $a_i$ decreases. For now, we take the cases where the leading digit is nonzero in binary. Note that if the binary representation has $n$ digits, with the leading digit nonzero, then its value in base $10$ will be strictly less than $2^n$ . Therefore, if we have the number of digits of $5^{2020}*a_i$ as $k$ , then we require $a_i \ge 2^k$ in order for $a_i$ to decreasing. However, note that $k=\lceil \log (5^{2020}*a_i) \rceil$ , so we require $a_i \ge 2^{\lceil \log (5^{2020}*a_i) \rceil}$ . Note that $2^{\log(5^{2020}*a_i)+1} \ge 2^{\lceil \log(5^{2020}*a_i) \rceil}$ (the equality case comes from when $\log(5^{2020}*a_i)$ is an integer, so we have to use the definition $\lfloor \log(5^{2020}*a_i) \rfloor+1$ instead), so when $a_i \ge 2^{\log (5^{2020}*a_i)+1}$ is satisfied, so does $a_i \ge 2^{\lceil \log (5^{2020}*a_i) \rceil}$ . To tackle $a_i \ge 2^{\log (5^{2020}*a_i)+1}$ , we may consider $a_i \ge 2^{\log (5^{2020}*a_i)} \implies (\log a_i)(\frac{1}{\log 2}-1) \ge 2020\log 5 \implies \log a_i \ge 2020\log 2$ , or $a_i \ge 2^{2020}$ . Therefore, note that for $a_i \ge 2^{\log (5^{2020}*a_i)+1}$ , we multiply an extra factor of $2$ , or $a_i \ge 2^{2021}$ . Thus, this takes care of the extremes of the side where $a_i$ decreases. Note that $a_i$ could be sufficiently high, however it will monotonously decrease until $a_{i+c}$ gets to $2^{2021}$ for some sufficiently large $c$ . Now consider when $a_i$ increases, which occurs when $a_i<2^{\log(5^{2020}*a_i)+1} \implies a_i<2^{2021}$ . Furthermore, any $a_i$ in this bound cannot pass $2^{2021}$ , as $\text{max}(5^{2020}*a_i)=2021$ . But any binary representation with $2021$ digits is strictly less than $2^{2021}$ , and so $a_{i+1}$ will be in the bound, even when maximized. In particular, consider the lower bound of any $a_2<2^{2021}$ , created from one iteration of $5^{2020}*a_1$ . Note we may do this as we require $a_{N}=a_{N+2^{2020}}$ . Therefore, if we considered the bounds of $a_1$ , then we included the cases when $a_1$ is arbitrarily small that could not be created for any $a_{1+c}$ for any positive $c$ , which creates a weak bound. (This is since if $a_1$ is very small, then $\lceil \log 5^{2020}*a_{1+c} \rceil>\lceil \log a_1 \rceil$ . But we have the case that the leading digits are non-zero in binary, so it is given that when $a_1$ is small then $a_{1+2^{2020}}>a_1$ , a contradiction). The minimal case of $a_2$ occurs when we choose $a_1=1$ , or the smallest possible of $a_1$ . Therefore, note that $\lceil \log 5^{2020} \rceil=\lceil 2020\log 5 \rceil=1412$ , and since any binary representation of $1412$ digits has a minimum bound of $2^{1411}$ , we have that as our minimum of $a_2$ . We introduce the following claim. **Claim 1:** If $a_1 < 2^{2021}$ and all numbers between $a_1$ and $a_k$ have their leading digit nonzero in binary, then for some sufficiently large $i$ , we have either $a_k \in [2^{2019}, 2^{2020})$ or $a_k \in [2^{2020}, 2^{2021})$ for any positive integer $k \ge i$ . **Proof:**Note that we have previously established that the minimum bound after one iteration of this process is $2^{1411}$ . We may use a similar logic, since if their leading digits in binary are always non-zero, the sequence keeps increasing. Therefore, we consider the minimum bound after the second iteration. Note that the minimum number of digits created by $5^{2020}*k$ for $k \in [2^{1411}, 2^{2021})$ occurs when $k=2^{1411}$ . Note that $\lceil \log 5^{2020}*2^{1411} \rceil=\lceil 2020\log 5+1411\log 2 \rceil=1837$ . Therefore, the minimum bound after two iterations is $2^{1836}$ . After the third iteration, we have $\lceil \log 5^{2020}*2^{1836} \rceil=\lceil 2020\log 5+1836\log 2 \rceil=1965$ , so the minimum bound is $2^{1964}$ . Repeatedly applying this gives the minimum as $2^{1411} \rightarrow 2^{1836} \rightarrow 2^{1964} \rightarrow 2^{2003} \rightarrow 2^{2014} \rightarrow 2^{2018} \rightarrow 2^{2019}$ . Note that from $2^{2019}$ , we see that $\lceil \log 5^{2020}*2^{2019} \rceil=2020$ and $5^{2020}*(2^{2020}-c)=10^{2020}-5^{2020}*c$ for a positive $c$ which has $2020$ digits. But any binary representation with $2020$ digits is bounded in the interval $[2^{2019}, 2^{2020})$ . Therefore, since both the bounds yield the same number of digits, any iterations forward will always be in that interval. However, there is the outlier if we picked $a_1 \in [2^{2020}, 2^{2021})$ . In particular, $5^{2020}*2^{2020}$ has $2021$ digits (We did not use logs for this since $\log(5^{2020}*2^{2020})$ is an integer. Refer to the first paragraph) and $\lceil \log 5^{2020}*2^{2021} \rceil=2021$ , so for any $a_1 \in [2^{2020}, 2^{2021})$ , $a_{1+c}$ will map the same interval. This gives the desired claim. \qedsymbol **Claim 2:** If $a_1 \ge 2^{2021}$ and all numbers between $a_1$ and $a_k$ have their leading digits nonzero in binary, then for some sufficiently large $i$ , we have it will decrease into the interval $a_k \in [2^{2020}, 2^{2021})$ for any positive integer $k \ge i$ . **Proof:** A similar logic can be applied for when $a_1 \ge 2^{2021}$ . We may make $a_1$ sufficiently large, with some $n$ digits. Note that we have shown that for any $a_1 \ge 2^{2021}$ , it is strictly decreasing. To show that it will eventually reach the interval of $[2^{2020}, 2^{2021})$ , we can note that $a_1 \ge 2^{2021}$ , so $5^{2020}*a_{i-1}$ for some $i$ will always contain at least $2021$ digits. We note that the leading digit is always nonzero in binary, and so $a_i \ge 2^{2020}$ . Since it monotonously decreases, it will eventually approach this interval. We define this as \emph{trapped}, as $a_i$ is trapped in the interval $[2^{2020}, 2^{2021})$ . Likewise, if the leading digit in binary is non-zero, then $a_i$ is also \emph{trapped} for $a_1<2^{2021}$ , in the intervals $[2^{2019}, 2^{2020})$ , or $[2^{2020}, 2^{2021})$ . **Claim 3:** If the leading digit in binary can be zero, then the bounds for $a_i$ (for sufficiently large $a_i$ ) become $[0, 2^{2021})$ for both $a_1<2^{2021}$ and $a_1 \ge 2^{2021}$ . **Proof:** Now consider the case where the leading digit can be zero in binary for the increasing portion. Note that this voids the \emph{trapped} condition as it can decrease within the interval, however it still bounds the values to be less than $2^{2021}$ or $a_i<2^{2021}$ . To see this, note that having the leading digit as zero will decrease the value of $a_{i+1}$ . But we have shown that even with the leading digit as nonzero in binary(which would actually increase), we have $a_{i+1}<2^{2021}$ . Thus, so must the value of $a_{i+1}$ when the leading digit can be zero in binary. However, note that this also changes the condition for the case $a_1 \ge 2^{2021}$ . Using the fact that the leading digit could be zero, $a_i$ can decrease so that it "escapes" the \emph{trapped} condition with $a_i<2^{2020}$ . For the lower bound, note that $a_i=2^{2021}$ suffices for $a_i=0$ , and it cannot be any lower, as the minimum $a_i$ created through binary is when all digits are $0$ . This gives the desired bounds as stated in the claim. \qedsymbol Since both $a_1<2^{2021}$ and $a_1 \ge 2^{2021}$ (for large enough $a_i$ ) yield the same interval in claim $3$ , it suffices to just consider $a_1<2^{2021}$ . Note that because of the representation in binary, all $a_1<2^{2021}$ could be formed by picking numbers from the set $S \in \{2^0, 2^1, ..., 2^{2019}, 2^{2020}\}$ , where each number can only be picked once. In particular, we write any $a_i=\sum_{p}2^{q}$ for $0 \le p,q \le 2020$ .(Note this includes $a_i$ that were not apart of the original $a_1$ ) Furthermore, let the smallest power of $2$ that occurs in any $a_i$ be $n_0$ , or the smallest term is $2^{n_0}$ . Note that since we chose it as the smallest term, there will be no powers of $2$ before $2^{n_0}$ , which also means that there will be no other terms that change the digit position of $2^{n_0}$ in binary representation other than $5^{2020}*2^{n_0}$ itself. But the digit representing $2^{n_0}$ in binary is the $n_0+1$ th digit from the decimal point. Therefore, $5^{2020}*2^{n_0}=5^{2020-n_0}10^{n_0}$ . Thus, the $n_0+1$ th digit from the decimal point of $5^{2020}*2^{n_0}$ is equivalent to the units digit of $5^{2020-n_0}$ , which is $5$ if $2020-n_0>0$ . But $5 \equiv 1 \pmod{2}$ , so the digit in binary that represents $2^{n_0}$ is always $1$ , which also means that the period of $2^{n_0}$ is $1$ . (Period is defined as the constant number of iterations it takes for the binary representation of the corresponding power of $2$ to return to its initial state) We denote this period as $k_0$ . The only case this is not satisfied is when $n_0=2020$ . But if $n_0=2020$ , since we picked $n_0$ to be the smallest power of $2$ , $a_i=2^{2020}$ . Thus, $5^{2020}*2^{2020}=10^{2020}$ . Taking each digit mod $2$ and in binary, we see that $a_{i+1}=2^{2020}$ , and so any $a_{i+c}=2^{2020}$ for $c \ge 1$ , which implies $a_i=a_{i+2^{2020}}$ . Therefore, this case doesn't cause any issue. Note that for the case when $a_i=2^{2020}$ , the period also coincides as $1$ . Likewise, we denote the period of the next smallest power of any $a_i$ as $2$ , $2^{n_1}$ as $k_1$ , and so on. Note that for $2^{n_1}$ , we have two cases: It has an even parity, or an odd parity. Consider if it was the parity where it remains the same. Then, the period would be the period of $2^{n_0}$ which is $k_0=1$ , since $n_1$ is the second smallest term, so its digit is influenced by $5^{2020}(2^{n_1}+2^{n_0})$ . On the other hand, if the parity changed, we would require twice the period to change it from a different parity and back. Therefore, we have $2k_0=2$ . Now consider the third smallest power of $2$ , $2^{n_2}$ with period $k_2$ . Instead of considering only $2^{n_0}$ , we also have to take into consideration of the period of $2^{n_1}$ . Therefore, in order for both periods to coincide, we instead consider $\text{lcm}(k_0, k_1)$ . Therefore, if we didn't have a parity change, the period would be $\text{lcm}(k_0, k_1)$ , and otherwise the period would be $2\text{lcm}(k_0, k_1)$ . We note from here that since $k_0=2^0$ , and the fact that the period of every subsequent term will either be a multiple of $1$ or $2$ of the lcm of the previous terms, every period will be a power of $2$ . This is due to the fact that if $b_0 \le b_1 ... \le b_{n}$ , we have $\text{lcm}(2^{b_0}, 2^{b_1}, ..., 2^{b_{n}})=2^{b_{n}}$ , and so we have $k_n=2^{b_{n}}, 2^{b_{n}+1}$ , both of which are powers of $2$ . Furthermore, since we begin with a power of $2$ , all periods will be powers of $2$ . However, the upper bound occurs when all terms $2^0, 2^1, ..., 2^{2019}, 2^{2020}$ are used, and we repeatedly multiply by $2$ to the lcm. Note this gives $k_0=2^0, k_1=2^1, k_2=2^2, ..., k_{2019}=2^{2019}, k_{2020}=2^{2020}$ . Therefore, we may express all $k_i$ for $0 \le i \le 2020$ as $2^n$ where $0 \le n \le 2020$ , so $2^n|2^{2020}$ . However, we did miss one case, which was if $a_i=0$ or $5^{2020}*a_i=0$ . *Let  $a'$  be the result when the operation in the problem is applied on some original number  $a$ . Then,  $\{0_2', 1_2', 10_2', 11_2',\cdots ,11\cdots 11_2'\}\equiv \mathcal S$ , i.e. applying  $'$  gives a permutation.*

Proof. Let  $f$  be a function on the obvious set defined such that  $f(x)=x'$ . If we can prove that  $f$  is surjective, then since  $\mathcal S$  is both the domain and the range,  $f$  must be bijective (and a permutation). We will actually give a way to algorithmically construct an input  $x=\overline{d_nd_{n-1}\cdots d_1}_2=\sum_{i=1}^n 2^{i-1}d_i$  given some desired output  $y\in \mathcal S$ , where each  $d_i\in \{0,1\}$ . (Note that  $x$  is in base  $2$ .) We start with the last digit of  $y$ : if it is `` $0$ " then we choose  $d_1=0$ , otherwise, if it is odd, then we choose  $d_1=1$ . Now we induct: say that we have already fixed the last  $k$  digits  $\overline{d_{k}\cdots d_1}$ , and we will show that we can determine a unique, working value for  $d_{k+1}.$  Notice that, if we add  $5^n\cdot 2^{k}=5^{n-k}\cdot 10^k$  to an existing base- $10$  number, then the last  $k$  digits will remain unchanged, but the  $k+1$ st-to-last digit will change parity ( $5^{n-k}$  is odd). On the other hand, if we do nothing, then each digit remains unchanged. Thus, if  $x=\overline{0\cdots 0d_k\cdots d_1}_2\cdot 5^n$  already gives a correct parity for what we want as an output for the  $k+1$  to last term, then we can choose  $d_{k+1}=0$ . Otherwise, what we want is of different parity, and we can choose  $d_{k+1}=1$ . Then, we can repeat this procedure to find some suitable input number for some desired output.
    
As an example, suppose that  $n=3$  and we want some number  $x=(\overline{d_3d_2d_1})_2$  such that  $f(x)=001.$  Since the last digit of  $125\cdot \overline{d_3d_2d_1}_2$  should be odd, we need to choose  $d_1=1$ . This means that  ${d_1}_2\cdot 125=125.$  Now, the second to last digit needs to be even. Since the second to last digit of  $125$  is already even, we choose  $d_2=0$ , so  $\overline{d_2d_1}_2\cdot 125=125.$  Finally, we want an even digit for the third-to-last digit but  $125$  has an odd third-to-last digit, so we should choose  $d_3=1$ . Hence  $x=101_2=5$ , which indeed works.

It is well-known that every permutation has a cyclic decomposition, so the sequence  $a, f(a), f^2(a),...$  will eventually cycle back to  $a$ . Furthermore, if we let  $c$  be any positive value such that  $f^c(a)=a$ , then we can say that the sequence  $a, f^z(a), f^{2z}(a),...$  also cycles to  $a$  since  $f^{cz}(a)=a$ .

Now we prove a final fact about  $f$ : the last  $j$  digits of  $f(a)$  (once again, in binary) for any  $j$  depends solely on the last  $j$  digits of  $a$ . This is easy: the last  $j$  digits of  $f(a)$  depends on the last  $j$  digits of  $5^{2020}\cdot a$  in base 10, which is just  $5^{2020}\cdot a\pmod{10^j}.$  By the Chinese remainder theorem, this is uniquely determined by the residues modulo  $2^{j}$  and  $5^{j}$ . Since  $5^{2020}\cdot a$  is clearly  $0\pmod{5^j}$ , it suffices to show that  $a\pmod{2^j}$  depends solely on the last  $j$  digits of  $a$  in binary, which it does. Hence this fact is true.

The main implication of this fact is that, if  $f^n(a)$  and  $a$  share the same last  $j$  digits in binary for some  $n$ , then the last  $j$  digits cycle at least every  $n$  applications of  $f$ , i.e.  $f^{n\ell}(a)$  also shares the last  $j$  digits in common with  $a$  for any  $\ell$ .

Now we are ready to finish the problem. If  $a$  is any number with  $\leq 2020$  digits in binary, then previously we have shown that  $f(a), f^2(a), ...$  are as well. Hence, if we show that the last  $k$  digits of the sequence  $a, f(a),f^2(a)$  cycles with periodicity dividing  $2^k$ , then we would be done, since the last  $k$  digits are \textit{all} of the digits. Hence, we induct, starting with the units digit in binary. Specifically, we claim that the last  $j$  digits of each of the terms in the sequence  $a, f(a), f^2(a),...$  cycles with periodicity dividing  $2^j$  for any integer  $j>0$ , and to show this, we induct on  $j$ , starting with  $j=1$ . Let  $c_j$  be the cycle length for the last  $j$  digits.

For the base case  $j=1$ , we have two cases:  $f(a)$  has the same last digit as  $a$ , and  $f(a)$  has a different last digit. In the first case, the last digit cycles immediately, so  $c_1=1$ . In the second case, I claim that  $f^2(a)$  must have the same last digit as  $a$ . FTSOC, assume otherwise; i.e.  $f^2(a)$  has the same last digit as  $f(a)$  and not  $a$ . Then, since the last digit of each term depends solely on the last digit of the previous term,  $f^3(a)$  also has the same last digit as  $f^2(a)$ ,  $f^4(a)$  the same as  $f^3(a)$ , and so on. This contradicts the fact that the sequence  $a, f(a), f^2(a),...$  cycles back to  $a$ , contradiction. Hence  $c_1=2$  in the second case. Both of these values divide  $2^1$ .

Now we proceed to show the inductive step, where we show that the claim holding for any  $j$  implies the claim for  $j+1$ . This is very similar to the proof of the base case. Consider the sequence 
\[a, f^{c_j}(a), f^{2c_{j}}(a),....\]
Each of the terms in this sequence has the same last  $j$  digits by construction. Consider the  $j+1$ th to last digit. We have two cases:  $f^{c_j}(a)$  has the same last digit as  $a$ , and  $f^{c_j}(a)$  has a different last digit. In the first case, the  $j+1$ th to last digit cycles immediately, so  $c_j=c_{j+1}$ . In the second case, I claim that  $f^{2c_j}(a)$  must have the same last digit as  $a$ . FTSOC, assume otherwise; i.e.  $f^{2c_j}(a)$  has the same  $j+1$ th-to-last digit as  $f^{c_j}(a)$  and not  $a$ . Then, since the last digit of each term depends solely on the last digit of the previous term,  $f^{3c_j}(a)$  also has the same last digit as  $f^{2c_j}(a)$ ,  $f^{4c_j}(a)$  the same as  $f^{3c_j}(a)$ , and so on. This contradicts the fact that the sequence  $a, f^{c_j}(a), f^{2c_j}(a),...$  cycles back to  $a$ , contradiction. Hence  $c_{j+1}=2c_j$  in the second case, and the inductive step is complete because  $c_j\mid 2^j$  implies both  $c_{j+1}\mid 2^{j+1}$ .

This claim must also be true for  $k$ , so  $c_k\mid 2^k$  and we are done.</details>

<details><summary>Solution (complicated, but 2 pages)</summary>For a base  $10$  positive integer  $n$ , define  $g(n)$  to be the number obtained from the operation in which we replace each digit with of  $n$  with its remainder when divided by  $2$ , and let  $f(g(n))$  be the number obtained when we read  $g(n)$  off in binary. **Lemma I:** If  $a_n < 2^{2021}$ , then  $a_i < 2^{2021}$   $\forall$   $i \ge n$  **Proof:** We are given  $a_n < 2^{2021}$ . We will proceed by induction, with base case  $i = n$ . Assume  $a_i < 2^{2021}$  for some  $i \ge n$ . Then  $5^{2020} \cdot a_i < 2 \cdot 10^{2020}$ , hence  $g(5^{2020} \cdot a_i)$  has at most  $2021$  digits, so we have  $a_{i + 1} = f(g(5^{2020} \cdot a_i)) < 2^{2021}$ , and by induction we are finished  $\blacksquare$  **Lemma II:** For any value of  $a_1$ ,  $\exists$   $n$  such that  $a_n < 2^{2021}$  **Proof:** For an arbitrary  $i$ , if  $a_i < 2^{2021}$ , then we are done, so assume  $a_i \ge 2^{2021}$ . Let  $\alpha > 2021$  be the positive integer such that  $2^{\alpha} > a_i \ge 2^{\alpha - 1}$ . Then  $5^{2020} \cdot a_i < 10^{2020} \cdot 2^{\alpha - 2020} < 10^{2020 + \frac{\alpha - 2020}{3}}$ . Hence,  $g(5^{2020} \cdot a_i)$  has at most  $2020 + \frac{\alpha - 2020}{3}$  digits, so  $a_{i + 1} = f(g(5^{2020} \cdot a_i)) < 2^{2020 + \frac{\alpha - 2020}{3}}$ . For  $\alpha > 2021$ , we have  $2^{2020 + \frac{\alpha - 2020}{3}} < 2^{\alpha - 1}$ , therefore  $a_{i + 1} < 2^{2020 + \frac{\alpha - 2020}{3} } < 2^{\alpha - 1} \le a_i$ . Inducting, we find that if  $a_i \ge 2^{2021}$ , the sequence will decrease until a term is reached that is less than  $2^{2021}$ , at which point we are finished  $\blacksquare$  **Lemma III**: If  $a_i \equiv a_j$  mod  $2^k$ ,  $i < j$ ,  $k \le 2020$ , then  $a_{n + i} \equiv a_{n + j}$  mod  $2^k$   $\forall$   $n$   $\in$   $\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ **Proof:** This clearly holds true for  $n = 0$ , so we proceed by induction. Assume we have  $a_{n + i} \equiv a_{n + j}$  mod  $2^k$  for some  $n$ , and we wish to prove  $a_{n + i + 1} \equiv a_{n + j + 1}$  mod  $2^k$ . 

If  $a_{n + i} \equiv a_{n + j}$  mod  $2^k$ , then  $5^{2020} \cdot a_{n + i} \equiv 5^{2020} \cdot a_{n + j}$  mod  $2^k$  and since  $5^{2020} \cdot a_{n + i} \equiv 5^{2020} \cdot a_{n + j} \equiv 0$  mod  $5^k$  as well, by the Chinese Remainder Theorem, we must have  $5^{2020} \cdot a_i \equiv 5^{2020} \cdot a_j$  mod  $10^k$ , so the last  $k$  digits of  $5^{2020}a_{n + i}$  and  $5^{2020}a_{n + j}$  are identical, and by extension, so are the last  $k$  digits of  $g(5^{2020}a_{n + i})$  and  $g(5^{2020}a_{n + j})$ . Finally, the remainders when  $a_{n + i + 1} = f(g(5^{2020}a_{n + i}))$  and  $a_{n + j + 1} = f(g(5^{2020}a_{n + j}))$  are divided by  $2^k$  are uniquely determined by the last  $k$  digits of  $g(5^{2020}a_{n + i})$  and  $g(5^{2020}a_{n + j})$ , therefore  $a_{n + i + 1} \equiv a_{n + j + 1}$  mod  $2^k$  as well, and by induction we are finished  $\blacksquare$  **Lemma IV:** The sequence  $(a_i)$  is eventually cyclic mod  $2^{2020}$ . Furthermore, the period divides  $2^{2019}$ . **Proof:** First note that  $(a_i)$  is constant modulo  $2$ . This is because if  $a_i$  is odd, then  $5^{2020}a_i$  is odd as well, so the final digit of  $g(5^{2020}a_i)$  is  $1$ , therefore  $a_{i + 1} = f(g(5^{2020}a_i))$  is odd. Similarly, if  $a_i$  is even, then  $5^{2020}a_i$  is even as well, so the final digit of  $g(5^{2020}a_i)$  is  $0$ , therefore  $a_{i + 1} = f(g(5^{2020}a_i))$  is even.

We now proceed by induction. Let  $b_k$  denote the period of  $(a_i)$  modulo  $2^k$  for  $0 \le k < 2020$  and for sufficiently large  $i$ . Assume  $b_k$  exists and  $b_k|2^{k - 1}$ . We wish to prove that  $b_{k + 1}$  exists and  $b_{k + 1}|2^k$ .

Since by the induction hypothesis,  $(a_i)$  is eventually cyclic mod  $2^k$  with period  $b_k|2^k$ . Then, when we take  $a_i$  modulo  $2^{k + 1}$  for sufficiently large  $i$ , since there are only two values in mod  $2^{k + 1}$  that are equivalent to  $x$  mod  $2^k$  for a given  $x$ , this means that two of  $a_i$ ,  $a_{i + b_k}$ ,  $a_{i + 2b_k}$  are congruent modulo  $2^{k + 1}$ . By **Lemma III**, this implies that  $(a_i)$  is eventually cyclic mod  $2^{k + 1}$  with period  $b_{k + 1}$  equal to either  $b_k$  or  $2b_k$ , hence  $b_{k + 1}|2^k$ , as desired. Therefore, by induction, this finishes the proof  $\blacksquare$ By **Lemma I** and **Lemma II**,  $\exists$   $n$  such that  $\forall$   $N > n$ ,  $a_N < 2^{2021}$ , and by **Lemma IV**, for  $n$  large enough,  $a_N \equiv a_{N + 2^{2019}}$  mod  $2^{2020}$   $\forall N > n$ . Then, two of  $a_N$ ,  $a_{N + 2^{2019}}$ ,  $a_{N + 2^{2020}}$  are congruent modulo  $2^{2021}$ . However, since  $a_N$ ,  $a_{N + 2^{2019}}$ ,  $a_{N + 2^{2020}} < 2^{2021}$ , this implies that two of  $a_N$ ,  $a_{N + 2^{2019}}$ ,  $a_{N + 2^{2020}}$  are equal. Thus,  $a_N = a_{N + 2^{2020}}$  for all sufficiently large  $N$ , as desired  $\blacksquare$</details>

We will prove the result when  $2020$  is replaced by any positive integer  $k.$  For a positive integer  $m$  expressed in base  $10,$  let  $f(m)$  denote the result of replacing each digit in  $m$  with its remainder when divided by  $2$  and then reading off the result in binary, and let  $g_{k}(m)=f(5^{k}m).$  Additionally, let the  $\emph{rank}$  of a positive integer  $m$  be the value of  $\nu_2(m).$ Write  $a_1=2^{k}q+r$  for positive integers  $q,r$  such that  $0\le r\le 2^{k}-1.$   $\textbf{Claim: }$  For all  $i,$  we have  $a_i=2^{k}f^{i-1}(q)+g_k^{i-1}(r).$   $\emph{Proof: }$  By definition, we have  $a_2=f(5^{k}a_1)=f(10^{k}q+5^{k}r).$  Since every nonzero digit of  $5^{k}r$  has value less than  $10^k$  and every nonzero digit of  $10^{k}q$  has value more than  $10^k,$  we may write  $f(10^{k}r+5^{k}r)=f(10^{k}q)+f(5^{k}r).$  Furthermore, since  $10^{k}q$  has  $k$  trailing zeroes, we have  $f(10^{k}q)=2^{k}f(q).$  Therefore,  $a_2=2^{k}f(q)+g_k(r),$  so we are done by induction.  $\blacksquare$   $\textbf{Claim: }$   $f^{i-1}(q)$  is constant for sufficiently large  $i.$   $\emph{Proof: }$  Consider a nonzero digit of a positive integer  $m$  with value  $c\times 10^d.$  By definition, this digit contributes at most  $2^d\le c\times 10^d$  to the value of  $f(m).$  Therefore,  $f(m)\le m$  for all  $m.$  Since  $f$  always outputs nonnegative integers, this implies the claim.  $\blacksquare$   $\textbf{Claim: }$   $g_k$  is a bijection on the set  $S_k=\{0,1,\dots,2^{k}-1\}.$   $\emph{Proof: }$  It suffices to show that for all  $j\in S_k,$  there exists  $i\in S_k$  such that  $g_k(i)=j.$  To prove this, we will induct on  $k,$  the base case being clear. Fix  $j\in S_k$  and express  $j$  in binary. Let  $d$  be the first digit of  $j,$  and let  $j'$  be the number resulting from removing  $d$  from  $j.$  By the inductive hypothesis, there exists  $i'\in S_{k-1}$  such that  $f(5^{k-1}i')=j'.$  Now choose one-digit  $a_k$  satisfying   $$ a_k\equiv d\pmod{2},\hspace{20pt}a_k\equiv -\frac{i'}{2^{k-1}}\pmod{5}. $$   Let  $i=\frac{1}{5}(i'+2^{k-1}a_k).$  Since  $i'<2^{k-1}$  and  $a_k<10,$  we know  $i<2^{k}.$  Moreover, \begin{align*}
f(5^{k}i)
&=f(5^{k-1}(i'+2^{k-1}a_k))
&=f(5^{k-1}i')+f(10^{k-1}a_k)
&=j'+2^{k-1}d=j.
\end{align*} (We can justify these manipulation in the same way as we did in the proof of the first claim)We have found  $i\in S_k$  such that  $g_k(i)=j,$  so we are done.  $\blacksquare$  Now construct a directed graph  $\mathcal{G}$  as follows.

    
- The vertices of  $\mathcal{G}$  are the elements of  $S_k.$
- For  $i,j\in S_k,$  there is an edge  $i\to j$  if and only if  $g_k(i)=j.$ [/list] Since  $g_k$  is a bijection on  $S_k,$  we know  $\mathcal{G}_k$  is the dijoint union of several cycles. $\textbf{Claim: }$  All cycles in  $\mathcal{G}_k$  contain  $2^t$  elements for some nonnegative integer  $t.$   $\emph{Proof: }$  First, notice that for all  $m\in S_k,$    $$ \nu_2(g_k(m))=\nu_{2}(f(5^{k}m))=\nu_{10}(5^{k}m))=\nu_2(m). $$   (Here,  $\nu_{10}(x)$  is defined as the largest integer  $e$  such that  $10^e\mid x.$ ) Therefore, the elements of each cycles of  $\mathcal{G}_k$  have the same rank, so we can consider each rank separately. By induction, we may assume the claim is true for  $\mathcal{G}_i$  for all  $i<k.$ \noindent\rule{17cm}{0.4pt}
[list]
- $\textbf{Rank }\mathbf{c}\textbf{, for some }\mathbf{c\ge 1}$  Write   $$ g_k(2^{c}m)=f(10^{c}5^{k-c}m)=2^{c}f(5^{k-c}m)=g_{k-c}(m). $$   Hence, the graph formed by the vertices of rank  $c$  in  $\mathcal{G}_k$  is isomorphic to the graph formed by the vertices of rank  $0$  in  $\mathcal{G}_{k-c}.$  We are done by the inductive hypothesis.
[/list]
\noindent\rule{17cm}{0.4pt}
[list]
- $\textbf{Rank }\mathbf{0}$  Consider some odd  $m\in S_k.$  Observe that   $$ g_k(m+2^{k-1})=f(5^{k}m+5\cdot 10^{k-1})\equiv f(5^{k}m)\equiv g_k(m)\pmod{2^{k-1}}. $$   Furthermore,   $$ g_k(m)=f(5^{k}m)=f(5^{k-1}(5m))=g_{k-1}(5m). $$   Therefore, the graph formed by the odd vertices of  $\mathcal{G}_k$  considered modulo  $16$  is isomorphic to the graph formed by the odd vertices in  $\mathcal{G}_{k-1}.$  For all  $m\in S_k,$  say the  $\emph{partner}$  of  $m$  is the other element of  $S_k$  which is congruent to  $m$  modulo  $16.$  For each cycle in  $\mathcal{G}_{k-1},$  there are two possibilities for the corresponding cycle in  $\mathcal{G}_{k}.$     [list]
- Go around the cycle once and return to the starting vertex.
- Go around the cycle once, and then go around the cycle again, choosing the  $\emph{partners}$  of the vertices we originally used.
    [/list] Therefore, each cycle of odd vertices in  $\mathcal{G}_{k}$  has either the same number or twice the number of vertices as the corresponding cycle in  $\mathcal{G}_{k-1}.$  By the inductive hypothesis, this implies that the number of vertices in each cycle is a power of  $2$ , as desired.

\noindent\rule{17cm}{0.4pt}
Having checked the claim for all possible ranks, we conclude.  $\blacksquare$  Now, combining claims 1, 2, and 4 implies the problem statement.

<details><summary>Short Solution</summary>Express  $a_s$  as  $$ b_1\cdot 2^{2020}+b_0 $$  Where  $b_0 < 2^{2020}$  Then notice that because   $$ 5^{2020}\cdot b_0 < 10^{2020}, b_1\cdot 2^{2020} \cdot 5^{2020} \ge 10^{2020} $$  The values of  $b_0,b_1$  will not affect each other in  $a_{s+1},a_{s+2},\cdots$ , as  $b_0$  is the sum of all binary digits with value less than  $2^{2020}$  and  $b_1 \cdot 2^{2020}$  is the sum of all binary digits with value greater than  $2^{2020}$ .  $
ewline$ But  $b_1$  will eventually become  $0$  or  $1$  and stay there for sufficiently large  $s$ . Due to the fact that it is being multiplied by  $2^{2020}$  in our expression for  $a_s$ , all we are doing to  $b_1$  when we go from  $a_s$  to  $a_{s+1}$  is turning its digits into  $0$ s or  $1$ s based on if they are even or odd, respectively, and then reading it mod  $2$ . Note that both of these operations will decrease the value of  $b_1$  unless we have  $b_1=0,1$ , and at this point  $b_1$  will stay constant.  $
ewline$ Thus, it is sufficient to prove that all  $a_s<2^{2020}$  satisfy the desired property.  $
ewline$ Now we do a digit-by digit induction. Let  $d_{i,j}$  be the  $i$ th digit from the right in the binary representation of  $a_j$ .  $
ewline$ We claim that the periods of these digits are all powers of two, and the period of  $d_{i,j}$  must be less than or equal to  $2^{i}$ . The base case,  $d_{1,j}$  is trivial and will always have a period of  $1$ .  $
ewline$ For the inductive step, we go from  $i=x \longrightarrow i=x+1$ .  $
ewline$ First, any carries from lower place values than  $x+1$  that might affect the value of  $d_{x+1,j}$  must be periodic  $2^x$ . This is because by our inductive assumption, the binary digits  $d_{0,j},d_{1,j},\cdots , d_{x,j}$  are all periodic with power of  $2$  of at most  $2^x$ , so any carries they bring over that affect  $d_{x+1,j}$  must be as well.  $
ewline$ Also, the digits  $d_{x+2,j},d_{x+3,j},\cdots$  cannot affect the value of  $d_{x+1,j}$  as we know that each represents a binary value  $2^k$  for some  $k \ge x+1$ , and their contribution to the value of  $a_{j+1}$  will be equal to   $$ 5^{2020} \cdot 2^k \cdot d_{k-1,j}=10^k\cdot q $$   for some integer  $q$ . As a result, whatever they contribute to  $a_{j+1}$  will have at least  $k \ge x+1$  zeroes trailing it, which goes past digit  $d_{x+1,j+1}$ .  $
ewline$ However, since the carries are periodic  $2^x$ , this means that the value of  $d_{x+1,j}$  either switches bit values after  $2^x$  iterations, or retains the same value. If it retains value then it will be periodic  $2^{x}<2^{x+1}$ , and we are done. Otherwise, once it has switched bit values, after another  $2^x$  iterations, it can either switch back, giving us a period of  $2^{x+1}$ , or stay the same, which is a period of  $2^{x}<2^{x+1}$  regardless. In every case the period is a power of  $2$  less than  $2^{x+1}$ , so we are done with the inductive step.  $
ewline$ Now as a result of our induction, each bitwise value of  $a_j$  is periodic at least  $2^{2020}$  for sufficiently large  $j$ , since we are dealing with numbers with less than  $2021$  digits implying  $a_j$  itself is also periodic in that way, so we conclude.  $\square$</details>

SolutionLet $2020 = k$ . The main idea is to show it cycles, and then lift cycles mod powers of $2$ . **Claim:** The sequence behaves in the following way with respect to size: - If $0 \leq a_i < 2^k$ , then $a_{i + 1}$ satisfies the same inequality. - If $2^k \leq a_i < 2^{k + 1}$ , then $a_{i + 1}$ satisfies the same inequality. - If $a_i \geq 2^{k + 1}$ , then $a_{i + 1} < a_i$ . *Proof*. In the first case, \[5^ka_i < 5^k\cdot 2^k = 10^k\] has at most $k$ digits in base $10$ , so the new number has at most $k$ digits in base $2$ and must be less than $2^k$ . In the second case, \[10^k \leq 5^ka_i< 2\cdot 10^k\] has exactly $k + 1$ digits in base $10$ , and the first digit is $1$ . So then $a_{i + 1}$ has exactly $k + 1$ digits in base $2$ , and must satisfy $2^k \leq a_i < 2^{k + 1}$ . In the third case, let $t \geq 1$ be the unique positive integer such that $2^{k + t} \leq a_i < 2^{k + t + 1}$ . Then \[5^ka_i < 10^k\cdot 2^{t + 1} \leq 4\cdot 10^{k + t - 1}\] has at most $k + t$ digits, so $a_{i + 1}$ has at most $k + t$ digits in binary and is strictly less than $2^{k + t}$ , and therefore strictly less than $a_i$ as well. $\blacksquare$ So eventually $a_i$ satisfies either $0 \leq a_i < 2^k$ or $2^k \leq a_i < 2^{k + 1}$ -- otherwise it decreases until this happens -- and then it remains in that interval forever. This deals with the size part and shows that the $a_i$ eventually cycle; now we use mods to deal with the cycle length. **Claim:** For each $\ell \leq k$ , $a_{i + 1}$ mod $2^\ell$ only depends on $a_i$ mod $2^\ell$ , and the function $a_i \to a_{i + 1}$ considered mod $2^\ell$ (which is well-defined by the previous statement) is a bijection. *Proof*. The first claim is because $a_{i + 1}$ mod $2^\ell$ depends only on $5^ka_i$ mod $10^\ell$ . But this is always $0$ mod $5^\ell$ , so its value mod $10^\ell$ only depends on $a_i$ mod $2^\ell$ . For the second, note that given $a_{i + 1}$ mod $2^\ell$ , we have the parities of the last $\ell$ digits of $5^ka_i$ (in base $10$ ). However, this is also a multiple of $5^\ell$ , so it's uniquely determined (we can build it from the right end, and we have exactly one choice at each step). So the function is reversible. $\blacksquare$ So then this function is a collection of cycles. **Claim:** Each cycle-length mod $2^\ell$ divides $2^\ell$ , for each $\ell$ . *Proof*. We induct on $\ell$ ; clearly for $\ell = 1$ this is true. Now suppose we lift from $2^{\ell - 1}$ to $2^\ell$ . Then each cycle-length either multiplies by $2$ or stays the same -- this is because if the cycle-length mod $2^{\ell - 1}$ was $c$ , then $a_{i + c}$ is either $a_i$ or $a_i + 2^{\ell - 1}$ , and the first case preserves $c$ and the second multiplies it by $2$ . $\blacksquare$ So then the cycle-length mod $2^k$ divides $2^k$ . But since the $a_i$ end up staying in an interval containing each residue mod $2^k$ exactly once, this means the actual cycle-length also divides $2^k$ .

<details><summary>Coordbash</summary>Denote  $A = (0, a), B = (-b, 0),$  and  $C = (c, 0)$  on the  $(x, y)$  coordinate plane. Now we will find the orthocenter and circumcenter  $H$  and  $O$  based on the aforementioned.
Recall the the former is the intersection of all three altitudes of  $ABC,$  so we only need to find the equations of two altitudes and equate them to find their intersection, the orthocenter. Using point slope formula, we can find that an altitude other than the one from  $A$  ( $x=0$ ) would be the one from  $B$  with equation  $y=\frac{c}{a}\left(x+b\right).$  Setting  $x=0$  in the aforementioned equation, we obtain that the intersection  $H$  occurs at  $(0, \frac{bc}{a})$ .

Recall that the latter is the intersection of all three perpendicular bisectors of  $ABC$ , so like the former, we only need to find the equations of two of the perpendicular bisectors and equate them to find their intersection, the circumcenter. A trivial perpendicular bisector is the one through  $BC$ , with the simple equation of  $x = \frac{c-b}{2}.$  A less trivial perpendicular bisector would be the one through  $AC$ , in which the equation is still easily obtained through using point slope formula on the points of triangle  $ABC$ :  $y=\frac{c}{a}x+\frac{\left(a^{2}-c^{2}\right)}{2a}.$  Setting  $x = \frac{c-b}{2}$  in the equation,  $\frac{c}{a}x + \frac{a^2-c^2}{2a}$ , we obtain that the intersection  $O$  occurs at   $$ (\frac{c-b}{2}, \frac{c}{a} \cdot \frac{c-b}{2} + \frac{a^2-c^2}{2a}) \implies \left(\frac{c-b}{2},\ \frac{a^{2}-bc}{2a}\right). $$  Now we'll find the coordinates for point  $T.$  Note that since  $AT$  is a tangent at  $A$ ,  $AO \perp AT,$  so we can first find the slope of line  $AO,$  which is   $$ \frac{\frac{a^{2}-bc}{2a} - a}{\frac{c-b}{2}} = \frac{-a^{2}-bc}{2a} \cdot \frac{2}{c-b} = \frac{a^2+bc}{ab-ac}. $$   Since  $AO \perp AT$ , the slope of  $AT$  is simply the opposite reciprocal of the aforementioned, or  $\frac{ac-ab}{a^2+bc},$  making the equation of  $AT$   $y=\frac{ac-ab}{a^{2}+bc}x+a.$  Since  $T$  in on line  $BC,$  we can find its coordinates by simply setting  $\frac{ac-ab}{a^{2}+bc}x+a = 0,$  in which we obtain  $T = \left(\frac{a^{3}+abc}{ab-ac},\ 0\right)$  upon doing so. Then, the midpoint of  $AT$ ,  $X$ , would simply be  $X = \left(\frac{a^{3}+abc}{2\left(ab-ac\right)},\frac{a}{2}\right).$  

If  $CH$  passes through  $X$  we need the slopes of  $CH$  and  $HX$  to be equal. The slope of  $HX$  can be found as   $$ \frac{\frac{a}{2} - \frac{bc}{a}}{\frac{a^{3}+abc}{2\left(ab-ac\right)}} = \frac{a^2-2bc}{2a} \cdot \frac{2(ab-ac)}{a^3+abc} = \frac{(a^2-2bc)(b-c)}{a^3+abc}. $$  The slope of  $CH$  can be found as simply  $\frac{-b}{a}.$  Thus, one of the extra conditions mentioned in the problem would be   $$ \frac{(a^2-2bc)(b-c)}{a^3+abc} = \frac{-b}{a}. $$  Now, given that condition, we need to prove that  $AO$  bisects  $CH.$  

Note that since we found the slope of  $AO$  earlier, it is easy to see that the equation for  $AO$  is simply  $y=a+\frac{\left(a^{2}+bc\right)}{ab-ac}x.$  Equating the equations of  $CH$  and  $AO,$  we obtain   $$ \frac{bc}{a}-\frac{b}{a}x = a+\frac{\left(a^{2}+bc\right)}{ab-ac}x \implies \frac{a^2+b^2}{ab-ac}x = \frac{bc}{a} - a \implies x = \frac{bc-a^2}{a} \cdot \frac{ab-ac}{a^2+b^2} = \frac{(bc-a^2)(b-c)}{a^2+b^2}, $$   the coordinate of the intersection between the two aforementioned lines. Since the midpoint of  $CH$  has  $x$ -coordinate  $\frac{c}{2},$  we now need to prove that   $$ \frac{(a^2-2bc)(b-c)}{a^3+abc} = \frac{-b}{a} \implies \frac{(bc-a^2)(b-c)}{a^2+b^2} = \frac{c}{2}. $$   Fortunately, the aforementioned is relatively trivial via simple rearrangement of variables:   $$ \frac{(a^2-2bc)(b-c)}{a^3+abc} = \frac{-b}{a} \implies -b(a^3+abc) = a(a^2-2bc)(b-c) $$      $$ \implies -a^3b - ab^2c = a^3b - a^3c - 2ab^2c + 2abc^2 \implies = -a^2b - b^2c =  a^2b - a^2c - 2b^2c + 2bc^2  $$     $$ \implies 2a^2b - a^2c- b^2c + 2bc^2 = 0. $$    $$ \frac{(bc-a^2)(b-c)}{a^2+b^2} = \frac{c}{2} \implies a^2c+b^2c = 2b^2c - 2bc^2 - 2a^2b + 2a^2c \implies b^2c - 2bc^2 - 2a^2b + a^2c = 0. $$   Since  $b^2c - 2bc^2 - 2a^2b + a^2c = 0$  and  $2a^2b - a^2c- b^2c + 2bc^2 = 0$  are equivalent (since one is just the opposite of another but both of them are set to  $0$ ), we are done.  $\boxed{}$</details>

Let  $D, E, F$  be the feet of the altitudes from  $A, B,$  and  $C$ , as shown and let  $AO$  intersect  $CH$  at  $Y$ . We use conventional notation, letting  $BC = a, AC = b, AB = c, \angle{BAC} = \angle{A}, \angle{ABC} = \angle{B},$  and  $\angle{ACB} = \angle{C}$ . $\textbf{Lemma 1:}$   $\triangle{ATC} \sim \triangle{BTA} \sim \triangle{HAY}$  $\textit{Proof:}$  First, we show  $\triangle{ATC} \sim \triangle{BTA}$ . Notice that  $\angle{TAB} = \angle{BCA} = \angle{TCA} = \angle{C}$  by inscribed angles and the fact that  $TA$  is tangent to the circumcircle of  $\triangle{ABC}$ . Also,  $\angle{ATB} = \angle{CTA}$ . Hence, by AA similarity, we know  $\triangle{ATC} \sim \triangle{BTA}$ . Also,  $\angle{HFB} + \angle{HDB} = 90^\circ + 90^\circ = 180^\circ$ , so  $BDHF$  is cyclic. Notice  $\angle{YHA} = \angle{FHD} = 180^\circ - \angle{FBD} = \angle{FBT} = \angle{ABT}$ . Also,  $\angle{HAY} =  90^\circ - \angle{BAD} - \angle{TAB} = 90^\circ - (90^\circ - \angle{B}) - \angle{C} = \angle{B} - \angle{C} = 180^\circ - (180^\circ - \angle{B}) - \angle{C} = 180^\circ - \angle{ABT} - \angle{TAB} = \angle{BTA}$ . Hence, by AA similarity, we have  $\triangle{BTA} \sim \triangle{HAY}$ , and therefore  $\triangle{ATC} \sim \triangle{BTA} \sim \triangle{HAY}$ . $\textbf{Lemma 2:}$   $\triangle{AYC} \sim \triangle{AHB}$  $\textit{Proof:}$  First,  $\angle{ACY} = \angle{ACF} = 90^\circ - \angle{A}$  and  $\angle{CYA} = 180^\circ - \angle{AYH} = 180^\circ - \angle{C}$ . Thus,  $\angle{CAY} = 180^\circ - \angle{ACY} - \angle{CYA} = 180^\circ - (90^\circ - \angle{A}) - (180^\circ - \angle{C}) = \angle{A} + \angle{C} - 90^\circ = (180^\circ - \angle{B}) - 90^\circ = 90^\circ - \angle{B}$ . But  $\angle{BAD} = 90^\circ - \angle{B} = \angle{BAH}$  so  $\angle{CAY} = \angle{BAH}$ . Also,  $\angle{ABH} = \angle{ABE} = 90^\circ - \angle{A} = \angle{ACY}$ . Hence, by AA similarity,  $\triangle{AYC} \sim \triangle{AHB}$ .

Now, we compute some lengths. First, we find  $AT$  and  $TB$ . We know from earlier  $\angle{XAB} = \angle{TAB} = \angle{C}$ . Then  $AX\cos{\angle{C}} = AF = AC\cos{\angle{A}} = b\cos{\angle{A}}$ . Hence,  $AX = \dfrac{b\cos{\angle{A}}}{\cos{\angle{C}}}$  and because  $AT = 2AX$ , we know  $AT = \dfrac{2b\cos{\angle{A}}}{\cos{\angle{C}}}$ . Also,  $\dfrac{TB}{AT} = \dfrac{AB}{AC} = \dfrac{c}{b}$ , by similar triangles, so  $TB = \dfrac{2b\cos{\angle{A}}}{\cos{\angle{C}}} \cdot \dfrac{c}{b} = \dfrac{2c\cos{\angle{A}}}{\cos{\angle{C}}}$ . 

Now, we find  $AH$ . Notice that  $AH\cos{\angle{HAB}} = AH\cos(90^\circ - \angle{B}) = AH\sin{\angle{B}} = AF = AC\cos{\angle{A}}$  so  $AH = \dfrac{b\cos{\angle{A}}}{\sin{\angle{B}}}$ . 

We proceed to find  $HY$ . Notice that  $\dfrac{HY}{AB} = \dfrac{AH}{TB}$ , by similar triangles, so  $HY = \dfrac{AH \cdot AB}{TB}$ . But we know  $AH = \dfrac{b\cos{\angle{A}}}{\sin{\angle{B}}}$ ,  $AB = c$ , and  $TB = \dfrac{2c\cos{\angle{A}}}{\cos{\angle{C}}}$ . So  $HY = \dfrac{b\cos{\angle{C}}}{2\sin{\angle{B}}}$ . 

But notice  $CD = b\cos{\angle{C}}$  and since  $\angle{CHD} = 90^\circ - \angle{HCD} = 90^\circ - (90^\circ - \angle{B}) = \angle{B}$  we know  $CH = \dfrac{CD}{\sin{\angle{B}}} = \dfrac{b\cos{\angle{C}}}{\sin{\angle{B}}}$ . Thus,  $CH = 2 \cdot HY$ , so  $Y$  is the midpoint of  $CH$ , as desired.  $\blacksquare$ Note: In this solution I divided by  $\cos{C}$  a few times. This is invalid when  $C = 90^\circ$ , but notice that if  $C = 90^\circ$  then  $AB$  is the hypotenuse of right triangle  $ABC$  which means  $AB > AC$  which is not allowed by the problem statement. I also divided by  $\sin{B}$  which is invalid if  $B = 0^\circ$  but notice that this would make the triangle degenerate, which is also not allowed.
