The answer is  $\boxed{2^{2n-2}}$ .

Call all cells in  $T$  colored, and all cells not in  $T$  uncolored. 

Lemma 1: Each one of the  $n$  horizontal rectangles is on a distinct row, and similarly the vertical rectangles are each on a distinct column.

Proof: FTSOC assume that there exist two horizontal rectangles that are contained within the same row. Then we can easily see that some row stays uncolored (because each horizontal rectangle can only be in one row), a contradiction because there exists a fully colored column.

Lemma 2: Given two colored cells on the same row, all cells on that row and between those two cells must be colored.

Proof: If otherwise, there would exist two rectangles on the same row, a contradiction by Lemma 1. The same logic applies for columns.

Now consider labeling each one of the  $n$  rows with a distinct number from  $1$  to  $n$  that corresponds to the number of colored cells in their row. Let these numbers be  $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$  from top to bottom. Define  $b_1,b_2,\dots,b_n$  similarly for the columns, from left to right.

Lemma 3: Suppose row  $a_k$  is the fully colored row for some  $1\leq k\leq n$ . Then  $a_1<a_2<\dots<a_k>a_{k+1}>\dots>a_n$ .

Proof: Consider some row  $a_i$  such that  $i<k$ . From Lemma 2, we know that for any colored cell in row  $a_i$ , the cells in the same column as this cell but in rows  $a_{i+1},a_{i+2},\dots,a_{k-1}$  must also be colored. It follows that  $a_i\leq a_{i+1},a_{i+2},\dots,a_{k-1}\leq a_k$ , and since all  $a_1,\dots,a_k$  are distinct we have  $a_i<a_{i+1},a_{i+2},\dots,a_{k-1}<a_k$ . Similarly for  $i>k$  we have  $a_i<a_{i-1},a_{i-2},\dots,a_{k+1}<a_k$ . This proves the lemma. Note that this also applies to  $b_1,b_2,\dots,b_n$ .

Now there are  $2^{n-1}$  ways to pick  $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$  satisfying Lemma 3 (if the fully colored row is  $a_k$ , there are  $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$  ways to order the rest, and we sum over  $1\leq k\leq n$ ) and similarly for  $b_1,b_2,\dots,b_n$ .

The final claim is this:

Claim: For any two sequences  $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$  and  $b_1,b_2,\dots,b_n$  satisfying Lemma 3, there is exactly one double staircase corresponding to these two sequences. 

Proof: We first place down the  $1\times n$  rectangle in its corresponding row. Then one of  $b_1$  and  $b_n$  is equal to  $1$ . WLOG suppose it is  $b_1$ . Then any new rectangles cannot intersect column  $b_1$  because it already has a colored cell. This means that there is only one choice for the  $1\times n-1$  rectangle: it must intersect columns  $b_2,b_3,\dots,b_n$ .

Now note that one of  $b_2$  and  $b_n$  is equal to  $2$ ; WLOG suppose it is  $b_2$ . Then any new rectangles cannot intersect column  $b_2$  because it already has two colored cells. Now apply the same logic to see that there is only one choice for the  $1\times n-2$  rectangle: it must intersect  $b_3,b_4,\dots,b_n$ .

Now apply this logic over and over to see that there is always exactly one position for the next rectangle. The number of ways to make a double staircase corresponding to the two sequences is just  $1^n=1$ , so the claim is proven.

Now there are  $2^{n-1}\cdot 2^{n-1}=2^{2n-2}$  ways to pick the two sequences, and we are done.  $\blacksquare$

solution_md:
Call a function  $g$  on the reals a staircase if:


- It is non-decreasing,
- item Every real number is in the domain of  $g$ ,
- item The range of  $g$  is an infinite arithmetic sequence with common difference 1, and
- item For every number  $k$  in the range of  $g$ , the values  $x$  for which  $g(x)=k$  are of the form  $[m,n)$ . Call each of these intervals a stair. Let the length of each stair be  $n-m$ , and let  $k$  be the "height" of the stair (the height can be negative).


Call a staircase  $g$  positive if it satisfies  $x<0$  where  $x$  is the smallest value that satisfies  $\lceil g(x)\rceil = 0$  (we can also show that if there exists some  $x<0$  such that  $g(x)\geq 0$ , then  $g$  is a positive staircase, which follows from all staircases being non-decreasing).

Call a staircase  $g$  normal if the length of each stair is constant. Call  $g$  very normal if in addition to being normal, the height of each stair of  $g$  is an integer.

Now, let  $g(x)=\left\lfloor \frac{\left\lfloor \tfrac{x+a}{b}\right\rfloor + c}{d} \right\rfloor$ , and let  $h(x)=\left\lfloor \frac{x+e}{f} \right\rfloor$ . 

Note that  $g$  is a staircase. We can easily check that the first three conditions for a function being a staircase are satisfied, while for the fourth, the values  $x$  satisfying  $g(x)=k$  for some integer  $k$  are the values satisfying   $$ kd-c\leq\left \lfloor \frac{x+a}{b} \right \rfloor<(k+1)d-c, $$   
or   $$ \lceil kd-c \rceil \leq \frac{x+a}{b} < \lceil (k+1)d-c \rceil, $$  from which it becomes clear that these values make up an interval of the form  $[m,n)$ . A similar check shows that  $h$  is also a staircase.

Then  $h$  is always a very normal positive staircase; furthermore, any very normal positive staircase can be expressed as a pair  $(e,f)$  as described by  $h$ . This is because  $f$  is the length of each stair, while  $e$  is the additive inverse of the smallest value  $x$  that satisfies  $h(x)=0$ . 

So, we need to show that  $g$  is a very normal positive staircase if and only if  $d$  is an integer. Plugging in  $x=-a<0$  gives a value greater than or equal to 0, so we see that  $g$  is a positive staircase. Also, the range of  $g$  is all integers. So, it suffices to show that  $g$  is normal (or that the length of each stair of  $g$  is constant) iff  $d$  is an integer.

First consider   $$ j(x)=\left\lfloor \frac{x+a}{b} \right\rfloor+c. $$  It's easy to see that  $j$  is a normal positive staircase. The heights of the stairs are equal to  $c+i$  for integral  $i$ . Now we can let   $$ g(x)=\left\lfloor \frac{j(x)}{d} \right\rfloor. $$  Let the stair satisfying  $g(x)=k$  be stair  $k$ , where  $k$  is an integer. Now for any stair  $k$ , we can see that the length of the stair is directly proportional to the number of integers  $i$  such that   $$ kd\leq c+i<(k+1)d. $$   

This is due to the range of  $j$  being only the numbers  $c+i$  for integral  $i$ , and because  $j$  is normal. The constant of proportionality is just the length of each stair of  $j$ , or  $b$ . So it suffices to show that there is always a constant amount of integers  $i$  satisfying the inequality for all integral   $k$  iff  $d$  is an integer.

If  $d$  is an integer, there will always be a constant amount of integers  $i$  satisfying this inequality for any  $k$ . This is because the solutions for any  $k$  are   $$ \lceil kd-c \rceil, \lceil kd-c \rceil + 1, \dots, \lceil kd-c\rceil + d - 1, $$   where the largest solution is equal to  $\lceil (k+1)d-c \rceil -1$ .

Finally, we must show that if there is a constant number of integers satisfying the inequality for all  $k$ , then  $d$  is an integer.

Note that across all  $k$ , the average number of integers  $i$  satisfying the inequality is  $\frac{(k+1)d-kd}{1}=d$ . But also the average number of integers  $i$  satisfying the inequality across all  $k$  is an integer itself, because we assumed that there is a constant number of integers  $i$  satisfying it over all  $k$ . Thus,  $d$  is an integer.

So, we are done.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Grogg and Winnie are playing a game using a deck of  $50$  cards numbered  $1$  through  $50$ . They take turns with Grogg going first. On each turn a player chooses a card from the deck—this choice is made deliberately, not at random—and then adds it to one of two piles (both piles are empty at the start of the game). After all  $50$  cards are in the two piles, the values of the cards in each pile are summed, and Winnie wins the positive difference of the sums of the two piles, in dollars. (For instance, if the first pile has cards summing to  $510$  and the second pile has cards summing to  $765$ , then Winnie wins  $ \$ 255$.) Winnie wants to win as much as possible, and Grogg wants Winnie to win as little as possible. If they both play with perfect strategy, find (with proof) the amount that Winnie wins.
solution_md:
The answer is  $75.$  The proof will be split into two parts: first proving Grogg can force  $|a_{50}-b_{50}| \leq 75$  no matter how Winnie plays, and then proving Winnie can achieve  $|a_{50}-b_{50}| \geq 75$  no matter how Winnie plays. Note this completes the proof, as then when both people play with best moves, the scenario will play out to the ultimate result of  $75.$  We first prove that Grogg can force an upper bound of  $75.$ To do this, we show that if Grogg plays in a certain way, he can always force Winnie to obtain  $|a_{50}-b_{50}| \leq 75,$  no matter what she plays. Grogg can force Winnie to obtain  $|a_{50}-b_{50}| \leq 75$  if he performs the following:


- Grogg always plays the largest valued card remaining in the lesser valued pile. 
[/list]
Since there are  $50$  cards in total, we may pair up the cards into pairs of  $2,$  which gives  $25$  pairs. Call these pairs  $k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_{25},$  where the subscript denotes which pair it is in the sequence of moves. For example,  $k_1$  is the first pair of values performed in the procedure, and so on. Denote by  $p_n$  the value of  $\text{pile}~1 - \text{pile}~2$  immediately after  $k_n$  has been performed. We now take a look at an arbitrary pair  $i+1.$  Assume that on the the previous  $i$ th pair, that  $p_{i} \geq 0.$  Since  $i$  pairs have already been executed, and Grogg always plays the largest valued card remaining, then on the  $i$ th pair, the card that could possibly be of the greatest remaining value is  $50-i.$ Clearly, Grogg plays the first move of every pair, as he is the first player in the sequence of moves. Thus after the first card has been played in the  $i$ th pair, the  $\text{pile}~1-\text{pile}~2$  is now  $p_i-(50-i).$  We now ``bound" depending on Winnie's move. On her move in the  $i$ th pair, she can play a card with minimum value of  $1$  and maximum value of  $(50-i)-1.$  Then, after Winnie's move, we can force  $p_{i+1}$  to be of a minimum of  $p_i-2(50-i)+1$  and a maximum of  $p_i-1.$  The lower bound reduces to  $p_i-2(50-i)+1=p_{i-1}+2i-99=2i-99,$  where the last comes from taking the smallest possible value  $p_{i}$  could have been. Thus  $p_{i+1}$  takes on values ranging from a lower bound of  $2i-99$  to an upper bound of  $p_{i}-1.$ Now we take care of the case when  $p_{i} < 0,$  where once again we consider  $i+1$  to be an arbitrary pair. The greatest remaining value is still  $50-i.$  In this case, since pile  $2$  has greater value than pile  $1,$  after Grogg's move in the pair, the difference of the two piles is now  $p_i+(50-i).$  We once again bound depending on Winnie's move, in the pair, which range from a minimum of  $1$  to a maximum of  $(50-i)-1.$  Since  $p_{i}<0,$  we have a minimal bound of  $p_{i}+1,$  and a maximum of  $p_i+(50-i)+((50-i)-1)=p_i+2(50-i)-1=2(50-i)-1=99-2i.$  Using similar logic as above, we substituted  $p_i=0$  for upper bound. Thus  $p_{i+1}$  takes on values ranging from a lower bound of  $p_i+1$  to an upper bound of  $99-2i.$ It suffices to show  $p_{25}$  takes on values ranging from a lower bound of  $-75$  to an upper bound of  $75.$  To do so, we proceed with induction. We prove that  $i-100 \leq p_i \leq 100-i$  for all pairs. First, for the base case it is easy to see  $-99 \leq p_1 \leq 99.$  For the inductive step, assume that on the  $k$ th pile, we have  $k-100 \leq p_k \leq 100-k.$  Then it suffices to prove that on the  $k+1$ th pile, that  $k-99 \leq p_{k+1} \leq 99-k.$  To show this, we consider two cases: when  $p_k \geq 0$  and  $p_k <0.$  For the former, we have  $2k-99 \leq p_{k+1} \leq p_k-1.$  Since  $p_k \leq 100-k,$  we may reduce our bounds to  $2k-99 \leq p_{k+1} \leq 99-k.$  For the latter, we have  $p_k+1 \leq p_{k+1} \leq 99-2k,$  and since  $k-100 \leq p_k,$  we may reduce our bounds to  $k-99 \leq p_{k+1} \leq 99-2k.$  Note  $k-99 \leq 2k-99$  holds for all  $k \geq 0,$  and  $99-2k \leq 99-k$  holds for all  $k \geq 0$  as well, so thus we have  $k-99 \leq p_{k+1} \leq 99-k,$  completing the induction. Since there are  $25$  pairs in total, we will have  $-75 \leq p_{25} \leq 75,$  so the result follows. Thus, no matter what Winnie plays, Grogg can always force an upper bound of  $75,$  that is,  $|a_{50}-b_{50}| \leq 75.$ Now we prove that no matter how Grogg plays, Winnie can perform an algorithm to force  $|a_{50}-b_{50}| \geq 75.$  Winnie performs the below algorithms, which depend on Grogg's moves. Denote the algorithms as  $(1), (2),$  and  $(3).$ [list]
- If Grogg picks a card  $n \leq 49$  with odd value, Winnie next picks the  $n+1$  valued card.
- If Grogg picks a card  $n \leq 48$  with even value, Winnie next picks the  $n-1$  valued card.
- If Grogg picks  $49$  or  $50,$  Winnie on her next move picks  $50$  or  $49,$  respectively.

Pair up card values in the form  $(1,2), (3,4), \ldots, (49,50),$  where every  $(a, a+1)$  is a pair, with card values  $a$  and  $a+1.$  For any card with value  $k \leq 48$  that Grogg picks as a move, Winnie on her next move can pick the other card in its corresponding pair, and place it in the opposite pile that Grogg previously placed  $k$  in. Thus, every pair from  $(1,2), \ldots, (47,48)$  creates either an increment or decrement of the difference of the piles by  $1.$  Since there are  $24$  pairs of cards in  $(1,2), \ldots, (47,48),$  any linear combination of these  $24$  increments or decrements by  $1$  will create a positive total difference of the sum of the values of the two piles ranging from  $0$  to  $24.$ If Winnie follows this procedure, Grogg will eventually pick either  $49$  or  $50.$  Following the algorithm described above, on Winnie's next move she picks the other value in the pair, and add it to the same pile as the one Grogg put the  $49$  or  $50$  valued card in. Ignoring the other pairs of increments or decrements, Winnie putting the other value in the pair  $(49,50)$  and adding it to the same pile Grogg put either  $49$  or  $50$  in will create a total pile difference of  $99.$  Aforementioned, linear combinations of the other  $24$  pairs range increments by  $0$  to increments by  $24.$  It follows that no matter what Grogg plays, if Winnie follows the above procedure, she can guarantee  $|a_{50}-b_{50}| \geq 99-24 = 75.$ Therefore, no matter what Winnie plays, Grogg can force  $|a_{50}-b_{50}| \leq 75,$  and no matter what Grogg plays, Winnie can force  $|a_{50}-b_{50}| \geq 75,$  so when both parties play optimally, equality is achieved, and the answer is  $\boxed{75}.$ **Remarks:** There were so many traps for this problem. Many people got  $27.$

stem_md: Given a sphere, a great circle of the sphere is a circle on the sphere whose diameter is also a diameter of the sphere. For a given positive integer  $n,$  the surface of a sphere is divided into several regions by  $n$  great circles, and each region is colored black or white. We say that a coloring is good if any two adjacent regions (that share an arc as boundary, not just a finite number of points) have different colors. Find, with proof, all positive integers  $n$  such that in every good coloring with  $n$  great circles, the sum of the areas of the black regions is equal to the sum of the areas of the white regions.

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>We claim the answer is  $\boxed{n \text{ odd}}$ .**Claim:** For every region  $\mathcal{R}$  on the surface of the sphere, there is another region on the sphere that can be mapped to  $\mathcal{A}$  by a homothety  $\mathcal H$  of ratio  $-1$  through the center of the sphere.


*Proof:* Consider edge  $e$  of a region formed by two great circles. In particular, this edge has length half the circumference of the great circle. Clearly, a homothety of  $-1$  through the center of the sphere maps it onto another identical edge. Similarly, all intersection between great circles can be mapped through the same homothety to another intersection. Thus, for every region  $\mathcal R$ , we can map all the edges and and vertices via  $\mathcal H$  to another identical region.

Now consider a region  $F$  and let the identical region opposite of it on the sphere be  $F'$ , as characterized above. **Claim:** Any path of minimum length, where we go from adjacent face to adjacent face, from  $F$  to  $F'$  must have length  $n+1$  (including  $F$  and  $F'$  themselves). 

*Proof:* We will show that for every great circle  $C$ , the region  $F'$  is on the other side of  $C$  than  $F$  is. Assume for the sake of contradiction that there exists a great circle  $C$  so that  $F'$  and  $F$  are on the same side. Then a homothety of  $-1$  centered at the center of the sphere takes  $F$  to the the other side from itself, but  $F'$  is not on that side, contradiction. 

    We also prove that any path from  $F$  which crosses each great circle exactly once must land at  $F'$ . Assume it lands at region  $X \neq F'$ . Then there must at least exist one great circle on which  $X$  and  $F'$  are on opposite sides of. But that implies that  $X$  is on the same side of said great circle as  $F$ , impossible. 

    Thus from  $F$ , it can cross over one if the great circles that bound  $F$  into another region  $R_1$ , and from  $R_1$ , it can cross over any great circle not yet crossed into  $R_2$ , and so on until it reaches  $F'$ . Since it crosses  $n$  great circles, that path consists of  $n+1$  regions.

Now for odd  $n$  consider the aforementioned minimal length path. Then, it must alternate between black and white faces, so  $F$  and  $F'$  will be different colors. Thus, the sum of the black and white areas will the the same. 

For even  $n$ , consider the following construction. Call the  $n$  great circles  $c_1, c_2,\dots,c_n$ . Assume they all share exactly one diameter. Assume that the smaller angle between  $c_1$  and  $c_2$  is  $\theta$ , and that in general for  $i>2$  that the angle between  $c_i$  and  $c_{i-1}$  is  $\theta$  and the angle between  $c_1$  and  $c_i$  is  $(i-1)\theta$ . Also,  $\theta < \tfrac{90^{\circ}}{n}$ . Below is what a cross section of the sphere looks like, for  $n=4$ .
[center]
[asy]
    unitsize(1.5cm);
    draw(circle((0,0), 1), blue);
    draw((-0.9,0.43)--(0.9,-0.43));
    draw((-1,0)--(1,0));
    draw((-0.98,0.19)--(0.98,-0.19));
    draw((-0.8,0.6)--(0.8,-0.6));
[/asy]
[/center]
Note that the two largest regions will be the same color, and because of our restrictions on  $\theta$  we must have that those two regions cover more than half of the surface area. Thus, the sum of the black and white areas cannot be the same.</details>

I claim that if in every good coloring the sum of the areas of the black regions is equal to the sum of the areas of the white regions, than  $n$  must be odd. The diagram below is provided for visualization purposes of the described algorithm (the red great circle is of no use).

[too lazy to insert diagram]

Position an arbitrary great circle to represent the horizontal axis. We first show that for every region on the above hemisphere an arbitrary great circle, there exists a corresponding region on the below hemisphere of this great circle which is the reflection of the region above, about the center of the sphere,  $O.$  Indeed, for every intersection above this great circle, there is a corresponding intersection below this great circle, the reflection over  $O,$  the center of the sphere. This is because when great circles intersect at a point, they intersect also at the antipode of that point. Similarly, every intersection a great circle has with the horizontal axis, there is a corresponding intersection, that is the antipode of the point about  $O.$  Therefore, because every point above the horizontal axis corresponds to an antipodal point under the base circle, every region will have a reflected version of that region which lies under the base circle. It readily follows since every region on the above hemisphere has a corresponding reflected region in the below hemisphere, the above and below hemispheres are reflections of each other about  $O.$  Since the above logic applies for any great circle we orient to be the horizontal axis, it follows that for every region, we may pick any great circle, and there is a reflected version of that region on the other hemisphere.

We now prove all odd  $n$  work through a parity argument. Let  $r$  and  $r'$  be two regions that are reflections of each other. Define a pathway to be a connection of  $r$  to  $r'$  that is drawn on the surface of the sphere such that this pathway projects to a straight line in a two dimensional plane, and does not intersect the intersection of two great circles. As for every region  $r$  its reflected region  $r'$  is a reflected version of that region on the opposite hemisphere, it follows that drawing a pathway between  $r$  and  $r'$  will intersect every great circle once. Note that every time the pathway from  $r$  to  $r'$  intersects with a great circle, the color of the region in the pathway changes, since two adjacent regions have different colors. Since there are an odd number of great circles, there will be an odd number of intersections, so no matter what color  $r$  is to begin with, due to parity  $r'$  will always be of the opposite color. Thus for any odd  $n,$  every region and its reflected region will be of different colors, and obviously reflected regions are of same surface area, so the total surface areas of black and white are equal.

It is easy to see that all even  $n$  fail from the above. Once again consider an arbitrary region  $r$  and its reflected region  $r'.$  Once again, the pathway from  $r$  to  $r'$  will intersect every great circle once. However, since this time  $n$  is even, no matter what color  $r$  is, following parity again,  $r'$  will be of the same parity. However, since the above and below hemispheres are reflections of each other about  $O,$  if two reflected regions are of same color, then it follows the surface areas of black and white are unequal, and thus all even  $n$  fail. After exhausting all cases, the answer is all odd  $n.$

The answer is all odd  $n \geq 1$ .
	First, we note that obviously  $n=1$  works, since it divides the sphere's 
	surface into 2 regions of equal area, which must have 2 different colors. 
	Now, we will prove that if  $k$  works, then  $k+1$  doesn't work, and if 
	 $k$  doesn't work, then  $k+1$  does work. (This clearly proves the 
	problem). 
	
	
	Obviously, we will place  $\geq 1$  great circles down. 
	
	
	Claim: Every region has an inverse-- that is, a region that has the 
	same area as it. 
	
	
	Proof: Note that all of the great
	circles after this one that are placed down are the same as themselves
	reflected across the center of the sphere. Because of this, the part of the 
	sphere that is above the selected great circle will be the same as 
	the part on the bottom, and because of this, each region will have an 
	inverse. 
	
	
	We will formally define the \textit{inverse} of a region  $T$  to be 
	the region resulting when  $T$  is reflected across the center of the sphere.
	
	We will also define a pair of inverses as the unordered pair  $(A, A^{-1})$  for some region  $A$ .
	
	
	For example, if I say "A pair of inverses are different colors", 
	I mean that the color of  $A$  is different than  $A^{-1}$ .
	Likewise, if I say "A pair of inverses are the same color", I mean
	that the color of  $A$  is the same as the color of  $A^{-1}$ .
	
	Now, with this claim, we note that the problem can only be satisfied if, 
	for all regions on the top of this equator: if their color is white, 
	then their inverse is black- else, if their color is black, then
	their inverse is white. 
	
	
	To show that this only occurs for odd  $n$ : we will prove that if  $k$  works, then  $k+1$  doesn't work, and if 
	 $k$  doesn't work, then  $k+1$  does work. (This clearly proves the 
	problem). 
	
	
		Now, define a \textit{path} from a region  $A$  to its inverse  $A^{-1}$ 	be a sequence of regions connected by arcs such that the first member
	of the path is  $A$  and the last region is  $A^{-1}$ . (This path
	may not have any region twice!!!).
	Clearly, we have that if the number of regions in a path  $P$  
	from  $X$  to  $X^{-1}$  is 
	even, then these vertices are of opposite color-- else, they are of
	the same color. (follows by very obvious induction from the fact that this holds when the length
	of the path is  $3$  or  $4$ ).
	(call this result REZ).

	Define the \textit{distance}  $D(P)_{A}$  from a region  $A$  to its inverse  $A^{-1}$ 	be the number of regions in the path  $P$ .
	
	
	Now, for any 2 inverse regions  $R$  and  $R^{-1}$ , we note that a great circle that we place
	down will either be the same as another line (which we 
	clearly don't need to consider), not intersecting either this region or
	its inverse, or intersecting both it and its inverse.
	
	
	(To prove that any great circle intersecting a region will also 
	intersect its inverse, we just need to make the realization that 
	in any region, its inverse will be its reflection across the 
	center of the circle (follows from great 
	circle properties) and that the great circle drawn is the same as its reflection 
	across the center of the circle, which thus means that for any point
	on the great circle, its reflection across the center of the circle
	is also on the great circle, from which the result follows).
	
	
	
	From here, we will split the problem into 2 cases-- if the great circle 
	mentioned before intersects both the region  $R$  and its inverse, 
	or if it intersects neither.
	
	
	Case 1: It intersects both the region  $R$  and its inverse. 
	
	
	In this case, we have that each of  $R$  and  $R^{-1}$  would be split into 
	two and there would be a great circle intersecting all members 
	of some path  $P$  from  $R$  to  $R^{-1}$ . Note that the regions resulting
	when  $R$  and  $R^{-1}$  are split will create 2 pairs of inverses
	 $(T, T^{-1})$ , and  $(Q, Q^{-1})$ , and we will also have that 
	\[
	D(P)_{R} + 1 = D(P')_{T} = D(P'')_{Q}
	\]
	where  $P'$  is the path resulting from replacing  $R$  with  $T$ , 
	and  $R^{-1}$  with  $Q^{-1}$  and  $T^{-1}$ , and  $P''$  is the path 
	resulting from replacing  $R$  with  $Q$  and  $T$ , and  $R^{-1}$  
	with  $Q^{-1}$ .
	
	
	(Note: below is the beginning of the theorem SPOCK, referenced in the future)
	Thus, by REZ, we know that if the great circle intersects  $R$ , then
	if  $R$  and  $R^{-1}$  were different colors, then  $Q$  and  $Q^{-1}$  would
	be the same color, as would  $T$  and  $T^{-1}$ -- else, 
	 $T$  and  $T^{-1}$  would be different colors, as would  $Q$  and  $Q^{-1}$ .
	(end of SPOCK).
	
	Case 2: It intersects neither the region  $R$  or its inverse. 
	Then, it must have intersected some other region  $K$  and its inverse
	 $K^{-1}$ , which would have done the process mentioned in Case 1. 
	
	
	Now, before finishing the problem, a lemma:
	
	
	Lemma 1. If there exists a pair of inverses that are different colors, 
	then all pairs of inverses are different colors. Else, if there exists a
	pair of inverses that are the same colors, then all pairs of inverses
	are the same color.
	
	
	\textit{Proof}: Consider a pair of regions  $A$  and  $B$ , such that  $A$  
	is connected to  $B$  by an arc. We would have that (since  $A^{-1}$  is connected to
	 $B^{-1}$  by an arc due to properties of reflection)  $A^{-1}$  is a 
	different color than  $B^{-1}$ , and  $A$  is a different color than  $B$ .
	Repeat this process until all vertices are covered, which would mean that if 
	 $A$  and  $A^{-1}$  were the same color, then all regions would be the same 
	color as their inverse- else, all regions would be a difference color 
	than their inverse.
	
	To finish the problem: 
	
	If all of the pairs of inverses are the same color for  $n=k$ , then 
	Case 1, Case 2, Lemma 1, and SPOCK, it should be clear that all of the pairs of inverses are different colors for 
	 $n=k+1$ . 
	
	
	Else, if all of the pairs of inverses are different colors for  $n=k$ , then by
	a similar explanation as when all of the pairs of inverses are different colors for  $n=k$ , 
	we can find that all of the pairs of inverses will then be the same colors for  $n=k+1$ .
	
	Now, we note that since  $n=1$  works (as I proved at the beginning
	of my writeup for this problem) then, by induction, all odd numbers work, and only
	all odd numbers- finishing the problem.

stem_md:
Prove that there is a unique  $1000$ -digit number  $N$  in base  $2022$  with the following properties:
[list=1]
[*] All of the digits of  $N$  (in base  $2022$ ) are  $1$ ’s or  $2$ ’s, and [/*]
[*]  $N$  is a multiple of the base- $10$  number  $2^{1000}$ . [/*]
[/list]
(Note that you must prove both that such a number exists and that there is not more than one such number. You do not have to write down the number! In fact, please don’t!)
solution_md:
$\textbf{\color{red}Lemma 1:}$  For all positive integers  $n$ , there exists a  $n$ -digit number  $a_n$  in base  $2022$  with the following properties: $1$ . All of the digits of  $a_n$  (in base  $2022$ ) are  $1$ 's or  $2$ 's, and $2$ .  $a_n$  is a multiple of the base- $10$  number  $2^n$ . $\textbf{\color{red}Proof:}$  We proceed by induction. For the base case  $n = 1$ , the only  $1$ -digit numbers in base  $2022$  containing only the digits  $1$  or  $2$  are  $1$  and  $2$ . Out of these, only  $2$  is divisible by  $2^1$ .

Now suppose the claim is true for  $n=1, 2, 3, ..., k$ .  $2022^k+a_k$  and  $2 \cdot 2022^k+a_k$  are both  $(k+1)$ -digit numbers in base  $2022$  where all of the digits are  $1$ 's or  $2$ 's. By hypothesis,  $2^k | a_k$ , so we can write that  $a_k=2^k \cdot p$  for some integer  $p$ . We can thus factorize  $2022^k+a_k$  and  $2 \cdot 2022^k+a_k$  as  $2^k(1011^k+p)$  and  $2^k(2 \cdot 1011^k+p)$ . Now we have two cases: $\textbf{Case 1:}$   $p$  is odd.
If  $p$  is odd, then  $2 | 1011^k+p$  but  $2 \nmid 2 \cdot 1011^k+p$ , so we can write that  $1011^k+p=2 \cdot q$  for some integer  $q$ . Therefore   $$ 2^k(1011^k+p)=2^{k+1} \cdot q $$   so we can let  $a_{k+1}=2022^k+a_k$ . $\textbf{Case 2:}$   $p$  is even.
If  $p$  is even, then  $2 | 2 \cdot 1011^k+p$  but  $2 \nmid 1011^k+p$ , so we can write that  $2 \cdot 1011^k+p=2 \cdot q$  for some integer  $q$ . Therefore   $$ 2^k(2 \cdot 1011^k+p)=2^{k+1} \cdot q $$   so we can let  $a_{k+1}=2 \cdot 2022^k+a_k$ . 

Thus the induction is complete and we are done.  $\blacksquare$   $\textbf{\color{red}Corollary to Lemma 1:}$   $2022^k+a_k$  and  $2 \cdot 2022^k+a_k$  cannot both be divisible by  $2^k$ , since  $p$  cannot be both odd and even at the same time. $\textbf{\color{red}Lemma 2:}$  For all positive integers  $n$ , if a  $n$ -digit number  $a^*_n$  is not divisible by  $2^n$ , then neither  $(2022^n+a^*_n)$  or  $(2 \cdot 2022^n+a^*_n)$  are divisible by  $2^{n+1}$ . $\textbf{\color{red}Proof:}$  Suppose the greatest power of  $2$  that divides  $a^*_n$  is  $2^k$ , where  $k$  is a positive integer less than  $n$ . Thus we can write that  $a^*_n=2^k \cdot p$ , for some odd positive integer  $p$ . 

Therefore,   $$ 2022^n+a^*_n=2^n \cdot 1011^n + 2^k \cdot p=2^k(2^{n-k} \cdot 1011^n + p). $$   Since  $k < n$ ,  $(n-k)$  is at least  $1$ , so  $(2^{n-k} \cdot 1011^n)$  is even. Since by hypothesis,  $p$  is odd,  $(2^{n-k} \cdot 1011^n + p)$  is also odd, since an even integer added to an odd integer gives an odd integer as the result. Therefore,  $2^k$  is the largest power of  $2$  that divides  $(2022^n+a^*_n)$ , and since  $k < n < n+1$ ,  $2^{n+1} \nmid (2022^n+a^*_n)$ .

Similarly,   $$ 2 \cdot 2022^n+a^*_n=2^{n+1} \cdot 1011^n + 2^k \cdot p=2^k(2^{n-k+1} \cdot 1011^n + p). $$   Since  $k < n$ ,  $(n-k+1)$  is at least  $2$ , so  $(2^{n-k+1} \cdot 1011^n)$  is even. Since by hypothesis,  $p$  is odd,  $(2^{n-k+1} \cdot 1011^n + p)$  is also odd, since an even integer added to an odd integer gives an odd integer as the result. Therefore,  $2^k$  is the largest power of  $2$  that divides  $(2 \cdot 2022^n+a^*_n)$ , and since  $k < n < n+1$ ,  $2^{n+1} \nmid (2 \cdot 2022^n+a^*_n)$ .

Therefore, neither  $(2022^n+a^*_n)$  or  $(2 \cdot 2022^n+a^*_n)$  are divisible by  $2^{n+1}$ .  $\blacksquare$  $\textbf{\color{red}Claim:}$  There exists only one  $n$ -digit integer containing only the digits  $1$  or  $2$  in base  $2022$  which is divisible by  $2^n$ . $\textbf{\color{red}Proof:}$  We proceed by induction. Consider the base case  $n=1$ . The only  $1$ -digit numbers in base  $2022$  containing only  $1$ 's and  $2$ 's as digits are  $1$  and  $2$ , of which only  $2$  is divisible by  $2^1$ .

Now, suppose there exists an  $n$ -digit integer  $a_n$  which is divisible by  $2^n$ . By   $\textbf{\color{red}Corollary to Lemma 1}$ , either appending a  $1$  at the beginning of  $a_n$  or appending a  $2$  at the beginning of  $a_n$  will produce an integer divisible by  $2^{n+1}$ , but both integers produced will not be divisible by  $2^{n+1}$ . By  $\textbf{\color{red}Lemma 2}$ , the integer produced that is not divisible by  $2^{n+1}$  will not produce any numbers divisible by  $2^p$ , where  $p > n+1$ , upon further iteration of the tree. Thus given an integer in base  $2022$  containing only  $1$ 's and  $2$ 's as digits and divisible by  $2^n$ , we can always produce a unique integer in base  $2022$  by appending a  $1$  or  $2$  at the beginning.

Thus, the induction is complete. Since our claim is true for all  $n$ , it is true for  $n=1000$ , so we are done.  $\blacksquare$

We prove a more general statement: for arbitrary  $2^k,$  there exists a number with  $k$  digits only consisting  $1$  or  $2$  in base  $2022$  that is equal to a multiple of  $2^k$  in base  $10.$  In particular, all  $2^k$  possibilities ( $2^k$  comes from  $2$  choices, either  $1$  or  $2,$  for each of the  $k$  digits) will cover all residues  $\pmod{2^k}.$  To prove this, we use induction.

The base case is obvious. When  $k=1,$  we have  $1$  or  $2,$  which cover all residues  $\pmod{2}.$  Now for the inductive step. First note any  $k$  digit number in base  $2022$  is expressed as \[a_1 (2022^{k-1})+a_2(2022^{k-2})+\cdots+a_k(2022^0),\] where  $a_i \in \{1,2\}$  for all  $1 \leq i \leq k.$  For our inductive step, we assume this number covers all residues  $\pmod{2^k}.$  Then a  $k+1$  digit number is expressed as \[a_0(2022^k)+a_1(2022^{k-1})+\cdots+a_k(2022^0),\] where once again  $a_i \in \{1,2\}$  for  $0 \leq i \leq k.$  Note that since  $2022=2 \cdot 3 \cdot 337,$  we have  $\nu_2 (2022^k)=\nu_2(2^k)=k.$  Since  $a_1(2022^{k-1})+\cdots+a_k(2022^0)$  covers all residues  $\pmod{2^k},$  that is, ranging from  $0$  to  $2^k-1,$  then when  $a_0=1,$  then all residues in the form of  $2^k+d$  for  $d \in \{0,1, \ldots, 2^k-1\}$  are covered. This gives us residues  $2^k$  through  $2^k+2^k-1=2^{k+1}-1$  covered, that is residues in the range  $[2^k,2^{k+1}).$  

When  $a_0=2,$  we have  $a_0(2022^k)$  as  $2 \cdot 2^k = 2^{k+1}.$  However, note that since we are taking  $\pmod{2^{k+1}},$  all residues  $[0,2^k)$  are covered. Combining the two intervals, we see the  $k+1$  digit number covers all residues taken  $\pmod{2^{k+1}},$  completing our induction. Substituting  $k=1000$  gives the desired result. Note that uniqueness is preserved as there are  $2^k$  possible numbers are  $2^k$  possible residues, so there is a one-to-one correspondence between our numbers and residues. Thus there is a unique  $1000$ -digit number  $N$  in base  $2022$  having all digits either  $1$  or  $2$  which is also a multiple of  $2^{1000}.$

Let  $S$  be the set of  $1000$ -digit numbers in base  $2022$ , all of whose digits are  $1$ 's or  $2$ 's. It follows that  $|S|=2^{1000}$ , since each of the  $1000$  digits in such a number has  $2$  possibilities:  $1$  or  $2$ .**Claim.** No two elements of  $S$  are equivalent modulo  $2^{1000}$ .**Proof.** For the sake of contradiction, let  $A=(a_{999}\dots a_0)_{2022}$  and  $B=(b_{999}\dots b_0)_{2022}$  be distinct elements of  $S$  that are equivalent modulo  $2^{1000}$ , whence  $$ a_{999}\cdot2022^{999}+\dots+a_0\cdot2022^0\equiv b_{999}\cdot2022^{999}+\dots+b_0\cdot2022^0\pmod{2^{1000}}, $$  where each of the  $a_k$  and  $b_k$  are  $1$  or  $2$ . Subtracting  $1\cdot2022^{999}+\dots+1\cdot2022^0$  from both sides, we have that  $$ a_{999}'\cdot2022^{999}+\dots+a_0'\cdot2022^0\equiv b_{999}'\cdot2022^{999}+\dots+b_0'\cdot2022^0\pmod{2^{1000}}, $$  where each of the  $a_k'$  and  $b_k'$  are  $0$  or  $1$ . Now, rid of all terms with coefficient (i.e. the corresponding  $a_k'$  or  $b_k'$ )  $0$ , and cancel out  $a_k'\cdot2022^k$  on the LHS with  $b_k'\cdot2022^k$  on the RHS where  $a_k'=b_k'$ . Then, we have  $$ 2022^{i_1}+\dots+2022^{i_m}\equiv2022^{j_1}+\dots+2022^{j_n}\pmod{2^{1000}}, $$  where the  $i_k$  and  $j_k$  are distinct and at least one of  $m$  and  $n$  is positive (i.e. at least one such  $i_k$  or  $j_k$  exists) since  $A$  and  $B$  are distinct by assumption. WLOG let  $i_1$  be the smallest of these. Analyzing  $\pmod{2^{i_1+1}}$  yields that all terms except  $2022^{i_1}$  disappear, but that leaves  $2022^{i_1}\equiv0\pmod{2^{i_1+1}}$ , contradiction.  $\Box$ As a result, the  $2^{1000}$  elements of  $S$  reduce to  $0,\dots,2^{1000}-1\pmod{2^{1000}}$ , because no two are equivalent modulo  $2^{1000}$  by the above claim. Hence, exactly one such element is a multiple of  $2^{1000}$ , as desired.  $\blacksquare$

Claim 1: If  $X = \{ a_1, a_2, ..., a_n\}$  forms a complete residue class

	also does if gcd $(k, n) = 1$ .
	
	
	Proof 1: If it doesn't, then by the Pigeonhole Principle, there must not exist 2

	However, this would mean  $k(a_i - a_t) \equiv 0$  (mod  $n$ ), which is obviously
	untrue since this would mean (since gcd $(k, n) = 1$ )  $a_i \equiv a_t$  (mod  $n$ ),
	which is a contradiction.
	
	
	Claim 2: If the set S =  $\{a_1, a_2, a_3, ... , a_{2^k}\}$  is a complete residue class
	(mod  $2^k$ ), then the set  $2S = \{2a_1, 2a_2, ... , 2a_{2^k}\}$  covers all even residues 
	(mod  $2^{k+1}$ ).

	 $K$  by  $M$ .

	which thus gets us that  $\frac{1}{2} \cdot J = S$ , or  $2S = J$ , 
	and since  $J$  is simply the set of even residues (mod  $2^{k+1}$ ), we are

	Now, we will continue to the solution of the problem. 
	Represent  $N$  as its base 10 representation,

	a_1 + 2022a_2 + 2022^2 a_3 + ... + 2022^{999} a_{1000}

	Of course, there are exactly  $2^{1000}$  different values for this number,

	Let the set  $M$  satisfy  $|M| = 2^{1000}$ , and all of its elements are

of which only  $2 + 1(2022) + 2(2022^2)$  is divisible by  $2^3=8$ .

By the hypothesis, this forms a complete residue class (mod  $2^t$ )

By Claim 1, we can multiply this  $N_t$  by 1011 without changing this fact, since gcd( $1011, 2^t) = 1$ .
Thus, we have that 
\[
1011a_1+1011\cdot2022a_2+1011\cdot2022^2a_3+...+1011\cdot2022^{t-1}a_t
\]
forms a complete residue class (mod  $2^t$ ) across all  $2^t$  choices of  $(a_1, a_2, ..., a_t)$ .
Now, by Claim 2, this means that multiplying this by 2
will cover all even residues (mod  $2^{t+1}$ ).
So, 
\[
2022a_1+2022^2a_2+...+2022^ta_t
\] 
covers all even residues (mod  $2^{t+1}$ ).
Now, to finish, let  $a_0 \in \{1, 2\}$ .
Then, this implies that 
\[
a_0+2022a_1+2022^2a_2+...+2022^ta_t
\] 
is a complete residue class (mod  $2^{t+1}$ ), which finishes the problem 
by induction if we simply add 1 to all of the indices of the  $a_i$ .

We prove the stronger problem where  $1000$  is replaced with any integer  $n\geq 1.$ For all positive integers  $n,$  let a  $n$ - $\textit{xook}$  number be a number with  $n$  digits in base  $2022$  whose base  $2022$  representation only consists of the digits  $1$  and  $2.$  We now proceed with induction.

If  $n=1,$  note that the only  $n$ - $\textit{xook}$  numbers are  $1_{2022}$  and  $2_{2022},$  of out which only the latter is divisible by  $2^n=2,$  so the base case holds.

Now, assume that there exists a positive integer  $k\geq 1$  such that there is a unique  $k$ - $\textit{xook}$  number.

Then, note that for any  $k+1$ - $\textit{xook}$  number  $m,$  we must have  $2^{k+1}\mid m.$  However, since  $m=\underline{a_{k+1}a_k\cdots a_1}_{2022}$  for some  $a_{k+1}, a_k, \cdots, a_1\in\{1,2\},$  then  $m\equiv a_{k+1}\cdot 2022^k+a_k\cdot 2022^{k-1}+\cdots+a_1\equiv a_k\cdot 2022^{k-1}+a_{k-1}\cdot 2022^{k-2}+\cdots+a_1\equiv\underline{a_ka_{k-1}\cdots a_1}_{2022}\equiv 0\pmod{2^k},$  so  $\underline{a_ka_{k-1}\cdots a_1}_{2022}$  is a  $k$ - $\textit{xook}$  number, and thus  $\{a_k, a_{k-1}, \cdots, a_1\}$  are uniquely determined. Denote  $\underline{a_ka_{k-1}\cdots a_1}_{2022}=p.$ Then,  $m=a_{k+1}\cdot 2022^k+p\equiv 0\pmod{2^{k+1}}.$  There are two cases:  $p\equiv 2^k\pmod{2^{k+1}},$  or  $p\equiv 0\pmod{2^{k+1}}.$ If  $p\equiv 2^k\pmod{2^{k+1}},$  then  $m=a_{k+1}\cdot 2022^k+p\equiv a_{k+1}2^k+2^k\equiv (a_{k+1}+1)2^k\equiv 0\pmod{2^{k+1}},$  so  $a_{k+1}\equiv 1\pmod{2}$  and thus  $a_{k+1}=1,$  so  $m$  is uniquely determined.

If  $p\equiv 0\pmod{2^{k+1}},$  then  $m=a_{k+1}\cdot 2022^k+p\equiv a_{k+1}2^k\equiv 0\pmod{2^{k+1}},$  so  $a_{k+1}\equiv 0\pmod{2},$  and  $a_{k+1}=2,$  so  $m$  is uniquely determined. (It is easy to check in both cases that this  $m$  is a  $k+1$ - $\textit{xook}$  number.)

As such, there is a unique  $k+1$ - $\textit{xook}$  number, so by the principle of mathematical induction, there exists a unique  $n$ - $\textit{xook}$  number for all positive integers  $n\geq 1,$  as desired.  $\Box$

We call a positive integer  $n$   $\textit{sixish}$  if  $n=p(p+6)$ , where  $p$  and  $p+6$  are prime numbers. For example,  $187=11\cdot17$  is sixish, but  $475=19\cdot25$  is not sixish. Define a function  $f$  on the positive integers such that  $f(n)$  is the sum of the squares of the positive divisors of  $n$ . For example,  $f(10)=1^2+2^2+5^2+10^2=130$ .

(a) Find, with proof, an irreducible polynomial function  $g(x)$  with integer coefficients such that  $f(n)=g(n)$  for all sixish  $n$ . ("Irreducible" means that  $g(x)$  cannot be factored as the product of two polynomials of smaller degree with integer coefficients.)

(b) We call a positive integer  $n$   $\textit{pseudo-sixish}$  if  $n$  is not sixish but nonetheless  $f(n)=g(n)$ , where  $g(n)$  is the polynomial function that you found in part (a). Find, with proof, all pseudo-sixish positive integers.

This gives us the possible divisors of  $n$  as  $1$ ,  $p$ ,  $p+6$ , and  $p(p+6)$ . Thus,  $f(n)$  is equivalent to   $$ 1 + p^{2} + (p+6)^{2} + (p(p+6))^{2}. $$  The polynomial  $g(x)$  we look for takes sixish  $n$  as an input, not some prime  $p$ . Ergo, we must substitute  $p$  for an expression in terms of  $n$ . Note that   $$ n = p(p+6) = (p+3)^{2} - 9, $$   and therefore,   $$ p = \sqrt{n+9} - 3. $$   

Substituting this back into the expression we got for  $f(n)$  in terms of  $p$  yields   $$ 1 + (\sqrt{n+9} - 3)^{2} + (\sqrt{n+9} + 3)^{2} + (n)^{2}. $$   Expanding will result in   $$ 1 + (n+9) - 6\sqrt{n+9} + 9 + (n+9) + 6\sqrt{n+9} + 9 + n^{2}. $$   Simplifying the right-hand side, we obtain   $$ n^{2} + 2n + 37. $$   Therefore, our irreducible polynomial is   $$ \boxed{g(x) = x^{2} + 2x + 37.} $$  Part B:

We want to find a positive integer  $n$  that is not sixish but still satisfies the equation we found in part A. Such an  $n$  is defined to be a  pseudo-sixish positive integer.

First, define the nontrivial divisors of  $n$  to be the divisors of  $n$  that are not  $1$  or  $n$ . Define  $Z(n)$  to be the sum of the squares of the nontrivial divisors of  $n$ .

Z(n) = 2n + 36.

Case I:  $n$  has one prime factor

We can equate  $n$  to  $a^{k}$ , where  $a$  is the prime factor of  $n$  has and  $k$  is a positive integer.

If  $k=1$ , then  $n = a$  is prime. This means  $n$  has no nontrivial divisors, and thus  $Z(n) = 0.$  This would simplify to   $$ 0 = 2a + 36 $$   from  $(4)$ . No  $a$  satisfy this equation. Therefore, no pseudo-sixish number cannot be prime. 

If  $k=2$ , then  $n = a^{2}$  and  $Z(n) = (a)^{2}.$  Therefore,   $$ a^{2} = 2(a^{2}) + 36 $$   so   $$ a^{2} + 36 = 0. $$   No  $a$  can satisfy this equation, which means that there is no pseudo-sixish number in the form of  $a^{2}$ .

If  $k=3$ , then  $n=a^{3}$  and  $Z(n) = (a)^{2} + (a^{2})^{2} = a^{2} + a^{4}.$  This gives   $$ a^{2} + a^{4} = 2(a^{3} + 36). $$   When the right-hand side is expanded and all terms are moved to the left-hand side, we get   $$ a^{4} - 2a^{3} + a^{2} + 36 = 0. $$   Note that  $a$  is a prime, positive integer. Combining this information with the rational roots theorem, we get the only possible values of  $a$  as  $a = 2$  and  $a = 3$ . We can plug in these two values to get  $a = 3$  as the only valid solution of this equation. Therefore,  $n = 3^{3} = 27$ , which means that  $27$  is a pseudo-sixish number.

If  $k = 4$ , then  $n = a^{4}$  and  $Z(n) = (a)^{2} + (a^{2})^{2} + (a^{3})^{2}.$  This gives   $$ a^{2} + a^{4} + a^{6} = 2a^{4} + 36. $$   When  $a = 2$ , the left-hand side is  $84$ , and the right-hand side is  $68$ . This indicates that  $a$  cannot be  $2$ . When  $a > 3$ , then  $a^{4} > 81 > 36$ . Also, note that  $a^{6} > 2a^{4}$  because  $a^{2} > 2$  for all prime  $a$ . Thus, the above equation has no solution, and no  $a$  exists when  $k \geq 5$ . Hence, no pseudo-sixish number is in the form of  $a^{k}$  when  $k \geq 5$ .

We have covered all possible  $k$ , and we got that  $\mathbf{27}$  is the only psuedo-sixish number that satisfies this case.

Case II:  $n$  has two (distinct) prime factors
If  $n$  has two prime factors, then   $$ n = a_{1}^{k_{1}}a_{2}^{k_{2}} $$   where  $a_{1}$  and  $a_{2}$  are the two distinct prime factors and  $k_{1}$  and  $k_{2}$  are the powers of  $a_{1}$  and  $a_{2}$  respectively.

First, consider the case where  $k_{1} = k_{2} = 1.$  This indicates that  $n = a_{1}a_{2}$  and  $Z(n) = (a_{1})^{2} + (a_{2})^{2}.$  It follows from  $(4)$  that   $$ a_{1}^{2} + a_{2}^{2} = 2a_{1}a_{2} + 36. $$   We can rewrite this as   $$ (a_{1}-a_{2})^{2} = 36 $$   or   $$ a_{1} - a_{2} = \pm6. $$  This is the definition of a sixish number (in disguise). Specifically, we have   $$ a_{1} = a_{2} \pm 6. $$   By definition, if  $a_{1} = a_{2} + 6$ , then  $n = a_{2}(a_{2}+6)$  is sixish. Note that if  $a_{1} = a_{2} - 6$ , then  $a_{2} = a_{1} + 6$ . It follows that  $n = a_{1}(a_{1} + 6)$ , which is also sixish by definition. Therefore, no psuedo-sixish number can be in the form of  $a_{1}a_{2}$ .

Next, consider the case where  $k_{1}$  and/or  $k_{2}$  is greater than or equal to  $2$ . a_{1}^{2k_{1}} + a_{2}^{2k_{2}} + a_{1}^{k_{1}}a_{2}^{k_{2}}(a_{1}^{k_{1}}a_{2}^{k_{2}-2} - 2) + B(n) = 36.
\end{align}
First, note that  $(a_{1}^{k_{1}}a_{2}^{k_{2}-2} - 2)$  is always nonnegative, as  $a_{2}^{k_{2}-2} \geq 1$  and  $a_{1}^{k_{1}} \geq 2.$ Next, note that  $k_{2} \ngeq 3$ . \begin{align}
a_{1}^{2k_{1}} + a_{2}^{4} + a_{1}^{k_{1}}a_{2}^{2}(a_{1}^{k_{1}} - 2) + B(n) = 36.
\end{align}
We can deduce that  $a_{2} < 3$ ; if  $a_{2} \geq 3$ ,   $$ a_{2}^{4} \geq 81 > 36. $$   This means that if  $a_{2} \geq 3$ ,  $(6)$  would not be satisifed for any inputs. Ergo,  $a_{2} < 3$  and  $a_{2} = 2$ .

Substituting  $a_{2} = 2$  into  $(6)$  gives   $$ a_{1}^{2k_{1}} + 16 + 4a_{1}^{k_{1}}(a_{1}^{k_{1}} - 2) + B(n) = 36. $$   This simplifies into 
\begin{align}
5a_{1}^{2k_{1}} - 8a_{1}^{k_{1}} + B(n) = 20.
\end{align}
The minimum value of  $a_{1}^{k_{1}}$  occurs when  $k_{1} = 1$  and  $a_{1} = 3$  (note that  $a_{1}$  cannot be  $2$  since  $a_{2} = 2$ ). All of this means that it is impossible for any combination of  $a_{1}$ ,  $a_{2}$ ,  $k_{1}$ , and  $k_{2}$  to give an  $n$  that satisfies  $(4)$ . Hence, no psuedo-sixish number has two prime factors.

We will prove that a pseudo-sixish number cannot have more than two prime factors through a proof by contradiction. Assume for the sake of contradiction that a psuedo-sixish number  $n$  has more than  $2$  prime factors.

Let  $n$  have  $x$  prime factors:  $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \hdots , a_{x}$ . Let  $k_{x}$  represent the power of  $a_{x}$ . Therefore,   $$ n = a_{1}^{k_{1}}a_{2}^{k_{2}}a_{3}^{k_{3}}\hdots a_{x}^{k_{x}}. $$

\begin{align}

\end{align}
where  $B(n)$  represents the sum of the squares of the other nontrivial divisors of  $n$  that have not been expressed (for example,  $(a_{1}^{2k_{1}}a_{2}^{2k_{2}})$  is part of  $B(n)$  as we have not explicitly written it). This can be rewritten as   $$ a_{1}^{2k_{1}} + a_{2}^{2k_{2}} + a_{3}^{2k_{3}} + a_{1}^{k_{1}-1}a_{2}^{k_{2}}a_{3}^{k_{3}}a_{4}^{k_{4}}\hdots a_{x}^{k_{x}}(a_{1}^{k_{1}-1}a_{2}^{k_{2}}a_{3}^{k_{3}}a_{4}^{k_{4}}\hdots a_{x}^{k_{x}} - 2a_{1}) + B(n) = 36. $$  Note that  $a_{2} > a_{1} \geq 2$ , and that  $a_{x} > a_{1}.$  Therefore,   $$ a_{1}^{k_{1}-1}a_{2}^{k_{2}}a_{3}^{k_{3}}a_{4}^{k_{4}}\hdots a_{x}^{k_{x}} > a_{2}a_{x} > 2a_{1} $$   and   $$ a_{1}^{k_{1}-1}a_{2}^{k_{2}}a_{3}^{k_{3}}a_{4}^{k_{4}}\hdots a_{x}^{k_{x}}(a_{1}^{k_{1}-1}a_{2}^{k_{2}}a_{3}^{k_{3}}a_{4}^{k_{4}}\hdots a_{x}^{k_{x}} - 2a_{1}) > 0. $$  Furthermore, by Lemma  $5.2$ ,   $$ a_{1}^{2} + a_{2}^{2} + a_{3}^{2} > 36. $$   Then   $$ a_{1}^{2k_{1}} + a_{2}^{2k_{2}} + a_{3}^{2k_{3}} > 36 $$   as  $k_{1}, k_{2},$  and  $k_{3}$  are greater than or equal to  $1$ .

Thus, we can conclude that   $$ a_{1}^{2k_{1}} + a_{2}^{2k_{2}} + a_{3}^{2k_{3}} + a_{1}^{k_{1}-1}a_{2}^{k_{2}}a_{3}^{k_{3}}a_{4}^{k_{4}}\hdots a_{x}^{k_{x}}(a_{1}^{k_{1}-1}a_{2}^{k_{2}}a_{3}^{k_{3}}a_{4}^{k_{4}}\hdots a_{x}^{k_{x}} - 2a_{1}) > 36. $$   Therefore,   $$ a_{1}^{2k_{1}} + a_{2}^{2k_{2}} + a_{3}^{2k_{3}} + a_{1}^{k_{1}-1}a_{2}^{k_{2}}a_{3}^{k_{3}}a_{4}^{k_{4}}\hdots a_{x}^{k_{x}}(a_{1}^{k_{1}-1}a_{2}^{k_{2}}a_{3}^{k_{3}}a_{4}^{k_{4}}\hdots a_{x}^{k_{x}} - 2a_{1}) + B(n) > 36. $$  Finally, let's manipulate this equation:   $$ a_{1}^{2k_{1}} + a_{2}^{2k_{2}} + a_{3}^{2k_{3}} + (a_{1}^{(k_{1}-1)}a_{2}^{k_{2}}a_{3}^{k_{3}}a_{4}^{k_{4}}\hdots a_{x}^{k_{x}})^{2} + B(n) > 2(a_{1}^{k_{1}}a_{2}^{k_{2}}a_{3}^{k_{3}}\hdots a_{n}^{k_{x}}) + 36. $$  A psuedo-sixish  $n$  must satisfy  $(8)$ . However, with some manipulation, we were able to prove that it is impossible for  $n$  to satisfy  $(8)$  due to the left-hand side of  $(8)$  being strictly greater than the right-hand side. Therefore, we have a contradiction, and no pseudo-sixish number has more than  $2$  prime factors.

Thus 27 is the only such number.</details>

        1. The pseudo-sixish number is of the form  $pq$ , for distinct primes  $p$  and  $q$ . Then note that

        But this just gives a sixish number.

        \[\left(\frac{X}{q}\right)^2+q^2 \ge 2X.\]
        Thus, it is required that 
        \[\left(\frac{X}{p}\right)^2+p^2+\left(\frac{X}{r}\right)^2+r^2 \le 37.\]

\[1\equiv 37 \pmod{p} \implies p \in \{2,3\}.\]

4^e &= 6 \cdot 2^{e}+112.

&= (n^2+1) + \sum_{d|n,1<d<\sqrt n}\left(\left(d-\frac nd\right)^2+2d\left(\frac nd\right)\right) + p(n)n 
&= (n^2+1) + \sum_{d|n,1<d<\sqrt n}\left(2n+\left(d-\frac nd\right)^2\right) + p(n)n. 
\end{align*}
\textbf{(a)} Consider the polynomial  $g(x)=x^2+2x+37$  which is irreducible as it has no real roots. Note that for all sixish  $n$  of the form  $p(p+6)$  for primes  $p$  and  $p+6,$ \begin{align*}
f(n) &= (n^2+1) + \sum_{d=p}\left(2n+\left(d-\frac nd\right)^2\right) + 0 
&= (n^2+1) +2n+\left(p-(p+6)\right)^2 
&= (n^2+1) +2n+36 
&= n^2 +2n+37 
&= g(n). 
\end{align*}

\textbf{(b)} Note that  $\boxed{27}$  is pseudo-sixish since  $f(27)=1^2+3^2+9^2+27^2=820=27^2+2\cdot 27+37=g(27).$  We claim that there are no other pseudo-sixish numbers. 

Consider a pseudo-sixish number  $n$ . Clearly 1 is not pseudo-sixish so  $n>1.$  Then we have 
\begin{align*}
f(n) &= g(n), 
(n^2+1) + \sum_{d|n,1<d<n}d^2&=(n^2+1)+2n+36,
\sum_{d|n,1<d<n}d^2&=2n+36,
\sum_{d|n,1<d<\sqrt n}\left(d^2+\left(\frac nd\right)^2\right) + p(n)n&=2n+36,
\sum_{d|n,1<d<\sqrt n}\left(2n+\left(d-\frac nd\right)^2\right) + p(n)n&=2n+36.
\end{align*}
Let a \textit{modest} divisor of  $n$  be a divisor  $d$  of  $n$  such that  $1<d<\sqrt n.$  We will do casework on the number of modest divisors of  $n$ . 

\textbf{Case 1:}  $n$  has no modest divisors.

Then we have  $$ \sum_{d\in\varnothing }\left(d^2+\left(\frac nd\right)^2\right) + p(n)n=2n+36, $$    $$ 0 + p(n)n=2n+36, $$    $$ n(p(n)- 2) = 36. $$  Since  $p(n)-2<0,$  we have  $n<0,$  a contradiction. 

\textbf{Case 2.1:}  $n$  has one modest divisor  $d$  and  $p(n)=1.$ Then  $n$  has 5 divisors (1,  $d$ ,  $\sqrt n$ ,  $\frac nd$ , and  $n$ ) so  $n=p^4$  for some prime  $p$ . (In fact we must have  $p=d$ .) We have  $$ \sum_{d|p^4,1<d<p^4}d^2=2p^4+36 $$    $$ p^2+p^4+p^6=2p^4+36, $$    $$ p^2(p^4-p^2+1)=36, $$    $$ p^2|36, $$    $$ p|6, $$    $$ p\in \{2,3\}, $$  neither of which of which satisfy the sextic.

\textbf{Case 2.2:}  $n$  has one modest divisor  $d$  and  $p(n)=0.$ Then  $n$  has 4 divisors (1,  $d$ ,  $\frac nd$  and  $n$ ) so  $n$  is of the form  $p^3$  for some prime  $p$  (which must be  $d$ ) or  $n=pq$  for primes  $p$  and  $q$  (one of which must be  $d$ ). If  $n$  is of the form  $p^3,$  we have  $$ \sum_{d|p^3,1<d<p^3}d^2=2p^3+36, $$    $$ p^2+p^4=2p^3+36, $$    $$ (p - 3) (p + 2) (p^2 - p + 6)=0, $$    $$ p=3, $$    $$ n=3^3=27. $$  If  $n$  is of the form  $n=pq,$  we have  $$ \sum_{d=p}\left(2pq+\left(d-\frac {pq}d\right)^2\right)+0=2pq+36, $$    $$ 2pq+(p-q)^2=2pq+36, $$    $$ (p-q)^2=36, $$    $$ |p-q|=6, $$  so  $n$  must be sixish, a contradiction.

stem_md:
Grogg’s favorite positive integer is  $n\ge2$ , and Grogg has a lucky coin that comes up heads with some fixed probability  $p$ , where  $0<p<1$ . Once each day, Grogg flips his coin, and if it comes up heads, he does two things:
[list=1]
[*] He eats a cookie. [/*]
[*] He then flips the coin  $n$  more times. If the result of these  $n$  flips is  $n-1$  heads and  $1$  tail (in any order), he eats another cookie. [/*]
[/list]
He never eats a cookie except as a result of his coin flips. Find all possible values of  $n$  and  $p$  such that the expected value of the number of cookies that Grogg eats each day is exactly  $1$ .
solution_md:
If the first flip lands tails with probability  $1-p$ , Grogg always eats  $0$  cookies. Meanwhile, if the first flip lands heads with probability  $p$ , Grogg eats  $1$  cookie to start with. Then, the probability that the next  $n$  flips land  $n-1$  heads and  $1$  tail is  $np^{n-1}(1-p)$ : the  $p^{n-1}(1-p)$  accounts for the individual outcomes of the flips, and the  $n$  for ordering the flips. Hence, the *expected* number of cookies following a first heads is  $1+p^{n-1}(1-p)$ , so the expected number of cookies across all scenarios is
\[(1-p)\cdot0+p\cdot\left(1+np^{n-1}(1-p)\right)=p+np^n-np^{n+1}.\]
Setting equal to  $1$  and rearranging, we have that
\[np^{n+1}-np^n-p+1=(np^n-1)(p-1)=0.\]
Assuming  $0<p<1$ , the only possibility is to have  $np^n-1=0$ , or, as a consequence,  $p=1/n^{1/n}$ . The requested answer is therefore  $\boxed{(n,p)=\left(n,1/n^{1/n}\right)\ |\ n\ge2}$ .

The answer is all positive integers  $n \geq 2$  where  $\displaystyle p = \left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{{n}}}$  for each  $n.$  On each day, the expected value of the number of cookies Grogg eats is the probability he eats exactly 1 cookie plus twice the probability he eats exactly 2 cookies, by the definition of expected value. We start by finding the probability he eats exactly 2 cookies. He must flip heads on the first coin, with probability  $p.$  Then, given he first flipped heads, the probability he gets  $n-1$  heads and  $1$  tail after flipping  $n$  more times is   $$ {{n} \choose {1}} p^{n-1}(1-p) = np^{n-1}(1-p), $$   by the binomial probability formula. The overall probability is thus  $np^{n}(1-p)$  he eats 2 cookies. The probability he eats 1 cookie is the probability he eats at least one cookie minus the probability he eats 2 cookies. The probability he eats at least one cookie is simply  $p,$  so the probability he eats exactly one cookie is  $p - np^{n}(1-p).$  Thus, the expected number of cookies Grogg eats every day is   $$ 1(p-np^{n}(1-p)) + 2(np^{n}(1-p)) = p +np^{n}(1-p) = 1. $$   Since  $1-p \neq 0,$  we have   $$ p +np^{n}(1-p) = 1 \Rightarrow np^{n}(1-p)=(1-p) \Rightarrow np^{n} = 1 \Rightarrow p = \displaystyle \left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{{n}}}. $$   It can easily be checked that  $p = (\frac{1}{n})^{\frac{1}{n}}$  satisfies the expected value equation, however we must ensure that  $0 < p < 1.$  Thus, it remains to show that  $\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{n}}$  is strictly between 0 and 1 for all positive integers  $n$  greater or equal to 2. Let  $m$  =  $\frac{1}{n}.$  It is clear that  $m$  is strictly positive and less than or equal to  $\frac{1}{2}.$  We will show  $m^{m}$  is strictly between 0 and 1 for all real numbers  $m$  on the interval  $(0,1) - $  a stronger statement than what is required. Consider the function  $y = x^{x}.$  Clearly,  $y$  is continuous and differentiable over the positive reals, so by logarithmic differentiation,   $$ \ln{y} = x\ln{x} \Rightarrow \frac{y'}{y} = 1 + \ln{x} \Rightarrow y' = x^{x}(1+\ln{x}) $$   for all  $x > 0.$  It is clear the only critical values occur at  $x=0$  and  $1+\ln{x}=0 \Rightarrow x = \frac{1}{e}.$  Now, on the interval  $(0,\frac{1}{e}),$   $y'$  is negative, so  $y$  is decreasing. For  $(\frac{1}{e},1), y'$  is positive, so  $y$  is strictly increasing. This means the function  $y = x^{x}$  has a global minimum at  $x = \frac{1}{e} \approx 0.3679, $  when  $y \approx 0.6922$  on the interval  $(0,1).$  Since on the interval  $(0,\frac{1}{e}),$   $y$  is strictly decreasing, it follows that  $0.6922<y(x) < y(0) = 1$  for all  $x$  on  $(0,\frac{1}{e}).$  On  $x \in (\frac{1}{e},1),$  we have  $0.6922 < x < y(1) = 1,$  since  $y$  is strictly increasing. Thus, we have shown for all  $x \in (0,1),$   $x^{x}$  is strictly between 0 and 1, which completes the proof.

stem_md: Let  $n\ge3$  be a positive integer. Alex and Lizzie play a game. Alex chooses  $n$  positive integers (not necessarily distinct), writes them on a blackboard, and does nothing further. Then, Lizzie is allowed to pick some of the numbers―but not all of them―and replace them each by their average. For example, if  $n=7$  and the numbers Alex writes on the blackboard to start are  $1,2,4,5,9,4,11$ , then on her first turn Lizzie could pick  $1,4,9$ , erase them, and replace them each with the number  $\tfrac{1+4+9}{3}$ , leaving on the blackboard the numbers  $\tfrac{14}{3},2,\tfrac{14}{3},5,\tfrac{14}{3},4,11$ . Lizzie can repeat this process of selecting and averaging some numbers as often as she wants. Lizzie wins the game if eventually all of the numbers written on the blackboard are equal. Find all positive integers  $n\ge3$  such that no matter what numbers Alex picks, Lizzie can win the game.
solution_md:
The answer is  $\boxed{\text{composite }n}$ .**Claim.** Composite  $n$  work.**Proof.** Partition the  $n$  integers into sets  $S_1,S_2,\dots,S_k$ , where  $k\ge1$  is a proper divisor of  $n$ . (Such a  $k$  exists since  $n$  is composite by assumption.) Then, average the elements in each set, so that if say  $a_i$  is the average of  $S_i$ ,  $\tfrac{n}{k}$   $a_1$ 's,  $\tfrac{n}{k}$   $a_2$ 's,  $\dots$ ,  $\tfrac{n}{k}$   $a_k$ 's remain. Now, these can be rearranged into  $\tfrac{n}{k}$  identical sets of the form  $\{a_1,a_2,\dots,a_k\}$ , and averaging each set yields a uniform  $\tfrac{a_1+a_2+\dots+a_k}{k}$ , as desired.  $\Box$ **Claim.** Prime  $n$  fail.**Proof.** Suppose Alex writes  $p-1$   $1$ 's and one  $2$ . As such, because the average of the numbers on the board remains invariant by nature of the game, Lizzie aims to convert all numbers into  $\tfrac{p+1}{p}$ , the initial average. Since  $\tfrac{p+1}{p}$  has denominator  $p$ , it suffices to show that at no moment can a number on the board have denominator dividing  $p$ , which would show Alex wins in a game with  $p$  numbers, as desired.

To do so, observe that if  $k$  rational numbers with denominators  $d_1,d_2,\dots,d_k$  are averaged, the denominator of their average is a factor of  $k\cdot\text{lcm}(d_1,d_2,\dots,d_k)$ , as the denominator of their sum is a factor of  $\text{lcm}(d_1,d_2,\dots,d_k)$  (provable by writing the sum with a common denominator). Hence, we can proceed with arbitrary induction (say, on the number of averagings made thus far), as follows.

Initially, none of the numbers have denominator dividing  $p$  as all of them are integers, thereby proving the base case. Now assume that at some moment, none of the numbers have denominator dividing  $p$ . In averaging some  $k<p$  of the numbers with denominators  $d_1,d_2,\dots,d_k$ , the denominator of the resulting average is a factor of  $N=k\cdot\text{lcm}(d_1,d_2,\dots,d_k)$ . But as  $p$  divides neither  $k$  nor  $\text{lcm}(d_1,d_2,\dots,d_k)$ , the latter by the inductive assumption, it doesn't divide  $N$  either. Ergo, *still* none of the numbers have denominator dividing  $p$ , which completes the inductive step and, consequently, the proof.  $\Box$

Find the smallest positive integer  $c_k$  (which may depend on  $k$ ) such that every lattice point can be colored with one of  $c_k$  colors, subject to the following two conditions:
[list=1]
[*] If  $(x,y)$  and  $(a,b)$  are two distinct neighboring points; that is,  $|x-a|\leq1$  and  $|y-b|\leq1$ , then  $(x,y)$  and  $(a,b)$  must be different colors. [/*]
[*] If  $(x,y)$  and  $(a,b)$  are two lattice points such that  $x\equiv a\pmod{k}$  and  $y\equiv b\pmod{k}$ , then  $(x,y)$  and  $(a,b)$  must be the same color. [/*]
[/list]

Start with a set  $A$  consisting of a single point.

stem_md: Let  $Z^+$  denote the set of positive integers. Determine , with proof, if there exists a function   $f:\mathbb{Z^+}\rightarrow\mathbb {Z^+}$  such that  $f(f(f(f(f(n)))))$  =  $2022n$  for all positive integers  $n$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>I claim that \boxed{\text{such a function  $f$  exists.}} For each  $n,$  let  $n = 2022^{a}\cdot k,$  for non-negative integers  $a,k$  and  $k$  not divisible by  $2022.$  Then,  $f$  is defined as follows:  $$  f(n) = 
\left\{
\begin{array}{cc}
   2022^{a+1}(k-8088)  & \text{ if } \left \lfloor \frac{k}{2022}  \right \rfloor \equiv 4 \pmod{5} 
   2022^{a}(k+2022)  &  \text{ otherwise }
   
\end{array}
\right\} $$   
In this solution,  $2022^{a+1}(k-8088)$  will be referred to as the ``top function,'' and  $2022^{a}(k+2022)$  will be referred to as the ``bottom function.'' 
 
Now, we will prove that for all  $n,$  exactly one of the five operations  $f$  of the operations of  $f(f(f(f(f(n)))))$  will be of the top function, and the other four will be of the bottom function. To show this, first note each iteration of the bottom function increases the value of  $\lfloor \frac{k}{2022} \rfloor$  by 1, and each iteration of the top function decreases the value of  $\lfloor \frac{k}{2022} \rfloor$  by 4. Now, using these facts, we make a table for the value of  $\lfloor \frac{k}{2022} \rfloor \pmod{5},$  based on each of the 5 starting cases for  $\lfloor \frac{k}{2022} \rfloor \pmod{5}.$ \begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{||c c c c c c||} 
 \hline $n$   &  $f(n)$  &  $f(f(n))$  &  $f(f(f(n)))$ & $f(f(f(f(n))))$ & $f(f(f(f(f(n)))))$   [0.5ex] 
 \hline\hline
 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 0 
 \hline
 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 0 & 1
 \hline
 2 & 3 & 4 & 0 & 1 & 2
 \hline
 3 & 4 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3
 \hline
 4 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 [1ex] 
 \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

It is clear from the table that no matter the initial choice of  $\lfloor \frac{k}{2022}\rfloor,$  the top function is applied once and the bottom function is applied four times. 
  Through these operations, the value of  $k$  does not change since  $2022+2022+2022+2022-8088 = 0,$  and the value of  $a$  increases by one since the top function is applied once and the bottom function does not change  $a.$  Thus, if the original value of  $n$  is  $2022^{a}k,$  the final value of  $f(f(f(f(f(n))))) = 2022^{a+1}k = 2022n,$  as desired.
[\hide]</details>

A more general version of this is true: Let  $f^k(x)$  be the function  $f(x)$  composed  $k$  times. We claim that for all positive integers  $k$  and  $n,$  there exists a function  $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$  such that  $f^k(x)=nx.$ Since there are infinitely many primes, let  $p$  be a prime not in the prime factorization of  $n.$  Let  $g(x)=\nu_p(x) \pmod{k},$  i.e. the residue of the exponent of  $p$  in the prime factorization of  $x,$  taken mod  $k.$  Then define  $f$  as follows:
\[f(x) = \begin{cases}
px & 0 \le g(x) \le k-2 
\dfrac{nx}{p^{k-1}} & g(x)=k-1
\end{cases}\]
This function is well-defined and takes natural numbers to natural numbers. (In particular, the latter case only 'kicks in' when  $g(x) \ge k-1,$  so dividing by  $p^{k-1}$  is no problem.) Furthermore, no matter what  $x$  is, when we iterate  $f(x)$   $k$  times, we'll cycle through all  $k$  possible values of  $g(x)$  exactly once, since  $g(f(x))=g(x)+1$  in both cases taken mod  $k.$  Therefore, in the process of this iteration we'll multiply by  $p$   $k-1$  times and by  $\dfrac{n}{p^{k-1}}$  once, so  $f^k(x)=p^{k-1} \cdot \dfrac{n}{p^{k-1}} \cdot x = nx.$ This is definitely not the only possible construction for  $f,$  but it's the cleanest construction I was able to find.

stem_md: A positive integer  $N$  is called *googolicious* if there are exactly  $10^{100}$  positive integers  $x$  that satisfy \[\left\lfloor \frac{N}{\left\lfloor \frac{N}{x} \right\rfloor } \right\rfloor = x,\] where  $z$  denotes the greatest integer less than  $z.$  Find, with proof, all googolicious integers  $N.$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>To solve this problem, consider two cases. 
Case 1:  $k^2\le{N}<(k)(k+1)$  for some positive integer  $k$ . 
In this case, consider if  $x<k$ . Now, consider the given equation.  $$ \lfloor{\frac{N}{\lfloor{\frac{N}{x}\rfloor}}\rfloor}=x $$  Let  $y$  be the largest positive integer such that  $xy\le{N}$ . Now, our equation becomes  $$ \lfloor{\frac{N}{y}\rfloor}=x $$  Now, let  $xy+r=N$  where  $r$  is a nonnegative integer. Note that  $r<x$ , otherwise  $y$  would not be the largest integer possible. However, we note that  $x<y$  as well, because we have that  $x<k$  and  $N\ge{x^2}$ . So, assuming  $x\ge{y}$  by contradiction, we would have  $x<$ ,  $y<k$ ,  $xy\ge{N}\ge{k^2}$ . Because all numbers involved are positive, we may multiply the first two expression to obtain  $xy<k^2$ , contradiction. Thus,  $x<y$ . 
Because  $r<y$  now holds, we can say that  $\lfloor{\frac{N}{y}\rfloor}$  must equal  $x$ . Thus, our equation is  $x=x$ , a true statement. Thus, all  $x<k$  work. 
\newline
\newline
Now, consider the case where  $x\ge{k}$ . Then,  $y\le{k}$ . Assume otherwise; that  $y>k$ . Then, we must have  $(k)(k+1+s)<(k)(k+1)$ , where  $s$  is some nonnegative integer. Expanding and simplifying, we have  $sk<0$ , contradiction because  $s, k$  are both nonnegative. Thus,  $y\le{k}$ . Instead of chasing possible values of  $x$ , we chase possible values of  $y$ . We know that  $\lfloor{\frac{N}{x}\rfloor} = y$ . We also know that there must be at least one solution to  $xy\le{N}$ , if  $y\le{N}$ . Returning to our equation  $xy+r=N$ , consider the highest integer possible value of  $x$  possible. Euclid's division lemma states that for a given positive integer  $y\le{N}$ , there is a unique positive integer  $x$  such that  $xy+r=N$  and  $0\le{r}<y$ . Then, because  $x\ge{y}>r$ , our equation simplifies to   $$ \lfloor{\frac{N}{y}\rfloor} = x $$    $$ x = x $$  Hence, for every  $y\le{k}$ , there is one and only one  $x$  that satisfies the equation. To show that no other combinations of  $x, y$  work, consider the following case:  $y\le{r}<x$ . Then,  $\lfloor{\frac{N}{x}\rfloor} = y$  would still clearly hold, but  $\lfloor{\frac{N}{y}\rfloor} = x$  would not hold, and would be a different value because  $r\ge{y}$  which would imply that there exists a higher possible  $x$ . So, for every  $y\le{k}$  (implying  $x\ge{k}$ , there exists one and only one  $x$  that satisfies the equation. Of course, we must set another obvious bound:  $y>0$ . 
\newline
\newline
Combining all of this information, there are  $k=\lfloor{\sqrt{N}\rfloor}-1$  solutions plus  $k=\lfloor{\sqrt{N}\rfloor}$  in this case, so  $2\lfloor{\sqrt{N}\rfloor}-1$  solutions exist in this case. 
\newline
\newline
Case 2:  $k(k+1)\le{N}<(k+1)^2$  for some positive integer  $k$ . 
We proceed in a similar manner. For  $x\le{k}$ ,  $y>k$  must hold, which can be easily proven using proof by contradiction similar to that found in the last case. Also,  $xy+r=N$  only has one solution where  $0\le{r}<y$  for a fixed  $x$ . So, there are  $k$  distinct solutions here. If  $x>k$  were to hold, then  $y\le{k}$  has to hold, which can also be easily proven using proof by contradiction. Also, for every  $xy+r=N$ , there exists exactly one unique  $x$  for each integer  $1\le{y}\le{k}$ , where  $0\le{r}<y<x$ . Again, if  $x>r\ge{y}$ , then  $\lfloor{\frac{N}{x}\rfloor} = y$  would hold, but  $\lfloor{\frac{N}{y}\rfloor} = x$  would not. Thus, there are  $k$  solutions here. In total, we would have   $$ 2\lfloor{\sqrt{N}\rfloor} $$   possible solutions for this case. 

The amount of possible solutions we desire is  $10^{100}$ . Using  $\mod{2}$ , we can quickly eliminate the first case. However, the second case may have some solutions. Indeed, we would have   $$ 2\lfloor{\sqrt{N}\rfloor}=10^{100} $$    $$ \lfloor{\sqrt{N}\rfloor}=10^{99}\cdot{5} $$    $$ 10^{198}\cdot{25}\le{N}<(10^{99}\cdot{5}+1)^2 $$  However, we must consider that for case 2 to apply,  $N\ge((10)^{99}\cdot{5})((10)^{99}\cdot{5}+1)$ . Thus, the set of googlicious numbers consists of   $$ \boxed{((10)^{99}\cdot{5})((10)^{99}\cdot{5}+1)\le{N}<(10^{99}\cdot{5}+1)^2} $$  and we are done.</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Define \(D(N)\) as the number of positive integers \(x\) such that \[\left\lfloor \frac{N}{\left\lfloor \frac{N}{x} \right\rfloor } \right\rfloor = x.\]

Consider the graph of \(f(x) = \frac{N}{\left\lfloor \frac{N}{x} \right\rfloor }.\) It is composed of several segments with different \(y\) coordinates. Each of these segments are determined by when \(\left\lfloor \frac{N}{x} \right\rfloor\) changes. This clearly happens when \(\frac{N}{x}\) is a positive integer, or when \(x = x_k = \frac{N}{k}\) for some integer \(k.\)  Therefore, \(f(x_k) = \frac{N}{\left\lfloor \frac{N}{x_k} \right\rfloor } = \frac{N}{\left\lfloor k \right\rfloor } = \frac{N}{k} = x_k.\) Each \(x_k\) corresponds to exactly one segment (where \(x_{k+1} < x \le x_k\) because \(\left\lfloor \frac{N}{x} \right\rfloor\) decreases when \(x\) is larger than \(x_k = \frac{N}{x}\)). Hence \(f(x) = \frac{N}{k}\) if \(\frac{N}{k+1} < x \le \frac{N}{k},\) where \(k\) is an integer.

This means that \(\lfloor f(x) \rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{N}{k} \right\rfloor.\) As a result, because we are taking the floor, there will be less segments on this graph than on the original graph. Now, suppose that for positive integers \(k_1 \ge k_2,\) \(\left\lfloor \frac{N}{k} \right\rfloor\) has the same positive integer value \(m\) for all positive integers \(k_2 \le k \le k_1.\) Then clearly we must have that this region where \(\lfloor f(x) \rfloor = m\) contains \(\frac{N}{k_1 +1} < x \le \frac{N}{k_1},\) \(\frac{N}{k_1} < x \le \frac{N}{k_1 - 1},\) and so on, up to \(\frac{N}{k_2 - 1} < x \le \frac{N}{k_2}.\) In other words, \(\frac{N}{k_1+1} < x \le \frac{N}{k_2}.\) Now we can arbitrarily set \(m = \left\lfloor \frac{N}{k_2} \right\rfloor\). If there were no integers in the possible values of \(x\) stated above, then \(m\) could not be achieved by any value of \(x.\) Otherwise, consider the largest integer \(z\) in this range. Clearly \(z + 1\) is outside this range, so \(z\)  must be the greatest integer less than \(\frac{N}{k_2}.\) In other words, by definition, \(z = \left\lfloor \frac{N}{k_2} \right\rfloor = m.\) This means that \(m\) lies in this range. Therefore, since \(m\) is a positive integer, there must be exactly one positive integer \(x\) in this range such that \(m = x\). In other words, \(\lfloor f(x) \rfloor = x.\) Hence, the graph of \(\lfloor f(x) \rfloor\), where \(x\) is a positive integer, consists of several segments with different positive \(y\)-coordinates, each of which intersects the line \(y = x\) exactly once.

As we found above, each distinct positive integer value of \(\left\lfloor \frac{N}{k} \right\rfloor\), where \(k\) is a positive integer, corresponds to one segment on this graph, and as we also found above, corresponds to one intersection point, or in other words, one positive integer \(x\) such that \[\left\lfloor \frac{N}{\left\lfloor \frac{N}{x} \right\rfloor } \right\rfloor = x.\] Therefore, we have shown that \(D(N)\) is the number of distinct positive integer values that \(\left\lfloor \frac{N}{k} \right\rfloor\) takes on when \(k\) is a positive integer.

Note that when \(k > N,\) \(\left\lfloor \frac{N}{k} \right\rfloor = 0,\) which is not a positive integer, so we only need to consider the case when \(k \le N.\) Divide this into 2 cases:**Case 1: \(1 \le k \le \lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor .\)** Call the count in this case \(S(N).\) Note that the derivative of \(\frac{N}{x}\) is \(-\frac{N}{x^2},\) which, when \(1 \le k \le \lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor ,\) is less than or equal to \(-1. \) This means that when \(x\) increases by \(1,\) \(\frac{N}{x}\) decreases by more than \(1,\) which clearly changes its floor. Therefore, every value of \(k\) in this range corresponds to one distinct value achieved by \(\left\lfloor \frac{N}{k} \right\rfloor\), so \(S(N) = \lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor,\) which clearly increases when \(N\) is a perfect square.**Case 2: \(\lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor + 1 \le x \le N.\)** Call this count \(L(N).\) Then in this case, by symmetry from the previous case, every single positive integer value of \(\left\lfloor \frac{N}{k} \right\rfloor\) less than or equal to \(\left\lfloor \frac{N}{\lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor + 1} \right\rfloor\) will be achieved. Hence \[L(N) = \left\lfloor \frac{N}{\lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor + 1} \right\rfloor.\] However, we are more interested on when \(L(N)\) increases.

Write \(N = m^2 + n,\) where \(m\) and \(n\) are positive integers and \(0 \le n \le 2m.\) Then \(\lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor = n\), so \[\left\lfloor \frac{N}{\lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor + 1} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{m^2 +
 n}{m + 1} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{m^2 - 1 + n + 1}{m + 1} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor m - 1 + \frac{n+1}{m + 1} \right\rfloor.\] If \(0 \le n \le m - 1,\) then this expression clearly evaluates to \(m - 1,\) since \(m - 1\) is an integer and \(\frac{n+1}{m+1} < 1,\) but when \(n = m,\) the expression evaluates to \(\lfloor m - 1 + 1 \rfloor = m,\) so \(L(N)\) increases when \(n = m,\) or \(N = m^2 + m\) for some positive integer \(m.\)
 
 Therefore, \(D(N) = S(N) + L(N)\) increases only when \(N\) is either a perfect square or an oblong number (a number of the form \(k^2 + k,\) where \(k\) is a positive integer). Additionally, we can compute that \(D(1) = 1\). Now, note that when we arrive at the next perfect square, \(D(N)\) increases by 2, so \(D(k^2) = 2k - 1.\) This means that all positive integer values of \(N\) that are between \(k^2\) and \(k^2 + k - 1,\) inclusive, for some positive integer \(k\), satisfies \(D(N) = 2k - 1.\) Since \(D(N)\) increases when \(N = k^2 + k\) for some positive integer \(k,\) we have that all positive integers \(N\) that are between \(k^2 + k\) and \((k+1)^2 - 1 = k^2 + 2k,\) inclusive, for some positive integer \(k,\) satisfy \(D(N) = 2k.\)
 
 Hence, for all positive integers \(N,\) we have that \(D(N) = 2k - 1\) if and only if \(N\) satisfies \(k^2 \le N \le k^2 + k - 1\) for some positive integer \(k,\) and \(D(N) = 2k\) if and only if \(N\) satisfies \(k^2 + k \le N \le k^2 + 2k\) for some positive integer \(k\).
 
 Now, we come back to the main question. By definition, a positive integer \(N\) is googolicious, if \(D(N) = 10^{100}.\) Clearly \(10^{100}\) is of the form \(2k = 2 \cdot \frac{10^{100}}{2} = 2a\), so \(N\) must satisfy \(a(a + 1) \le N \le a(a + 2).\) Since this condition is necessary and sufficient for \(D(N) = 2a,\) the only googolicious positive integers \(N\) are all of those that are in between \(\frac{10^{100}}{2} \left(\frac{10^{100}}{2} + 1 \right)\) and \(\frac{10^{100}}{2} \left(\frac{10^{100}}{2} + 2 \right),\) inclusive.</details>

Main Claim: A point  $P$  is snug if and only if  $PO+PH\leq R$ , which  $R$  is the circumradius.

Consider the ellipse  $\mathcal{E}$  of points with  $PO+PH=R$ . We claim that this ellipse is tangent to all three sides of the triangle. To do this, we show that over points  $P$  on side  $BC$ , the minimum value of  $PH+PO$  is  $R$ . Let  $H'$  be the reflection of  $H$  over  $BC$ . Clearly,  $PH+PO=PH'+PO$ , which is at least  $R$  with equality when  $P=BC\cap OH'$ . (remember those riddles about someone going out, touching a wall, and then going somewhere else?) Thus, the ellipse is tangent to  $BC$ , and similarly with the other three sides.

To finish the proof, we show that any point outside this ellipse is not snug. Suppose a point  $P$  is outside this ellipse. Let  $\ell$  be a line tangent to the ellipse that separates the ellipse from point  $P$ , and suppose  $\ell$  intersects the circumcircle at  $B$  and  $C$ . By Poncelet's porism, there exists  $A$  on the circumcircle such that  $AB$  and  $AC$  are both tangent to  $\mathcal{E}$ , hence giving a triangle  $ABC$  that does not contain  $P$ , done.

Thus the answer is  $20\pi$ .

stem_md: Suppose that the  $101$  positive integers \[2024, 2025, 2026, \ldots  , 2124 \]are concatenated in some order to form a  $404$ -digit number. Can this number be prime?
solution_md: <details><summary>weird reverse construction</summary>Denote any permutation of the set  $\lbrace 2024,2025,\ldots,2124 \rbrace$  as  $a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_{100}$ . Then the number formed by concatenation of the  $a_i$  can be written as  $\sum_{i=0}^{100} a_i10^{4i}$ . Call this number  $p$ . We will prove that  $p$  can never be prime as it will always be divisible by  $101$ . Consider the number  $$ q=p-209474=p-\sum_{i=0}^{100} i+2024=p-\sum_{i=0}^{100} a_i. $$  Note that  $209474=2074*101$ , so if we can prove that  $q | 101$  too, then  $p | 101$  and thus  $p$  is never prime. But since  $p=\sum_{i=0}^{100} a_i10^{4i}$ , we have that  $$ q=p-\sum_{i=0}^{100} a_i=\sum_{i=0}^{100} a_i10^{4i}-\sum_{i=0}^{100} a_i=\sum_{i=0}^{100} a_i(10^{4i}-1). $$  But  $10^{4i}-1$  is always divisible by  $10^4-1=9999=99*101$ , so  $q|101$  and thus  $p|101$  and  $p$  can never be prime, so the answer is  $\boxed{no}$ .</details>

Let  $a_0,a_1,a_2,\ldots a_{100}$  be a permutation of  $2024,2025,2026,\ldots 2124$  in the order of their appearance from right to left, and let  $N$  be the resulting 404-digit concatenated number.
