This is a pretty instructive problem! I'll try to write how I would motivate this "wishful thinking" approach. Maybe it's an early Christmas vibe :)
Suppose that the $101$ positive integers \[2024, 2025, 2026, \ldots , 2124 \]are concatenated in some order to form a $404$ -digit number. Can this number be prime?
So, we look at this and go: well that's an insanely huge number. If ever it turned out to be a prime, it would be disastrous to verify: after all, the thing is, like, bigger than $10^{400}$ so surely it'll be insane to verify. So it makes sense to try to prove it would always be composite. Even if this line of thinking were to fail, it just generally makes sense to look at divisibility, so why not? Now for it to be composite regardless of how you arrange these four-digit numbers together, is a bit crazy. Surely, we can't find a good way to factor all of these misbegotten permuted digit monstrous numbers. Unless... we don't have to --- that is, there is a common factor dividing them all somehow, or at the very least, a common technique to do so. That would be really wishful, but hey, nothing better to try so far, so why not? Now let's picture what this hypothetical, frankly, too good to be true, would entail. First, we want a common divisor to them all. Second, it needs to have an easily verifiable divisibility test. Third, the divisibility test should respond well to four-digit blocks moving and scurrying around. If we can create such a tool, we would simply need to verify that it works, i.e., the number we conjure divides all of them. So, maybe it's worth asking, what do divisibility tests even look like, before we try finding a yet-to-be-decided make-believe number with vague divisibility properties we want. We know some famous ones: $7, 9, 11$ , and maybe even $13$ , if we are fancy. Notice that all of them have the trend "find the smallest number of the form $k$ such that $10^k \pm 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ and see that the remainder mod $p$ for the number is obtained by (alternating) sums of blocks of $k$ -digit blocks so obtained". If we were to extend this idea, need to find a number $p \mid 10^4 \pm 1$ , just to ensure that the $4$ -digit blocks work out. Now, we ideally want to avoid the alternating sums, as it becomes less clear what sets of remainders across all permutations we can have in that situation, so let us take $p \mid 10^4-1$ . This nicely factors as $9 \times 11 \times 101$ , but each of $9$ and $11$ divide $10^2-1$ , so would actually give $2$ -digit divisibility tests, so the only natural choice is $p=101$ . In that case, because $10^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ , any permuted number $$ N = \overline{a_1a_2 \dots a_{404}} \equiv \sum_{k=0}^{100} \overline{a_{4k+1}a_{4k+2}a_{4k+3}a_{4k+4}} \equiv \sum_{k = 2024}^{2124} k \equiv 0 \pmod{101} $$ so $101$ indeed divides all permuted numbers. Since all of them are obviously bigger than that, it means none of them can be primes, as we originally hoped. Done.**Remark:** Of course, a lot of this would be completely "obvious" to a well-trained student, so the write-up above is probably overly specific and jarring in that sense. But I personally find it interesting how we develop instincts to know that this kind of thing will work, and spontaneously see it, as we improve at problem-solving. Wishful thinking is quite a useful tool sometimes, especially when constructing tools (like coming up with interim lemmas to solve a hard problem or making observations as a necessary backward step that has to be true). I do wonder if writing solutions to problems like this in a wishful-style like the above is actually helpful for intuition, or if it is simply hindsight-writing an instinct that students simply develop over the course of their training, and it makes little sense to try and motivate it. Curious if there are community thoughts on this :)

stem_md:
Let  $n \geq 2$  be a positive integer, and suppose buildings of height  $1, 2, \ldots, n$  are built
in a row on a street. Two distinct buildings are said to be  $\emph{roof-friendly}$  if every building
between the two is shorter than both buildings in the pair. For example, if the buildings are
arranged  $5, 3, 6, 2, 1, 4,$  there are  $8$  roof-friendly pairs:  $(5, 3), (5, 6), (3, 6), (6, 2), (6, 4), (2, 1),$  $(2, 4), (1, 4).$  Find, with proof, the minimum and maximum possible number of roof-friendly
pairs of buildings, in terms of  $n.$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>The minimum is  $\boxed{n-1},$  and the maximum is  $\boxed{2n-3}.$  Let the building heights be  $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots a_n,$  in order of buildings from left to right. 
First, for the minimum, note that consecutive buildings will always be roof-friendly pairs since there are no buildings between them. Since there are  $n$  buildings, there are  $n-1$  pairs of consecutive buildings, so there are at least  $n-1$  roof-friendly pairs. To show a construction of exactly  $n-1$  roof-friendly pairs, consider the permutation  $1,2,3,\ldots n,$  where  $a_i = i$  for all  $1 \leq i \leq n.$  We claim that no two non-adjacent buildings form a roof-friendly pair. To prove this, assume for the sake of contradiction that there exists non-adjacent buildings  $a_x = x$  and  $a_y = y$  with  $x < y$  that are a roof friendly pair. However, note that since  $x$  and  $y$  are not adjacent, there exists some  $z$  such that  $x < z < y$  and thus clearly  $x$  and  $y$  are not a roof-friendly pair, reaching our desired contradiction. Thus, we have proven a construction for the minimum.
 
For the maximum, we start with the following lemma:
\theoremstyle{definition}
\newtheorem*{lemma}{Lemma}

\begin{lemma}
   We say a roof-friendly pair  $(a_x,a_y)$  with  $x < y$  \textit {contains} a building  $z$  if  $x < z < y.$  For any positive integer  $k,$  there exists at most one roof-friendly pair such that the maximum height of the buildings the roof-friendly pair contains is  $k.$ \end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We use contradiction. Suppose we have two roof-friendly pairs  $(a_w,a_x)$  and  $(a_y,a_z)$  such that the maximum building each pair contains is  $a_t = k.$  Note that  $t$  is unique since there is exactly one building of each height. Also, WLOG assume that  $w < y.$  We have the inequality   $$ w < y < t, $$   since both pairs must contain  $a_t.$  However, we must have   $$ a_w > a_y > a_t=k, $$   by the definition of a roof-friendly pair. This contradicts the supposed maximum of  $k$  as the maximum height of any building  $(a_w,a_x)$  contains, because  $(a_w,a_x)$  also contains  $a_y > a_t=k.$  Thus, we have reached our desired contradiction.
\end{proof}
Now, note that the tallest possible building that can be contained is  $n-2,$  since there must exist at least two buildings (forming the roof-friendly pair) taller than all buildings the pair contains. This means the buildings  $1,2,3,\ldots n-2$  are counted as the maximum contained building at most once, so there is an upper bound of  $n-2$  roof-friendly pairs that contain at least one building. Since there are  $n-1$  pairs of consecutive buildings that form roof-friendly pairs (and contain 0 buildings), our total upper bound is  $n-2+n-1 = 2n-3.$  It remains to show a construction for when this upper bound can be achieved. Consider the following arrangement of buildings:   $$ n,1,2,3,4,5,\ldots, n-1. $$   Note that there are  $n-1$  roof-friendly pairs from consecutive buildings. Additionally, we claim that the building with height  $n$  forms a roof friendly pair with all other buildings. To show this, consider a building of height  $k \leq n-1.$  Since the buildings after  $n$  strictly increase in height, the building with height  $k$  is taller than all buildings between  $n$  and  $k.$  Additionally,  $n$  is clearly taller than all other buildings, thus we have shown that the buildings with heights  $n$  and  $k$  form a roof-friendly pair. This accounts for an additional  $n-2$  pairs, bringing the total number of roof-friendly pairs to  $2n-3.$  This proves the upper bound is attainable, and finishes the problem.</details>

<details><summary>solution</summary>We claim that the minimum is  $\boxed{n-1}$  

We have the construction  $1, 2, 3 \ldots n$  which obviously has  $n-1$  roof friendly pairs. There exists no construction with less roof friendly pairs because each of the  $n-1$  pairs of neighbors must be roof friendly. 

We claim that the maximum is  $\boxed{2n-3}$  

We have the construction  $n, n-2, n-4 \ldots 1, 2, 4, 6 \ldots n-1$  if  $n$  is odd, and we have  $n-1, n-3, n-5 \ldots 1, 2, 4, 6, \ldots n$  if  $n$  is even. We can obviously see that this obtains  $2n-3$ . We now claim that this is the maximum. 

Consider a certain number  $a < n-1$ . We consider the number of roof friendly pairs that contain  $a$  and contain a number larger than  $a$ . We can see that there exist at most  $2$  such pairs. 

For the sake of contradiction assume there are  $3$  such pairs, say  $(a, b), (a, c), (a, d)$  where  $b, c, d > a$  Then we would need  $2$  of  $b, c, d$  to lie on the same side of  $a$ . Without loss of generality, let them be  $b, c$  This means that both of  $(a, b)$  and  $(a, c)$  cannot both be roof friendly because either if  $c$  lies in between  $a$  and  $b$  we have contradiction and if  $b$  lies in between  $a$  and  $c$  we have contradiction. 

Thus we have at most  $2n-4$  roof friendly pairs from the first  $n-2$  numbers combined with a larger number. We can see that there just exists one more  $(n-1, n)$  this brings our count to  $2n-3$ . (note  $n-1$  can never obtain  $2$  pairs with greater terms because there only exists one greater term).</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>We will first show that the minimum number of roof-friendly pairs is  $\boxed{n - 1}.$  Let building  $i$  denote the building with height  $i.$ Obviously, every pair of adjacent buildings are roof-friendly, so each contribute  $1$  to the count. There are  $n - 1$  pairs of adjacent buildings, so the number of roof-friendly pairs is at least  $n - 1.$ The equality case requires a bit more care. Arrange all of the buildings in increasing order, from left to right. That is, we arrange the buildings as follows:  $1,2,\dots, n.$  Then if there are two buildings  $i$  and  $j$  with  $|j-i| \ge 2,$  then building  $i + 1$  is in between buildings  $i$  and  $j.$  Since building  $i + 1$  is taller than building  $i,$  the pair  $(i,j)$  is not roof-friendly if  $|j-i| \ge 2.$  Therefore, in this configuration, the only roof-friendly pairs are of the form  $(i,i+1),$  where  $1 \le i \le n - 1.$  There are  $n - 1$  of these pairs, so this configuration attains our minimum  $n - 1.$ Now we will show that the maximum number of roof-friendly pairs is  $\boxed{2n - 3}.$  This part is a bit harder than finding the minimum.

We will first show that equality holds. Arrange the buildings as follows:  $n, 1, 2, 3, \dots, n - 1.$  Obviously, among the last  $n - 1$  buildings, there are  $n - 2$  roof-friendly pairs as proven above, so now we just have to account for the roof-friendly pairs that include building  $n.$  It turns out that the pair  $(n,i)$  is always roof-friendly for  $1 \le i \le n - 1.$  This is because when  $i \ge 2,$  all the buildings in between  $n$  and  $i$  are  $1,2,\dots, i - 1,$  whose heights are less than  $i$  and clearly less than  $n;$  and when  $i = 1,$  the pair  $(n,1)$  is obviously roof-friendly because they are adjacent. There are  $n - 1$  buildings in  $1,2,\dots, n - 1,$  so there are  $n - 1$  roof-friendly pairs that include building  $n.$  This gives a total of  $(n-1) + (n-2) = 2n - 3,$  which shows that  $2n - 3$  is possible.

Now we will prove that we cannot do better than  $2n - 3.$  Assume that there is an assortment of  $n$  buildings of distinct height such that the number of roof-friendly pairs is at least  $2n - 2.$  Call such an assortment  $n$ -\textit{bad}. Consider what happens if we remove the smallest building, the one of size  $1.$  This building is part of at most  $2$  roof-friendly pairs, with the buildings right next to it, since if the buildings  $1$  and  $j$  are not adjacent, then there is a building of size  $k > 1$  in between the two buildings, making the pair  $(1,j)$  not roof-friendly. Therefore, after removing the smallest building, we have an  $(n-1)$ -bad assortment of buildings. If we remove the smallest building from that, we get an  $(n-2)$ -bad assortment. We continue this process until we get a  $3$ -bad assortment with at least  $2(3) - 2 = 4$  roof-friendly pairs. However, the number of roof-friendly pairs is at most equal to the number of total pairs of buildings, which is  $\binom{3}{2} = 3 < 4.$  This is a contradiction.

Therefore, the minimum number of roof-friendly pairs is  $\boxed{n-1},$  achieved with  $1,2,\dots, n$ , and the maximum number of roof-friendly pairs is  $\boxed{2n-3},$  achieved with  $n, 1, 2, \dots, n-1,$  as claimed.</details>

We will show that the maximum possible number of roof-friendly pairings is  $2n-3$  for  $n \geq 2$ , and otherwise  $0$ . 

We proceed by induction with  $n = 2$  as our base case. For  $n = 2$ , there is only one pair of buildings, which must be roof-friendly, so our maximum is  $1 = 2(2) - 3$ .

Assume that for some  $k$ , any configuration of  $k$  roofs has a maximum of  $2k-3$  roof-friendly pairings. We will show that a configuration of  $k+1$  buildings has at most  $2k-1$  roof-friendly pairings. 

Take an arbitrary configuration with  $k$  buildings. Increase the height of each building by one, and observe that the number of roof-friendly pairings is the same. Then, add at some position a building of height  $1$ . Observe that no original roof-friendly pairing is removed, and the only roof-friendly pairings that are added are pairings containing the new building. However, because this building is the shortest building, it can be in a maximum of two roof-friendly pairings (each of which are with adjacent buildings). Thus, there are now at most  $2k-3+2 = 2k-1$  roof-friendly pairings. Finally, we will show that every configuration of  $k+1$  buildings can be reached by incrementing the height of each building of a configuration of  $k$  buildings by  $1$  and adding a building of height  $1$ . This is true because we can reverse the process: remove the building of height  $1$  and decrement every building's height by  $1$  in a configuration of  $k+1$  buildings to achieve a configuration of  $k$  buildings. Thus, the proof is complete.

Here is an example that achieves the value of  $2n-3$ : for even  $n$  put the buildings in the order  $n, n-2, n-4, \ldots, 2, 1, 3, 5, \ldots n-1$ , and for odd  $n$  put the buildings in the order  $n, n-2, n-4, \ldots 1, 2, 4, 6, \ldots n-1$ . 

This works because each of the  $n-1$  pairs of consecutive buildings are roof-friendly pairs, as well as the  $n-2$  pairs  $(2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 5), \ldots (n-1, n)$ .

By arranging the buildings in order of strictly increasing or strictly decreasing height, these  $n-1$  adjacent pairs are the only roof-friendly pairs.

The maximum number of roof-friendly pairs is  $2n-3$ . We prove this via induction.
\vspace{12pt}

\textbf{Base Case:}
Say there are exactly  $2$  buildings. Obviously, there is only  $1$  possible roof-friendly pair, and  $2\cdot2-3=1$ , as desired.
\vspace{12pt}

\textbf{Induction Step:}
Assume that, for  $k$  buildings arranged optimally, there are  $2k-3$  roof-friendly pairs. When adding the  $k+1$  building, it cannot be added between any other buildings, since if it breaks  $x$  roof-friendly pairs, it can establish at most  $x+1$  new roof-friendly pairs, increasing the number of pairs by at most  $1$ *, rather than the optimal  $2$ .

By adding the  $k+1$  building to an edge, we create  $1$  roof-friendly pair with the adjacent building and  $1$  roof-friendly pair with the building of height  $k$ , increasing the number of pairs by  $2$  if the adjacent building and the  $k$ th building are distinct, and by  $1$  otherwise.

Therefore, if the  $k$ th building is on an edge, the  $k+1$  building should be placed on the opposite edge. By induction, if the set of  $k$  buildings were optimal, than building  $k$  must be on an edge and opposite of building  $k-1$ . Since adding the building  $k+1$  to an edge opposite of building  $k$  increases the number of pairs by exactly  $2$ , there are at most
\begin{align*}
    2k-3+2&=2(k+1)-3\text{ pairs},
\end{align*}
as desired.  $\blacksquare$ \vspace{12pt}

*\textbf{Proof:}
Consider an arrangement of  $k$  buildings and pick two buildings to put building  $k+1$  in between of. Let there be  $x$  roof-friendly pairs which pass over this point and call such pairs "cross-pairs" (if buildings  $a$  and  $b$  are roof-friendly and on opposite sides of the space where building  $k+1$  will be added, the pair  $(a,b)$  is a cross-pair). When building  $k+1$  is added, all cross-pairs are "broken" since building  $k+1$  is the tallest.

Notice that, since we are considering any non-edge location for building  $k+1$ , maximizing the number of cross-pairs is equivalent to maximizing the number of roof-friendly pairs in general. Since our induction step assumes our arrangement is optimal, the buildings are always arranged in such a way such that cross-pairs are maximal.

Denote  $a_i$  and  $b_j$ , where  $1\leq i\leq k-1$  and  $j=k-i$ , as the orderings of the heights of all buildings to the right and left of building  $k+1$ , respectively. Here, building  $a_1$  is next to building  $k+1$  and  $i$  increases for  $a_i$  further from building  $k+1$ , and likewise for  $b_j$ . A total of  $$ i+j=k $$  new roof-friendly pairs are formed between building  $k+1$  and the rest of the buildings, which is possible whenever  $r>s\implies a_r>a_s$  and likewise for  $b_j$ . Since our arrangement is optimal,  this is the case and so building  $k+1$  is between those of heights  $1$  and  $2$ .

Without loss of generality, assume that  $a_1=2$  and  $b_1=1$  such that  $a_i=2i$  and  $b_j=2i-1$ . Before building  $k+1$  is added, there are cross-pairs between  $b_1$  and  $a_1$ ,  $a_1$  and  $b_2$ ,  $b_2$  and  $a_2$ , and so on. This accounts for a total of  $$ 2(i-1)+1=2i-1 $$  roof-friendly pairs that are broken when building  $k+1$  is added to the ordering. If  $k$  were even, then  $2i-1=k$ , and, if  $k$  we odd, then  $2i-1=k-1$ . Therefore, by adding building  $k+1$  between two other buildings, we can increase the number of roof-friendly pairs by  $$ k-k=0 $$  if  $k$  is even, and by  $$ k-(k-1)=1 $$  if  $k$  is odd.  $\blacksquare$</details>

We claim that the maximum is  $2n-3$ , let  $a_k=2k-3$  for all  $k<n$ . We use strong induction to prove that  $a_n=2n-3$ . Place building  $n-1$  on the left and  $n$  on the right, then place  $n-2$  in between (optimal compared to not in between). Next, suppose  $x$  are between  $n-1$  and  $n-2$  while  $n-x-3$  are between  $n-2$  and  $n$ . If  $a_n$  is the number of ways, then we have   $$ a_n \leq a_{x+2} + a_{n-x-1} + 1 = 2(x+2)-3 + 2(n-x-1)-3 + 1= 2n-3 $$   for all  $a$ , where we add  $1$  for the roof-friendly pair  $(n-1,n)$ .

<details><summary>big brane sol</summary>The buildings heights are essentially an ordered permutation of the set  $\lbrace 1,2,\ldots,n \rbrace$ . Denote one such permutation as  $\lbrace a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n \rbrace$  where the  $a_i$  are not necessarily equal to  $i$ . Then we can assign each value to a point on the plane. We do this so we can arrange the points equally spaced on a circle. We connect two points with an edge if they form a roof-friendly pair. 

Note that any pair of adjacent integers is considered a roof-friendly pair by definition, so then we connect every pair of points  $(a_i,a_{i+1})$ . This corresponds to drawing all edges of a regular  $n$ -gon except the edge  $a_na_1$ , which gives  $n-1$  edges. This minimum value can be achieved simply when all the values are consecutive in the permutation  $\lbrace 1,2,\ldots,n \rbrace$ , so the minimum number of roof-friendly buildings is  $n-1$ .

Now we take four arbritrary points  $a_w,a_x,a_y,a_z$  such that  $w<x<y<z$ . Then we note that neither  $(a_w,a_y)$  or  $(a_x,a_z)$  can be a roof-friendly pair. This operation corresponds to drawing two edges that intersect. Thus our problem is simply finding the maximum number of diagonals we can draw in an  $n$ -gon without any two diagonals intersecting anywhere other than the vertices (so we consider the edges as diagonals). But this is simply the total number of edges in a triangulation of the  $n$ -gon, which is  $2n-3$ . This maximum value can be achieved by simply moving the  $n$  to the end in the permutation  $\lbrace n,1,2,\ldots,n-1 \rbrace$ , so the maximum number of roof-friendly buildings is  $2n-3$ .</details>

<details><summary>sol</summary>We can see that from Vieta's formula that the given is equivalent to proving that \[ 2a^3 - (x+x^2+x^4+y+y^2+y^4)a^2 + (x^3+x^5+x^6+y^3+y^5+y^6)a - x^7 - y^7\] has  $3$  real roots (call this polynomial  $f(a)$ ). Note that a cubic polynomial can't have  $2$  real roots (nonreal roots come in conjugate pairs). So, we just need to prove that it has  $2$  roots (then the third comes implicitly). 

Notice that the condition for  $x$  and  $y$  is symmetric. That is  $1\leq \sqrt{x} \leq y \leq x^2$  implies that  $1 \leq \sqrt{y} \leq x \leq y^2$ . Thus we can assume without loss of generality that  $x \geq y$ . 

Since  $f$  is continuous we claim that if \[f(0) < 0, f(x) > 0, \text{ and } f(x^2)<0\] hold then we are done. This is because there must be a root between  $0$  and  $x$ , and there must be a root between  $x$  and  $x^2$ . 

\textbf{Case 1:}  $f(0)<0$ This is simple since we know that  $x$  and  $y$  are positive. Thus  $f(0) = -x^7-y^7 < 0$ . 

\textbf{Case 2:}  $f(x) > 0$ We can see that 
\begin{align*} 
f(x) &=  2x^3 - x^3 - x^4 - x^6 - x^2y - x^2y^2 - x^2y^4 + x^4 + x^6 + x^7 + xy^3 + xy^5 + xy^6 - x^7 - y^7  
 &=  x^3 - x^2y -x^2y^2-x^2y^4+xy^3+xy^5+xy^6-y^7  
 &= (x-y)(x-y^2)(x-y^4)
\end{align*}
 We can see that the first term is positive and the last two are negative (or  $0$  which is case  $4$ ). Thus  $f(x) > 0$ \textbf{Case 3:}  $f(x^2) < 0$ We can see that \begin{align*} 
f(x^2) &=  2x^6 - x^5 - x^6 - x^8 - x^4y-x^4y^2-x^4y^4+x^5+x^7+x^8+x^2y^3+x^2y^5+x^2y^6-x^7-y^7  
 &=  x^6 - x^4y - x^4y^2 - x^4y^4 + x^2y^3 + x^2y^5 + x^2y^6 - y^7 
 &= (x-y)(x^2-y)(x+y)(x-y^2)(x+y^2)
\end{align*}
 We can see form our conditions that all of those terms are positive except  $x-y^2$  which is negative (or  $0$  which is case  $4$ ). 

 \textbf{Case 4:}  $f(x^2) = 0$  or  $f(x) = 0$  We can see that if  $f(x) = 0$  then we either have  $x = y$  or  $x = y^2$  (we can't have  $x = y^4$ ). If either of those are true then  $f(x^2) = 0$ . 

 If  $f(x^2) = 0$  then we have  $x = y$ , or  $x = y^2$ . This implies that  $f$  has two roots.</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Define  $f(t) = (t-x)(t-x^2)(t-x^4)$  and  $g(x) = (t-y)(t-y^2)(t-y^4)$  with  $h(t) = \frac{f(t) + g(t)}{2}$ . We will first show that  $h(x)$  has roots  $a,b,c.$  Equivalently, we will show that  $f(t) + g(t)$  has roots  $a,b,c.$  Expanding  $f(t) + g(t),$  we get
\[
f(t) + g(t) = 2t^3 - (x + x^2 + x^4 + y + y^2 + y^4)t^2 + (x^3 + x^5 + x^6 + y^3 + y^5 + y^6)t - (x^7 + y^7).
\]
Thus by Vieta's Formulas and the given conditions,  $h(t)$  has roots  $a,b,c.$ Let  $j(t) = f(t) - g(t).$  We wish to show that  $h(t)$  has  $3$  not necessarily distinct real roots.**Claim:** The roots of  $j(t)$  are  $t_1$  and  $t_2,$  where  $x \le t_1 \le x^2$  and  $x^2 \le t_2 \le x^4.$ *Proof:*We will use the Intermediate Value Theorem. Obviously plugging  $x, x^2, x^4$  into  $f$  will give  $0,$  so we just need to evaluate  $g(x), g(x^2), g(x^4).$  We have that   $$ g(x) = (x-y)(x-y^2)(x-y^4), $$     $$ g(x^2) = (x^2 - y)(x^2 - y^2)(x^2 - y^4), $$   and   $$ g(x^4) = (x^4 - y)(x^4 - y^2)(x^4 - y^4). $$   Let's compare the first two expressions. We are given that  $y \ge \sqrt{x};$  thus squaring both sides, we get  $x-y^2 \le 0.$  If we instead raise both sides to the fourth power, we get  $x^2 - y^4 \le 0.$  Since  $x \ge 1$  (otherwise  $\sqrt{x} \ge x^2$  and  $y$  does then not exist), we also must have  $x - y^4 \le 0.$ Finally, since  $y \le x^2,$  we have that  $x^2 - y \ge 0.$  Therefore, the sign of  $g(x)$  is the same as the sign of  $(x-y) \cdot (-1) \cdot (-1) = x - y,$  while the sign of  $g(x^2)$  is the same as the sign of  $(x-y)(1)(-1) = y-x.$  Since  $x-y$  and  $y-x$  have opposite signs, by the Intermediate Value Theorem,  $j(t)$  has a root between  $x$  and  $x^2$ .

Now let's find the other root by finding the sign of  $g(x^4).$  We already derived that  $x^2 \ge y;$  thus  $x^4 \ge y^2$  and  $x^4 - y^2 \ge 0.$  Since  $y \ge 1$  ( $y \ge \sqrt{x} \ge 1$ ), we also must have that  $x^4 - y \ge 0.$  Finally,  $x^4 - y^4 = (x-y)(x^3 + x^2y + xy^2 + y^3).$  Because  $x^3 + x^2 y + xy^2 + y^3$  is positive (since  $x,y > 0$ ), the sign of  $x^4 - y^4$  is the same as that of  $x-y.$  Therefore, the sign of  $g(x^4)$  is the same as that of  $(x-y)\cdot 1 \cdot 1 = x - y.$  The sign of  $g(x^4)$  is the same as that of  $y-x,$  so by the Intermediate Value Theorem,  $j(t)$ 's other root is between  $x^2$  and  $x^4.$  This proves the claim.

Consequently,  $f(t)$  and  $g(t)$  intersect at two points  $P = (t_1, s_1)$  and  $Q = (t_2, s_2)$  such that  $t_1 < t_2,$   $s_1 \ge 0,$  and  $s_2 \le 0.$  Note that  $h(t)$  also intersects  $f(t)$  and  $g(t)$  at these two points since if  $f(t) = g(t),$  then  $f(t) = \frac{f(t) + g(t)}{2} = h(t).$ Since  $h$  passes through  $P$  and  $Q$  with opposite  $y$  coordinates, by the Intermediate Value Theorem,  $h$  must have a root between  $t_1$  and  $t_2,$  inclusive. Also,  $h$  decreases to  $-\infty$  as  $x \to -\infty.$  Since  $s_1 \ge 0,$  by the Intermediate Value Theorem,  $h$  must have a root less than or equal to  $t_1.$  Similarly,  $h$  must have a root greater than or equal to  $t_2.$  We have found our three roots for  $h,$  so we are done.</details>

Thus $f(0) = -x^7-y^7 < 0$ . \textbf{Case 2:} $f(x) > 0$ We can see that \begin{align*} f(x) &= 2x^3 - x^3 - x^4 - x^6 - x^2y - x^2y^2 - x^2y^4 + x^4 + x^6 + x^7 + xy^3 + xy^5 + xy^6 - x^7 - y^7 &= x^3 - x^2y -x^2y^2-x^2y^4+xy^3+xy^5+xy^6-y^7 &= (x-y)(x-y^2)(x-y^4) \end{align*} We can see that the first term is positive and the last two are negative (or $0$ which is case $4$ ). If either of those are true then $f(x^2) = 0$ . If $f(x^2) = 0$ then we have $x = y$ , or $x = y^2$ . This implies that $f$ has two roots.

Additionally, the product-to-sum and difference-to-product identities are all clearly reversible. This concludes the proof.

The shaded area is  $\frac{IG+JF}{2} \cdot h_2 + \frac{KE+LD}{2} \cdot h_4 + \frac{MC+AB}{2} \cdot h_6,$  while the non-shaded area is  $\frac{IG \cdot h_1}{2}+\frac{JF+KE}{2} \cdot h_3+\frac{LD+MC}{2} \cdot h_5 + \frac{AB \cdot F_1 N}{2}.$  The shaded area is  $l^2 ( (\cos(\frac{\pi}{13})+\cos(\frac{6\pi }{26})+\cos(\frac{10\pi}{26})cos(\frac{12\pi}{26})-cos(\frac{8\pi}{26})+0.5)(\sin(\frac{4\pi}{26}))+(2\cos(\frac{\pi}{13})+\cos(\frac{6\pi}{26}))(\sin(\frac{6\pi}{26})) +(2\cos(\frac{\pi}{13})+2\cos(\frac{6\pi}{26})+2\cos(\frac{10\pi}{26})-\cos(\frac{12\pi}{26}))(\sin(\frac{12\pi}{26})) ),$  while the non-shaded area is  $l^2 (\sin(\frac{\pi}{13}) \cdot \cos(\frac{\pi}{13})+(2\cos(\frac{\pi}{13}) + 2\cos(\frac{6\pi}{26}) + \cos(\frac{10\pi}{26}))(\sin(\frac{10\pi}{26}))+(2\cos(\frac{\pi}{13} )+2\cos(\frac{6\pi}{26}) +2\cos(\frac{10\pi}{26})- 2\cos(\frac{12\pi}{26})- \cos(\frac{8\pi}{26}))(\sin(\frac{8\pi}{26}))+0.25 \cdot \tan(\frac{4\pi}{26})).$  Both of these expressions have a  $l^2,$  so we can divide by  $l^2$ . stem_md: Malmer Pebane's apartment uses a six-digit access code, with leading zeros allowed. He noticed that his fingers leave  that reveal which digits were pressed. He decided to change his access code to provide the largest number of possible combinations for a burglar to try when the digits are known. For each number of distinct digits that could be used in the access code, calculate the number of possible combinations when the digits are known but their order and frequency are not known. For example, if there are smudges on  $3$  and  $9,$  two possible codes are  $393939$  and  $993999.$  Which number of distinct digits in the access code offers the most combinations?

solLet $f(x)$ be the number of possible combinations for the access code given that it has $x$ distinct digits, for all integers $1\leq x \leq 6.$ Clearly, $f(1)=1.$ We claim that $f(n)=n^6-\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \dbinom{n}{i}f(i)\right) $ for all integers $2\leq n \leq 6.$ $$ $$ Proof: $$ $$ Note that the number of ways to have a $6$ digit access code using a given set of $n$ digits is $n^6$ if not all of the digits must be used. We now proceed with complementary counting. $$ $$ Note that since $n$ is an integer $2\leq n \leq 6,$ this means that $n^6$ equals the sum of the number of ways to have a $6$ digit access code using $a$ of the digits in the set of $n$ digits, where $a$ is any arbitrary positive integer less than or equal to $n.$ Note that when $a=n,$ we can only choose one set with $a$ elements that is a subset of our original set of $n$ digits, so the number of $6$ digit access code formable using all $n$ of the digits in the set of $n$ digits is $f(n).$ As such, $f(n)$ is $n^6$ minus the number of $6$ digit access codes that can be formed by only using a proper subset of the original set of $n$ digits. $$ $$ As such, $f(n)$ is equal to $n^6$ minus the number of six digit access codes that can be formed by only using exactly $b$ of the digits in the original set, where $b$ ranges from the integers from $1$ to $n-1.$ Note that for any particular value of $b,$ there are $\dbinom{n}{b}$ subsets of the set of $n$ digits with $b$ digits. Also, for any subset $C$ of the set of $n$ digits with $b$ elements, the number of ways to form a $6$ digit access code using all of the elements in $C$ is $f(b),$ so the number of ways to form a $6$ digit access code using exactly $b$ digits from the subset of the $n$ digits is $\dbinom{n}{b}f(b)$ for all integer $1\leq b \leq n-1.$ $$ $$ Note that a $6$ digit access code cannot be formed without using any digits, so the number of ways to form a $6 $ digit access code by only using digits from a proper subset of the set of $n$ digits is $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \displaystyle\dbinom{n}{i}f(i).$ $$ $$ As such, $f(n)=n^6-\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\dbinom{n}{i}f(i)\right)$ for all integers $2\leq n \leq 6,$ as desired. $$ $$ Now, we can just calculate $f(i)$ for all integers $2\leq i \leq 6.$ $$ $$ We have \begin{align*} f(2)=2^6-\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{1}\dbinom{2}{i}f(i)\right)=64-2&=62, f(3)=3^6-\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{2}\dbinom{3}{i}f(i)\right)=729-3\cdot 62-3\cdot 1=729-189&=540 f(4)=4^6-\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{3}\dbinom{4}{i}f(i)\right)=4096- 4\cdot540-6\cdot 62-4\cdot 1=4096-2536&=1560 f(5)=5^6-\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{4}\dbinom{5}{i}f(i)\right)=15625-5\cdot 1560-10\cdot 540-10\cdot 62-5\cdot 1=15625-13825&=1800 f(6)=6^6-\left(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{5}\dbinom{6}{i}f(i)\right)=46656-6\cdot 1800-15\cdot 1560-20\cdot 540-15\cdot 62-6\cdot 1=46656-45936&=720 \end{align*} $$ $$ As such $\boxed{f(1)=1\text{, }f(2)=62\text{, }f(3)=540\text{, }f(4)=1560\text{, }f(5)=1800\text{, and }f(6)=720},$ so having $\boxed{5}$ distinct digits gives the highest amount of possible access codes.

\end{enumerate}
        We use a different strategy for  $n=4,5,6.$ \begin{enumerate}

stem_md: The incircle of triangle  $ABC$  with  $AB\neq AC$  has center  $I$  and is tangent to  $BC, CA,$ and  $AB$  at  $D, E,$  and  $F$  respectively. The circumcircle of triangle  $ADI$  intersects  $AB$  and $AC$  again at  $X$  and  $Y.$  Prove that  $EF$  bisects  $XY.$
solution_md:
First I thought there was a projective sol, but I gave up so I got the following ill-advised bary solution:
-----
We proceed using barycentric coordinates. Let  $\triangle ABC$  be our reference triangle, so that  $A$ ,  $B$ , and  $C$  have respective unhomogenized barycentric coordinates  $(1:0:0)$ ,  $(0:1:0)$ , and  $(0:0:1)$ .

Define the side lengths  $a=BC$ ,  $b=CA$ , and  $c=AB$ . By Ravi Substitution, we note that  $AE=AF=s-a$ ,  $BD=BF=s-b$ , and  $CD=CE=s-c$ , where  $s$  is the semiperimeter of  $\triangle ABC$  In particular, using the areal definition of barycentric coordinates,   $$ D=\left(\frac{[DBC]}{[ABC]},\frac{[ADC]}{[ABC]},\frac{[ABD]}{[ABC]}\right)=\left(0,\frac{CD}{BC},\frac{BD}{DC}\right)=\left(0,\frac{s-c}{a},\frac{s-b}{a}\right)=(0:s-c:s-b). $$   Similarly, it follows that   $$ E=(s-c:0:s-a) $$   and   $$ F=(s-b:s-a:0). $$   It is also well known that   $$ I=(a:b:c). $$  Now let  $\omega$  be the circumcircle of  $\triangle ADI$ . This must have an equation of the form   $$ -a^2yz-b^2zx-c^2xy+(ux+vy+wz)(x+y+z)=0, $$   for some constants  $u,v,w\in\mathbb{R}$ . Substituting the values  $A=(1:0:0)=(x:y:z)$  into the above, we get that  $u=0$ .

Similarly, we substitute  $D=(0:s-c:s-b)=(x:y:z)$  into the same circle equation to get that   $$ -a^2(s-c)(s-b)+(v(s-c)+w(s-b))(2s-c-b)=0, $$   which simplifies to   $$ (s-c)v+(s-b)w=-a(s-c)(s-b), $$   as  $s=\frac{a+b+c}2$  is the semiperimeter of  $\triangle ABC$ . Finally, substituting in  $I=(a:b:c)=(x:y:z)$  gives   $$ -a^2bc-ab^2c-abc^2+(au+bv+cw)(a+b+c)=0, $$   which simplifies to having   $$ bv+cw=abc, $$   using the fact that  $u=0$  as found previously.

We thus have the system
\begin{align*}
    (s-c)v+(s-b)w&=-a(s-c)(s-b),
    bv+cw&=abc,
\end{align*}
which we solve, say using Cramer's Rule, to get that   $$ (v,w)=\left(-\frac{ac(s-b)}{b-c},\frac{ab(s-c)}{b-c}\right). $$   Plugging in the values of  $u$ ,  $v$ , and  $w$  into the original expression, it thus follows that the equation of  $\omega$  is given by   $$ -a^2yz-b^2zx-c^2xy+\left(-\frac{ac(s-b)y}{b-c}+\frac{ab(s-c)z}{b-c}\right)(x+y+z)=0. $$  Now consider the point  $X$ , which is given to be the second intersection of  $AB$  and  $\omega$ . Note the condition that  $X\in AB$  is given by the determinant condition   $$ \begin{vmatrix}1&0&00&1&0x&y&z\end{vmatrix}=0, $$   as  $A$  and  $B$  have respective barycentric coordinates  $(1:0:0)$  and  $(0:1:0)$ . It thus follows that  $z=0$ .

Hence, we must have that  $X=(x_X,y_X,0)$  for some  $x_X$  and  $y_X$ ; note that  $y_X\neq0$  as  $A\neq X$ . Plugging this into the circle condition, we find that   $$ -c^2x_Xy_X-\frac{ac(s-b)y_X(x_X+y_X)}{b-c}=0, $$   which simplifies to having   $$ cx_X=-\frac{a(s-b)(x_X+y_X)}{b-c}, $$   which further becomes   $$ (c(b-c)c+a(s-b))x_X=-a(s-b)y_X, $$   giving   $$ X=(x_X,y_X,0)=(-a(s-b):c(b-c)+a(s-b):0). $$   Note that this is valid as we are using unhomogenized barycentric coordinates, meaning that  $X\in AB$  is uniquely determined only by the  $\frac{x_X}{y_X}$ .

Similarly,  $Y$  is defined to be the second intersection of  $AC$  and  $\omega$ , so that the condition that  $Y\in AC$  is given by the determinant condition for unhomogenized coordinates   $$ \begin{vmatrix}1&0&00&0&1x&y&z\end{vmatrix}=0, $$   which implies that  $y=0$ . Thus we set  $Y=(x_Y,0,z_Y)$  for  $x_Y$  and  $z_Y$ ; substitution in the circle condition then gives that   $$ -b^2z_Yx_Y+\frac{ab(s-c)z_Y(x_Y+z_Y)}{b-c}=0, $$   which simplifies to having   $$ bx_Y=\frac{a(s-c)(x_Y+z_Y)}{b-c} $$   and thus   $$ (b(b-c)-a(s-c))x_Y=a(s-c)z_Y. $$   Taking unhomogenized coordinates, it then follows that   $$ Y=(x_Y,0,z_Y)=(a(s-c):0:b(b-c)-a(s-c)). $$  Note that the homogenized barycentric coordinates for  $X$  and  $Y$  are then respectively given by   $$ X=\left(-\frac{a(s-b)}{c(b-c)},\frac{c(b-c)+a(s-b)}{c(b-c)},0\right)=\left(-\frac{a(s-b)}{c(b-c)},1+\frac{a(s-b)}{c(b-c)},0\right) $$   and   $$ Y=\left(\frac{a(s-c)}{b(b-c)},0,\frac{b(b-c)-a(s-c)}{b(b-c)}\right)=\left(\frac{a(s-c)}{b(b-c)},0,1-\frac{a(s-c)}{b(b-c)}\right), $$   as  $(-a(s-b))+(c(b-c)+a(s-b))+0=c(b-c)$  and  $(a(s-c))+0+(b(b-c)-a(s-c))=b(b-c)$ . In particular, it follows that  $x_X=-\frac{a(s-b)}{c(b-c)}$ ,  $y_X=1+\frac{a(s-b)}{c(b-c)}$ ,  $x_Y=\frac{a(s-c)}{b(b-c)}$ , and  $z_Y=1-\frac{a(s-c)}{b(b-c)}$ .

Now let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $XY$ . Then  $M$  is the basic average of  $X$  and  $Y$ ; in particular, we have that  $M=\frac{X+Y}2$ , where  $X+Y$  denotes the componentwise addition of homogenized barycentric coordinates. As a result, it follows that
\begin{align*}
M&=\frac{X+Y}2
&=\frac{(x_X,y_X,0)+(x_Y,0,z_Y)}2
&=\left(\frac{x_X+x_Y}2,\frac{y_X}2,\frac{z_Y}2\right)
&=(x_X+x_Y:y_X:z_Y)
&=\left(-\frac{a(s-b)}{c(b-c)}+\frac{a(s-c)}{b(b-c)}:1+\frac{a(s-b)}{c(b-c)}:1-\frac{a(s-c)}{b(b-c)}\right)
&=(-ab(s-b)+ac(s-c):bc(b-c)+ab(s-b):bc(b-c)-ac(s-c)).
\end{align*}

Now note that, by expansion of minors,
\begin{align*}
&\ \ \ \ \begin{vmatrix}-ab(s-b)+ac(s-c)&bc(b-c)+ab(s-b)&bc(b-c)-ac(s-c)s-c&0&s-as-b&s-a&0\end{vmatrix}
&=(-ab(s-b)+ac(s-c))\begin{vmatrix}0&s-as-a&0\end{vmatrix}
&\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ -(bc(b-c)+ab(s-b))\begin{vmatrix}s-c&s-as-b&0\end{vmatrix}
&\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ +(bc(b-c)-ac(s-c))\begin{vmatrix}s-c&0s-b&s-a\end{vmatrix}
&=(ac(s-c)-ab(s-b))(-(s-a)^2)
&\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ -(bc(b-c)+ab(s-b))(-(s-a)(s-b))
&\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ +(bc(b-c)-ac(s-c))(s-c)(s-a)
&=-ac(s-c)(s-a)^2+ab(s-b)(s-a)^2
&\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ +bc(b-c)(s-a)(s-b)+ab(s-b)^2(s-a)
&\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ +bc(b-c)(s-a)(s-c)-ac(s-c)^2(s-a)
&=ab(s-a)(s-b)((s-a)+(s-b))-ac(s-a)(s-c)((s-a)+(s-c))+bc(b-c)(s-a)((s-b)+(s-c))
&=abc(s-a)(s-b)-abc(s-a)(s-c)+abc(s-a)(b-c)
&=abc(s-a)((s-b)-(s-c)+(b-c))
&=0,
\end{align*}
as  $s=\frac{a+b+c}2$  by definition.

Since the three rows in the above determinant   $$ \begin{vmatrix}-ab(s-b)+ac(s-c)&bc(b-c)+ab(s-b)&bc(b-c)-ac(s-c)s-c&0&s-as-b&s-a&0\end{vmatrix}, $$   from top to bottom, are respectively the unhomogenized barycentric coordinates of  $M$ ,  $E$ , and  $F$ , it thus follows that  $M$ ,  $E$ , and  $F$  are collinear. In particular, since  $M$  is the midpoint of  $XY$ , this means that  $EF$  bisects  $XY$ , as desired.  $\blacksquare$

Let  $m$  and  $n$  be positive integers. Let  $S$  be the set of all points  $(x, y)$  with integer
coordinates such that  $1 \leq x,y \leq m+n-1$  and  $m+1 \leq x +y \leq 2m+n-1.$  Let  $L$  be the
set of the  $3m+3n-3$  lines parallel to one of  $x = 0, y = 0,$  or  $x + y = 0$  and passing through
at least one point in  $S$ . For which pairs  $(m, n)$  does there exist a subset  $T$  of  $S$  such that
every line in  $L$  intersects an odd number of elements of  $T$ ?

We say that three numbers are balanced if either all three numbers are the same, or they are all different. A grid consisting of hexagons is presented in Figure 1. Each hexagon is filled with the number 1, 2, or 3, so that for any three hexagons that are mutually adjacent and oriented with two hexagons on the bottom and one hexagon on the top (as in Figure 3), the three numbers in the hexagons are balanced. Prove that when the grid is filled completely, the three numbers in the three shaded hexagons are balanced.

(An example of a partially filled-in grid is shown in Figure 2. There are other ways of filling in the grid.)

**Attachments:**

( $0 \leq k \leq n).$  To illustrate this, the first three rows and the last row have been filled in in the following figure:

Now, we present a claim to simply the problem.
Lemma:
Three not necessarily distinct positive integers  $a,b,c$ , each from the set  $\{1,2,3\}$  are balanced if and only if  $a+b+c \equiv 0 \pmod{3}.$ Proof:
If case: if  $a+b+c \equiv 0 \pmod{3},$  then we see by inspection that either  $a=b=c$  or  $(a,b,c)$  is some permutation of  $(1,2,3)$ . This is exactly what it means to be balanced, as desired.
 
Only if case: If  $(a,b,c)$  is balanced, then either  $a=b=c$  or  $(a,b,c)$  is a permutation of  $(1,2,3),$  by definition. This clearly implies  $a+b+c \equiv 0 \pmod{3},$  as desired.


Define  $S_n$  to be   $$ S_n = \sum_{k=0}^n {n \choose k} a_{n,k}. $$   This leads us to our key lemma.
 
Lemma:  $$ S_n \equiv (-1)^{n}a_{0,0} \pmod{3}, \text{ 
 }\forall n \geq 0. $$  Proof:
We use induction. The base case is trivial ( $n= 0,$  so  $S_n = a_{0,0} \equiv (-1)^{0}a_{0,0} \mod{3}$ ), so we prove the inductive step. Suppose that   $$ S_m \equiv (-1)^{m}a_{0,0} \pmod{3} $$   for an integer  $m \geq 0,$  and we will prove   $$ S_{m+1} \equiv (-1)^{m+1}a_{0,0} \pmod{3}. $$   By the balanced condition in the problem, we write the following  $m+1$  equations relating the  $m$  and  $m+1$  rows (since the statement that three numbers are balanced is equivalent to their sum being divisible by 3, proved above).
\begin{align*}
    a_{m,0} + a_{m+1,0} + a_{m+1,1} \equiv 0  \pmod{3}
    a_{m,1} + a_{m+1,1} + a_{m+1,2} \equiv 0 \pmod{3}
    \cdots 
    a_{m,m} + a_{m+1,m}+ a_{m+1,m+1} \equiv 0 \pmod{3}
\end{align*}
We multiply each equation by  ${m \choose k}$  as follows:

\begin{align*}
    {m\choose 0} a_{m,0} + {m\choose 0}a_{m+1,0} + {m\choose 0}a_{m+1,1} \equiv 0 \pmod{3}
   {m\choose 1} a_{m,1} + {m\choose 1}a_{m+1,1} + {m\choose 1}a_{m+1,2} \equiv 0 \pmod{3}
    \cdots \cdots \cdots\cdots
   {m\choose m} a_{m,m} + {m\choose m}a_{m+1,m}+ {m\choose m}a_{m+1,m+1} \equiv 0 \pmod{3}
\end{align*}
Adding up all  $m+1$  of these equations, we have:
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{k=0}^m {m \choose k} a_{m,k} +{m\choose 0} a_{m+1,0} + \left({m\choose 0}+{m\choose 1}\right)a_{m+1,1}+\left({m\choose 1}+{m\choose 2}\right)a_{m+1,2} + \cdots 
    \cdots +\left({m\choose m-1}+{m\choose m}\right)a_{m+1,m} + {m \choose m}a_{m+1,m+1} \equiv 0 \pmod{3}.
\end{align*}
Using  ${m \choose 0} = 1 = {m+1 \choose 0},$   ${m \choose m} = 1 = {m+1 \choose m+1},$  and Pascal's identity ( ${m \choose k} + {m \choose k+1} = {m+1 \choose k+1})$ , we simply this to 
\begin{align*} 
S_m + {m+1\choose 0} a_{m+1,0}+  {m+1\choose 1} a_{m+1,1} + {m+1\choose 2}a_{m+1,2} + \cdots + {m+1\choose m+1}a_{m+1,m+1} \equiv 0 \pmod{3}
S_m + \sum_{k=0}^{m+1} {m+1 \choose k} a_{m+1,k} 
S_m + S_{m+1} \equiv 0 \pmod{3} 
S_{m+1} \equiv -(1)S_{m} \pmod{3}  
S_{m+1} \equiv (-1)^{m+1}a_{0,0} \pmod{3},
\end{align*}
where the last step follows from the inductive hypothesis.

To finish, note that   $$ S_9 = \sum_{k=0}^9 {9 \choose k}a_{9,k} \equiv (-1)^{9}a_{0,0} \equiv -a_{0,0} \pmod{3} $$   by our key lemma. Also, since 
\begin{align*}
    {9 \choose 1} = {9 \choose 8} = 9 
    {9 \choose 2} = {9 \choose 7} = 36 
    {9 \choose 3} = {9 \choose 6} = 84 
    {9 \choose 4} = {9 \choose 5} = 126,  
\end{align*}
which are all divisible by 3, we have   $$ S_9 = \sum_{k=0}^9 {9 \choose k}a_{9,k} \equiv {9 \choose 0}a_{9,0}+{9 \choose 9}a_{9,9} \equiv -a_{0,0} \pmod{3}, $$   so   $$ a_{9,0}+a_{9,9}\equiv -a_{0,0} \pmod{3} \Longrightarrow a_{9,0}+a_{9,9}+a_{0,0} \equiv 0 \pmod{3}, $$   which is exactly what we needed to prove, since this means that the ``points" of the triangle must be balanced, as desired.</details>

I think it's worthwhile to post my pretty clean solution.

First, we note that three integers  $a,b,c$  whose values are either  $1,2,$  or  $3$  are balanced if and only if  $a + b + c \equiv 0 \pmod{3}.$  Obviously for any integer  $a,$  we have that  $a + a + a \equiv 0 \pmod{3},$  and we also know that  $1 + 2 + 3 \equiv 0 \pmod{3}.$  However, if  $a$  and  $b$  are different, then  $a + a + b \equiv 2a + b \equiv b - a \not \equiv 0 \pmod{3}.$  Hence three numbers whose values are among  $1,2,3$  are balanced if and only if their sum is divisible by  $3.$ Now we can get to the main part of the problem. We will first show that in a 4x4 triangular grid, the numbers in the corners are balanced. Label the numbers in the bottom row as  $a,b,c,d.$  Then mod  $3,$  the numbers in the second row from the bottom are  $-a - b, -b - c, - c - d.$  The numbers in the second row from the top are then  $a + 2b + c$  and  $b + 2c + d$  mod  $3,$  and finally the number at the top is then  $-a - d.$  Since  $a + d + (-a-d) = 0,$  the numbers at the corners of a 4x4 triangular grid are balanced.

Now we return back to the problem of showing that the corners of a 10x10 triangular grid are balanced. Let the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth numbers on the 10th row be  $a,b,c,d.$  Then the first, fourth, and seventh numbers on the seventh row, by the claim, are  $-a-b, -b-c, -c-d$  mod  $3.$  Continuing, the first and fourth numbers on the fourth row are  $a+2b+c,b+2c+d$  mod  $3.$  Finally, mod  $3,$  the number on the top row is  $-a - d$  mod  $3.$  Since  $a + d + (-a-d) = 0,$  we are done.

Solution from *Twitch Solves ISL*: We need the following key observation:**Lemma:** [Known by people who play too much SET] Three numbers $x,y,z \in \{1,2,3\}$ are balanced if and only if \[ x + y + z \equiv 0 \pmod 3. \] Work modulo $3$ and let the bottom row be \[ a_0, \dots, a_9 \] in order. Then the second-to-bottom row (in order) is \[ -(a_0 + a_1), \; -(a_1 + a_2), \; \dots, \; -(a_8 + a_9). \] and the third-to-bottom row is \[ a_0 + 2a_1 + a_2, \; a_1 + 2a_2 + a_3, \; \dots, \; a_7 + 2a_8 + a_9. \] and so on; the pattern is given by binomial coefficients. One can then check the entry in the top row \[ -\sum_{k=0}^9 \binom9k a_k \equiv -(a_0+a_9) \pmod 3 \] since every binomial coefficient $\binom9k$ is divisible by $3$ for $0 < k < 9$ , which implies the result.

stem_md:
Grogg takes an a × b × c rectangular block (where a, b, c are positive integers), paints
the outside of it purple, and cuts it into abc small 1 × 1 × 1 cubes. He then places all the
small cubes into a bag, and Winnie reaches in and randomly picks one of the small cubes.
If the probability that Winnie picks a totally unpainted cube is 20%, determine all possible
values of the number of cubes in the bag.
solution_md:
Without loss of generality, assume that  $a \le b \le c.$  First note that  $a,b,c \ge 3,$  since if any of them were less than or equal to  $2,$  then the prism that Grogg constructs would just be a slab with no unpainted cube at all.

Now, we see that a cube is unpainted if and only if it is part of the interior  $(a-2) \times (b-2) \times (c-2)$  cube inside of the bigger cube. This means that the probability that a cube is unpainted is
\[
\frac{(a-2)(b-2)(c-2)}{abc} = \frac{1}{5}.
\]**Claim:**  $a \le 4.$ *Proof:* Assume otherwise; that is, assume that  $a,b,c \ge 5.$  Then
\[
\frac{(a-2)(b-2)(c-2)}{abc} = \left(1-\frac{2}{a}\right)\left(1-\frac{2}{b}\right)\left(1-\frac{2}{b}\right).
\]
Noting that  $\frac{2}{a} \le \frac{2}{5},$  we see that  $1 - \frac{2}{a} \ge \frac{3}{5},$  and similarly for  $b$  and  $c.$  Therefore,
\[
\frac{(a-2)(b-2)(c-2)}{abc} \ge \left(\frac{3}{5}\right)^3 = \frac{27}{125} > \frac{1}{5},
\]
which is a contradiction.  $\square$ This means that we only need to consider two cases for  $a$ :**Case 1:**  $a = 3.$  Then we need
\[
\frac{(3-2)(b-2)(c-2)}{3bc} = \frac{(b-2)(c-2)}{3bc} = \frac{1}{5}.
\]
Cross-multiplying, we get
\[
5(b-2)(c-2) = 5bc - 10b - 10c + 20 = 3bc.
\]
Subtracting  $3bc$  from both sides and then dividing both sides by  $2,$  we get
\[
bc - 5b - 5c + 10 = 0.
\]
Adding  $15$  to both sides and factoring the left-hand side, we get
\[
(b-5)(c-5) = 15.
\]
Note that  $b - 5 \le c - 5$  from what we assumed at the beginning. Thus there are only four subcases that we need to consider. If  $b - 5 = 1$  and  $c - 5 = 15,$  then  $b = 6$  and  $c = 20.$  This gives a total number of cubes equal to  $3 \cdot 6 \cdot 20 = 360.$  If  $b - 5 = 3$  and  $c - 5 = 5,$  then  $b = 8$  and  $c = 10.$  This gives a total number of cubes equal to  $3 \cdot 8 \cdot 10 = 240.$  If  $b - 5 = -15$  and  $c - 5 = -1,$  then  $b = -10,$  which is absurd. Finally, if  $b - 5 = -5$  and  $c - 5 = -3,$  then  $b = 0,$  which is also absurd. Therefore, this case only gives the values  $360$  and  $240$  for the total number of cubes.**Case 2:**  $a = 4.$  Then we need
\[
\frac{(4-2)(b-2)(c-2)}{4bc} = \frac{(b-2)(c-2)}{2bc} = \frac{1}{5}.
\]
Cross-multiplying, we get
\[
5(b-2)(c-2) = 5bc - 10b - 10c + 20 = 2bc.
\]
Subtracting  $2bc$  from both sides, we get
\[
3bc - 10b - 10c + 20 = 0.
\]
Multiplying both sides by  $3$ , we get
\[
9bc - 30b - 30c + 60 = 0.
\]
Adding  $40$  to both sides and factoring, we get
\[
(3b-10)(3c-10) = 40.
\]
Note that  $3b - 10 \le 3c - 10$  from what we assumed at the beginning, and that both factors are equivalent to  $2$  mod  $3.$  Additionally, since  $a = 4 \le b \le c,$  both  $3b-10$  and  $3c-10$  are positive. This means that there are only  $2$  cases to consider. If  $3b - 10 = 2$  and  $3c - 10 = 20,$  we get  $b = 4$  and  $c = 10,$  giving a cube total of  $4 \cdot 4 \cdot 10 = 160.$  If  $3b - 10 = 5$  and  $3c - 10 = 8,$  we get  $b = 5$  and  $c = 6,$  giving a cube total of  $4 \cdot 5 \cdot 6 = 120.$  Hence this case only gives the values  $120$  and  $160$  for the total number of cubes.

Therefore, the only possible values of the number of cubes in the bag are  $\boxed{\text{120, 160, 240, and 360}}.$

WLOG assume that  $a \leq b \leq c.$  Note that since all of the  $1\times 1\times 1$  small cubes on the sruface of the cube are painted, only the  $1\times 1\times 1$  small cubes on the inside of the larger cube are totally unpainted. This is a cube of dimensions  $(a-2) \times (b-2) \times (c-2).$  Thus, since the probability Winnie selects a totally unpainted cube is  $20\%,$  we have:  $$ \frac{(a-2)(b-2)(c-2)}{abc}  = \frac{1}{5}. $$   We perform casework on  $a.$  Clearly, we require  $a \geq 3$  for at least one cube to be unshaded.

    Case #1:  $a=3.$  We have:
\begin{align*}
    \frac{(b-2)(c-2)}{3bc}  = \frac{1}{5} \Longrightarrow 
   5(b-2)(c-2)  = 3bc \Longrightarrow 
   5bc-10b-10c+20=3bc \Longrightarrow 
   bc - 5b - 5c + 25 = 15 \Longrightarrow 
   (b-5)(c-5) = 15. 
\end{align*}
    Since  $b,c$  are integers we check all factor pairs of  $15: (1,15), (3,5),$  to find possible values of  $b$  and  $c.$  Since we assumed  $b \leq c,$  we get  $(b,c) = (6,20)$  and  $(8,10)$  as solutions. These give the solutions  $3\cdot 6\cdot 20 = 360$  and  $3\cdot 8\cdot 10 = 240.$   Case #2:  $a=4.$  We have:
    \begin{align*}
    \frac{2(b-2)(c-2)}{4bc}  = \frac{1}{5} \Longrightarrow 
   10(b-2)(c-2)  = 4bc \Longrightarrow 
   10bc-20b-20c+40=4bc \Longrightarrow 
   3bc - 10b - 10c + 20= 0 \Longrightarrow 
   9bc - 30b - 30c + 60= 0 \Longrightarrow 
   (3b-10)(3c-10) = 40. 
\end{align*}
    Since  $b,c$  are integers, we check all factor pairs of  $40: (1,40), (2,20), (4,10), (5,8)$  to find possible values of  $b$  and  $c.$  Both factors must be  $2 \pmod{3},$  so only  $(2,20), (5,8)$  give solutions. Since assumed  $b \leq c,$  so we find that we must have either  $(b,c) = (4,10)$  or  $(5,6).$  These give the solutions  $4\cdot 4\cdot 10 = 160$  and  $4\cdot 5\cdot 6 = 120.$     Case #3:  $a \geq 5.$  We have:
\begin{align*}
    \frac{(a-2)(b-2)(c-2)}{abc}  = \frac{1}{5} \Longrightarrow 
    \frac{5(b-2)(c-2)}{bc} = \frac{a}{a-2} \Longrightarrow 
    5\left(1-\frac{2}{b}\right)\left(1-\frac{2}{c}\right)=1+\frac{2}{a-2}.

Since  $a \geq 5,$  the right-hand side is less than or equal to  $1+\frac{2}{5-2} = \frac{5}{3}.$  However, since  $b,c \geq a \geq 5,$  the left hand side is greater than or equal to  $5(1-\frac{2}{5})(1-\frac{2}{5}) = \frac{9}{5}.$  Since  $\frac{9}{5} > \frac{5}{3},$  there are no solutions for this case.

We find bounds on  $a$ ,  $b$ , and  $c$ . 

We have the equation   $$ \frac{20}{100} = \frac15 = \frac{(a-2)(b-2)(c-2)}{abc} = \frac{a-2}{a} \cdot \frac{b-2}{b} \cdot \frac{c-2}{c}. $$  Suppose WLOG  $a \le b \le c$ . Then  $\dfrac{a-2}{a} \le \dfrac{b-2}{b} \le \dfrac{c-2}{c}$ , and in particular we have   $$ \dfrac15 \le \dfrac{a-2}{a} \le \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{1}{5}}. $$   This simplifies to   $$ \dfrac15 \le 1 - \dfrac{2}{a} \le \dfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]{5}}, $$   or   $$ \frac45 \ge \dfrac{2}{a} \ge 1 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]{5}}, $$   or   $$ \frac52 = 2.5 \le a \le \frac{2}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{5}}} \approx 4.817. $$  This bounds  $a$  to be  $3$  or  $4$ . 

If  $a=3$  then we have  $\dfrac35 = \dfrac{b-2}{b} \cdot \dfrac{c-2}{c}$ , and in particular   $$ \dfrac35 \le 1 - \dfrac{2}{b} \le \frac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt5}. $$   So   $$ \dfrac25 \ge \frac{2}{b} \ge 1-\frac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt5}, $$   or   $$ 5 \le b \le \frac{2}{1-\frac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt5}} \approx 8.873. $$  So we have the bounds  $5 \le b \le 8$ . Solving for  $c = 5 \cdot \frac{b-2}{b-5}$  for  $5 \le b \le 8$  only yields positive integers for  $(a,b,c) = (3,6,20)$  and  $(a,b,c) = (3,8,10)$ . 

If  $a=4$  then we have  $\dfrac25 = \dfrac{b-2}{b} \cdot \dfrac{c-2}{c}$ , and in particular   $$ \dfrac25 \le 1 - \dfrac{2}{b} \le \frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt5}. $$   So   $$ \dfrac35 \ge \frac{2}{b} \ge 1-\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt5}, $$   or   $$ 3 \le b \le \frac{2}{1-\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt5}} \approx 5.44. $$  So (recalling  $4 = a \le b$ ) we have the bounds  $4 \le b \le 5$ . Solving for  $c = 10 \cdot \frac{b-2}{3b-10}$  yields positive integers for  $(a,b,c) = (4,4,10)$  and  $(a,b,c) = (4,5,6)$ .

The number of  $1 \times 1 \times 1$  cubes that are entirely unshaded are  $(a-2)(b-2)(c-2).$  The total number of  $1 \times 1 \times 1$  cubes is  $abc.$  Thus we desire all possible values of  $abc$  over the condition  $\tfrac{(a-2)(b-2)(c-2)}{abc}=\tfrac{1}{5}.$  Without loss of generality, assume  $a \ge b \ge c \ge 3$  (observe we may do this as we may permute the values of  $a,b,c$  in our resulting triples to undo the restriction. Also observe this does not affect the number of cubes we put in the bag, since  $abc$  is the same regardless of how  $a,b,c$  are permuted). Note that if  $c \ge 5,$  then 
\begin{align*}
5=\frac{abc}{(a-2)(b-2)(c-2)}&=\left(1+\frac{2}{a-2}\right)\left(1+\frac{2}{b-2}\right)\left(1+\frac{2}{c-2}\right) 
&\le\left(1+\frac{2}{c-2}\right)^3 
&\le \frac{125}{27},
\end{align*}
a contradiction. Thus, either  $c=4$  or  $c=3.$ In the former case, we obtain  $6ab-20a-20b+40=0$  upon substitution. Multiplying both sides by  $3$  and adding  $80$  to both sides, we obtain  $18ab-60a-60b+200=80.$  Factoring the left hand side, we obtain  $2(3a-10)(3b-10)=80 \implies (3a-10)(3b-10)=40.$  Considering factor pairs  $(1,40), (2,20), (4,10), (5,8),$  we find the valid triples  $(a,b,c)=(10,4,4),(6,5,4).$  From these, we obtain possible values of  $abc=160, 120.$ In the latter case, we obtain  $2ab-10a-10b+20=0$  upon substitution. Adding  $30$  to both sides, we have  $2ab-10a-10b+50=30.$  Factoring the left hand side, we obtain  $2(a-5)(b-5)=30 \implies (a-5)(b-5)=15.$  Considering factor pairs  $(1,15), (3,5),$  we find the valid triples  $(20,6,3), (10,8,3).$  From these, we obtain possible values of  $abc=360, 240.$ Thus, we may have  $160, 120, 360,$  or  $240$  cubes in the bag.

stem_md: Let  $\omega$  be the unit circle in the  $xy$ -plane in  $3$ -dimensional space. Find all points  $P$  not on the  $xy$ -plane that satisfy the following condition: There exist points  $A,B,C$  on  $\omega$  such that  $$  \angle APB = \angle APC = \angle BPC = 90^\circ. $$
solution_md:
By far the best problem this year... I have never enjoyed a geometry problem this much

We claim that the answer is  $\boxed{\text{All points on the unit sphere pushed towards the }xy\text{ plane by a }\sqrt{2}\text{ factor}}$ This is equivalent to all triples  $(x, y, z)$  such that  $\boxed{x^2+y^2+2z^2 = 1}$ First view the problem as picking three points  $A$ ,  $B$ , and  $C$ , and then drawing three spheres with centers at the midpoint of  $AB$ ,  $AC$ , and  $BC$  and touching those respective sides. We can see that  $P$  is the intersection of all  $3$  of these spheres. There exist two such points,  $P$ , since the intersection of two spheres (note these spheres are close enough for this to happen) is a circle. The intersection of a sphere and a circle is two points. **Claim 1:**
The projection of  $P$  onto the  $xy$  plane is the orthocenter of  $ABC$ *proof:*First of all, going back to the logic above we can see that the intersection of two spheres is a circle. We can see that the two point of this circle which pass through the  $xy$  plane is the diameter by symmetry. 

WLOG let those two spheres have diameter  $AB$  and  $AC$ . We can see that the other point in the diameter of their intersectional sphere is  $D$  where  $AD \perp BC$ ,  $D$  lies on  $BC$ . Now we can see that the projection of  $P$  must lie on every altitude of the triangle. Thus, it must be the orthocenter. $\square$ Now we simply have to find the distance from the  $xy$  plane of a certain point (this is just  $PH$ ). Let  $H$  be the orthocenter, and  $E$ , and  $F$ , be the feet of the altitudes from  $B$  and  $C$ . We can see that there are exactly two points on the circle with diameter  $AD$  that when projected onto the  $xy$  plane are the orthocenter. Thus, these must be the two  $P$  points we desire. 

We can see that  $\triangle AHP \sim \triangle PHD$ . Thus,  $PH = \sqrt{AH\cdot HD}$  (the choice of  $A$  is not unique). Notice that  $AH \cdot HD = BH \cdot HE = CH \cdot HF = \frac{\text{Pow}(H)}{2}$  Where  $\text{Pow}(n)$  is the power of the point  $n$  with respect to the unit circle. Notice that this is true since the reflection of  $H$  over  $D$ ,  $E$ , or  $F$  lies on the unit circle. 

Let  $O$  be the origin. We can see that  $OH^2 = x^2 + y^2$ , and  $z = \sqrt{\frac{\text{Pow}(H)}{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{1 - OH^2}{2}}$ . Thus we can see that  $x^2 + y^2 + 2z^2 = 1$ , or we can see that the distance must be decreased by a  $\sqrt{2}$  factor for each point.

My solution was very similar to @above. I also utilized the claim he presented (specifically, the foot from  $P$  to the  $xy$ -plane is the orthocenter of  $\triangle ABC$ ). However, instead of using Power of a Point and Similar Triangles, I used the Pythagorean Theorem and a vector bash to show that  $P$  lies on the ellipsoid.

Let  $O$  be the origin and therefore the circumcenter of  $\triangle ABC,$  and let  $H$  be the orthocenter of  $\triangle ABC.$  Then according to the claim, we have  $z^2 = PH^2$  and  $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = OH^2 + PH^2.$  We would therefore like to show that
\[
OH^2 + 2PH^2 = 1.
\]
Now, again by the claim, we have that  $AP^2 = PH^2 + AH^2$  and  $BP^2 = PH^2 + BH^2.$  Adding the two, we get
\[
AP^2 + BP^2 = AH^2 + BH^2 + 2 PH^2.
\]
Since  $P$  lies on  $S_C,$  by the Pythagorean Theorem we know that  $AP^2 + BP^2 = AB^2.$  Thus
\[
AB^2 = AH^2 + BH^2 + 2PH^2,
\]
so
\[
2 PH^2 = AB^2 - AH^2 - BH^2.
\]
Substituting into the equation we would like to show, we now want to show that
\[
OH^2 + AB^2 - AH^2 - BH^2 = 1.
\]
To do so, we will use vectors. Let  $a,b,c$  be the vectors corresponding to  $A,B,C,$  respectively, from the origin. It is well-known that the vector representation of  $h$  is  $h = a + b + c.$  This means that
\[
OH^2 = |a+b+c|^2 = (a+b+c) \bullet (a+b+c) = a \bullet a + b \bullet b + c \bullet c + 2(a \bullet b + b \bullet c + c \bullet a) = 3 + 2(a \bullet b + b \bullet c + c \bullet a)
\]
since the dot product is commutative and distributive, and  $a \bullet a = b \bullet b = c \bullet c = |a|^2 = |b|^2 = |c|^2 = 1.$  We also know that
\[
BH^2 = |h-b|^2 = |a+c|^2 = (a+c) \bullet (a+c) = a \bullet a + c \bullet c + 2 \cdot a \bullet c = 2 + 2 \cdot a \bullet c
\]
and similarly
\[
AH^2 = 2 + 2 \cdot b \bullet c.
\]
Now, 
\[
AB^2 = |a-b|^2 = (a-b) \bullet (a-b) = a \bullet a + b \bullet b - 2 \cdot a \bullet b = 2 - 2 \cdot a \bullet b.
\]
Therefore,
\[
OH^2 + AB^2 - AH^2 - BH^2 = (3 + 2(a \bullet b + b \bullet c + c \bullet a)) + (2 - 2 \cdot a \bullet b) - (2 + 2 \cdot b \bullet c) - (2 + 2 \cdot a \bullet c) = 1.
\]
This concludes our proof that  $P$  lies on the ellipsoid.**Remark:** People who have taken AoPS's Olympiad Geometry class might recognize the claim as a Writing Problem in one of the weeks.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Any point  $P$  lying on the ellipse  $x^2+y^2+2z^2=1$ , but not on the  $xy$ -plane, satisfies the condition.

To begin, let  $Q$  be the foot of the altitude of  $P$  unto face  $ABC$  of tetrahedron  $ABCP$ . We claim that  $Q$  is the orthocenter of  $\triangle{ABC}$ .

To prove this, note that  $AP \perp \text{plane } BCP \therefore AP \perp BC$ , and  $PQ \perp \text{plane } ABC \therefore PQ \perp BC$ . Putting these together, we get  $BC \perp \text{plane } APQ \therefore AQ \perp BC$ ; hence,  $AQ$  is an altitude of  $\triangle{ABC}$ . We then repeat this logic for  $B$  and  $C$  to find that  $AQ, BQ,$  and  $CQ$  are all altitudes of  $\triangle{ABC}$ . Therefore,  $Q$  is its orthocenter.

Next, let  $A=(\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha), B=(\cos\beta, \sin\beta)$ , and  $C=(\cos\gamma, \sin\gamma)$ . We now claim that  $Q=(\cos\alpha+\cos\beta+\cos\gamma, \sin\alpha+\sin\beta+\sin\gamma)$ .

To prove this, let  $O$  be the circumcenter of  $\triangle{ABC}$  and  $G$  be the centroid of  $\triangle{ABC}$ .  $G=(\frac{\cos\alpha+\cos\beta+\cos\gamma}{3}, \frac{\sin\alpha+\sin\beta+\sin\gamma}{3})$  and  $A, B, C \in \omega \therefore O=(0, 0, 0)$ . Using the Euler line of  $\triangle{ABC}$ , we have that  $O, G, \text{ and } Q$  are collinear and  $3OG=OQ$ . Therefore,  $Q=(\cos\alpha+\cos\beta+\cos\gamma, \sin\alpha+\sin\beta+\sin\gamma)$ .

Now, let  $P=(x, y, z)$ . We know  $x$  and  $y$  by knowing the coordinates of  $Q$ . Hence, using the Pythagorean identity:
\[
\begin{split}
x & = \cos\alpha+\cos\beta+\cos\gamma 
x^2 & = (\cos\alpha+\cos\beta+\cos\gamma)^2 
& = \cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta+\cos^2\gamma + 2(\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\cos\gamma+\cos\beta\cos\gamma) 
y & = \sin\alpha+\sin\beta+\sin\gamma 
y^2 & = \left(\sin\alpha+\sin\beta+\sin\gamma\right)^2 
& = \sin^2\alpha+\sin^2\beta+\sin^2\gamma + 2(\sin\alpha\sin\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\gamma+\sin\beta\sin\gamma) 
x^2+y^2 & = 3 + 2(\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\cos\gamma+\cos\beta\cos\gamma + \sin\alpha\sin\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\gamma+\sin\beta\sin\gamma)
\end{split}
\]

Next, we find the vectors between the pair of points  $A$  and  $P$ ,   $\overrightarrow{\rm AP},$  and between the pair of points  $B$  and  $P$ ,  $\overrightarrow{\rm BP}$ :
\[
\begin{split}
\overrightarrow{\rm AP} & = \langle \cos\alpha+\cos\beta+\cos\gamma-\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha+\sin\beta+\sin\gamma-\sin\alpha, z \rangle 
& = \langle \cos\beta+\cos\gamma, \sin\beta+\sin\gamma, z \rangle 
\overrightarrow{\rm BP} & = \langle \cos\alpha+\cos\beta+\cos\gamma-\cos\beta, \sin\alpha+\sin\beta+\sin\gamma-\sin\beta, z \rangle 
& = \langle \cos\alpha+\cos\gamma, \sin\alpha+\sin\gamma, z \rangle
\end{split}
\] $\angle APB = 90° \therefore \overrightarrow{\rm AP} \cdot \overrightarrow{\rm BP} = 0$ . Hence, we have:
\[ \overrightarrow{\rm AP} \cdot \overrightarrow{\rm BP} = 0 \]
\[(\cos\beta+\cos\gamma)(\cos\alpha+\cos\gamma) + (\sin\beta+\sin\gamma)(\sin\alpha+\sin\gamma) + z^2 = 0 \]
\[\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\cos\gamma+\cos\beta\cos\gamma+\cos^2\gamma + \sin\alpha\sin\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\gamma+\sin\beta\sin\gamma+\sin^2\gamma + z^2 = 0 \]
\[1 + \cos\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\cos\gamma+\cos\beta\cos\gamma + \sin\alpha\sin\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\gamma+\sin\beta\sin\gamma + z^2 = 0 \]
\[z^2 = -1 - \cos\alpha\cos\beta-\cos\alpha\cos\gamma-\cos\beta\cos\gamma - \sin\alpha\sin\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\gamma+\sin\beta\sin\gamma \]
\[2z^2 = -2 - 2(\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\cos\alpha\cos\gamma-\cos\beta\cos\gamma - \sin\alpha\sin\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\gamma+\sin\beta\sin\gamma) \]

We now have the following equations:
\[
\begin{split}
x^2+y^2 = 3 + 2(\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\cos\gamma+\cos\beta\cos\gamma + \sin\alpha\sin\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\gamma+\sin\beta\sin\gamma)  
\hspace{0.3cm} 2z^2 = -2 - 2(\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\cos\alpha\cos\gamma-\cos\beta\cos\gamma - \sin\alpha\sin\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\gamma+\sin\beta\sin\gamma)
\end{split}
\]
We sum them to attain  $x^2 + y^2 + 2z^2 = 1$ , giving us the condition which  $P$  is subject to. We must then omit the case in which  $P$  lies on the  $xy$ -plane (these extraneous solutions are generated by the fact that the dot product is still zero even if  $P$  is coincident with  $A$ ,  $B$ , or  $C$  and hence not all angles are defined). This gives us our final result:  $P$  can lie on the ellipse  $x^2+y^2+2z^2=1$  but not on the  $xy$ -plane.  $\blacksquare$</details>

stem_md:
In this problem, a *simple polygon* is a polygon that does not intersect itself and has no holes, and a *side* of a polygon is a maximal set of collinear, consecutive line segments in the polygon. In particular, we allow two or more consecutive vertices in a simple polygon to be identical, and three or more consecutive vertices in a simple polygon to be collinear. By convention, polygons must have at least three sides. A simple polygon is *convex* if every one of its interior angles is  $180^\circ$  degrees or less. A simple polygon is concave if it is not *convex*. 

Let P be the plane. Prove or disprove each of the following statements: $(a)$  There exists a function  $f : P \to P$  such that for all positive integers  $n \geq 4$ , if  $v_1, v_2, \ldots , v_n$  are 
           the vertices of a simple concave  $n$ -sided polygon in some order, then  $f(v_1), f(v_2), \ldots, f(v_n)$  are the 
           vertices of a simple convex polygon in some order (which may or may not have  $n$  sides). $(b)$  There exists a function  $f : P \to P$  such that for all positive integers  $n \geq 4$ , if  $v_1, v_2, \ldots , v_n$  are 
           the vertices of a simple convex  $n$ -sided polygon in some order, then  $f(v_1), f(v_2), \ldots, f(v_n)$  are the 
           vertices of a simple concave polygon in some order (which may or may not have  $n$  sides).

**Part a**: There is such a function. Redefine  $P=\mathbb{R}^2$ . Let  $\mathbb{S}^1$  be the unit circle  $\{(x,y)\mid x^2+y^2=1\}$ . We begin with a claim.**Claim**: There sets  $\mathbb{S}^1$  and  $\mathbb{R}^2$  are in bijection.

*Proof*: It is well-known that there exists a bijection from  $\mathbb{R}^2$  to  $\mathbb{R}$ . This follows since  $$ |\mathbb{R}^2|=|\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}|=|\mathbb{R}|^2=2^{2\cdot \aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}=|\mathbb{R}|, $$  for example. Notice that this means that  $|\mathbb{S}^1|\le |\mathbb{R}|$ , as  $\mathbb{S}^1$  is a subset of  $\mathbb{R}^2$ . Since the cardinality of  $\mathbb{R}$  is equal to the cardinality of  $(0,1)$ , as was famously proven by Cantor, in order to establish our claim, it hence suffices to show that there is an injection from  $(0,1)$  to  $\mathbb{S}^1$ . An example of such an injection is given by  $g: (0,1)\to \mathbb{S}^1$  with  $g(t)=(\sin t, \cos t)$ . Injectivity follows obviously from the fact that  $1<2\pi$ . Therefore  $|\mathbb{S}^1|=|\mathbb{R}|=|\mathbb{R}^2|$ , so there must be a bijection between the two sets.

Now, let  $f$  be some bijection from  $\mathbb{R}^2$  to  $\mathbb{S}^1$ . I claim that  $f$  satisfies the desired property. Any polygon in  $\mathbb{R}^2$  with finitely many vertices  $n\ge 4$  gets mapped to a cyclic  $n$ -gon, which by default is convex (cyclic polygons are convex, all angles are less than  $180$  degrees by inscribed angle theorem). We're done.**Part b**: There is no such function. Assume for the sake of contradiction that there is such a function. Consider the image of the unit circle, let it be some point set  $T$ . We need a lemma which, in combination with the happy ending problem, solve the problem at hand.**Lemma 1**: There exist  $5$  points in  $T$  such that no three are collinear.

*Proof*: The main idea is that the image of an  $n$ -gon inscribed in the unit circle (which is convex) is non-degenerate. Additionally,  $T$  is infinite, because if it were finite then there would be a quadrilateral mapping to a single point (because the unit circle contains infinitely many points, and so some point in  $T$  would get mapped to infinitely many times), a contradiction. Draw lines through every pair of points in  $T$ . If there were finitely many lines, then we may pick four points on one of these lines (since  $T$  is infinite). The preimage of these four points must be convex, as it is inscribed in the unit circle, so this would contradict the assumption. Thus there are infinitely many lines, and we may pick  $5$  points such that no three are on the same line, as desired.

By Lemma 1, there exist  $5$  points in  $T$  such that no three are collinear. Thus, by the happy ending problem, there exists a convex quadrilateral consisting of points in  $T$ . Now, the preimage of this quadrilateral must be a polygon inscribed in the unit circle -- i.e. a convex polygon (with at least  $4$  sides). This is a contradiction, so no such function exists.

Here's an outline for my solution to this problem.
Part a: The answer is yes. For any point  $X,$  draw a ray from the origin to  $X,$  and let  $f(X)$  be the intersection between the ray and the unit circle. Every polygon inscribed in a circle is convex, and it can be shown that every concave polygon will produce at least three distinct points on the circle after applying the function, so this function works.

Part b: The answer is no. Look at a regular pentagon. Every four-tuple of vertices in the regular pentagon form a convex quadrilateral. After applying the function, we'd expect to find five points, no three collinear, for which every four-tuple of them forms a concave quadrilateral (since concave polygons can't have fewer than four sides). This is impossible by happy ending theorem. Therefore such a function can't exist.

<details><summary>Here's the solution sketch I submitted with the proposal. There are probably cleaner approaches to part (b).</summary>(a): **True.** Project everything onto the unit circle (and the origin to  $(1,0)$ ). Any polygon formed by connecting vertices on the unit circle is convex, so it remains to show that the image of the vertices of a concave polygon under this function always contains at least three points (which can then be connected to form a polygon).

Take a concave  $n$ -gon. The convex hull of these points is not an  $n$ -gon, so we can find four vertices of this  $n$ -gon forming a concave quadrilateral. Note that no three vertices of this quadrilateral can lie on a single line. If one vertex of the quadrilateral is the origin, then this means the other three vertices must lie on different angles around the circle, and we're done (since the image is at least a triangle). If no three vertices lie on different angles around the circle, then we must have two vertices lying on each of two radial lines (whose angles don't differ by  $180^{\circ}$ ). But then the original quadrilateral must be convex, contradiction.

(b): **False.** We present a disproof for  $n=4$ . Suppose that  $f$  exists. We claim the image of any  $n$  points must be exactly  $n$  points, by induction: The base case is trivial. suppose this is true for  $k$  points, and consider the image of  $k+1$  points. By the inductive hypothesis, the image of  $k$  of these points, say points  $1$  through  $k,$  must be  $k$  points. If point  $k+1$  gets sent to the same place as point  $i$  where  $1 \le i \le k,$  then points  $i, k+1, x, y$  where  $x, y \neq i$  get set to a triangle, not a quadrilateral, which is a contradiction. In particular, this means there are infinitely many points in the image of the plane.

Among any  $5$  points in general position, there are  $4$  forming a convex quadrilateral: If the convex hull of  $5$  points is a quadrilateral or pentagon, we're done. If it's a triangle, draw the line passing through the two interior points. One half-plane formed by this line must have  $2$  of the other  $3$  points (by Pigeonhole); add those in to the points on the line to get a convex quadrilateral. Hence, if the image of some  $5$  points is  $5$  points in general position, there must be a convex quadrilateral among these points, which means a convex quadrilateral gets sent to another convex quadrilateral, a contradiction.

Finally, if the image of the plane does not have  $5$  points in general position, it must have at most  $4$  points in general position, which means that all the points in the image lie on at most  $\binom{4}{2}=6$  lines. Now, let  $S$  be a point-set composed of a point  $Q$  and all the points at distance  $1$  from  $Q.$  By infinite Pigeonhole (using the claim from the first paragraph), there are infinitely many points in  $f(S)$  lying on one of the  $6$  lines above. Taking  $f(Q)$  along with the image of three points sent to  $S$  gives us a concave quadrilateral which gets sent to either a line or a triangle, a contradiction.</details>

It turns out to actually be the same “number” of points! In set theory there is this notion of cardinality, which is essentially size. For finite sets it’s just the number of elements in the set. However, things get funky when we’re working with infinite sets. The cardinality of two sets are the same if there is a bijection between them. It happens to be true that the cardinality of the natural numbers (which is given the name $\aleph_0$ ) is less than the cardinality of the real numbers (which is $2^{\aleph_0}$ ). Here’s the crazy thing: It’s possible to have two sets $A$ and $B$ such that $A\subset B$ but $A$ and $B$ have the same cardinality (i.e. they can get mapped to each other)! For example, $(0,1)$ and $\mathbb{R}$ have the same cardinality, i.e. they are the same “size of infinity”. There are some very interesting arguments by a mathematician named Cantor to prove this. If you are interested I highly suggest looking at some of his work. Here’s an easy example of this phenomenon: I claim that the even positive integers are the same cardinality as the positive integers. Indeed, there’s a bijection between the two sets: Take the function $f$ from the even naturals to all the naturals defined by $f(n)=n/2$ . An exercise for the reader is to check that this is a bijection.

stem_md:
Lizzie and Alex are playing a game on the whiteboard. Initially,  $n$  twos are written
on the board. On a player’s turn they must either 
       1. change any single positive number to 0, or
       2. subtract one from any positive number of positive numbers on the board.
The game ends once all numbers are 0, and the last player who made a move wins. If Lizzie
always plays first, find all  $n$  for which Lizzie has a winning strategy.
solution_md:
sol hopefully correctWe claim the answer is $\boxed{\text{all positive integer values of }n\text{ such that }n\not\equiv 0 \text{ }(\text{mod }3)}.$ (Note that it can be technically said that $n=0$ works as well since all numbers on a board with $0$ twos does have all of the numbers on the board equal to $0,$ but I will assume that this is not what the problem meant) We proceed as follows. $$ $$ We claim that for any combination of $0's,$ $1's,$ and $2's$ on the board, the player whose turn it is can either guarantee a win, or their opponent can guarantee a win. $$ $$ Proof: $$ $$ Note that any $0's$ on the board do not change the moves that any player can make, and all $0's$ do not change when the game ends, so we just need to prove that for any combination of $1's$ and $2's,$ the player whose turn it is can guarantee a win, or their opponent can guarantee a win. (Note: from now on, we will just discard the $0's$ in combinations. We will also use "combination" and "sequence" interchangeably.) $$ $$ Note that for any sequence of $1's$ with nonzero length, the player whose turn it is can just subtract $1$ from all numbers on the board, so the player whose turn it is can always guarantee a win. $$ $$ We claim that any sequence of $1's$ combined with one $2$ can on the board guarantees a win for one of the $2$ players. We proceed with induction. $$ $$ Note that if there is just one $2$ on the board, the player whose turn it is can just turn it into a $0,$ so if there is just one $2$ on the board, the person whose turn it is can guarantee a win. $$ $$ Assume there is a nonnegative integer $n$ such that for all nonnegative integers $y\leq n,$ if there are $y$ $1's$ and one $2$ written on the board, one of the players can guarantee a win. We claim that if there are $n+1$ $1's$ and one $2$ written on the board, then one of the players can guarantee a win. $$ $$ Note that if the board contains $n+1$ $1's$ and one $2$ , for any move that the player whose turn it is makes, the state of the board will be either a sequence of $1's$ of nonnegative length, or a sequence of $1's$ with a length that is less than or equal to $y$ followed by a $2,$ for which one of the players can guarantee a win. As such, after any move that the player whose turn it is makes, one of the players can guarantee a win.
