If  $i + j = 1$ , the tuples are  $(0, 1), (1, 0).$  Either case is winning by using move  $(1).$  If  $i + j = 2$ , then the tuples are  $(0, 2), (1, 1), (2, 0).$  The first and last can be finished by using move  $(1)$  rendering them winning. For the tuple  $(1, 1)$ , observe that move  $(1)$  will yield the opponent:  $(0, 1)$  or  $(1, 0)$ , and move  $(2)$  will yield:  $(0, 1), (2, 0), (1, 0)$ , all of which are winning states. So  $(1,1)$  is losing. Hence, the base case is resolved. 

Assume that the claim holds for  $\lfloor \frac{i + j}{3} \rfloor \in \{0, 1, \dots, k-1\}$  for  $k \in \mathbb{N}.$ \begin{itemize}
	\item Let  $i + j = 3k$ . First consider pairs \textbf{excluding}  $(0, 3k)$ . If  $j \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$ , observe that we can use move  $(2)$  with  $[i, 0]$  to obtain the pair  $(0, j)$  which is losing by the inductive hypothesis ( $0 + j < 3k$ ). If  $j \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ , then we can use move  $(2)$  with  $[i - 1, 0]$  to obtain  $(1, j)$  which is losing ( $1 + j < 2 + 3k-2 = 3k$ ). Finally if  $j \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$ , we use move  $(2)$  with  $[i, 1]$  to obtain  $(1, j-1)$  which is losing ( $1 + (j - 1)  <3k$ ). 
	
	For the pair  $(0, 3k)$ , the use of move  $(1)$  will result in  $(0, 3k-1)$ , a winning state. The use of move  $(2)$  with arbitrary  $[0, y]$  yields  $(y, 3k - y).$  From the previous cases, no result will be a losing state and we conclude that  $(0, 3k)$  is losing. 
	
	\item Now take  $i + j = 3k + 1.$  As before, if  $j \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$  apply move  $(2)$  with  $[i, 0]$  to get  $(0, j)$  which is losing by the above case and inductive hypothesis. If  $j \equiv 1 \pmod{3},$  then tautologically  $j = 3k + 1$   or  $j \ne 3k+1.$  In the former case, just move  $(1)$  to yield a losing state from above. Otherwise, use move  $(2)$  with  $[i-1, 0]$  to yield  $(1, j)$  which is losing by induction. Finally, if  $j \equiv 2 \pmod{3},$  then apply move  $2$  with  $[i,1]$  to yield  $(1, j-1)$  which is losing by induction.
	
	\item Finally take  $i + j = 3k + 2.$  First consider pairs \textbf{excluding}  $(1, 3k+1)$ . If  $j \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$ , then we can apply move  $(2)$  with  $[i, 0]$  to yield  $(0, j)$ , a losing state by induction. If  $j \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ , then  $i > 1$  from the assumption, so we can move  $(2)$  with  $[i-1, 0]$  to yield  $(1, j)$  which is losing by induction. Finally if  $j \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$ , then we can move  $(2)$  with  $[i, 1]$  to yield  $(1, j-1)$  which is losing by induction. 
	
	Now  $(i, j) = (1, 3k+1).$  Applying move  $(1)$  yields either  $(0, 3k+1), (1, 3k)$ , both of which are winning by the above cases. Using move  $(2)$  yields either  $(1 + y, 3k + 1 - y)$  or  $(y, 3k + 1 - y)$  (based on  $x = 0, 1$ .) In the former case, as  $i \ge 2$ , the cases are all winning from the previous paragraph. All later cases are winning by conclusions in the previous case. Thus  $(1, 3k+1)$  is losing.
\end{itemize}

So we have proven that for  $\lfloor \frac{i + j}{3} \rfloor = k$ , the claim holds. Hence the claim holds for all non-negative integers  $k$ , for all values of  $i + j$ , and so for all pairs  $(i,j).$  

It is clear that Lizzie wins if her starting conditions are winning. By our claim, it is evident that Lizzie wins if and only if  $n \equiv 1, 2\pmod{3}.$</details>

stem_md: During a lecture, each of  $26$  mathematicians falls asleep exactly once, and stays asleep for a nonzero amount of time. Each mathematician is awake at the moment the lecture starts, and the moment the lecture finishes. Prove that there are either  $6$  mathematicians such that no two are asleep at the same time, or  $6$  mathematicians such that there is some point in time during which all  $6$  are asleep.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Ridiculously Overcomplicated</summary>Each mathematician's sleeping period can be considered as an interval  $[s,t)$ , where  $s$  is the moment when the mathematician fall asleep, and  $t$  is the moment when the mathematician wake up.  $s$  and  $t$  could be in arbitrary units, such as seconds, minutes, etc.
We will first sort the mathematicians in the increasing order of the wake up time of their sleeping periods. If two or more mathematicians have the same wake up time, they can be sorted in arbitrary order and the following arguments still apply.
Denote the sorted mathematicians  $a_1, a_2, \dots a_{26}$ , with their respective sleeping interval being  $[s_i, t_i)$ , for all  $i \in \{ 1, 2, \dots 26 \}$ . The wake up time  $t_i$  has the following property since they are sorted.  $$ t_i \leq t_j, 1 \leq i< j \leq 26 $$  All the mathematicians can be partitioned into  $M$  disjoint sets  $G_1, G_2,\dots, G_M$  based on the following process. Each iteration of the process will identify one set of mathematicians. Denote the iteration of the following process by  $n$ , and we want to find a set  $G_n$  during each iteration. The below are the initial values of variables at the beginning of the process, and the values will be updated during each duration. The number of disjoint sets  $M$  is automatically determined when the process terminates.
\begin{align*}
    n&=1 
    S&=\{a_k, 1\leq k \leq 26\} 
\end{align*}
So initially the set  $S$  includes all the mathematicians, and it will be always non-empty until the process terminates. The process is described as below.
1. Since the set  $S$  is non-empty, we can choose the mathematicians who has the earliest wake up time  $t_k$ . So we have 
     $t_k = \min_{a_i\in~S} t_i \label{q4_min_t}$     Note that there could be multiple mathematicians who have the same smallest wake up time. 

    2. Consider the set of all the mathematicians from the set  $S$  who fall asleep before the smallest wake up time  $t_k$ .
     $G_n=\{a_j | s_j<t_k, a_j\in~S\} \label{q4_set_g}$     The mathematician(s)  $a_k$  with the wake up time  $t_k$  is clearly in this set, so this set is nonempty. Note that there could be multiple mathematicians who have the same wake up time  $t_k$ . 
     3. Update the set  $S$  by removing all the mathematicians in  $G_n$  from the set  $S$ .   $$ S \leftarrow S - G_n $$       4. If the set  $S$  becomes empty, all the mathematicians has been partitioned into disjoint sets and this process terminates. Otherwise, the iteration value  $n$  is incremented by 1 and the above process repeats.

Note that every iteration of the process eliminates at least one person from  $S$ . Because  $S$  has finite size, the process must terminate. 
Also notice that every step is taking into account previous iterations. For example, when  $n=2$  and we are on Step 1, the set  $S$  we consider does not have the elements that were eliminated in Step 3 of iteration  $n=1$ . 
When the above process terminates, the number of iterations (the value of  $n$ ) is the number of disjoint sets.\newline\newline**Claim 1**: Assume that there are  $M$  disjoint sets  $G_i~(1\leq i\leq M)$  generated from the above process. For each set  $G_i~(1\leq i\leq M)$ , there is some point in time during which all the mathematicians in the set are asleep}. 
*Proof*: Choose any set  $G_i~(1\leq i\leq M)$ . From the equation above, all the mathematicians in the set  $G_i$  fall asleep before the smallest wake up time  $t_k$ . Consider the mathematician  $a_l$  who is the last person to fall asleep in the set  $G_i$ , so we have  $$ s_l = \max_{a_j\in G_i}s_j $$  If there are multiple such mathematicians, we can randomly choose one. This means that all the mathematicians in the set  $G_i$  fall asleep on or before  $s_l$  and wake up no earlier than  $t_k$ . This follows from the definition of  $t_k$ . We also have  $s_l<t_k$  because of Eq.~(\ref{q4_set_g}). This means that all the mathematicians are ssleep during the interval  $[s_l,t_k)$ , which is an nonempty interval. This completes the proof. $\blacksquare$ **Claim 2**: Assume that there are  $M$  disjoint sets  $G_i~(1\leq i\leq M)$  generated from the above process. If we choose a mathematician with a earliest wake up time from each set  $G_i~(1\leq i\leq M)$ , we will have  $M$  mathematicians. All such  $M$  mathematicians have disjoint sleeping intervals, which means that no two are asleep at the same time.}\newline
*Proof*: In the first set  $G_1$ , there exists a mathematician  $a_{g_1}$  with the earliest wake up time because the set  $G_1$  is generated according to the equations above. There could be multiple mathematicians who has the earliest wake up time, and we can just randomly choose one in that case. Assume that this mathematician has the sleeping interval  $[s_{g_1}, t_{g_1})$ .

Similarly for the set  $G_2$ , there exists a mathematician  $a_{g_2}$  with the earliest wake up time. Assume that such mathematician from the set  $G_2$  has the sleeping interval  $[s_{g_2}, t_{g_2})$ . We must have  $s_{g_2} \geq t_{g_1}$ . I will prove  $s_{g_2} \geq t_{g_1}$  below by using contradiction.

Assume  $s_{g_2} < t_{g_1}$ . So the mathematician  $a_{g_2}$  should belong to the set  $G_1$  instead of the set  $G_2$  based on the equations above. This is contradictory to the condition that the mathematician  $a_{g2}$  belong to the set  $G_2$ . So we must have  $s_{g_2} \geq t_{g_1}$ . $s_{g_2} \geq t_{g_1}$  means that the two sleeping interval  $[s_{g_1}, t_{g_1})$  and  $[s_{g_2}, t_{g_2})$  do not intersect. So the mathematician  $a_{g_1}$  and  $a_{g_2}$  are not asleep at the same time.

By the similar reasoning, all such  $M$  mathematicians with the earliest wake up time in each set have disjoint sleeping intervals, which means that no two are asleep at the same time. This completes the proof. $\blacksquare$ If there exists one set  $G_i$  which has 6 or more mathematicians, there is some point in time during which all these 6 or more mathematicians are asleep according to the Claim 1.
Otherwise if each of the sets  $G_i~(1\leq i\leq M)$  has at most 5 mathematicians, the number of sets  $M$  is at least 6 according to Pigeonhole principle since there are 26 mathematicians. According to the Claim 2, we can choose 6 mathematicians (one from each set with the earliest wake up time) such that no two are asleep at the same time. This completes the proof, as we have shown that always one of the two conditions in the problem is satisfied.  $\blacksquare$</details>

**arfkete** has an absolutely life changing solution to this problem

Suppose that a closet in the lecture room contains five distinguishable pairs of self-cleaning pajamas. Whenever a mathematician falls asleep, they instantly select a pair of pajamas (if available), wear that same pair of pajamas the whole time while sleeping, and instantly return the pajamas to the closet once they wake up. If there are no pajamas left in the closet, the mathematician falls asleep without pajamas.

If a mathematician at any point sleeps without pajamas, that means no pajamas were available, so five other mathematicians were asleep at the moment said mathematician fell asleep, meaning there are, at the moment that that mathematician falls asleep,  $6$  mathematicians sleeping at once, satisfying the condition.

If all mathematicians wear some pair of pajamas during their sleep, then by pigeonhole principle we must be able to select some at least six mathematicians that all wore the same pair of pajamas (If each pair of pajamas were worn by at most five mathematicians, then this would only cover  $5 \cdot 5 = 25 < 26$  mathematicians.) No two of these mathematicians could have been asleep at once since that would imply they were wearing the same pair of pajamas at the same time, which is impossible. Therefore, there are either six mathematicians who were all asleep at once or six mathematicians no two of which were asleep at the same time, as desired.

We can designate one of the individuals in the group of 6 non-overlapping people as the first person to wake up after falling asleep. We use all the time up to  $t_5$  to construct a group of 5 mathematicians. This implies that the latest moment at which the first person in our group of 6 non-overlapping people wakes up is at  $t_6.$  

The second person's latest waking time can occur after 4 other mathematicians have already woken up and 5 people have fallen asleep (including this person). Thus, the second person's latest waking time is  $t_{6+4+5+1} = t_{16}.$ We can apply the same reasoning for the 3rd, 4th, and 5th person in the group, resulting in their latest waking times being \(t_{26}, t_{36}, \text{and } t_{46}\), respectively. After the 5th person in our group of 5 non-overlapping sleepers, there are still 4 people asleep and \(26 - 5\cdot5 = 26 - 25 = 1\) person who hasn’t slept yet. This person, who hasn’t slept, can fall asleep at any time before \(t_{51}\) and wake up any time after falling asleep, but before or at \(t_{52}\). This ensures that we have a group of 6 people whose sleep intervals never overlap.

Since we have maximized the amount of time taken for each new person to be in the set and we still get a set of 6 people when at anything there are not  $6$  people sleeping together, the conditions will always be satisfied.

We aim to prove the contrapositive: If there is no group of 6 mathematicians such that no two are asleep at the same time, then there exists a group of 6 mathematicians who are all asleep at some common point in time.

Assume that it is not possible to select 6 mathematicians such that no two are asleep at the same time. This implies that in any group of 6 mathematicians, there must be some overlap in their sleep intervals. Consider the case where at most 5 mathematicians can be selected whose sleep intervals are disjoint, i.e., no two are asleep at the same time. Beyond this, any additional mathematician must have a sleep interval that overlaps with at least one of the 5. If the contrapositive holds for 5 mathematicians with disjoint intervals, then it will also hold for any smaller number.

This is because, if someone both falls asleep and wakes up within the interval \( [s_i, w_i) \), they are among the original 5 mathematicians by our construction. If a person falls asleep between \( w_i \) and \( s_{i+1} \), they will wake up between \( w_{i+1} \) and \( s_{i+2} \) if they sleep the minimum amount of time. In this case, they are also part of the 5 mathematicians, according to the construction.

Thus, anyone who sleeps between \( w_i \) and \( s_{i+1} \) will wake up between \( w_{i+1} \) and \( s_{i+2} \). This shows that each person falls asleep during one of the following five intervals will wake up in the same interval:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Between the start and \( w_1 \),
    \item Between \( w_1 \) and \( w_2 \),
    \item Between \( w_2 \) and \( w_3 \),
    \item Between \( w_3 \) and \( w_4 \),
    \item Between \( w_4 \) and \( w_5 \).
\end{itemize}

Since all mathematicians in the same group fall asleep during the same time interval, they must have a point in common where they are all asleep simultaneously.

\[
\left\lceil \frac{21}{5} \right\rceil = 5
\]

additional mathematicians. Thus, this group of 5, along with one of the mathematicians from the group of 5 non-overlapping individuals, will form a group of 6 mathematicians who are all asleep at the same time.

Therefore, if there are no 6 mathematicians such that no two are asleep at the same time, then there must be a group of 6 mathematicians who are asleep together.

Thus, there are either 6 mathematicians such that no two are asleep at the same time, or 6 mathematicians such that there is some point in time during which all 6 are asleep. This completes the proof.</details>

First, take the mathematician who goes to sleep the latest. (If there are any ties, choose one of these mathematicians who go to sleep the latest at random. For simplicity, we call mathematician  $a_i$  the \textit{ $i$ th insomniac.} Call a mathematician who is not a insomniac a \textit{light sleeper.} There are thus  $26-k$  light sleepers.

If  $k \ge 6,$  then by definition the first  $6$  insomniacs are such that no two are sleeping at the same time, which satisfies the problem condition, and we are done. Thus assume that  $k \le 5.$ Now let mathematician  $j$  be a light sleeper. We say that they \textit{fall for} the  $i$ th insomniac if they go to sleep before the  $i$ th insomniac falls asleep and after the  $(i+1)$ st insomniac falls asleep. (Mathematician  $j$  falls for the  $k$ th insomniac if they go to sleep before the  $k$ th insomniac.) By definition, every light sleeper falls for exactly one insomniac.

If they wake up before the insomniac falls asleep, then by definition they would have been the  $(i+1)$ st insomniac, which is a contradiction. If they fall asleep after the  $i$ th insomniac falls asleep, then that violates the definition of mathematician  $j$  falling for the  $i$ th insomniac. Thus they fall asleep before the insomniac falls asleep and wake up after the insomniac falls asleep, so we conclude that mathematician  $j$  is asleep the moment when the  $i$ th insomniac falls asleep.

Therefore, the at least five light sleepers who fall for the  $i$ th insomniac are all asleep the moment when this insomniac falls asleep. This gives us six mathematicians who are asleep at the same time.

This is impossible, so there is some set such that all mathematicians in it woke up before the  $i$ th, and we can put the  $i$ th mathematician in that set.

But this is a funny one in that it caves to machinery (albeit machinery we *definitely* don't expect USAMTS competitors to know). Here's the rough ideas behind four different solutions. Most of them rely on reducing to the following "weaker" version:
During a lecture, each of $26$ mathematicians fell asleep exactly once. Prove that there are either $6$ mathematicians such that no two were asleep at the same time, or $6$ mathematicians **such that for each pair of mathematicians, there was some point in time during which both mathematicians were asleep.**
Here's how this strengthens to the original problem: Represent mathematician $i$ 's sleeping time as an interval of real numbers $[a_i,b_i),$ and sort the intervals so that $a_1 \le \cdots \le a_n.$ If there was some point during which mathematician $i$ and $j$ were both asleep, we know that $a_i < b_j$ for all $i$ and $j.$ Hence for any $i$ we know that $a_i \le a_n < b_i,$ so all mathematicians were asleep at time $a_n.$ (You could also say this is Helly's theorem in one dimension, though I didn't think of this before reading through this thread.) - **Solution 1 (elementary):** Build an interval digraph, where there's a directed edge from $i$ to $j$ iff mathematician $i$ 's sleeping time falls entirely before mathematician $j$ 's. Imagine the directed edges were weighted so the "head" of each arrow is heavy, then pick the digraph up by all the vertices with indegree $0.$ If there's a path of length $6,$ there's $6$ mathematicians who slept in sequence, and otherwise there's a "layer" with $6$ vertices (i.e. no arrows between them), so each pair of mathematicians is asleep at some time and you get the weak version above. - **Solution 2 (elementary):** Consider the first mathematician to wake up from a nap. If five other mathematics are asleep that wakeup moment, then we had $6$ mathematicians asleep at once. If not, we have $21$ or more mathematicians who have not yet started their nap. Repeat this argument with these $21$ mathematicians, and if we're not done, do that for the $16$ remaining mathematicians, and so on. Either we'll finish before we get to the end (so there are $6$ asleep at once) or we have $1$ mathematician left at the end, in which case there are $6$ asleep in sequence. - **Solution 3 (machinery):** Apply a version of Dilworth's Theorem to the induced interval poset (where $i \le j$ iff mathematician $i$ 's sleeping time is entirely before mathematician $j$ ) to get the weak version. - **Solution 4 (machinery):** Consider the induced interval graph (where an edge is present iff the corresponding intervals overlap). For interval graphs, $\chi(G)=\omega(G).$ Substituting this into the inequality $\chi(G) \cdot \alpha(G) \geq |G|,$ we get $\alpha(G) \cdot \omega(G) \geq |G|.$ Then $\alpha(G)$ is the largest number of mathematicians whose sleep times didn't overlap, and $\omega(G)$ is the largest number of mathematicians who did (pairwise). If the weak version is false, we know $25 \geq \alpha(G) \cdot \omega(G) \geq 26,$ contradiction.

The intervals of when each mathematician is sleeping can be represented as a closed subinterval of the interval  $[0,1]$ . Let the set of these  $26$  subintervals be  $S$  (if two mathematicians' sleep is represented by the same interval, these are two distinct elements in  $S$ ). Define a poset  $S:=(S,\ \geq)$  (partialy ordered set) on  $S$  as follows:  $I\leq J$  iff either  $I$  and  $J$  are the same element of  $S$  (not only the same interval; recall what we said earlier), or  $I$  and  $J$  are disjoint and there exists  $i\in I$  and  $j\in J$  for which  $i\leq j$ . For example, two elements  $I$  and  $J$  of  $S$  can be the same interval, but there is no relation between them: neither  $I\leq J$  nor  $J\leq I$ . It is easy to verify that this is a poset. Note in particular that any two disjoint intervals are comparable.

A chain in  $S$  is a set of disjoint intervals, which corresponds to a set of mathematicians such that no two were asleep at the same time.

An antichain in  $S$  is a subset  $A\subseteq S$  such that every pair of intervals in  $A$  intersect. For each  $I\in A$ , its minimum  $\min(I)$  exists because  $I$  is a closed interval. We claim that the number
\[
m:=\max_{I\in A}(\min(I))
\]
is in every interval in  $A$ . Suppose  $I\in A$  has  $\min(I)=m$ . Every  $J\in A$  and  $I$  must intersect, so  $m$  must be in their intersection since  $\min(J)\leq\min(I)$ . Thus  $m\in J$  so  $m$  is in every interval in  $A$ .

The above claim is Helly's theorem for  $d=1$ .

Hence, an antichain in  $S$  corresponds to a set of mathematicians such that there was some point in time ( $m$ ) during which all of them were asleep.

If the largest antichain has size  $s$ , by Dilworth's theorem there exists a chain decomposition of size  $s$ . By pigeonhole, one of the chains in this chain decomposition has size at least  $\frac{26}{s}$ . Since either  $s$  or  $\frac{26}{s}$  is at least  $6$ , we are done by the preceding remarks.

To prove this, we will try to use a graphical approach. We can denote each student’s
sleep interval as an interval (or a horizontal segment) starting at the time the student sleeps
and ending at the time the student wakes up. Two students’ sleep schedules intersect if there
is a non-zero length in the intersection between the two segments if they were on a number
line. For the proof, we shall show a system of how we can graph this on a cartesian plane in
an orderly fashion to create a one-to-one correspondence between their sleep schedules and
the graph that should hopefully allow us to see why there will be either 6 mathematicians
such that no two are asleep at the same time, or 6 mathematicians such that there is some
point in time during which all 6 are asleep. First, let us number the students from 1 -
26 in increasing order of the time at which they fall asleep (if there is a tie between 2 or
more people then we can randomly choose the ordering between them). On the cartesian
coordinate system, on the horizontal line y = 1, we can plot the student’s sleep schedule as
a horizontal segment as mentioned above. For example, if the student sleeps from minute
1 to minute 5 (units don’t matter as long as they are uniform), our segment would be the
segment from when connecting the points (1,1) and (5,1). We then move onto number 2’s
sleep schedule. If theirs intersects with the first student if graphed on y =1, we graph theirs
on y = 2 instead so it will be above. If not, it will still be graphed on y = 1. For the every
student afterwards, we graph their segment that represents their sleep schedule on y = 1
if it doesn’t intersect any of the other segments on y = 1, otherwise, we graph on y =2 if
it doesn’t intersect any segments on y = 2, if not we go to y = 3 and so on. In simpler
terms, we work from bottom to top (or create a new line above) and see if the segment can
be placed there without intersecting any other segments. In the end, we should have 26
segments that are graphed so that none of them directly intersect any other segment in the
graph. An example for 5 students and their intervals is presented in Figure 4.1, which is
attached at the end of this problem solution.
There are two properties of this arrangement that I will now show:
The first is the group of students that make up the segments on each of the horizontal
lines (y = 1, y = 2, y = 3, and any of the others) are all a group of mathematicians such that
no two are asleep at the same time. This is because since they are on the same horizontal
line, their sleep schedule segments do not intersect by definition of how we arranged them
and, thus, they never share any moments where two of them are asleep simultaneously.
The second is that the number of horizontal lines, (k where the highest horizontal line
we have a segment on is y = k) show the greatest number of mathematicians you can choose
from this group such that there is some point in time during which all of them are asleep.
To prove this, we must show how the nature of the way we arranged these segments onto
the cartesian coordinates represent this idea. Our arranging of students based on increasing
order of the time they begin sleeping is very crucial for this proof. First, let us prove that
a segment on the highest line must intersect at least one segment in each of the lines below

has a non-zero length of intersection with the segment on the highest line such that the

SolName the mathematicians $1$ , $\ldots$ , $26$ and let their sleeping intervals be $[s_{i}, e_{i})$ . WLOG, assume that $s_{1} \le s_{2} \le \cdots \le s_{26}$ . Now, suppose that we cannot pick 6 mathematicians such that no two were asleep at the same time and 6 mathematicians such that there is some point in time during which all 6 are asleep. Thus, the following claim takes place.**Claim.** For a positive integer $k=1,2,\ldots,21$ , there exists integer $i$ , where $k \le i \le k+5$ , such that the interval $[s_{i}, e_{i})$ lies within the interval $[s_{k}, s_{k+5}]$ , or in other words, $s_{k} \le s_{i} < e_{i} \le s_{k+5}$ . *Proof.* Note that for each $i \ge k$ , $s_{k} \le s_{i} < e_{i}$ . Now, suppose that for each $k \le i \le k+5$ , $s_{k+5} < e_{i}$ . Thus, there exists a point of time $t$ such that $s_{k+5} < t < \min(e_{k}, \ldots, e_{k+5})$ , when 6 mathematicians from $k$ to $k+5$ were sleeping, which is a contradiction. Hence, it follows that there exists such mathematician $i$ that $s_{k} \le s_{i} < e_{i} \le s_{k+5}$ . $\square$ From this claim, it follows that there exists 5 mathematicians whose sleeping intervals fall withing the ranges $[s_1, s_6]$ , $[s_6, s_{11}]$ , $[s_{11}, s_{16}]$ , $[s_{16}, s_{21}]$ , $[s_{21}, s_{26}]$ , so their sleeping intervals do not intersect pairwise. However, there is also mathematician 26 whose sleeping interval $[s_{26}, e_{26})$ doesn't overlap with other 5, so we proved that there are 6 mathematicians such that no two were asleep at the same time. $\blacksquare$ **Addendum.** Even if at some point in time one mathematician wakes up and another falls asleep, say at time point $s_6$ , these intervals do NOT intersect, as the mathematician is already awake at the moment the mathematician wakes up.

stem_md: A regular hexagon is placed on top of a unit circle such that one vertex coincides with the center of the circle, exactly two vertices lie on the circumference of the circle, and exactly one vertex lies outside of the circle. Determine the area of the hexagon.

Let the hexagon be  $ABCDEF,$  and let  $A$  be the vertex equal to the center of the circle. Note that  $AD=2AB>AB\sqrt{3}=AC=AE>AB=AF,$  so  $D$  is the vertex of the hexagon which is farthest away from  $A,$  so  $D$  must be the vertex of the hexagon outside of the circle. Then, the  $4$  vertices of the hexagon not equal to  $A$  or  $D$  are either on the circle or inside it, and since  $AC=AE>AB=AF,$   $C$  and  $E$  are on the circle, and  $B$  and  $F$  are inside it.

Since  $AB=BC,$   $AG=GC=\dfrac{1}{2},$  and  $\angle ABG=\angle CBG=\dfrac{120^{\circ}}{2}=60^{\circ}.$  Thus,  $AGB$  is a  $30^{\circ}$ - $60^{\circ}$ - $90^{\circ}$  triangle, and  $GB=\dfrac{AG}{\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6}.$  Then,  $AB=2GB=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3},$  so by the area formula of a regular hexagon,  $[ABCDEF]=\dfrac{3AB^2\sqrt{3}}{2}=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)^2=\boxed{\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}.$  (This area formula can be proven by splitting the regular hexagon into  $6$  equilateral triangles.)</details>

\newline For D:  $0^2 + (-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}3)^2 = \frac 43 > 1$ .

From this, we can see that B and F are on the inside of the circle, C and E are on the boundary of the circle, and D is outside the circle.

To show the first condition, all we have to do is just apply the distance formula. To simplify our calculations, we note that quadrilateral  $ABCD$  reflects over the x-axis to quadrilateral  $DEFA$ .

From this reflection, we have that  $\overline{AB} = \overline{FA}, \overline{BC} = \overline{EF}, \text{and } \overline{CD} = \overline{DE}$ .

stem_md:
Let  $f(x) = x^2 + bx + 1$  for some real number  $b$ . Across all possible values of  $b$ , find all
possible values for the number of integers  $x$  that satisfy  $f(f(x) + x) < 0$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>probably much longer than it needs to be</summary>We claim the answer is  $\boxed{0,\text{ }1,\text{ and }2}.$  Note that when  $b=2,$  then  $f(x)\geq 0$  for all real  $x$  via the trivial inequality, so  $f(f(x)+x)<0$  for no integers   $x,$  and thus,  $0$  is obtainable. Also, when  $b=3,$  then if  $x$  is an integer such that  $f(f(x)+x)<0,$  then  $f(x)+x$  is an integer. Note that the condition that  $f(y)=y^2+3y+1<0$  for some integer  $y$  is equivalent to the condition that  $\left(y+\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2<\dfrac{5}{4},$  which is equivalent to the condition that  $-\dfrac{3}{2}-\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}<y<-\dfrac{3}{2}+\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2},$  and note that the only integers  $y$  satisfying this are  $-1$  and  $-2.$  Thus, if  $x$  is an integer such that  $f(f(x)+x)<0,$  then  $f(x)+x=x^2+4x+1$  is  $-1$  or  $-2.$  If  $f(x)+x=-1,$  then  $x^2+4x+2=0,$  and  $x$  is not an integer, and if  $f(x)+x=-2,$  then  $x^2+4x+3=0,$  so  $x=-3$  or  $x=-1.$  These both clearly work, so  $2$  is obtainable. Note that when  $b=\dfrac{10}{3},$  then the condition that  $f(y)=y^2+\dfrac{10y}{3}+1<0$  for some real number  $y$  is equivalent to the condition that  $y^2+\dfrac{10y}{3}+1+\dfrac{16}{9}=\left(y+\dfrac{5}{3}\right)^2<\dfrac{16}{9},$  which is equivalent to the condition that  $-\dfrac{5}{3}-\dfrac{4}{3}=-3<y<-\dfrac{5}{3}+\dfrac{4}{3}=-\dfrac{1}{3}.$  Thus, if  $x$  is an integer such that  $f(f(x)+x)<0,$  we have  $-3<f(x)+x=x^2+\dfrac{13x}{3}+1<-\dfrac{1}{3},$  which is equivalent to the condition that  $\dfrac{133}{36}-3=\dfrac{25}{36}<x^2+\dfrac{13x}{3}+1+\dfrac{133}{36}=x^2+\dfrac{13x}{3}+\dfrac{169}{36}=\left(x+\dfrac{13}{6}\right)^2<\dfrac{133}{36}-\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{121}{36},$  which is equivalent to the condition that  $x+\dfrac{13}{6}\in \left(-\dfrac{11}{6}, -\dfrac{5}{6}\right)\cup \left(\dfrac{5}{6},\dfrac{11}{6}\right),$  which is equivalent to the condition that  $x\in(-4,-3)\cup \left(-\dfrac{4}{3},-\dfrac{1}{3}\right),$  and the only integer that satisfies this is  $x=-1,$  which does satisfy  $f(f(x)+x)<0,$  so  $1$  is obtainable.

We now claim that no other possible amounts are possible. We proceed as follows. 

For some real number  $b\in(-\infty, -2]\cup[2,\infty),$  let  $P$  the condition that  $x$  is an integer and  $f(f(x)+x)<0.$  Now, let  $Q$  be the condition that  $f(y)=y^2+by+1<0.$  Note that by the quadratic formula, the roots of  $f(x)$  are  $\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2},$  so  $Q$  is equivalent to the condition that and   $$ f(y)=\left(y-\left(\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}\right)\right)\left(y-\left(\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}\right)\right)<0. $$  Note that since  $\sqrt{b^2-4}>0,$   $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}<\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2},$  we now have that  $Q$  is equivalent to the condition that  $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}<y<\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}.$  

Now, note that  $P$  is equivalent to the condition such that  $x$  is an integer and  $Q$  is true for  $y=f(x)+x.$  As such,  $P$  is equivalent to the condition that  $x$  is an integer and  $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}<f(x)+x=x^2+(b+1)x+1<\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}$ .

As such,  $P$  to be true, we must have  $x^2+(b+1)x+1<\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2},$  so we must have  $x^2+(b+1)x+1+\dfrac{b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}<0.$  Note that by the quadratic formula, the roots of  $x^2+(b+1)x+1+\dfrac{b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}$  are  $x=\dfrac{-(b+1)\pm\sqrt{(b+1)^2-4-4\left(\dfrac{b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}\right)}}{2}=\dfrac{-b-1\pm\sqrt{b^2+2b+1-4-2(b-\sqrt{b^2-4})}}{2}=\dfrac{-b-1\pm\sqrt{b^2+2\sqrt{b^2-4}-3}}{2}=\dfrac{-b-1\pm\sqrt{(\sqrt{b^2-4})^2+2\sqrt{b^2-4}+1}}{2}.=\dfrac{-b-1\pm\sqrt{(\sqrt{b^2-4}+1)^2}}{2}=\dfrac{-b-1\pm(\sqrt{b^2-4}+1)}{2}.$  

Thus, for  $P$  to be true, we must have  $x^2+(b+1)x+1+\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}=\left(x-\left(\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}\right)\right)\left(x-\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2}\right)\right)<0,$  and since  $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}<\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}+1+\sqrt{b^2-4}=\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2},$  this is equivalent to  $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}<x<\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2}.$  

Also, for  $P$  to be true, we must have  $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}<x^2+(b+1)x+1,$  which is equivalent to  $0<x^2+(b+1)x+1+\dfrac{b+\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}.$  By the quadratic formula, the roots of  $x^2+(b+1)x+1+\dfrac{b+\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}$  are  $x=\dfrac{-(b+1)\pm\sqrt{(b+1)^2-4-4\left(\dfrac{b+\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}\right)}}{2}=\dfrac{-b-1\pm\sqrt{b^2+2b+1-4-2(b+\sqrt{b^2-4})}}{2}=\dfrac{-b-1\pm\sqrt{b^2-2\sqrt{b^2-4}-3}}{2}=\dfrac{-b-1\pm\sqrt{(\sqrt{b^2-4})^2-2\sqrt{b^2-4}+1}}{2}=\dfrac{-b-1\pm\sqrt{(\sqrt{b^2-4}-1)^2}}{2}=\dfrac{-b-1\pm(\sqrt{b^2-4}-1)}{2}.$  Thus, for  $P$  to be true, we must have  $0<x^2+(b+1)x+1+\dfrac{b+\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}=\left(x-\left(\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}\right)\right)\left(x-\left(\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}\right)\right).$  

We split this into  $2$  cases.

Case  $1:$    $\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}\leq\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}.$  

Then,  $0<\left(x-\left(\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}\right)\right)\left(x-\left(\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}\right)\right)$  is equivalent to  $x\in \left(-\infty, \dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}\right)\cup\left(\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2},\infty\right).$  Since  $P$  is equivalent to the condition that  $x$  is an integer and  $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}<x^2+(b+1)x+1<\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2},$  it is also equivalent to the condition that  $x$  is an integer and  $x\in \left(\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}, \dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2}\right)$  and  $x\in \left(-\infty, \dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}\right)\cup\left(\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2},\infty\right).$  The last part of this condition is equivalent to  $x<\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}=\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2}-1$  or  $x>\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2},$  so  $P$  is equivalent to the condition that  $x$  is an integer and  $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}<x<\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2}-1<\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2}$  or  $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}=\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}-1<\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}<x<\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2}.$  Since  $\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}\leq \dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2},$  these cannot happen simultaneously, and  $\sqrt{b^2-4}\leq 1.$  Note that since  $\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}\right)-\left(\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}\right)=\sqrt{b^2-4}\leq1,$  at most  $1$  integer can satisfy the second inequality, and note that, for all real  $z,$  if  $z$  satisfies the second inequality iff  $z-1$  satisfies the first inequality. Thus, if  $0$  integers satisfy the second inequality,  $0$  satisfy  $P,$  and if exactly  $1$  integer satisfies the second inequality,  $2$  satisfy  $P,$  so the only possible values that could occur in this case are  $0$  and  $2.$  

Case  $2:$   $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}<\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}.$  

Then,  $0<\left(x-\left(\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}\right)\right)\left(x-\left(\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}\right)\right)$  is equivalent to  $x\in\left(-\infty,\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}\right)\cup\left(\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2},\infty\right).$  Since  $P$  is equivalent to the condition that  $x$  is an integer and  $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}<x^2+(b+1)x+1<\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2},$  it is also equivalent to the condition that  $x$  is an integer and  $x\in\left(\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2},\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2}\right)$  and  $x\in\left(-\infty,\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}\right)\cup\left(\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2},\infty\right).$  Note that the last part of this condition is equivalent to  $x<\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}$  or  $x>\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2},$  so  $P$  is equivalent to the condition that  $x$  is an integer and  $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}=\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}-1<x<\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}<\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}+\sqrt{b^2-4}=\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2}$  or  $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}<\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}+\sqrt{b^2-4}=\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2}=\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2}-1<x<\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2}.$  Note that since  $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}<\dfrac{-b+\sqrt{b^2-4}-2}{2},$  these inequalities cannot happen simultaneously. Note that both inequalities have exactly  $1$  integer solution except when  $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}$  is an integer for the first inequality, which is  $\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2}-1<x<\dfrac{-b-\sqrt{b^2-4}}{2},$  and  $\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2}$  is an integer for the second inequality, which is  $\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2}-1<x<\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2-4}-b}{2},$  since in both inequalities, the difference between the upper and lower bounds is  $1.$  As such, if neither value is an integer, then the number of possible values is  $2,$  if exactly one of these values is an integer, then the number of possible values is  $1,$  and if both of these values are integers, then the number of possible values is  $0.$  Thus, the only possible values for the number of integers satisfying  $P$  that could occur in this case are  $0,$   $1,$  and  $2.$ As such, we have shown that in the case where  $b\in(-\infty, -2]\cup [2,\infty),$  the only possible values that could occur are  $0,$   $1,$  and  $2.$  We now deal with the case when  $b\in(-2,2).$  

Then,  $b^2<4.$  Assume for the sake of contradiction that  $a$  is a real number such that  $f(a)=a^2+ba+1<0.$  Then,  $a^2+ba+1+\dfrac{b^2}{4}-1=a^2+ba+\dfrac{b^2}{4}=\left(a+\dfrac{b}{2}\right)^2<\dfrac{b^2}{4}-1<\dfrac{4}{4}-1=0,$  but by the trivial inequality,  $\left(a+\dfrac{b}{2}\right)^2\geq 0,$  a contradiction, so there exist no real numbers  $a$  such that  $f(a)<0.$  Thus,  $f(f(x)+x)<0$  for  $0$  integers  $x,$  and as such, if  $b\in(-2,2),$  there are  $0$  possible integer values of  $x.$  

Thus, we have shown that  $0,$   $1,$  and  $2$  are achievable, and we have shown that no other values are possible, as desired.  $\Box$</details>

Let  $p$  and  $q$  be the roots of  $f.$  Note that  $g(x)=f(f(x)+x)$  is a quartic.

\bigskip
\textbf{Claim:} The (not necessarily distinct) roots of  $g$  are  $p,q,p-1,q-1.$  $\textit{Proof:}$  

Because  $g$  is a quartic,  $g$  has at most four roots. We therefore must prove that  $g(p)=g(q)=g(p-1)=g(q-1)=0.$  
The first two are easy; we have:
\begin{align*}
g(p)&=f(f(p)+p)
&=f(0+p)
&=f(p)
&=0
\end{align*}
 and similarly for  $q.$  For  $p-1,$  we have:
 \begin{align*}
    g(p-1)&=f(f(p-1)+p-1)
    &=f((p-1)^2+b(p-1)+1+p-1)
    &=f(p^2-2p+1+bp-b+1 +p-1)
    &=f(p^2+bp+1-2p-b+1+p-1)
    &=f(-p-b)
    &=(p+b)^2+b(-p-b)+1
    &=p^2+2pb+b^2-pb-b^2+1
    &=p^2+pb+1
    &=0.
 \end{align*}
 A similar process works for  $q-1$  as well, so we are done.  $\blacksquare$ \bigskip

We now only have to consider a few cases. For each of these, without loss of generality let  $p\geq q.$ \bigskip

\textbf{Case 1:}  $p=q.$ By Vieta's formulas,  $pq =1,$  and thus  $p=q=\pm1.$  This means either  $f(x)=(x+1)^2,$  or  $f(x)=(x-1)^2.$  However, then by the trivial inequality,  $f(k)\geq0$  in both cases for all real  $k,$  and thus  $f(f(x)+x)\geq0$  for all  $x$  in this case, so there are  $\boxed{0}$  integer solutions to  $g(x)<0$  here.
\newpage
\textbf{Case 2:}  $p=q+1.$  Again, Vieta yields  $pq=1,$  so  $q(q+1)=1.$  Solving this quadratic yields  $q=\tfrac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2},$  so  $p=\tfrac{\sqrt{5}+1}{2},$  and thus  $f(x)=x^2-x\sqrt{5}+1$  in this case. 

 Now, because  $x^4$  dominates the rest of the terms in  $g,$  we have that  $g(x)$  is monotonically decreasing until it's first root, and monotonically increasing past it's last root. Thus, the only time  $g$  could be negative is between it's largest and smallest roots, which are  $q-1=\tfrac{\sqrt5-3}{2}\approx=-0.3$  and  $p=\tfrac{\sqrt5+1}{2}\approx1.6.$  The only integers in this range are  $0$  and  $1.$  One can check that  $g(0),g(1)<0,$  so there are  $\boxed{2}$  integer solutions to  $g(x)<0$  in this case.
\bigskip

 \textbf{Case 3:}  $p\neq q$  and  $p\neq q+1.$  

 Because there are no double roots in this case,  $g(x)$  is never tangent to the  $x$ -axis, so each time it intersects the  $x$ -axis it changes it's sign. Similar reasoning to case  $2$  yields that  $g(x)$  will be negative on the intervals  $(q-1,q)$  and  $(p-1,p).$  Now, both of   $p$  and  $q$  can not be integers, otherwise  $p=q$  because  $pq=1.$  If one of them is an integer, there will be no integers in it's respective interval, however the other root of  $f$  will have an integer solution in it's interval. There would be  $\boxed{1}$  integer solution to  $g(x)<0$  in this case.

 Otherwise, both of  $p$  and  $q$  are not integers, so there is an integer solution in each of their intervals, yielding  $\boxed{2}$  integer solutions to  $g(x)<2$  here.
\bigskip

In summary, there are  $\boxed{0,1,\text{or } 2}$  integer solutions for  $g(x)<0.$   $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
A sequence of integers  $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k$  is called fibtastic if the difference between any two consecutive elements in the sequence is a Fibonacci number.

The integers from  $1$  to  $2024$  are split into two groups, each written in increasing order.
Group A is  $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_m$  and Group B is  $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n.$ Find the largest integer  $M$  such that we can guarantee that we can pick  $M$  consecutive elements from either Group A or Group B which form a fibtastic sequence.

As an illustrative example, if a group of numbers is  $2, 4, 11, 12, 13, 16, 18, 27, 29, 30,$  the
longest fibtastic sequence is  $11, 12, 13, 16, 18,$  which has length  $5.$
solution_md:
<details><summary>hopefully my abuse of jargon isn't going to get docked</summary>(We will refer to group  $A$  as  $A,$  and group  $B$  as  $B.$  We will also refer to  $A$  and  $B$  as  $\textit{sets};$  assume these sets are always listed in increasing order so that  $\{4,1434,5,2\}$  is not a valid set, for example. For this reason, we will use ``set" and ``sequence" interchangebly.)

We claim the answer is  $\boxed{3}.$ We first show that it is obtainable for  $3$  to be the largest value of  $M$  for some  $A,$   $B.$ Consider the scenario when  $A$  is the set of positive integers less than or equal to  $2024$  which have residues modulo- $6$  in the set  $\{1,2,3\},$  and  $B$  is the set of positive integers less than or equal to  $2024$  which have residues modulo- $6$  in the set  $\{4,5,0\},$  so  $A$  is the sequence  $\{1,2,3,7,8,9,\dots, 2023, 2024\}$  and  $B$  is the set  $\{4,5,6,10,11,12,\dots, 2020, 2021, 2022\}.$  Clearly,  $A\cup B=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,\cdots, 2022,2023,2024\},$  and  $A$  and  $B$  do not share any elements, so this is a valid partition.

Clearly, it is possible to obtain  $3$  by choosing the set  $\{1,2,3\}$  from  $A.$  We now claim that getting bigger than  $3$  is impossible.

Proof:

Note that after any  $0\pmod{3}$  number in either set, the next number is  $4$  above it, which is not a Fibonacci number. Also, before any  $1\pmod{3}$  number in either set, the number before it is  $4$  below it.

Now, assume for the sake of contradiction that it is possible to get a set with  $4$  elements from consecutive terms in either  $A$  or  $B$  that is fibtastic. Then, both of the middle  $2$  terms of the set must be  $2\pmod{3},$  or else there would be a difference of  $4$  between consecutive terms of the set, but since a  $2\pmod{3}$  term in both  $A$  and  $B$  must be immediately preceded by a  $1\pmod{3}$  term and immediately followed by a  $0\pmod{3}$  term, this is impossible, a contradiction. 

As such, it is impossible to get a set with  $4$  elements from consecutive terms in either  $A$  or  $B$  that is fibtastic, so it is impossible to get a set with more than  $4$  elements from consecutive terms in either  $A$  or  $B$  that is fibtastic, and the desired claim follows. 

Thus,  $3$  is obtainable for the largest possible value of  $M$  for some  $A,$   $B.$ We now show that, for all partitions into  $2$  sets  $A,$   $B,$  that  $3$  is achievable.

Assume for the sake of contradiction that there exists a partition into  $2$  sets  $A,$   $B$  such that  $3$  is not obtainable. Also, WLOG, let  $2\in A.$ We have  $2$  cases:  $1\in A$  or  $1\in B.$ Case  $1:$   $1\in A.$ Then, if  $3\in A,$  we can choose  $\{1,2,3\}$  from  $A$  to get a fibtastic sequence of length  $3$  from  $A,$  a contradiction, so  $3\in B.$  Similarly, if  $4\in A,$  then we can choose  $\{1,2,4\}$  from  $A$  to get a fibtastic sequence of length  $3$  from  $A,$  so  $4\in B.$  Also, if  $5\in A,$  then we can choose  $\{1,2,5\}$  from  $A$  to get a fibtastic sequence of length  $3$  from  $A,$  so  $5\in B,$  but then we can choose  $\{3,4,5\}$  from  $B$  to get a fibtastic sequence of length  $3,$  a contradiction, so it is impossible to have  $3$  be unobtainable in this case.

Case  $2:$   $1\in B.$  

We now have  $2$  subcases:  $3\in A$  and  $3\in B.$  

Subcase  $1:$   $3\in A.$  

Then, if  $4\in A,$  then we can choose  $\{2,3,4\}$  from  $A$  to get a fibtastic sequence of length  $3,$  a contradiction, so  $4\in B.$  Then, if  $5\in A,$  then we can choose  $\{2,3,5\}$  from  $A$  to get a fibtastic sequence of length  $3,$  so  $5\in B.$  Thus, we can choose  $\{1,4,5\}$  from  $B$  to get a fibtastic sequence of length  $3$  from  $B,$  a contradiction, so it is impossible to have  $3$  be unobtainable in this case.

Subcase  $3:$   $3\in B.$ Then, if  $4\in B,$  then we can choose  $\{1,3,4\}$  from  $B$  to get a fibtastic sequence of length  $3,$  a contradiction, so  $4\in A.$  Also, if  $5\in B,$  then we can choose  $\{1,3,5\}$  from set  $B$  to get a fibtastic sequence of length  $3,$  so  $5\in A,$  but then we can choose  $\{2,4,5\}$  from  $A$  to get a fibtastic sequence of length  $3,$  a contradiction, so it is impossible to have  $3$  be unobtainable in this case.

Thus, it is impossible for  $3$  to be unobtainable in any cases, and thus  $3$  is always obtainable, and thus, the answer is  $3,$  as desired.  $\Box$</details>

Can someone check this?The answer is $3$ . We first show that there is a possible way to pick three consecutive elements from Group $A$ or Group $B$ such that they form a fibtastic series. Consider all the numbers congruent to $1, 2, $ or $3 \mod 6$ in the range from $1$ to $2024$ , and let these be in Group $A$ . Likewise, all the numbers congruent to $4, 5,$ or $0 \mod 6$ should be in Group $B$ . For illustration, Group $A$ would have elements $1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9...2023, 2024$ , and Group $B$ would have elements $4, 5, 6, 10, 11, 12...2020, 2021, 2022$ . Observe that in Group $A$ , the longest fibtastic sequence that we could have would have length $3$ as if we include two elements with a difference of $4$ , then the sequence would not be fibtastic. The same reasoning applies to Group $B$ . Thus, the maximum length of a fibtastic sequence with these groupings is $3$ , showing that it is achievable. This same grouping also shows that the maximum fibtastic sequence length of all groupings cannot be more than three, since this grouping is a counterexample, showing that $3$ is a possible maximum. For example, if we claim the maximum fibtastic sequence length is $4$ , this grouping is a counterexample to the statement. This shows that there exists a grouping where the maximum fibtastic sequence length is not $4$ . Finally, we show that all groupings have a fibtastic sequence with a length of at least $3$ . For the sake of contradiction, assume a grouping of the numbers exists from $1$ to $2024$ , such that the maximum fibtastic sequence length in both groups is less than $3$ . We will try to construct a possible grouping that satisfies our claim. Without loss of generality, let the number $1$ be in Group $A$ . If $2$ is in Group $A$ , then in order not to form a fibtastic sequence of length three in Group $A$ , the next number in Group $A$ must be at least $6$ . However, this makes Group $B$ have the numbers $3, 4,$ and $5$ which is undesirable. This means that $2$ has to be in Group B. We can repeat the same process for $3$ . If $3$ is in Group $A$ , then in order not to form a fibtastic sequence of length three in Group $A$ , the next number in Group $A$ must be at least $7$ . However, this allows for the numbers $4, 5,$ and $6$ to be in Group $B$ , which is again undesirable. Finally, if we do this process for $4$ as well, we find that $4$ must also be in Group B, which forms a fibtastic sequence of at least length $3$ , contradiction. This means that there does not exist a grouping of numbers such that the maximum length of a fibtastic sequence in either group is at least three. $\square$

We claim that the largest integer $M$ such that we can guarantee that we can pick $M$ consecutive elements from either Group A or Group B which form a fibtastic sequence is $$ \boxed{M=3} $$ A construction for $M=3$ is as follows: $$ \text{Group A} = \{1,2 \} \cup\{3k, 3k+1, 3k+2 \mid k =2n \text{ }\forall \text{ } n \le 337 \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}\} $$ $$ \text{Group B} = \{3k, 3k+1, 3k+2 \mid k = 2n - 1 \text{ } \forall \text{ } n \le 337 \in \mathbb{Z}^+ \} $$ Written out in increasing order, this is $$ \text{Group A} = 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14, \dots, 2024 $$ $$ \text{Group B} = 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, \dots 2021 $$ \newline This partition into sub-sequences clearly yields $M=3$ . This is observable by selecting $6,7,8$ from Group A. (one of many options) \newline Also, $M \ge 4$ is not present in this partition, because choosing any four consecutive terms in either $A$ or $B$ guarantees that the difference between some two consecutive terms is $$ 3 \cdot 2(n+1) - 3 \cdot 2n + 2= (6n+6) - (6n+2) = 4 $$ which is not a Fibonacci number. Now we are left to show that $M<3$ can not be achieved. For convenience purposes, let $a_{n}$ be the $n$ th term of sequence A and $b_{n}$ be the $n$ th term of sequence B. \textbf{Case 1: }Show that $M=1$ can not be achieved. Assume for the sake of contradiction that $M=1$ is achievable. Without loss of generality, assume that $a_{i} = 1$ for some $i$ . Then, by the increasing order condition, $i=1$ . Since we must have $M=1$ , $a_{2} - a_{1} = a_{2} -1$ should not be a Fibonacci number. Since the smallest non-Fibonacci positive integer is $4$ , $a_{2} - 1 \ge 4 \Longleftrightarrow a_{2} \ge 5$ . However, this implies that $2, 3,$ and $4$ must be in Group B, and consecutively too, given that they are consecutive positive integers. This forms a fibtastic sub-sequence of length $3$ , which is a contradiction. Hence $M \neq 1$ \textbf{Case 2:} Show that $M=2$ can not be achieved. Assume for the sake of contradiction that $M=2$ is achievable. Without loss of generality, assume $a_{i} =1$ for some $i$ . Then, by the increasing order condition, $i=1$ . In the previous case, we showed that if $a_{2} - a_{1} \ge 4$ , we are left with $M\ge 3 > 2$ . Hence, $a_{2} - a_{1}$ must be a Fibonacci number less than $4$ . Our possibilities for $a_{2}$ are $a_{2} = a_{1} + 1, a_{1}+2, a_{1} + 3 = 2, 3, 4$ . Now, we can establish our contradiction. Since we must have $M=2$ , $a_{3}-a_{2}$ should not be a Fibonacci number. Because $a_{2} \ge 2$ and the smallest non-Fibonacci positive integer is $4$ , $a_{3} - 2 \ge 4 \Longleftrightarrow a_{3} \ge 6$ . However, this implies that $3,4$ , and $5$ must be in Group B, and consecutively too, given that they are consecutive positive integers. This forms a fibtastic sub-sequence of length $3$ , which is a contradiction. Hence $M \neq 2$ As a result, we have proved that $M=3$ is achievable in some partition, and $M<3$ is not. Thus, the largest integer $M$ such that we can guarantee that we can pick $M$ consecutive elements from either Group A or Group B which form a fibtastic sequence is $$ \boxed{M=3} $$

I claim that the answer is  $M = 3.$  We first prove that this is the maximum. By picking  $A = \{2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10, \ldots, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2024\},$  which are values  $2, 3, 4\pmod 6$  and then  $B = \{1, 5, 6, 7, 11, \ldots, 2021, 2022, 2023\},$  which are  $1, 5, 6 \pmod 6.$  We clearly see that the maximum is a sequence of length 3, because 4 is not a Fibonacci number. 

Let  $M(n)$  be the answer to the more general problem, where rather than 2024, we substitute  $n.$  We claim that  $M(n)\leq M(n + 1).$  To see this, begin by splitting  $\{1, 2, \ldots, n + 1\}$  into 2 different groups  $A, B.$  WLOG, assume that  $n + 1 \in B.$  Since  $A \cup B \backslash\{n + 1\} = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\},$  we have that we can form a \emph{fibtastic} sequence from just these two groups. However, adding a new term to consider will result in  $M(n + 1) \geq M(n).$ Now, we prove that  $M(5) = 3.$  We can just go through all of the cases:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item  $\max(|A|, |B|) = 5$     \begin{enumerate}
        \item  $(A, B) = (\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}, \phi)$  has 5.
    \end{enumerate} 
    \item  $\max(|A|, |B|) = 4$     \begin{enumerate}
        \item  $(A, B) = (\{1, 2, 3, 4\}, \{5\})$  has 4.
        \item  $(A, B) = (\{1, 2, 3, 5\}, \{4\})$  has 4.
        \item  $(A, B) = (\{1, 2, 4, 5\}, \{3\})$  has 4.
        \item  $(A, B) = (\{1, 3, 4, 5\}, \{2\})$  has 4.
        \item  $(A, B) = (\{2, 3, 4, 5\}, \{1\})$  has 4.
    \end{enumerate}
    \item  $\max(|A|, |B|) = 3.$  WLOG let  $|A| = 3, |B| = 2$     \begin{enumerate}
        \item  $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$  has 3
        \item  $A = \{1, 2, 4\}$  has 3
        \item  $A = \{1, 2, 5\}$  has 3
        \item  $A = \{1, 3, 4\}$  has 3
        \item  $A = \{1, 3, 5\}$  has 3
        \item  $A = \{1, 4, 5\}$  has 3
        \item  $A = \{2, 3, 4\}$  has 3
        \item  $A = \{2, 3, 5\}$  has 3
        \item  $A = \{2, 4, 5\}$  has 3
        \item  $A = \{3, 4, 5\}$  has 3
    \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
Thus,  $M = M(2024) \geq M(5) = 3,$  and hence  $M = \boxed3.$

stem_md:
In how many ways can a  $3\times 3$  grid be filled with integers from  $1$  to  $12$  such that all three of the following conditions are satisfied: 
(a) both  $1$  and  $2$  appear in the grid, 
(b) the grid contains at most  $8$  distinct values, and 
(c) the sums of the numbers in each row, each column, and both main diagonals are all the same?
Rotations and reflections are considered the same.
solution_md:
<details><summary>14 pages (still not my longest usamts writeup tho)</summary>We claim the answer is  $\boxed{3}.$  We provide the three grids below.
[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,3)--(2,3)--(2,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(2,3)--(0,3));
draw((0,2)--(3,2)--(3,1)--(0,1));
pair A=(1/2,1/2), B=(3/2, 1/2), C=(5/2,1/2), D=(1/2,3/2), E=(3/2,3/2), F=(5/2,3/2), G=(1/2, 5/2), H=(3/2,5/2), I=(5/2,5/2);
label(" $2$ ", A);
label(" $5$ ", B);
label(" $2$ ", C);
label(" $3$ ", D);
label(" $3$ ", E);
label(" $3$ ", F);
label(" $4$ ", G);
label(" $1$ ", H);
label(" $4$ ", I);
[/asy]
[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,3)--(2,3)--(2,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(2,3)--(0,3));
draw((0,2)--(3,2)--(3,1)--(0,1));
pair A=(1/2,1/2), B=(3/2, 1/2), C=(5/2,1/2), D=(1/2,3/2), E=(3/2,3/2), F=(5/2,3/2), G=(1/2, 5/2), H=(3/2,5/2), I=(5/2,5/2);
label(" $2$ ", A);
label(" $1$ ", B);
label(" $3$ ", C);
label(" $3$ ", D);
label(" $2$ ", E);
label(" $1$ ", F);
label(" $1$ ", G);
label(" $3$ ", H);
label(" $2$ ", I);
[/asy]
[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,3)--(2,3)--(2,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(2,3)--(0,3));
draw((0,2)--(3,2)--(3,1)--(0,1));
pair A=(1/2,1/2), B=(3/2, 1/2), C=(5/2,1/2), D=(1/2,3/2), E=(3/2,3/2), F=(5/2,3/2), G=(1/2, 5/2), H=(3/2,5/2), I=(5/2,5/2);
label(" $6$ ", A);
label(" $3$ ", B);
label(" $3$ ", C);
label(" $1$ ", D);
label(" $4$ ", E);
label(" $7$ ", F);
label(" $5$ ", G);
label(" $5$ ", H);
label(" $2$ ", I);
[/asy]
These grids work. We now prove these are the only ones.

Since there are at most  $8$  distinct values in the grid, there must be at least two cells of the grid that have the same number. We do casework on where the two cells with the same number are.
\[\]
\[\]
Case  $1$ : There exists a pair of two equal cells such that one of the cells is a corner cell.

Label the numbers in the grid as  $a_1,$   $a_2,$   $\cdots,$   $a_9,$  as shown below. (We will use this for every case.)

[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,3)--(2,3)--(2,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(2,3)--(0,3));
draw((0,2)--(3,2)--(3,1)--(0,1));
pair A=(1/2,1/2), B=(3/2, 1/2), C=(5/2,1/2), D=(1/2,3/2), E=(3/2,3/2), F=(5/2,3/2), G=(1/2, 5/2), H=(3/2,5/2), I=(5/2,5/2);
label(" $a_7$ ", A);
label(" $a_8$ ", B);
label(" $a_9$ ", C);
label(" $a_4$ ", D);
label(" $a_5$ ", E);
label(" $a_6$ ", F);
label(" $a_1$ ", G);
label(" $a_2$ ", H);
label(" $a_3$ ", I);
[/asy]

Since we do not care about rotations and reflections, WLOG let the top left corner of the grid ( $a_1$ ) be the corner cell that is the same as another corner cell. We now do casework on what the other cell is.

Subcase  $1$ :  $a_1=a_2.$ Note that this is equivalent to the case where  $a_1=a_4$  via a reflection and a rotation.

We now have the grid below.

[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,3)--(2,3)--(2,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(2,3)--(0,3));
draw((0,2)--(3,2)--(3,1)--(0,1));
pair A=(1/2,1/2), B=(3/2, 1/2), C=(5/2,1/2), D=(1/2,3/2), E=(3/2,3/2), F=(5/2,3/2), G=(1/2, 5/2), H=(3/2,5/2), I=(5/2,5/2);
label(" $a_7$ ", A);
label(" $a_8$ ", B);
label(" $a_9$ ", C);
label(" $a_4$ ", D);
label(" $a_5$ ", E);
label(" $a_6$ ", F);
label(" $a_1$ ", G);
label(" $a_1$ ", H);
label(" $a_3$ ", I);
[/asy]
Note that  $a_1+a_5+a_9=a_1+a_5+a_8,$  so  $a_8=a_9.$  We mark this on our grid. 

[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,3)--(2,3)--(2,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(2,3)--(0,3));
draw((0,2)--(3,2)--(3,1)--(0,1));
pair A=(1/2,1/2), B=(3/2, 1/2), C=(5/2,1/2), D=(1/2,3/2), E=(3/2,3/2), F=(5/2,3/2), G=(1/2, 5/2), H=(3/2,5/2), I=(5/2,5/2);
label(" $a_7$ ", A);
label(" $a_8$ ", B);
label(" $a_8$ ", C);
label(" $a_4$ ", D);
label(" $a_5$ ", E);
label(" $a_6$ ", F);
label(" $a_1$ ", G);
label(" $a_1$ ", H);
label(" $a_3$ ", I);
[/asy]
Now,  $2a_1+a_3=a_1+a_5+a_8,$  so  $a_3=a_5+a_8-a_1,$  and  $2a_8+a_7=a_1+a_5+a_8,$  so  $a_7=a_1+a_5-a_8.$ We now have  $a_1+a_4+a_7=2a_1+a_5-a_8+a_4=a_1+a_5+a_8,$  so  $a_4=2a_8-a_1,$  and  $a_3+a_6+a_8=2a_8+a_5-a_1+a_6=a_1+a_5+a_8,$  so  $a_6=2a_1-a_8.$ Also,  $a_3+a_5+a_7=(a_5+a_8-a_1)+a_5+(a_5+a_1-a_8)=3a_5=a_1+a_5+a_8,$  so  $a_5=\dfrac{a_1+a_8}{2}.$  As such,  $a_3=a_5+a_8-a_1=\dfrac{3a_8-a_1}{2},$  and  $a_7=a_1+a_5-a_8=\dfrac{3a_1-a_8}{2}.$  We can now further update our grid.
[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,3)--(2,3)--(2,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(2,3)--(0,3));
draw((0,2)--(3,2)--(3,1)--(0,1));
pair A=(1/2,1/2), B=(3/2, 1/2), C=(5/2,1/2), D=(1/2,3/2), E=(3/2,3/2), F=(5/2,3/2), G=(1/2, 5/2), H=(3/2,5/2), I=(5/2,5/2);
label(" $\frac{3a_1-a_8}{2}$ ", A);
label(" $a_8$ ", B);
label(" $a_8$ ", C);
label(" $2a_8-a_1$ ", D);
label(" $\frac{a_1+a_8}{2}$ ", E);
label(" $2a_1-a_8$ ", F);
label(" $a_1$ ", G);
label(" $a_1$ ", H);
label(" $\frac{3a_8-a_1}{2}$ ", I);
[/asy]
We know that there must be a  $1$  in the grid somewhere. We do casework on where the  $1$  is.

If  $a_1=1,$  then  $2a_1-a_8=2-a_8$  is a positive integer, so since  $a_8$  is a positive integer,  $a_8=1,$  which yields that every cell of the grid contains a  $1,$  but then the grid does not contain a  $2.$  Thus,  $a_1\neq 1.$  Similarly,  $a_8\neq 1.$  


If  $\dfrac{a_1+a_8}{2}=1,$  then  $a_1+a_8=2,$  so since  $a_1$  and  $a_8$  are positive integers,  $a_1=a_8=1,$  but  $a_1\neq 1.$  Thus,  $\dfrac{a_1+a_8}{2}\neq 1.$ We now have  $4$  cases:  $2a_8-a_1=1,$   $2a_1-a_8=1,$   $\dfrac{3a_1-a_8}{2}=1,$  and  $\dfrac{3a_8-a_1}{2}=1.$  However, since  $a_1$  and  $a_8$  are symmetric,  $2a_8-a_1=1$  and  $2a_1-a_8=1$  are symmetric cases, and  $\dfrac{3a_8-a_1}{2}=1$  and  $\dfrac{3a_1-a_8}{2}=1$  are symmetric cases, so we only have to deal with the cases that  $2a_8-a_1=1$  and  $\dfrac{3a_8-a_1}{2}=1.$ If  $2a_8-a_1=1,$  then we know that  $a_1=2a_8-1,$  and since  $2a_1-a_8$  is in the grid, we have that  $12\geq 2a_1-a_8=3a_8-2,$  so  $a_8\leq \dfrac{14}{3},$  and since  $a_8$  is a positive integer,  $a_8\in\{1,2,3,4\}.$  However, since we know  $a_8\neq 1,$   $a_8\in\{2,3,4\}.$ If  $a_8=2,$  then  $a_1=2a_8-1=3,$  so the center cell of the grid is  $\dfrac{a_1+a_8}{2}=\dfrac{5}{2},$  which is not an integer. Thus,  $a_8\neq 2.$  Similarly, if  $a_8=4,$  then  $a_1=2a_8-1=7,$  so the center cell of the grid is  $\dfrac{a_1+a_8}{2}=\dfrac{11}{2},$  which is not a integer, so  $a_8\neq 4.$  

If  $a_8=3,$  then  $a_1=2a_8-1=5.$ We can then calculate  $\dfrac{a_1+a_8}{2}=4,$   $2a_1-a_8=7,$   $\dfrac{3a_1-a_8}{2}=6,$  and  $\dfrac{3a_8-a_1}{2}=2,$  so we can fill in the grid as shown below.
[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,3)--(2,3)--(2,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(2,3)--(0,3));
draw((0,2)--(3,2)--(3,1)--(0,1));
pair A=(1/2,1/2), B=(3/2, 1/2), C=(5/2,1/2), D=(1/2,3/2), E=(3/2,3/2), F=(5/2,3/2), G=(1/2, 5/2), H=(3/2,5/2), I=(5/2,5/2);
label(" $6$ ", A);
label(" $3$ ", B);
label(" $3$ ", C);
label(" $1$ ", D);
label(" $4$ ", E);
label(" $7$ ", F);
label(" $5$ ", G);
label(" $5$ ", H);
label(" $2$ ", I);
[/asy]
Note that this is the third grid from our list of grids at the top, so in this case that  $2a_8-a_1=1,$  there exist no additional grids that are not in the list of grids provided at the start.

We also need to deal with the case that  $\dfrac{3a_8-a_1}{2}=1.$  Then,  $3a_8-a_1=2,$  so  $a_1=3a_8-2.$  Then, since  $2a_1-a_8$  is in the grid,  $12\geq 2a_1-a_8=2(3a_8-2)-a_8=5a_8-4,$  so  $a_8\leq \dfrac{16}{5},$  and since  $a_8$  is a positive integer,  $a_8\in\{1,2,3\}.$  However,  $a_8\neq 1,$  so  $a_8\in\{2,3\}.$  

If  $a_8=2,$  then  $a_1=3a_8-2=4,$  so  $2a_8-a_1=0$  is in the grid, a contradiction, so  $a_8\neq 2.$  If  $a_8=3,$  then  $a_1=3a_8-2=7,$  so  $2a_8-a_1=-1$  is in the grid, a contradiction, so  $a_8\neq 3.$  Thus, there are no possible grids when  $\dfrac{3a_8-a_1}{2}=1.$ As such, all possible grids in this subcase are in the list of  $3$  grids provided at the start of this solution.

Subcase  $2$ :  $a_1=a_3.$ Note that this is equivalent to the  $a_1=a_7$  case via a rotation.

We mark this on our grid. 
[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,3)--(2,3)--(2,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(2,3)--(0,3));
draw((0,2)--(3,2)--(3,1)--(0,1));
pair A=(1/2,1/2), B=(3/2, 1/2), C=(5/2,1/2), D=(1/2,3/2), E=(3/2,3/2), F=(5/2,3/2), G=(1/2, 5/2), H=(3/2,5/2), I=(5/2,5/2);
label(" $a_7$ ", A);
label(" $a_8$ ", B);
label(" $a_9$ ", C);
label(" $a_4$ ", D);
label(" $a_5$ ", E);
label(" $a_6$ ", F);
label(" $a_1$ ", G);
label(" $a_2$ ", H);
label(" $a_1$ ", I);
[/asy]
Note that  $a_1+a_5+a_9=a_1+a_5+a_7,$  so  $a_7=a_9.$  We mark this on our diagram.
[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,3)--(2,3)--(2,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(2,3)--(0,3));
draw((0,2)--(3,2)--(3,1)--(0,1));
pair A=(1/2,1/2), B=(3/2, 1/2), C=(5/2,1/2), D=(1/2,3/2), E=(3/2,3/2), F=(5/2,3/2), G=(1/2, 5/2), H=(3/2,5/2), I=(5/2,5/2);
label(" $a_7$ ", A);
label(" $a_8$ ", B);
label(" $a_7$ ", C);
label(" $a_4$ ", D);
label(" $a_5$ ", E);
label(" $a_6$ ", F);
label(" $a_1$ ", G);
label(" $a_2$ ", H);
label(" $a_1$ ", I);
[/asy]
Now,  $a_1+a_5+a_7=a_1+a_4+a_7,$  so  $a_4=a_5,$  and  $a_1+a_6+a_7=a_1+a_5+a_7,$  so  $a_4=a_5=a_6.$  As such,  $a_1+a_4+a_7=a_4+a_5+a_6=3a_4,$  so  $a_4=\dfrac{a_1+a_7}{2}.$  Now,  $a_1+a_2+a_1=2a_1+a_2=a_4+a_5+a_6=3a_4=\dfrac{3a_1+3a_7}{2},$  so  $a_2=\dfrac{3a_7-a_1}{2},$  and  $a_7+a_8+a_7=2a_7+a_8=a_4+a_5+a_6=3a_4=\dfrac{3a_1+3a_7}{2},$  so  $a_8=\dfrac{3a_1-a_7}{2}.$  We can fill this into the grid.
[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,3)--(2,3)--(2,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(2,3)--(0,3));
draw((0,2)--(3,2)--(3,1)--(0,1));
pair A=(1/2,1/2), B=(3/2, 1/2), C=(5/2,1/2), D=(1/2,3/2), E=(3/2,3/2), F=(5/2,3/2), G=(1/2, 5/2), H=(3/2,5/2), I=(5/2,5/2);
label(" $a_7$ ", A);
label(" $\frac{3a_1-a_7}{2}$ ", B);
label(" $a_7$ ", C);
label(" $\frac{a_1+a_7}{2}$ ", D);
label(" $\frac{a_1+a_7}{2}$ ", E);
label(" $\frac{a_1+a_7}{2}$ ", F);
label(" $a_1$ ", G);
label(" $\frac{3a_7-a_1}{2}$ ", H);
label(" $a_1$ ", I);
[/asy]
We know there must be a  $1$  somewhere in the grid. We now do casework on where the  $1$  is.

If  $a_1=1,$  then  $\dfrac{3a_1-a_7}{2}=\dfrac{3-a_7}{2}$  is a positive integer, and since  $a_7$  is a positive integer,  $a_7=1,$  so we now have that  $\dfrac{a_1+a_7}{2}=\dfrac{3a_7-a_1}{2}=\dfrac{3a_1-a_7}{2}=1,$  so every number in the grid is a  $1,$  and there are no  $2$ 's, a contradiction, so  $a_1\neq 1.$  Similarly,  $a_7\neq 1.$  

If  $\dfrac{a_1+a_7}{2}=1,$  then  $a_1+a_7=2,$  and since  $a_1$  and  $a_7$  are positive integers,  $a_1=a_7=1,$  but  $a_1,a_7\neq 1,$  so  $\dfrac{a_1+a_7}{2}\neq 1.$  Thus, there are only  $2$  cases:  $\dfrac{3a_7-a_1}{2}=1$  and  $\dfrac{3a_1-a_7}{2}=1.$  However, since  $a_1$  and  $a_7$  are symmetric, these cases are symmetric, so we only need to deal with one of the cases, so we will deal with the  $\dfrac{3a_7-a_1}{2}=1$  case.

Then,  $3a_7-a_1=2,$  so  $a_1=3a_7-2.$  We have that  $\dfrac{3a_1-a_7}{2}=\dfrac{3(3a_7-2)-a_7}{2}=\dfrac{8a_7-6}{2}=4a_7-3$  is part of the grid, so  $12\geq 4a_7-3,$  so  $a_7\leq \dfrac{15}{4}.$  Since  $a_7$  is a positive integer,  $a_7\in\{1,2,3\},$  but since  $a_7\neq 1,$   $a_7\in\{2,3\}.$ If  $a_7=3,$  then  $a_1=3a_7-2=7,$  so  $\dfrac{a_1+a_3}{2}=5$  and  $\dfrac{3a_1-a_7}{2}=9,$  so we can fill in the grid like shown. (The grid is on the next page.)
[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,3)--(2,3)--(2,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(2,3)--(0,3));
draw((0,2)--(3,2)--(3,1)--(0,1));
pair A=(1/2,1/2), B=(3/2, 1/2), C=(5/2,1/2), D=(1/2,3/2), E=(3/2,3/2), F=(5/2,3/2), G=(1/2, 5/2), H=(3/2,5/2), I=(5/2,5/2);
label(" $3$ ", A);
label(" $9$ ", B);
label(" $3$ ", C);
label(" $5$ ", D);
label(" $5$ ", E);
label(" $5$ ", F);
label(" $7$ ", G);
label(" $1$ ", H);
label(" $7$ ", I);
[/asy]
However, since there are no  $2$ 's in this grid, this is not a valid solution. 

If  $a_7=2,$  then  $a_1=3a_7-2=4,$  so  $\dfrac{a_1+a_7}{2}=3,$  and  $\dfrac{3a_1-a_7}{2}=5,$  and we can fill out the grid as shown below. 
[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,3)--(2,3)--(2,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(2,3)--(0,3));
draw((0,2)--(3,2)--(3,1)--(0,1));
pair A=(1/2,1/2), B=(3/2, 1/2), C=(5/2,1/2), D=(1/2,3/2), E=(3/2,3/2), F=(5/2,3/2), G=(1/2, 5/2), H=(3/2,5/2), I=(5/2,5/2);
label(" $2$ ", A);
label(" $5$ ", B);
label(" $2$ ", C);
label(" $3$ ", D);
label(" $3$ ", E);
label(" $3$ ", F);
label(" $4$ ", G);
label(" $1$ ", H);
label(" $4$ ", I);
[/asy]
Note that this is the same thing as the first grid from the list of grids from the start. Since there are no more cases in this subcase, this means that all possible grids in this subcase are in the list of grids provided at the start.
Subcase  $3$ :  $a_1=a_6$ By a rotation and a reflection, this is equivalent to the  $a_1=a_8$  case. 

We label the grid as shown below. 
[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);
draw((1,0)--(1,3)--(2,3)--(2,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(2,3)--(0,3));
draw((0,2)--(3,2)--(3,1)--(0,1));
pair A=(1/2,1/2), B=(3/2, 1/2), C=(5/2,1/2), D=(1/2,3/2), E=(3/2,3/2), F=(5/2,3/2), G=(1/2, 5/2), H=(3/2,5/2), I=(5/2,5/2);
label(" $a_7$ ", A);
label(" $a_8$ ", B);
label(" $a_9$ ", C);
label(" $a_4$ ", D);
label(" $a_5$ ", E);
label(" $a_1$ ", F);
label(" $a_1$ ", G);
label(" $a_2$ ", H);
label(" $a_3$ ", I);
[/asy]
Note that  $a_1+a_5+a_9=a_1+a_4+a_5,$  so  $a_4=a_9.$   $a_1+a_4+a_7=a_3+a_1+a_9=a_3+a_1+a_4,$  so  $a_7=a_3.$  We can label this on our diagram. 
[asy]
size(10cm, 5cm);
draw((0,0)--(3,0)--(3,3)--(0,3)--cycle);

We will fill it out so that every row, column, and diagonal has the same sum.  $$ \begin{pmatrix}a&b&\text{blank}\text{blank}&c&\text{blank}\text{blank}&\text{blank}&d\end{pmatrix} $$  The common sum is  $a+c+d$  so, using the middle column, we get   $$ \begin{pmatrix}a&b&\text{blank}\text{blank}&c&\text{blank}\text{blank}&a-b+d&d\end{pmatrix}. $$  Using the bottom row, we get   $$ \begin{pmatrix}a&b&\text{blank}\text{blank}&c&\text{blank} b+c-d&a-b+d&d\end{pmatrix}. $$  Using the left column, we get   $$ \begin{pmatrix}a&b&\text{blank}-b+2d&c&\text{blank} b+c-d&a-b+d&d\end{pmatrix}. $$  Using the top  $2$  rows, we get  $$ \begin{pmatrix}a&b&-b+c+d-b+2d&c&a+b-d b+c-d&a-b+d&d\end{pmatrix}. $$  Using the diagonals, we see that  $a+c+d=(b+c-d)+c+(-b+c+d)$  so  $a+d=2c$ . Therefore, let  $a=c-x$ ,  $d=c+x$ , and  $b=c+x-y$  so our square becomes   $$ \begin{pmatrix}c-x&c+x-y&c+yc+x+y&c&c-x-y c-y&c-x+y&c+x\end{pmatrix}. $$  Let  $S$  be the set of magic squares of the above form with both a  $1$  and a  $2$  and at most  $8$  distinct numbers and let the group of symmetries of a square,  $D_4$ , act on  $S$ . Then, our answer is the number of orbits of  $S$  under the action of  $D_4$  or  $|S/D_4|$ . For every  $g\in D_4$ , let  $S^g$  be the set of  $s\in S$  such that  $gs=s$ . Similarly, for every  $s\in S$ , let  $G_s$  be the set of  $g\in D_4$  such that  $gs=s$ . Then, Burnside's Lemma states that   $$ |S/D_4|=\frac{1}{|D_4|}\sum_{g\in D_4}|S^g|=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{s\in S}|G_s|. $$  We now utilize the following Python3 code to compute  $|S/D_4|$ .
