stem_md: Prove that there is no polynomial  $P(x)$  with integer coefficients such that  $$ P(\sqrt[3]{5} + \sqrt[3]{25}) = 2\sqrt[3]{5}+3\sqrt[3]{25} $$
solution_md:
<details><summary>im not sure if my notation is bad</summary>(In this solution, we will take  $x\pm y$  to mean a quantity which could be either  $x-y$  or  $x+y,$  as in the quadratic formula. Also, we will say that  $x\pm y=z\pm a$  so long as at least one of the following is true:  $x-y=z-a,$   $x-y=z+a,$   $x+y=z-a,$  or  $x+y=z+a.$  We will also take  $x\pm y=c$  to mean that  $x-y=c$  or  $x+y=c.$ )

For the sake of contradiction, assume that there exists a polynomial  $P$  with integer coefficients such that  $P(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})=2\sqrt[3]{5}+3\sqrt[3]{25}.$  We proceed as follows.

We first prove a couple lemmas.

Lemma  $0$ :  $\sqrt[3]{25}$  is irrational. 

Proof: Assume for the sake of contradiction that  $\sqrt[3]{25}$  is rational. Then, there exist integers  $p,$   $q,$  such that  $\gcd(p,q)=1$  and  $\sqrt[3]{25}=\dfrac{p}{q}.$  Thus,  $25=\dfrac{p^3}{q^3}.$  Now,  $p^3=25q^3\equiv 0\pmod{5},$  so  $5\mid p,$  and  $p=5k$  for some integer  $k.$  Now,  $125k^3=p^3=25q^3,$  so  $q^3=5k^3\equiv 0\pmod{5},$  so  $5\mid q.$  However, we then have  $5\mid \gcd(p,q)=1,$  a contradiction, so  $\sqrt[3]{25}$  is irrational, as desired.
\[\]
Lemma  $1$ :  $\sqrt[3]{5}$  is irrational.

Proof: Assume for the sake of contradiction that  $\sqrt[3]{5}$  is rational. Then, there exist integers  $p,$   $q$  such that  $\sqrt[3]{5}=\dfrac{p}{q},$  but then  $\dfrac{p^2}{q^2}=(\sqrt[3]{5})^2=\sqrt[3]{25},$  so  $\sqrt[3]{25}$  is rational, but by Lemma  $0,$   $\sqrt[3]{25}$  is irrational, a contradiction, so  $\sqrt[3]{5}$  is irrational, as desired. 
\[\]
Lemma  $2$ :  $\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25}$  is irrational.

Proof: Assume for the sake of contradiction that  $\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25}$  is rational. Then,  $\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25}=c,$  for some rational  $c.$  Thus,  $1+\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25}=1+c,$  so  $(1+c)(\sqrt[3]{5}-1)=(\sqrt[3]{25}+\sqrt[3]{5}+1)(\sqrt[3]{5}-1)=4.$  Since  $4\neq 0,$  we have that  $1+c\neq 0,$  so  $\sqrt[3]{5}-1=\dfrac{4}{1+c},$  and  $\sqrt[3]{5}=1+\dfrac{4}{1+c}.$  Since  $c$  is rational and  $1+c\neq 0,$  we have that  $1+\dfrac{4}{1+c}=\sqrt[3]{5}$  is rational, but by lemma  $1,$   $\sqrt[3]{5}$  is irrational, a contradiction, so  $\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25}$  is irrational, as desired. 
\[\]
Lemma  $3$ : If  $q$  and  $s$  are rationals so that  $qs$  is the square of a rational, then there exists a rational  $a$  and integers  $b,$   $c$  such that  $q=ab^2$  and  $s=ac^2.$ Proof: If  $q=0,$  then set  $b=0,$   $a=s,$  and  $c=1,$  which yields  $q=ab^2$  and  $s=ac^2.$   If  $s=0,$  then set  $c=0,$   $a=q,$  and  $b=1,$  which  $q=ab^2$  and  $s=ac^2.$  If  $q,s\neq 0,$  then note that  $sq=d^2\neq 0$  for some rational  $d,$  and  $\dfrac{s}{q}=\dfrac{sq}{q^2}=\dfrac{d^2}{q^2}=\left(\dfrac{d}{q}\right)^2.$  Since  $q\neq 0$  and  $d$  and  $q$  are rational, we have that  $0\neq \dfrac{d}{q}=\dfrac{f}{g}$  for some integers  $f$  and  $g,$  so  $\dfrac{s}{q}=\left(\dfrac{d}{q}\right)^2=\dfrac{f^2}{g^2}.$  Since  $f\neq 0,$  we have  $\dfrac{s}{f^2}=\dfrac{q}{g^2}.$  Then, we can set  $a=\dfrac{s}{f^2}=\dfrac{q}{g^2},$   $b=g$  and  $c=f,$  yielding  $q=ab^2$  and  $s=ac^2,$  as desired. 
\[\]
Lemma  $4$ : If  $r_1,$   $r_2,$   $r_3,$  and  $r_4$  are rationals so that  $r_2$  and  $r_4$  are not the square of any rational, then  $r_1-\sqrt{r_2}\neq r_3+\sqrt{r_4}.$  

Proof: Assume for the sake of contradiction that there exist rationals  $r_1,$   $r_2,$   $r_3,$   $r_4,$  such that  $r_2$  and  $r_4$  are not the squares of rationals and  $r_1-\sqrt{r_2}=r_3+\sqrt{r_4}.$  Then,  $\sqrt{r_2}+\sqrt{r_4}=r_1-r_3,$  so  $(r_1-r_3)^2=(\sqrt{r_2}+\sqrt{r_4})^2=r_2+r_4+2\sqrt{r_2r_4}.$  Now,  $\sqrt{r_2r_4}=\dfrac{(r_1-r_3)^2-r_2-r_4}{2},$  so  $r_2r_4=\left(\dfrac{(r_1-r_3)^2-r_2-r_4}{2}\right)^2,$  and since  $\dfrac{(r_1-r_3)^2-r_2-r_4}{2}$  is a rational,  $r_2r_4$  is the square of a rational. As such, by Lemma  $3,$  there exists integers  $b,$   $c,$  and a rational  $a$  such that  $r_2=ab^2$  and  $r_4=ac^2.$  If  $a$  is the square of a rational, then  $r_2=(b\sqrt{a})^2,$  and since  $b\sqrt{a}$  is rational,  $r_2$  is the square of a rational, a contradiction. Thus,  $a$  is not the square of a rational.

Now,  $(r_1-r_3)^2=r_2+r_4+2\sqrt{r_2r_4}=ab^2+ac^2+2\sqrt{a^2b^2c^2}=ab^2+ac^2\pm2abc=a(b^2\pm2bc+c^2)=a(b\pm c)^2.$  If  $b\pm c=0,$  then  $b=\pm c,$  so  $b^2=c^2,$  and  $r_2=r_4,$  so  $r_1-r_3=\sqrt{r_2}+\sqrt{r_4}=2\sqrt{r_2},$  so  $r_2=\left(\dfrac{r_1-r_3}{2}\right)^2,$  so since  $\dfrac{r_1-r_3}{2}$  is rational,  $r_2$  is the square of a rational, a contradiction, so  $b\pm c\neq 0,$  so  $a=\dfrac{(r_1-r_3)^2}{(b\pm c)^2}=\left(\dfrac{r_1-r_3}{b\pm c}\right)^2,$  so since  $\dfrac{r_1-r_3}{b\pm c}$  is a rational,  $a$  is the square of a rational, but we proved earlier that  $a$  is not the square of a rational, a contradiction. Thus, the lemma holds true. 
\[\]
Lemma  $5$ : If  $r_1,$   $r_2,$   $r_3,$  and  $r_4$  are rationals such that  $r_2$  and  $r_4$  are not the squares of any rational, and  $r_1+\sqrt{r_2}=r_3+\sqrt{r_4},$  then  $r_1=r_3$  and  $r_2=r_4.$ Proof: Let  $r_1,$   $r_2,$   $r_3,$  and  $r_4$  be rationals such that  $r_2$  and  $r_4$  are not the square of rationals and  $r_1+\sqrt{r_2}=r_3+\sqrt{r_4}.$  Then,  $r_1-r_3=\sqrt{r_4}-\sqrt{r_2},$  so  $(r_1-r_3)^2=(\sqrt{r_4}-\sqrt{r_2})^2=r_2+r_4-2\sqrt{r_2r_4},$  so  $\sqrt{r_2r_4}=\dfrac{r_2+r_4-(r_1-r_3)^2}{2},$  and  $r_2r_4=\left(\dfrac{r_2+r_4-(r_1-r_3)^2}{2}\right)^2,$  so since  $\dfrac{r_2+r_4-(r_1-r_3)^2}{2}$  is a rational,  $r_2r_4$  is a square of a rational. Thus, by Lemma  $3,$   $r_2=ab^2$  and  $r_3=ac^2$  for some integers  $b,$   $c$  and some rational  $a.$  If  $a$  was the square of a rational, then  $r_2=ab^2=(b\sqrt{a})^2,$  and since  $\sqrt{a}$  is rational,  $r_2$  would be the square of a rational, a contradiction, so  $a$  is not the square of a rational. Now,  $(r_1-r_3)^2=r_2+r_4-2\sqrt{r_2r_4}=ab^2+ac^2-2\sqrt{a^2b^2c^2}=ab^2+ac^2\pm2abc=a(b^2\pm2bc+c^2)=a(b\pm c)^2.$  If  $b\pm c\neq 0,$  then  $a=\dfrac{(r_1-r_3)^2}{(b\pm c)^2}=\left(\dfrac{r_1-r_3}{b\pm c}\right)^2,$  and since  $\dfrac{r_1-r_3}{b\pm c}$  is rational,  $a$  is the square of a rational, but  $a$  is not the square of a rational, a contradiction. Thus,  $b\pm c=0.$  Now,  $(r_1-r_3)^2=a(b\pm c)^2=0,$  so  $r_1-r_3=0$  and  $r_1=r_3,$  so  $r_1+\sqrt{r_2}=r_3+\sqrt{r_4}=r_1+\sqrt{r_4},$  and so  $\sqrt{r_2}=\sqrt{r_4},$  and  $r_2=r_4,$  as desired. 
\[\]
Lemma  $6$ : If  $r_1,$   $r_2,$   $r_3,$  and  $r_4$  are rationals such that  $r_2$  and  $r_4$  are not the squares of any rational, and  $r_1-\sqrt{r_2}=r_3-\sqrt{r_4},$  then  $r_1=r_3$  and  $r_2=r_4.$ Proof: Let  $r_1,$   $r_2,$   $r_3,$  and  $r_4$  be rationals such that  $r_2$  and  $r_4$  are not the squares of rationals and  $r_1-\sqrt{r_2}=r_3-\sqrt{r_4}.$  Note that  $r_1+\sqrt{r_4}=r_3+\sqrt{r_2},$  so by Lemma  $5,$   $r_1=r_3$  and  $r_4=r_2,$  as desired. 
\[\]
Lemma  $7$ : If  $f_1,$   $f_2,$   $f_3,$   $f_4,$   $f_5,$  and  $f_6$  are integers such that  $f_1+f_2\sqrt[3]{5}+f_3\sqrt[3]{25}=f_4+f_5\sqrt[3]{5}+f_6\sqrt[3]{25},$  then  $f_1=f_4,$   $f_2=f_5,$   $f_3=f_6.$  

Proof: Assume for the sake of contradiction that there exist integers  $f_1,$   $f_2,$   $f_3,$   $f_4,$   $f_5,$  and  $f_6$  such that  $f_1+f_2\sqrt[3]{5}+f_3\sqrt[3]{25}=f_4+f_5\sqrt[3]{5}+f_6\sqrt[3]{25}$  but either  $f_1\neq f_4,$   $f_2\neq f_5,$  or  $f_3\neq f_6.$  Then, we have  $(f_5-f_2)\sqrt[3]{5}+(f_6-f_3)\sqrt[3]{25}=f_1-f_4.$  We now split this into a couple of cases. 

Case  $1:$   $f_5=f_2,$  and  $f_6=f_3.$  (which implies  $f_5-f_2=f_6-f_3=0$ )

Then, we must have  $f_1\neq f_4.$  However,  $f_1-f_4=(f_5-f_2)\sqrt[3]{5}+(f_6-f_3)\sqrt[3]{25}=0,$  so  $f_1=f_4,$  a contradiction.
\[\]
Case  $2$ :  $f_5-f_2=f_6-f_3\neq 0.$  

Then, we have that  $f_1-f_4=(f_5-f_2)\sqrt[3]{5}+(f_6-f_3)\sqrt[3]{25}=(f_5-f_2)(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25}),$  so  $\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25}=\dfrac{f_1-f_4}{f_5-f_2},$  so  $\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25}$  is rational, but by Lemma  $2,$   $\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25}$  is irrational, a contradiction.
\[\]
Case  $3$ :  $f_5-f_2\neq f_6-f_3.$ Then, we have that  $f_1-f_4=(f_5-f_2)\sqrt[3]{5}+(f_6-f_3)\sqrt[3]{25}.$  Denote  $f_7=f_1-f_4,$   $f_8=f_5-f_2,$  and  $f_9=f_6-f_3.$  If  $f_8=0\neq f_9,$  then  $f_7=f_9\sqrt[3]{25},$  so  $\sqrt[3]{25}=\dfrac{f_7}{f_9},$  and  $\sqrt[3]{25}$  is rational, but by Lemma  $0,$   $\sqrt[3]{25}$  is irrational, a contradiction. If  $f_9=0\neq f_8,$  then  $f_7=f_8\sqrt[3]{5},$  so  $\sqrt[3]{5}=\dfrac{f_7}{f_8},$  so  $\sqrt[3]{5}$  is rational, but by Lemma  $1,$   $\sqrt[3]{5}$  is irrational, a contradiction. Thus,  $f_8,f_9\neq 0.$  Denote  $x=\sqrt[3]{5}.$  Note that  $f_9\sqrt[3]{25}+f_8\sqrt[3]{5}-f_7=f_9x^2+f_8x-f_7=0.$  Since  $f_9\neq 0,$  by the quadratic formula,  $x=\dfrac{-f_8\pm\sqrt{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}}{2f_9}=-\dfrac{f_8}{2f_9}\pm \sqrt{\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}}.$  If  $\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}$  is the square of a rational, then  $x=-\dfrac{f_8}{2f_9}\pm \sqrt{\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}}$  would be rational,  but by Lemma  $1,$   $x=\sqrt[3]{5}$  is irrational, a contradiction, so  $\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}$  is not the square of a rational. Also, note that  $f_9\sqrt[3]{25}+f_8\sqrt[3]{5}-f_7=\dfrac{5f_9}{\sqrt[3]{5}}+f_8\sqrt[3]{5}-f_7=\dfrac{5f_9}{x}+f_8x-f_7=0.$  Thus,  $f_8x^2-f_7x+5f_9=0,$  so by the quadratic formula,  $x=\dfrac{f_7\pm\sqrt{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}}{2f_8}=\dfrac{f_7}{2f_8}\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}}.$  If  $\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}$  was the square of a rational, then  $x=\dfrac{f_7}{2f_8}\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}}$  would be a rational, but by Lemma  $1,$   $x=\sqrt[3]{5}$  is an irrational, a contradiction, so  $\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}$  is not the square of a rational. 

We now have  $-\dfrac{f_8}{2f_9}\pm \sqrt{\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}}=x=\dfrac{f_7}{2f_8}\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}}.$  
We can now split this case into a number of subcases. 

Subcase  $1$ :  $-\dfrac{f_8}{2f_9}- \sqrt{\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}}=x=\dfrac{f_7}{2f_8}+\sqrt{\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}}$  or  $-\dfrac{f_8}{2f_9}+ \sqrt{\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}}=x=\dfrac{f_7}{2f_8}-\sqrt{\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}}.$ Since  $\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}$  and  $\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}$  are not the squares of rationals, by Lemma  $4,$   $-\dfrac{f_8}{2f_9}- \sqrt{\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}}\neq \dfrac{f_7}{2f_8}+\sqrt{\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}}$  and  $-\dfrac{f_8}{2f_9}+ \sqrt{\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}}\neq \dfrac{f_7}{2f_8}-\sqrt{\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}},$  a contradiction.

Subcase  $2$ :  $-\dfrac{f_8}{2f_9}- \sqrt{\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}}=x=\dfrac{f_7}{2f_8}-\sqrt{\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}}$  or  $-\dfrac{f_8}{2f_9}+ \sqrt{\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}}=x=\dfrac{f_7}{2f_8}+\sqrt{\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}}.$ Since  $\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}$  and  $\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}$  are not the squares of rationals, by Lemma  $5$  if  $-\dfrac{f_8}{2f_9}+ \sqrt{\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}}=x=\dfrac{f_7}{2f_8}+\sqrt{\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}}$  and Lemma  $6$  if  $-\dfrac{f_8}{2f_9}- \sqrt{\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}}=x=\dfrac{f_7}{2f_8}-\sqrt{\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}},$  we have  $-\dfrac{f_8}{2f_9}=\dfrac{f_7}{2f_8}$  and  $\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}=\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}.$ Then,  $\left(-\dfrac{f_8}{2f_9}\right)^2=\dfrac{f_8^2}{4f_9^2}=\left(\dfrac{f_7}{2f_8}\right)^2=\dfrac{f_7^2}{4f_8^2}.$  Thus,  $\dfrac{f_8^2+4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}-\dfrac{f_8^2}{4f_9^2}=\dfrac{4f_9f_7}{4f_9^2}=\dfrac{f_7}{f_9}=\dfrac{f_7^2-20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}-\dfrac{f_7^2}{4f_8^2}=-\dfrac{20f_8f_9}{4f_8^2}=-\dfrac{5f_9}{f_8}.$ Now,  $-\dfrac{f_8}{f_9}=\dfrac{f_7}{f_8},$  so  $\left(-\dfrac{f_8}{f_9}\right)\left(\dfrac{f_7}{f_8}\right)=-\dfrac{f_7}{f_9}=\left(-\dfrac{f_8}{f_9}\right)^2=\dfrac{f_8^2}{f_9^2},$  so  $-\dfrac{f_8^2}{f_9^2}=\dfrac{f_7}{f_9}=-\dfrac{5f_9}{f_8},$  so  $\dfrac{f_8^3}{f_9^3}=5.$  Thus,  $\sqrt[3]{5}=\dfrac{f_8}{f_9},$  so  $\sqrt[3]{5}$  is rational, but by Lemma  $1,$   $\sqrt[3]{5}$  is irrational, a contradiction.

Thus, in every case, we get a contradiction, so the lemma holds true, as desired.
\[\]
Lemma  $8$ : For all nonnegative integers  $n,$  there exist integers  $a_n,$   $b_n,$  and  $c_n$  such that  $(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})^n=a_n+b_n\sqrt[3]{5}+c_n\sqrt[3]{25}.$ Proof: We proceed with induction.

For the base case at  $n=0,$  we have that  $(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})^0=1=1+0\sqrt[3]{5}+0\sqrt[3]{25},$  so the base case holds.

Now, assume there exists a nonnegative integer  $k$  such that  $(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})^k=a_k+b_k\sqrt[3]{5}+c_k\sqrt[3]{25}$  for some integers  $a_k,$   $b_k,$  and  $c_k.$  

Then,  $(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})^{k+1}=(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})^k=(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})(a_k+b_k\sqrt[3]{5}+c_k\sqrt[3]{25})=5(b_k+c_k)+(a_k+5c_k)\sqrt[3]{5}+(a_k+b_k)\sqrt[3]{25},$  so  $(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})^{k+1}=a_{k+1}+b_{k+1}\sqrt[3]{5}+c_{k+1}\sqrt[3]{25}$  for some integers  $a_{k+1},$   $b_{k+1},$  and  $c_{k+1}.$  Thus, by the principle of mathematical induction, the lemma holds true.
\[\]
From here on out, denote  $a_n,$   $b_n,$  and  $c_n$  for integers  $n\geq 0$  to be the unique integers such that  $(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})^n=a_n+b_n\sqrt[3]{5}+c_n\sqrt[3]{25}.$  By Lemma  $7,$  these are indeed unique for any nonnegative integers  $n.$  
\[\]
\[\]

Substituting, we get

Expanding this, we get: 

\[ a_n \sqrt[3]{25} + 5a_n + 5b_n \sqrt[3]{5} + 5b_n + c_n \sqrt[3]{25} + c_n \sqrt[3]{5}. \]

This can be written as:

Therefore, we have:

\[ b_{n+1} = a_n + c_n, \]

\[ c_{n+1} = 5a_n + 5b_n. \]

Note that this means \(a_n\), \(b_n\), and \(c_n\) will always be integers. 

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get: 

\[ a_{n+1} - b_{n+1} = 5 b_n - a_n. \]

So, 

\[ a_{n+1} - b_{n+1} = 4 b_n - (a_n - b_n). \]

We claim that \(a_n - b_n \equiv 0 \pmod{4}\) for all integers \(n \geq 0\). We proceed by induction.

substituting \(a_n \sqrt[3]{5} + b_n \sqrt[3]{25} + c_n\) for \( (\sqrt[3]{5} + \sqrt[3]{25})^n \), we get:

Taking this modulo 4, we get \( 0 \equiv -1 \pmod{4} \) because \(a_n - b_n \equiv 0 \pmod{4}\) for all integers \(n \geq 0\). This is a contradiction. Therefore, no such polynomial \(P(x)\) with integer coefficients exists, and the proof is complete.

\[ \alpha^{k + 1} = (\sqrt[3]{5} + \sqrt[3]{25})(p + q\sqrt[3]{5} + r\sqrt[3]{25}) = 5(q + r) + (p + 5r)\sqrt[3]{5} + (p + q)\sqrt[3]{25} \]
By the induction hypothesis,  $q + r$  is even,  $p + 5r$  is odd, and  $p + q$  is also odd, so our lemma is proved. 



Note that because the sum of two odd numbers is even, our lemma implies that  $f(\alpha^k) = 0$ . We can extend this result to outputs of any integer polynomial. 



Claim: For all integer polynomials  $P$ ,  $f(P(\alpha)) = 0$  
Proof. Let the polynomial be  $P(x) = \sum_{i = 1}^n a_i x^i$ . Then:
\[
\begin{split}
 P(\alpha) &= f(a_n\alpha^n + a_{n - 1}\alpha^{n - 1} +  \dots +  a_1\alpha + a_0) 
 &= f(a_n\alpha^n) + f(a_{n - 1}\alpha^{n - 1}) + \dots + f(a_1\alpha) + f(a_0) 
 &= a_nf(\alpha^n) + a_{n -1} f(\alpha^{n - 1}) +\dots + a_1f(\alpha) + 0 
 &= 0 + 0 + \dots + 0 
 &= 0 
 \end{split}
\]



To finish, note that  $f(2\sqrt[3]{5} + 3\sqrt[3]{25}) \equiv 2 + 3 \equiv 1 \not\equiv 0 \pmod{2}$  By our claim, there is thus no integer polynomial  $P$  such that  $P(\alpha) = 2\sqrt[3]{5} + 3\sqrt[3]{25}$ .

    &= 2\sqrt[3]{5}+3\sqrt[3]{25}.

Since  $a,b,c$  are all integers we require  $5a+b=2$ ,  $a+b=3$ , and  $10a+c=0$ . Taking the first two equations modulo  $4$ , we obtain  $a+b \equiv 2 \pmod{4}$  and  $a+b \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$  respectively, absurd, since  $2 \not \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ . Thus no such polynomial  $P$  exists.

<details><summary>hidden for length</summary>\textbf{Claim:} Any power of  $\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25}$  is of the form  $a+b\sqrt[3]{5}+c\sqrt[3]{25}.$ \textit{Proof:}

 By the Binomial Theorem, any term in the expansion of  $(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})^n$  will be a product of integers,  $\sqrt[3]{5}$ 's, and  $\sqrt[3]{25}$ 's. Because  $\sqrt[3]{25}=(\sqrt[3]{5})^2,$  this term will be of the form  $x(\sqrt[3]{5})^y$  for integers  $x$  and  $y,$  and because  $(\sqrt[3]{5})^3=5,$  once we factor out all  $\sqrt[3]{5^3}$  terms, we will be left with either  $(\sqrt[3]{5})^0,(\sqrt[3]{5})^1,$  or  $(\sqrt[3]{5})^2,$  which are either integers,  $\sqrt[3]{5},$  or  $\sqrt[3]{25},$  as desired.

\textit{Remark:} This also implies that whenever we plug  $\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25}$  into an integer polynomial, we will get a result of this form, because all the terms are integer multiples of powers of  $\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25}.$ \bigskip

The following is the key:

\textbf{Lemma 1:}

If  $(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})^n=a+b\sqrt[3]{5}+c\sqrt[3]{25},$  then both of  $b$  and  $c$  are odd.

\textit{Proof:}

Note that  $(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})^n=(\sqrt[3]{5})^n(1+\sqrt[3]{5})^n.$  Split into three cases:
\bigskip

\textbf{Case 1:}  $n\equiv0\pmod3.$  

Then, we need the  $\sqrt[3]{5}$   and  $\sqrt[3]{25}$  terms of  $(1+\sqrt[3]{5})^n$  to be odd, because  $(\sqrt[3]{5})^n$  is an integer power of  $5.$  By the Binomial Theorem, we have:
\begin{align*}
(1+\sqrt[3]{5})^n&=1+\tbinom{n}{1}\sqrt[3]{5}+\tbinom{n}{2}\sqrt[3]{25}+\tbinom{n}{3}\cdot5+\ldots
\end{align*}
The coefficient of the integer term is  $\tbinom{n}{0}+\tbinom{n}{3}+\tbinom{n}{6}+\cdots,$  which is equal to  $\tfrac{(1+1)^n+(1+e^{2\pi i/3})^n+(1+e^{4\pi i/3})^n}{3}=\tfrac{2^n+2}{3}$  by a roots of unity filter. However, we have  $\tbinom n1+\tbinom n4+\cdots+\tbinom{n}{n-2}=\tbinom{n}{n-1}+\tbinom{n}{n-4}+\cdots+\tbinom n2,$  so the  $\sqrt[3]{5}$  and  $\sqrt[3]{25}$  terms are equal, and are both half the sum of all binomial terms minus the integer terms, which is  $\tfrac{2^n-\tfrac{2^n+2}{3}}{2}=\tfrac{2^n-1}{3}.$  This is odd, so this case is proven.
\bigskip

\textbf{Case 2:}  $n\equiv1\pmod3$ This time, we want the integer and  $\sqrt[3]{5}$  terms of  $(1+\sqrt[3]{5})^2$  to have odd coefficients. Again, we use roots of unity filter; the integer coefficient is  $\tbinom n0+\tbinom n3+\cdots+\tbinom{n}{n-1}=\tfrac{(1+1)^n+(1+e^{2\pi i/3})^n+(1+e^{4\pi i/3})^n}{3}=\tfrac{2^n+e^{4\pi i/3}+e^{2\pi i/3}}{3}=\tfrac{2^n-1}{3}$  which is odd. However, we have  $\tbinom n0+\tbinom n3+\cdots+\tbinom{n}{n-1}=\tbinom nn+\tbinom n{n-3}+\cdots+\tbinom{n}{1},$  so the integer coefficient is equal to the  $\sqrt[3]{5},$  so both are odd, as desired.
\bigskip

\textbf{Case 3:}  $n\equiv2\pmod3$ We want the  $\sqrt[3]{25}$  and integer coefficients to be odd this time around. Roots of unity filter one more time; as seen from previous cases the integer coefficient is  $\tfrac{(1+1)^n+(1+e^{2\pi i/3})^n+(1+e^{4\pi i/3})^n}{3}=\tfrac{2^n-e^{2\pi i/3}-e^{4\pi i/3}}{3}=\tfrac{2^n+1}{3},$  which is odd. We also have  $\tbinom n0+\tbinom n3+\cdots+\tbinom{n}{n-2}=\tbinom nn+\tbinom n{n-3}+\cdots+\tbinom{n}{2},$  so the  $\sqrt[3]{25}$  term is the same as the integer coefficient, which we know is odd.  $\blacksquare$  
\bigskip

\newpage
Let  $f(x)=a_nx^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\ldots+a_0$  for integers  $a_i.$  Then, we have that  $f(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})=a+b\sqrt[3]{5}+c\sqrt[3]{25}$  for integers  $a,b,c.$  Define  $(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})^n=k_n+b_n\sqrt[3]{5}+c_n\sqrt[3]{25}$  for integers  $k_n,b_n,c_n.$  If  $f(\sqrt[3]{5}+\sqrt[3]{25})=2\sqrt[3]{5}+3\sqrt[3]{25},$  then, by grouping we must have  $a_nb_n+a_{n-1}b_{n-1}+\ldots+a_1b_1=2$  and  $a_nc_n+a_{n-1}c_{n-1}+\ldots+a_1c_1=3.$  Subtracting these yields  $a_n(c_n-b_n)+a_{n-1}(c_{n-1}-b_{n-1})+\ldots+a_1(c_1-b_1)=1.$  Yet, by Lemma 1,  $b_n$  and  $c_n$  are odd, so  $c_i-b_i$  is even for all  $i,$  and thus the RHS is odd while the LHS is even. Therefore, there are no  $a_i$  that make this true, so there are no functions  $f$  that satisfy this.  $\blacksquare$</details>

Let  $x_1 \le x_2 \le \dots < x_n$  (with  $n \ge 2$ ) and let  $S$  be the set of all the  $x_i$ . Let  $T$  be a randomly chosen subset of  $S$ . What is the expected value of the indexed alternating sum of  $T$  ? Express your answer in terms of the  $x_i$ .
Note: We define the indexed alternating sum of  $T$  as
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{|T|} (-1)^{i+1}(i) T[i],
\]
where  $T[i]$  is the ith element of  $T$  when listed in increasing order. For example, if  $T = \{1, 3, 5\}$ then the indexed alternating sum of  $T$  is
\[
1 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 3 + 3 \cdot 5 = 10.
\]
Alternating sums of empty sets are defined to be  $0$ .

<details><summary>sol</summary>(We will denote the set  $S=\{x_1,x_2,\cdots, x_n\}$  with  $n$  elements to be  $S_n$  throughout the problem. Also, we will consider  $\subseteq$  to be the notation that a set is a [not necessarily proper] subset of another set, so for example,  $\{1,2\}\subseteq\{1,2,3\},$  and  $\{1,2,3\}\subseteq\{1,2,3\}.$  As in the problem statement,  $A[i]$  will be the  $i$  element of  $A$  when  $A$  is listed in increasing order for any set  $A$  with at least  $i$  elements.)

We claim the answer is  $\boxed{\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}}.$  

We first prove a lemma. 

Lemma  $1$ : For all positive integers  $n,$   $\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i (i+1)\dbinom{n}{i}=0.$ Proof: By the binomial theorem,  $0=(1-1)^n=\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^i(1)^{n-i}(1)^i\dbinom{n}{i}=\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^i\dbinom{n}{i}.$  Thus, it is sufficient to prove that  $\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^i (i+1)\dbinom{n}{i}-\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n}(-1)^i\dbinom{n}{i}=\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^ii\dbinom{n}{i}=0.$ We now proceed as follows. 

Consider a committee of  $n$  people. We want to select one person as the ``head of problem writing" and a nonnegative amount of other people as ``problem writers". (We will also consider the head of problem writing to be a problem writer.)

Let  $A_o$  be the amount of ways to assign roles such that there are an odd number of problem writers, and let  $A_e$  be the amount of ways to assign roles such that there are an even amount of problem writers.

We can count  $A_o$  and  $A_e$  in two different ways. 

We can first choose a person to be the ``head of problem writing". There are  $n$  ways to choose a person from the  $n$  people on the committee to be the head of problem writing, and then we can choose people from the remaining  $n-1$  people to be additional problem writers. 

If we want an even number of problem writers, then we need an odd number of additional problem writers in addition to the head of problem writing, and hence  $A_e=n\displaystyle\sum_{0\leq k\leq n-1, k\equiv 1 \pmod{2}}\dbinom{n-1}{k}=n\left(\dbinom{n-1}{1}+\dbinom{n-1}{3}+\cdots\right)$  based off casework on how many additional problem writers we want. Similarly,  $A_o=n\displaystyle\sum_{0\leq k\leq n-1, k\equiv 0 \pmod{2}}\dbinom{n-1}{k}=n\left(\dbinom{n-1}{0}+\dbinom{n-2}{2}+\cdots\right).$ By the binomial theorem,  $0=(1-1)^{n-1}=\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (-1)^i\dbinom{n}{i}=\dbinom{n-1}{0}-\dbinom{n-1}{1}+\dbinom{n-1}{2}-\cdots+(-1)^{n-1}\dbinom{n-1}{n-1},$  so  $\dbinom{n-1}{0}+\dbinom{n-1}{2}+\cdots=\displaystyle\sum_{0 \leq k\leq n-1, k\equiv 0 \pmod{2}}\dbinom{n-1}{k}=\displaystyle\sum_{0 \leq k\leq n-1, k\equiv 1 \pmod{2}}\dbinom{n-1}{k}= \dbinom{n-1}{1}+\dbinom{n-1}{3}+\cdots,$  so  $A_e=n\displaystyle\sum_{0\leq k\leq n-1, k\equiv 1 \pmod{2}}\dbinom{n-1}{k}=n\displaystyle\sum_{0 \leq k\leq n-1, k\equiv 0 \pmod{2}}\dbinom{n-1}{k}=A_o.$ We now compute  $A_e$  and  $A_o$  in another way. 

Consider choosing the problem writers first, and then designating one to be the head of problem writing. If we choose  $k$  problem writers, then the amount of ways to designate roles is  $k\dbinom{n}{k}.$  Thus, by doing casework on  $k,$  we yield  $A_e=\displaystyle\sum_{0\leq k \leq n, k\equiv 0\pmod{2}}k\dbinom{n}{k}=0\dbinom{n}{0}+2\dbinom{n}{2}+\cdots,$  and  $A_o=\displaystyle\sum_{0\leq k \leq n, k\equiv 1\pmod{2}} k\dbinom{n}{k}=1\dbinom{n}{1}+3\dbinom{n}{3}+\cdots.$  

Now,  $0=A_e-A_o=0\dbinom{n}{0}-1\dbinom{n}{1}+2\dbinom{n}{2}-3\dbinom{n}{3}+\cdots=\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n} (-1)^ii\dbinom{n}{i}.$  Since this is sufficient to prove the lemma, the lemma holds true, as desired.
\[\]
We now proceed with induction on  $n$  to prove the original claim on the expected value.

We first deal with the base case of  $n=2.$  In this case, there are  $4$  subset of  $S_2,$  so we can simply run through them all.

If the randomly chosen subset is  $\{\},$  then the indexed alternating sum of the subset is  $0.$  If the randomly chosen subset is  $\{x_1\},$  then indexed alternating sum of the subset is  $x_1,$  if the randomly chosen subset is  $\{x_2\},$  then the indexed alternating sum of the subset is  $x_2,$  and if the randomly chosen subset is  $\{x_1,x_2\},$  then the indexed alternating sum of the subset is  $x_1-2x_2.$ Since there are only  $4$  subsets of  $S_2$  and each one is equally likely to be chosen, the expected value of the indexed alternating sum of a subset of  $S_2$  is  $\dfrac{0+x_1+x_2+(x_1-2x_2)}{4}=\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}.$  Thus, the base case holds. 

Now, assume that there exists an integer  $k\geq 2$  such that the expected value of  $S_k$  is  $\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}.$ Then, the expected value of the indexed alternating sum for subsets of  $S_{k+1}$  is the sum of the indexed alternating sums of all  $2^{k+1}$  subsets of  $S_{k+1}$  divided by  $2^{k+1}.$  We split this sum into two sums: the sum of the indexed alternating sums of the subsets without  $x_{k+1}$  as an element, and the sum of the indexed alternating sums with  $x_{k+1}$  as an element.

The sum of the indexed alternating sums of the subsets without  $x_{k+1}$  as an element is simply the sum of the indexed alternating sums of the subsets of  $S_k$ , and since there are  $2^k$  such subsets, and the expected value of the indexed alternating sum is  $\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4},$  the total sum of all the indexed alternating sums is  $2^k\left(\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}\right).$ We now deal with the sum of the indexed alternating sums of the subsets with  $x_{k+1}$  as an element. We can further split this sum into two parts: the terms with  $x_{k+1}$  and the terms without  $x_{k+1}.$  

Let  $T$  be an arbitrary subset of  $S_{k+1}$  that contains  $x_{k+1}.$  If  $|T|=1,$  then the indexed alternating sum of  $T$  is simply  $x_{k+1}.$  If  $|T|\neq1,$  then the indexed alternating sum of  $T$  is  $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{|T|}(-1)^{i+1}(i)T[i]=\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{|T|-1}(-1)^{i+1}(i)T[i]+(-1)^{|T|+1}|T|x_{k+1}.$  Note that  $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{|T|-1}(-1)^{i+1}(i)T[i]$  is the indexed alternating sum of  $T\backslash \{x_{k+1}\},$  which is a subset of  $S_k.$  Also, for every subset  $T_1$  of  $S_k,$   $T_1\cup \{x_{k+1}\}$  will be a valid subset  $T$  of  $S_{k+1}$  containing  $x_{k+1},$  and also for that valid subset  $T,$   $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{|T|-1}(-1)^{i+1}(i)T[i]$  is the indexed alternating sum of  $T_1.$  As such, there is a one-to-one bijection between subsets of  $S_k$  with at least  $1$  element to subsets of  $S_{k+1}$  with  $x_{k+1}$  as an element and with at least  $2$  elements. Note that  $\displaystyle\sum_{T_1\subseteq S_k, |T_1|\geq 1}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{|T_1|}(-1)^{i+1}(i)T_1[i]$  is the sum of the indexed alternating sums of all the subsets of  $S_k$  except for the empty set, and since the indexed alternating sum of the empty set is  $0,$  this is simply equal to the sum of the indexed alternating sums of all the subsets of  $S_k,$  which we computed earlier to be  $2^k\left(\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}\right).$ We now consider  $\displaystyle\sum_{T\subseteq S_{k+1}, x_{k+1}\in T, |T|\geq 2}(-1)^{|T|+1}|T|x_{k+1}.$  We do casework on  $|T|$  to evaluate this sum. Note that for all integers  $2\leq a \leq k+1,$  then the amount of subsets  $T$  of  $S_{k+1}$   that have  $x_{k+1}$  as an element and  $|T|=a$  is the number of ways to choose  $a-1$  elements from the set  $\{x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_k\},$  which is simply  $\dbinom{k}{a-1}.$ As such, from casework on  $a,$   $\displaystyle\sum_{T\subseteq S_{k+1}, x_{k+1}\in T, |T|\geq 2}(-1)^{|T|+1}|T|x_{k+1}=\displaystyle\sum_{a=2}^{k+1} (-1)^{a+1}a\dbinom{k}{a-1}x_{k+1}=\displaystyle\sum_{a=1}^{k}(-1)^{a+2}(a+1)\dbinom{k}{a}x_{k+1}=\displaystyle\sum_{a=1}^{k}(-1)^{a}(a+1)\dbinom{k}{a}x_{k+1}.$ Now, the sum of all the indexed alternating sums of the subsets of  $S_{k+1}$  with  $x_{k+1}$  as an element is 
\begin{align*}
    &x_{k+1}+\displaystyle\sum_{T_1\subseteq S_k, |T_1|\geq 1}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{|T_1|}(-1)^{i+1}(i)T_1[i]+\displaystyle\sum_{T\subseteq S_{k+1}, x_{k+1}\in T, |T|\geq 2}(-1)^{|T|+1}|T|x_{k+1}&=(-1)^0(0+1)\dbinom{k}{0}x_{k+1}+2^k\left(\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}\right)+\displaystyle\sum_{a=1}^{k}(-1)^{a}(a+1)\dbinom{k}{a}x_{k+1}&=2^k\left(\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}\right)+\displaystyle\sum_{a=0}^{k}(-1)^{a}(a+1)\dbinom{k}{a}x_{k+1}&=2^k\left(\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}\right)+x_{k+1}\displaystyle\sum_{a=0}^{k}(-1)^{a}(a+1)\dbinom{k}{a}.
\end{align*}

By Lemma  $1,$   $\displaystyle\sum_{a=0}^{k}(-1)^{a}(a+1)\dbinom{k}{a}=0,$  so the sum is  $2^k\left(\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}\right)+x_{k+1}\displaystyle\sum_{a=0}^{k}(-1)^{a}(a+1)\dbinom{k}{a}=2^k\left(\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}\right).$ As such, the sum of all the indexed alternating sums of all the subsets of  $S_{k+1}$  is  $2^k\left(\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}\right)+2^k\left(\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}\right)=2^{k+1}\left(\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}\right).$  Since there are  $2^{k+1}$  subsets of  $S_{k+1},$  and each is equally likely to be chosen, the expected value of the indexed alternating sum of a randomly chosen subset of  $S_{k+1}$  is  $\dfrac{2^{k+1}\left(\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}\right)}{2^{k+1}}=\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}.$ As such, by the principle of mathematical induction, the expected of the indexed alternating sum of a randomly chosen subset of  $S_n$  is  $\dfrac{2x_1-x_2}{4}$  for all integers  $n\geq 2,$  as desired.  $\Box$</details>

Thus, because  $YA=YB,$  we have  $\angle YAB=\angle YBA=\angle B,$  so  $\angle AYD=2\angle B.$  Thus,  $\angle AYD=\angle APD,$  so  $APYD$  is cyclic, as desired.  $\blacksquare$ Define  $Y$  as above, and let  $M,N$  be the midpoints of  $AB$  and  $AD.$  Note that  $CE\perp AB$  is the equivalent of  $E$  being on the perpendicular bisector of  $AB.$  $\textbf{Only If:}$ If  $EPQ$  is equilateral, then  $QE=QP,$  so because  $QE=QA=QD$  we would need  $QP=QE=QA=QD,$  so  $APED$  would be cyclic. However,  $(APD)$  can only meet  $BD$  at 2 points at most, and we already know that  $D$  and  $Y$  are on both this circle and line by Lemma  $1,$  so we must have  $Y=E.$   $\blacksquare$   $\textbf{If:}$  

By Lemma  $1,$   $APED$  is cyclic with center  $Q,$  so  $QE=QP.$  We also have that  $\angle AMP+\angle ANP=90^\circ+90^\circ=180^\circ$ , so  $AMPN$  is cyclic. Thus,  $\angle MPN=180^\circ-\angle A=120^\circ.$  However, because  $E,P,$  and  $M$  all lie on the perpendicular bisector of  $AB,$  they are collinear, so  $\angle NPE=180^\circ-\angle NPM=60^\circ.$  Yet,  $N,P,Q$  all lie on the perpendicular bisector of  $AD,$  so they are collinear, and thus  $\angle QPE=\angle NPE=60^\circ.$  Thus, because  $QE=QP,$  we have  $\angle QEP=\angle QPE=60^\circ,$  so  $\angle PQE=180^\circ-\angle QEP-\angle QPE=60^\circ.$  Therefore,  $EPQ$  is equilateral.  $\blacksquare$

If  $\triangle EPQ$  is an equilateral triangle:

- $\triangle PAB = \triangle PBE$  by ASA, as  $PA=PB$ ,  $\angle PAE = \angle PBE$  and  $\angle APE = \angle BPE$ .
- $AE=BE$ , so  $E$  lies on a perpendicular bisector of  $AB$ .  $CA=CB$ , so  $C$  also lies on a perpendicular bisector of  $AB$ , and  $AB \perp CE$ .
[/list]</details>

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>[list]

- $AE=BE$
- $\triangle PAE = \triangle PBE$  by SSS ->  $\angle PAE = \angle PBE$ .
- By angle chasing,  $\angle PBE = \angle PDE = 30^{\circ}$ , so  $\angle PAE = \angle PDE$  and ADEP is concyclic.
- $Q$  is the center of (ADEP), so  $\angle PQE = 2\angle PAE=60^{\circ}$ .
- By  $PQ=QE$  and  $\angle PQE = 60^{\circ}$ , we can show that  $\triangle PQE$  is equilateral.

stem_md: $ABCD$  is a convex quadrilateral where  $\angle A = 45^\circ$  and  $\angle C = 135^\circ$ .  $P$  is a point strictly inside  $\triangle ABC$  such that  $\angle BAP = \angle CAD$  and  $\angle BCP = \angle ACD$ . Prove that  $PB \perp PD$  if and only if  $AC \perp BD$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>xooksxooksxooksxooksxooksxooks</summary>(Note: In this solution, the measure of an arc refers to the degree measure of that arc.)
[asy]
import olympiad;
unitsize(6 cm);
pair D=(0,0), B=(2-2sqrt(3)/3,0), C=(2-sqrt(3), 1-2sqrt(3)/3), A=(2-sqrt(3), 1), E=(2-sqrt(3),0), P=(1-sqrt(3)/3, 1-sqrt(3)/3);
draw(A--B--C--D--A);
draw(B--D);
draw(A--C);
label(" $A$ ", A, N);
label(" $B$ ", B, E);
label(" $C$ ", C, S);
label(" $D$ ", D, W);
label(" $E$ ", E, SW);
label(" $P$ ", P, NE);
draw(A--P--C);
draw(circumcircle(A,B,C));
draw(B--P);
[/asy]
Firstly, since  $\angle BAD+\angle BCD=45^{\circ}+135^{\circ}=180^{\circ},$   $ABCD$  is cyclic. 

We now prove that  $PB\perp PD$  if  $AC\perp BD.$ Assume  $AC\perp BD,$  and let  $AC$  and  $BD$  intersect at  $E.$  Also, denote  $\angle CAD=\theta.$   Then,  $\angle BAC=\angle BAD-\angle CAD=45^{\circ}-\theta.$  

Now, since  $ABCD$  is cyclic,  $\angle BDC=\angle BAC=45^{\circ}-\theta,$  so since  $\angle DEC=90^{\circ},$   $\angle DCE=180^{\circ}-\angle DEC-\angle BDC=90^{\circ}-(45^{\circ}-\theta)=45^{\circ}+\theta.$  Now,  $\angle BAP=\angle CAD=\theta,$   $\angle BCP=\angle ACD=\angle DCE=45^{\circ}+\theta,$  and  $\angle ACB=\angle BCD-\angle ACD=135^{\circ}-(45^{\circ}+\theta)=90^{\circ}-\theta.$ As such,  $\angle CAP=\angle BAC-\angle BAP=(45^{\circ}-\theta)-\theta=45^{\circ}-2\theta=(90^{\circ}-\theta)-(45^{\circ}+\theta)=\angle ACB-\angle BCP=\angle PCA,$  so  $PA=PC.$ Since  $PA,$   $PB,$  and  $PC$  are concurrent at  $P$  inside  $\triangle ABC,$  by trig ceva,  $\dfrac{\sin \angle BCP}{\sin \angle PCA}\cdot \dfrac{\sin \angle CAP}{\sin \angle PAB}\cdot \dfrac{\sin \angle ABP}{\sin \angle PBC}=\dfrac{\sin(45^{\circ}+\theta)}{\sin(45^{\circ}-2\theta)}\cdot\dfrac{\sin(45^{\circ}-2\theta)}{\sin\theta}\cdot \dfrac{\sin \angle ABP}{\sin \angle PBC}=\dfrac{\sin(45^{\circ}+\theta)}{\sin \theta}\cdot \dfrac{\sin \angle ABP}{\sin \angle PBC}=1,$  so  $\dfrac{\sin \angle ABP}{\sin \angle PBC}=\dfrac{\sin \theta}{\sin(45^{\circ}+\theta)}.$ Since  $ABCD$  is cyclic,  $\angle ABD=\angle ACD=45^{\circ}+\theta$  and  $\angle CBD=\angle CAD=\theta,$  so  $\angle ABC=\angle ABD+\angle CBD=(45^{\circ}+\theta)+\theta=45^{\circ}+2\theta=\angle ABP+\angle PBC,$  so  $\angle PBC=45^{\circ}+2\theta-\angle ABP.$ Now,  $\sin\angle ABP\sin(45^{\circ}+\theta)=\sin \theta\sin\angle PBC=\sin\theta\sin(45^{\circ}+2\theta-\angle ABP).$  By product-to-sum,  $\dfrac{\cos(45^{\circ}+\theta-\angle ABP)-\cos(45^{\circ}+\theta+\angle ABP)}{2}=\sin(45^{\circ}+\theta)\sin\angle ABP=\sin(45^{\circ}+2\theta-\angle ABP)\sin\theta=\dfrac{\cos(45^{\circ}+\theta-\angle ABP)-\cos(45^{\circ}+3\theta-\angle ABP)}{2}.$ As such,  $\cos(45^{\circ}+\theta-\angle ABP)-\cos(45^{\circ}+\theta+\angle ABP)=\cos(45^{\circ}+\theta-\angle ABP)-\cos(45^{\circ}+3\theta-\angle ABP),$  so  $0=\cos(45^{\circ}+\theta+\angle ABP)-\cos(45^{\circ}+3\theta-\angle ABP)=\cos(45^{\circ}+2\theta-(\theta-\angle ABP))-\cos(45^{\circ}+2\theta+(\theta-\angle ABP)).$  As such, by sum-to-product,  $0=\dfrac{\cos(45^{\circ}+2\theta-(\theta-\angle ABP))-\cos(45^{\circ}+2\theta+(\theta-\angle ABP))}{2}=\sin(45^{\circ}+2\theta)\sin(\theta-\angle ABP).$  Note that  $0^{\circ}<\angle CAD=\theta<\angle BAD=45^{\circ},$  so  $45^{\circ}<2\theta+45^{\circ}<135^{\circ},$  so  $\sin(45^{\circ}+2\theta)\neq 0,$  and  $\sin(\theta-\angle ABP)=0.$  Since  $0^{\circ}<\theta<45^{\circ}$  and  $0^{\circ}<\angle ABP<\angle ABC=45^{\circ}+2\theta,$  so  $-135^{\circ}<-45^{\circ}-2\theta<\theta-\angle ABP<45^{\circ},$  and since  $\sin(\theta-\angle ABP)=0,$  so  $\theta-\angle ABP=0,$  and  $\angle ABP=\theta=\angle PAB,$  so  $PB=PA=PC.$ As such,  $P$  is the circumcenter of  $\triangle ABC,$  Since  $ABCD$  is cyclic,  $P$  is the center of the circumcircle of  $ABCD,$  so  $\angle DPB=2\angle BAD=90^{\circ},$  so  $DP\perp PB.$ As such,  $PB\perp PD$  if  $AC\perp BD.$ We now prove that  $AC\perp BD$  if  $PB\perp PD.$ [asy]
import olympiad;
unitsize(6 cm);
pair D=(0,0), B=(2-2sqrt(3)/3,0), C=(2-sqrt(3), 1-2sqrt(3)/3), A=(2-sqrt(3), 1), E=(2-sqrt(3),0), P=(1-sqrt(3)/3, 1-sqrt(3)/3);
draw(A--B--C--D--A);
draw(B--D);
draw(A--C);
label(" $A$ ", A, N);
label(" $B$ ", B, E);
label(" $C$ ", C, S);
label(" $D$ ", D, W);
label(" $E$ ", E, SW);
label(" $P$ ", P, NE);
draw(circumcircle(A,B,C));
draw(B--P--D);
draw(A--P--C);
[/asy]
Again, denote  $E$  as the intersection of  $AC$  and  $BD.$  Also, denote  $\angle BAP=\angle CAD=\theta,$   $\angle BCP=\angle ACD=\alpha,$  and denote  $O$  as the circumcenter of  $ABCD.$  

Since  $ABCD$  is cyclic,  $\angle CBD=\angle CAD=\theta,$  and  $\angle ABD=\angle ACD=\alpha,$  so  $\angle ABC=\angle ABD+\angle CBD=\alpha+\theta.$ Note that  $\angle APB+\angle BPC=(180^{\circ}-\angle BAP-\angle ABP)+(180^{\circ}-\angle BCP-\angle PBC)=360^{\circ}-\theta-\alpha-(\angle ABP+\angle PBC)=360^{\circ}-\theta-\alpha-\angle ABC=360^{\circ}-2\theta-2\alpha.$  As such,  $\angle APC=360^{\circ}-(\angle APB+\angle BPC)=360^{\circ}-(360^{\circ}-2\theta-2\alpha)=2\theta+2\alpha.$ Note that  $0^{\circ}<2\theta=\angle CAD+\angle BAP=\angle BAD-\angle CAP=45^{\circ}-\angle CAP<45^{\circ}$  and  $0^{\circ}<2\alpha=\angle ACD+\angle BCP=\angle BCD-\angle ACP=135^{\circ}-\angle ACP<135^{\circ},$  so  $0^{\circ}<2\theta+2\alpha<180^{\circ}.$  As such, arc  $CDA$  has measure  $0^{\circ}<2\theta+2\alpha=2\angle ABC<180^{\circ},$  so arc  $ABC$  has arc measure of more than  $180^{\circ},$  so  $O$  lies on the same of  $AC$  as  $P.$  As such,  $\angle AOC=2\angle ABC=2\theta+2\alpha=\angle APC,$  so  $A,$   $O,$   $P,$  and  $C$  are concyclic. Since  $P$  and  $O$  are on the same side of  $AC,$  we also have that  $P$  lies on arc  $AOC.$ Also,  $\angle BPD=90^{\circ},$  so since  $\angle BOD=2\angle BAD=90^{\circ},$  so  $P$  lies on the circumcircle of  $BOD,$  which is the circle with diameter  $BD.$

unitsize(6 cm);
pair D=(0,0), B=(2-2sqrt(3)/3,0), C=(2-sqrt(3), 1-2sqrt(3)/3), A=(2-sqrt(3), 1), E=(2-sqrt(3),0), P=(1-sqrt(3)/3, 1-sqrt(3)/3);
draw(A--B--C--D--A);
draw(B--D);
draw(A--C);

label(" $D$ ", D, W);
label(" $O$ ", P, NE);
draw(circumcircle(A,B,C));
pair F=(1-sqrt(3), 1-sqrt(3)/3);
draw(arc(F, C, A));

As such,  $P$  is one of the intersections between the circle with diameter  $BD$  and the circumcircle of  $AOC.$  Clearly,  $O$  lies on both of the circles, so one of these intersections is  $O.$  

Claim  $1$ :  $C$  lies within the circle with diameter  $BD$ Proof: Clearly, if  $C$  lied on the circle with diameter  $BD,$  then  $135^{\circ}=\angle BCD=90^{\circ},$  a contradiction. Assume for the sake of contradiction that  $C$  lies outside the circle with diameter  $BD.$  Let  $E^{\prime}$  be the foot of the perpendicular from  $C$  to  $BD,$  and let  $H$  be the intersection point between  $CE^{\prime}$  and the circle with diameter  $BD$  that lies on the same side of  $BD$  as  $C.$

label(" $H$ ", H, dir(65));

pair G=(B+D)/2;

Then, since  $C$  lies outside the circle with diameter  $BD,$   $H$  is closer to  $BD$  than  $C.$  Since  $H$  lies on the circle with diameter  $BD,$   $\angle BHD=90^{\circ}.$  Note that  $135^{\circ}=\angle BCD=180^{\circ}-\angle BDC-\angle CBD=180^{\circ}-(\angle CDH+\angle BDH)-(\angle CBH+\angle HBD)=(180^{\circ}-\angle BDH-\angle HBD)-\angle CDH-\angle CBH=90^{\circ}-\angle CDH-\angle CBH<90^{\circ},$  a contradiction. Thus,  $C$  lies inside the circle with diameter  $BD,$  as desired.

Claim  $2$ :  $A$  lies outside of the circle with diameter  $BD.$  

Proof: If  $A$  lied on the circle with diameter  $BD,$  then  $45^{\circ}=\angle BAD=90^{\circ},$  a contradiction.

Assume for the sake of contradiction that  $A$  lies inside the circle with diameter  $BD.$  Let  $E^{\prime\prime}$  be the foot of the altitude from  $A$  to  $BD,$  and let  $I$  be the intersection between  $AE^{\prime\prime}$  and the circle with diameter  $BD.$  Since  $A$  lies inside the circle with diameter  $BD,$   $A$  is closer to  $BD$  than  $I.$ [asy]
import olympiad;
unitsize(6 cm);
pair D=(0,0), B=(2-2sqrt(3)/3,0), C=(2-sqrt(3), 1-2sqrt(3)/3), A=(2-sqrt(3), 1), E=(2-sqrt(3),0), P=(1-sqrt(3)/3, 1-sqrt(3)/3);
draw(A--B--C--D--A);
draw(B--D);
label(" $A$ ", A, NE);
label(" $B$ ", B, E);
label(" $C$ ", C, S);
label(" $D$ ", D, W);
pair H=(E+C)/2;
label(" $E^{\prime\prime}$ ", E, S);

pair I=A+(0, 1/(2sqrt(3)));
draw(I--E);
draw(D--I--B);
pair F=(1-sqrt(3), 1-sqrt(3)/3);
draw(" $I$ ", I, N);
pair G=(B+D)/2;


[/asy]
Since  $I$  lies on the circle with diameter  $BD,$   $\angle BID=90^{\circ},$  so  $90^{\circ}=\angle DIB=180^{\circ}-\angle BDI-\angle DBI=180^{\circ}-(\angle ADI+\angle BDA)-(\angle ABI+\angle DBA)=180^{\circ}-(\angle BDA+\angle DBA)-(\angle ADI+\angle ABI)=\angle BAD-(\angle ADI+\angle ABI)<\angle BAD=45^{\circ},$  a contradiction, so  $A$  lies outside of the circle with diameter  $BD,$  as desired. 

Now, consider the shortest path with positive length along the circumcircle of  $AOC$  starting at  $A$  and ending at  $A$  moving clockwise, and denote it  $p.$ [asy]
import olympiad;
unitsize(6 cm);
pair D=(0,0), B=(2-2sqrt(3)/3,0), C=(2-sqrt(3), 1-2sqrt(3)/3), A=(2-sqrt(3), 1), E=(2-sqrt(3),0), P=(1-sqrt(3)/3, 1-sqrt(3)/3);
draw(A--B--C--D--A);
draw(B--D);
draw(A--C);
label(" $A$ ", A, N);
label(" $B$ ", B, E);
label(" $C$ ", C, S);
label(" $D$ ", D, W);
label(" $O$ ", P, NE);
draw(circumcircle(A,B,C));
pair F=(1-sqrt(3), 1-sqrt(3)/3);
draw(circle(F, 2sqrt(3)/3));
pair G=(B+D)/2;
draw(circle(G, 1-sqrt(3)/3));
dot(P);
[/asy]
Note that  $p$  starts at  $A,$  a point outside of the circle with diameter  $BD,$  and eventually gets to  $C,$  a point inside of the circle with diameter  $BD.$  Also, it ends at  $A,$  a point outside of the circle with diameter  $BD,$  so  $p$  must cross the circle with diameter  $BD$  at least twice, once before reaching  $C$  and once after. Also, since two circles can intersect in at most two points,  $p$  intersects the circle with diameter  $BD$  exactly twice. Clearly,  $O$  is one of these intersections as  $O$  lies on both the circumcircle of  $AOC$  and the circle with diameter  $BD,$  and since the path along arc  $AOC$  starting at  $A$   and going to  $C$  goes clockwise,  $O$  is the intersection that  $p$  goes through before hitting  $C.$  

The other intersection between  $p$  and the circle with diameter  $BD$  occurs on the part of  $p$  after hitting  $C,$  but since  $P$  lies on the arc  $AOC,$   $P$  is not equal to this other intersection. Since there are only two intersections between  $p$  and the circle with diameter  $BD,$  and  $P$  must be one of them, this means that  $P=O,$  so  $P$  is the circumcenter of  $ABCD.$ [asy]

ABP=\sin(45^{\circ}+2\theta-\angle ABP)\sin\theta=\dfrac{\cos(45^{\circ}+\theta-\angle ABP)-\cos(45^{\circ}+3\theta-\angle ABP)}{2}.$ As such, $\cos(45^{\circ}+\theta-\angle ABP)-\cos(45^{\circ}+\theta+\angle ABP)=\cos(45^{\circ}+\theta-\angle ABP)-\cos(45^{\circ}+3\theta-\angle ABP),$ so $0=\cos(45^{\circ}+\theta+\angle ABP)-\cos(45^{\circ}+3\theta-\angle ABP)=\cos(45^{\circ}+2\theta-(\theta-\angle ABP))-\cos(45^{\circ}+2\theta+(\theta-\angle ABP)).$ As such, by sum-to-product, $0=\dfrac{\cos(45^{\circ}+2\theta-(\theta-\angle ABP))-\cos(45^{\circ}+2\theta+(\theta-\angle ABP))}{2}=\sin(45^{\circ}+2\theta)\sin(\theta-\angle ABP).$ Note that $0^{\circ}<\angle CAD=\theta<\angle BAD=45^{\circ},$ so $45^{\circ}<2\theta+45^{\circ}<135^{\circ},$ so $\sin(45^{\circ}+2\theta)\neq 0,$ and $\sin(\theta-\angle ABP)=0.$ Since $0^{\circ}<\theta<45^{\circ}$ and $0^{\circ}<\angle ABP<\angle ABC=45^{\circ}+2\theta,$ so $-135^{\circ}<-45^{\circ}-2\theta<\theta-\angle ABP<45^{\circ},$ and since $\sin(\theta-\angle ABP)=0,$ so $\theta-\angle ABP=0,$ and $\angle ABP=\theta=\angle PAB,$ so $PB=PA=PC.$ As such, $P$ is the circumcenter of $\triangle ABC,$ Since $ABCD$ is cyclic, $P$ is the center of the circumcircle of $ABCD,$ so $\angle DPB=2\angle BAD=90^{\circ},$ so $DP\perp PB.$ As such, $PB\perp PD$ if $AC\perp BD.$ We now prove that $AC\perp BD$ if $PB\perp PD.$ [asy] import olympiad; unitsize(6 cm); pair D=(0,0), B=(2-2sqrt(3)/3,0), C=(2-sqrt(3), 1-2sqrt(3)/3), A=(2-sqrt(3), 1), E=(2-sqrt(3),0), P=(1-sqrt(3)/3, 1-sqrt(3)/3); draw(A--B--C--D--A); draw(B--D); draw(A--C); label(" $A$ ", A, N); label(" $B$ ", B, E); label(" $C$ ", C, S); label(" $D$ ", D, W); label(" $E$ ", E, SW); label(" $P$ ", P, NE); draw(circumcircle(A,B,C)); draw(B--P--D); draw(A--P--C); [/asy] Again, denote $E$ as the intersection of $AC$ and $BD.$ Also, denote $\angle BAP=\angle CAD=\theta,$ $\angle BCP=\angle ACD=\alpha,$ and denote $O$ as the circumcenter of $ABCD.$ Since $ABCD$ is cyclic, $\angle CBD=\angle CAD=\theta,$ and $\angle ABD=\angle ACD=\alpha,$ so $\angle ABC=\angle ABD+\angle CBD=\alpha+\theta.$ Note that $\angle APB+\angle BPC=(180^{\circ}-\angle BAP-\angle ABP)+(180^{\circ}-\angle BCP-\angle PBC)=360^{\circ}-\theta-\alpha-(\angle ABP+\angle PBC)=360^{\circ}-\theta-\alpha-\angle ABC=360^{\circ}-2\theta-2\alpha.$ As such, $\angle APC=360^{\circ}-(\angle APB+\angle BPC)=360^{\circ}-(360^{\circ}-2\theta-2\alpha)=2\theta+2\alpha.$ Note that $0^{\circ}<2\theta=\angle CAD+\angle BAP=\angle BAD-\angle CAP=45^{\circ}-\angle CAP<45^{\circ}$ and $0^{\circ}<2\alpha=\angle ACD+\angle BCP=\angle BCD-\angle ACP=135^{\circ}-\angle ACP<135^{\circ},$ so $0^{\circ}<2\theta+2\alpha<180^{\circ}.$ As such, arc $CDA$ has measure $0^{\circ}<2\theta+2\alpha=2\angle ABC<180^{\circ},$ so arc $ABC$ has arc measure of more than $180^{\circ},$ so $O$ lies on the same of $AC$ as $P.$ As such, $\angle AOC=2\angle ABC=2\theta+2\alpha=\angle APC,$ so $A,$ $O,$ $P,$ and $C$ are concyclic. Since $P$ and $O$ are on the same side of $AC,$ we also have that $P$ lies on arc $AOC.$ Also, $\angle BPD=90^{\circ},$ so since $\angle BOD=2\angle BAD=90^{\circ},$ so $P$ lies on the circumcircle of $BOD,$ which is the circle with diameter $BD.$ [asy] import olympiad; unitsize(6 cm); pair D=(0,0), B=(2-2sqrt(3)/3,0), C=(2-sqrt(3), 1-2sqrt(3)/3), A=(2-sqrt(3), 1), E=(2-sqrt(3),0), P=(1-sqrt(3)/3, 1-sqrt(3)/3); draw(A--B--C--D--A); draw(B--D); draw(A--C); label(" $A$ ", A, N); label(" $B$ ", B, E); label(" $C$ ", C, S); label(" $D$ ", D, W); label(" $O$ ", P, NE); draw(circumcircle(A,B,C)); pair F=(1-sqrt(3), 1-sqrt(3)/3); draw(arc(F, C, A)); pair G=(B+D)/2; draw(circle(G, 1-sqrt(3)/3)); dot(P); [/asy] As such, $P$ is one of the intersections between the circle with diameter $BD$ and the circumcircle of $AOC.$ Clearly, $O$ lies on both of the circles, so one of these intersections is $O.$ Claim $1$ : $C$ lies within the circle with diameter $BD$ Proof: Clearly, if $C$ lied on the circle with diameter $BD,$ then $135^{\circ}=\angle BCD=90^{\circ},$ a contradiction. Assume for the sake of contradiction that $C$ lies outside the circle with diameter $BD.$ Let $E^{\prime}$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $BD,$ and let $H$ be the intersection point between $CE^{\prime}$ and the circle with diameter $BD$ that lies on the same side of $BD$ as $C.$ [asy] import olympiad; unitsize(6 cm); pair D=(0,0), B=(2-2sqrt(3)/3,0), C=(2-sqrt(3), 1-2sqrt(3)/3), A=(2-sqrt(3), 1), E=(2-sqrt(3),0), P=(1-sqrt(3)/3, 1-sqrt(3)/3); draw(A--B--C--D--A); draw(B--D); draw(C--E); label(" $A$ ", A, N); label(" $B$ ", B, E); label(" $C$ ", C, S); label(" $D$ ", D, W); pair H=(E+C)/2; label(" $E^{\prime}$ ", E, N); draw(D--H--B); label(" $H$ ", H, dir(65)); pair F=(1-sqrt(3), 1-sqrt(3)/3); pair G=(B+D)/2; [/asy] Then, since $C$ lies outside the circle with diameter $BD,$ $H$ is closer to $BD$ than $C.$ Since $H$ lies on the circle with diameter $BD,$ $\angle BHD=90^{\circ}.$ Note that $135^{\circ}=\angle BCD=180^{\circ}-\angle BDC-\angle CBD=180^{\circ}-(\angle CDH+\angle BDH)-(\angle CBH+\angle HBD)=(180^{\circ}-\angle BDH-\angle HBD)-\angle CDH-\angle CBH=90^{\circ}-\angle CDH-\angle CBH<90^{\circ},$ a contradiction. Thus, $C$ lies inside the circle with diameter $BD,$ as desired. Claim $2$ : $A$ lies outside of the circle with diameter $BD.$ Proof: If $A$ lied on the circle with diameter $BD,$ then $45^{\circ}=\angle BAD=90^{\circ},$ a contradiction. Assume for the sake of contradiction that $A$ lies inside the circle with diameter $BD.$ Let $E^{\prime\prime}$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$ to $BD,$ and let $I$ be the intersection between $AE^{\prime\prime}$ and the circle with diameter $BD.$ Since $A$ lies inside the circle with diameter $BD,$ $A$ is closer to $BD$ than $I.$ [asy] import olympiad; unitsize(6 cm); pair D=(0,0), B=(2-2sqrt(3)/3,0), C=(2-sqrt(3), 1-2sqrt(3)/3), A=(2-sqrt(3), 1), E=(2-sqrt(3),0), P=(1-sqrt(3)/3, 1-sqrt(3)/3); draw(A--B--C--D--A); draw(B--D); label(" $A$ ", A, NE); label(" $B$ ", B, E); label(" $C$ ", C, S); label(" $D$ ", D, W); pair H=(E+C)/2; label(" $E^{\prime\prime}$ ", E, S); pair I=A+(0, 1/(2sqrt(3))); draw(I--E); draw(D--I--B); pair F=(1-sqrt(3), 1-sqrt(3)/3); draw(" $I$ ", I, N); pair G=(B+D)/2; [/asy] Since $I$ lies on the circle with diameter $BD,$ $\angle BID=90^{\circ},$ so $90^{\circ}=\angle DIB=180^{\circ}-\angle BDI-\angle DBI=180^{\circ}-(\angle ADI+\angle BDA)-(\angle ABI+\angle DBA)=180^{\circ}-(\angle BDA+\angle DBA)-(\angle ADI+\angle ABI)=\angle BAD-(\angle ADI+\angle ABI)<\angle BAD=45^{\circ},$ a contradiction, so $A$ lies outside of the circle with diameter $BD,$ as desired. Now, consider the shortest path with positive length along the circumcircle of $AOC$ starting at $A$ and ending at $A$ moving clockwise, and denote it $p.$ [asy] import olympiad; unitsize(6 cm); pair D=(0,0), B=(2-2sqrt(3)/3,0), C=(2-sqrt(3), 1-2sqrt(3)/3), A=(2-sqrt(3), 1), E=(2-sqrt(3),0), P=(1-sqrt(3)/3, 1-sqrt(3)/3); draw(A--B--C--D--A); draw(B--D); draw(A--C); label(" $A$ ", A, N); label(" $B$ ", B, E); label(" $C$ ", C, S); label(" $D$ ", D, W); label(" $O$ ", P, NE); draw(circumcircle(A,B,C)); pair F=(1-sqrt(3), 1-sqrt(3)/3); draw(circle(F, 2sqrt(3)/3)); pair G=(B+D)/2; draw(circle(G, 1-sqrt(3)/3)); dot(P); [/asy] Note that $p$ starts at $A,$ a point outside of the circle with diameter $BD,$ and eventually gets to $C,$ a point inside of the circle with diameter $BD.$ Also, it ends at $A,$ a point outside of the circle with diameter $BD,$ so $p$ must cross the circle with diameter $BD$ at least twice, once before reaching $C$ and once after. Also, since two circles can intersect in at most two points, $p$ intersects the circle with diameter $BD$ exactly twice. Clearly, $O$ is one of these intersections as $O$ lies on both the circumcircle of $AOC$ and the circle with diameter $BD,$ and since the path along arc $AOC$ starting at $A$ and going to $C$ goes clockwise, $O$ is the intersection that $p$ goes through before hitting $C.$ The other intersection between $p$ and the circle with diameter $BD$ occurs on the part of $p$ after hitting $C,$ but since $P$ lies on the arc $AOC,$ $P$ is not equal to this other intersection. Since there are only two intersections between $p$ and the circle with diameter $BD,$ and $P$ must be one of them, this means that $P=O,$ so $P$ is the circumcenter of $ABCD.$ [asy] import olympiad; unitsize(6 cm); pair D=(0,0), B=(2-2sqrt(3)/3,0), C=(2-sqrt(3), 1-2sqrt(3)/3), A=(2-sqrt(3), 1), E=(2-sqrt(3),0), P=(1-sqrt(3)/3, 1-sqrt(3)/3); draw(A--B--C--D--A); draw(B--D); draw(A--C); label(" $A$ ", A, N); label(" $B$ ", B, E); label(" $C$ ", C, S); label(" $D$ ", D, W); label(" $E$ ", E, SW); label(" $P$ ", P, NE); draw(circumcircle(A,B,C)); draw(B--P--D); draw(A--P--C); [/asy] Note that $\angle PAC=\angle BAD-\angle CAD-\angle BAP=45^{\circ}-2\theta,$ and $\angle PCA=\angle BCD-\angle ACD-\angle PCB=135^{\circ}-2\alpha.$ Since $P$ is the circumcenter of $ABCD,$ $PA=PC,$ so $45^{\circ}-2\theta=\angle PAC=\angle PCA=135^{\circ}-2\alpha,$ so $2\alpha=2\theta+90^{\circ},$ and $\alpha=\theta+45^{\circ}.$ Now, since $ABCD$ is cyclic, $\angle ABD=\angle ACD=\alpha=\theta+45^{\circ},$ and $\angle BAC=\angle BAD-\angle CAD=45^{\circ}-\theta,$ so $\angle BEA=180^{\circ}-\angle BAC-\angle ABD=180^{\circ}-(45^{\circ}-\theta+45^{\circ}+\theta)=90^{\circ},$ so $AC\perp BD,$ and $AC\perp BD$ if $PB\perp PD.$ As such, $PB\perp PD$ iff $AC\perp BD,$ as desired. $\Box$

SolutionThe solutions are $(a,b,c)=(1,0,0),(1,1,2),$ and $(2,0,1).$ Rearranging the given equation $2^a \cdot 5^b-3^c=1,$ we get $2^a \cdot 5^b=3^c+1.$ We use casework. Our cases are $a \ge 1$ and $b \ge 1,$ $a=0,$ and $b=0.$ \textbf{Case 1 : $a \ge 1$ and $b \ge 1$ } In this case, $2^a \cdot 5^b$ ends in a $0.$ So, $3^c$ must end in a $9.$ This only happens when $c \equiv 2 \mod 4.$ Note that $81(3^x+1)-80=3^{x+4}+1.$ Let $\frac{3^x+1}{10}=y_x.$ Then, the equation $81(3^x+1)-80=3^{x+4}+1$ is the same as $810y_x-80=10y_{x+4}.$ Dividing by $81y_x-8=y_{x+4}.$ Let $c_k=4k-2,$ and also let $\frac{3^{c_k}+1}{10}=d_k.$ Since $c_{k+1}=c_k+4,$ by $81y_x-8=y_{x+4},$ we get $81d_k-8=d_{k+1}.$ The units digit of $d_1=\frac{3^2+1}{10}=1$ is $1.$ By the equation $81d_k-8=d_{k+1},$ we get $81d_1-8=d_2.$ So, the units digit of $d_2$ is the same as the units digit of $81(1)-8=73.$ So, the units digit of $d_2$ is equal to $3.$ The units digit of $d_3$ is the same as $81$ times the units digit of $d_2$ minus $8,$ which is the same as $81(3)-8=243-8=235.$ So, the units digit of $d_3$ is $5.$ Repeating the same method gives us the units digit of $d_4,d_5,$ and $d_6.$ They are respectively $7,9,$ and $1.$ Since we are using the same algorithm, the units digit of $d_k$ repeats $1,3,5,7,9,1,3,5,7,9$ , and so on. Since $y_x=\frac{3^x+1}{10}=\frac{2^a \cdot 5^b}{10}=2^{a-1} \cdot 5^{b-1},$ the units digit of $y_x$ must be $0,2,4,5,6,8,$ or $1$ if $a=1$ and $b=1.$ So, the units digit of $d_k$ must be $5$ or $d_k=1.$ If $d_k=1,c=2.$ So, one solution appears : $(a,b,c)=(1,1,2).$ Now, let the units digit of $d_k$ be $5.$ Then, $\frac{d_k}{5}$ ends in an $1,3,5,7,$ or $9.$ If it is $1,$ stop. If it is a $5,$ keep dividing by $5.$ If it is a different number, $2^x \cdot 5^y$ cannot equal it. Then, we get $d_k=5^x$ for some positive integer $x.$ There are no solutions in this case. \textbf{Case 2 : $a=0$ } Then, since $2^a=1$ for $a=0,$ the given equation is the same as $5^b-3^c=1.$ For all nonnegative integers $b$ and $c,$ both $5^b$ and $3^c$ are odd. So, $5^b-3^c$ must be an even number. Since $1$ is a odd number, we have a contradiction. So, there are no solutions in this case. \textbf{Case 3 : $b=0$ } Since $5^b=1$ for $b=0,$ the given equation is the same as $2^a-3^c=1,$ or $2^a=3^c+1.$ Taking $\mod 3,$ we get $2^a=3^c+1 \equiv 1 \mod 3.$ If $c=0,$ we get $a=1.$ We get another solution, $(a,b,c)=(1,0,0).$ I don't know what to do from here, but I found that $(a,b,c)=(2,0,1)$ also works.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let  $\angle{BAP}=\angle{CAD}=\alpha$  and  $\angle{BCP}=\angle{ACD}=\beta$ , and denote  $K$  as the intersection of  $\overline{AC}$  and  $\overline{BD}$ .

Since the opposite angles of quadrilateral  $ABCD$  have a sum of  $180^{\circ}$ ,  $ABCD$  is a cyclic quadrilateral. Therefore,  $\angle{CBD}= \angle{CAD}=\alpha$  and  $\angle{ABD}=\angle{ACD}=\beta$ , so  $\angle{ABC}=\angle{CBD}+\angle{ABD}=\alpha+\beta$ .

First, we prove that if  $\overline{AC} \perp \overline{BD}$ , then  $\overline{PB} \perp \overline{PD}$ . 

Note that  $\angle{CAP}=45^{\circ}-\angle{CAD}-\angle{BAP}=45^{\circ}-2\alpha$ . Also, we have  $\angle{BDC}=\angle{BAC}=45^{\circ}-\angle{CAD}=45^{\circ}-\alpha$ . Since  $\triangle{CKD}$  is a right triangle,  $\angle{KDC}+\angle{KCD}=90^{\circ}\Rightarrow 45^{\circ}-\alpha+\beta=90^{\circ}\Rightarrow \beta = \alpha + 45^{\circ}$ . Thus,  $\angle{ACP}=135^{\circ}-\angle{ACD}-\angle{BCP}=135^{\circ}-2\beta=45^{\circ}-2\alpha=\angle{CAP}$ , so  $AP=CP$ .

Now, we claim that  $\angle{ABP}=\alpha$ . Assume that  $\angle{ABP}<\alpha$ . This suggests  $\angle{CBP}>\beta$ , since  $\angle{ABC}=\alpha+\beta$ . The former statement gives  $AP<BP$  in  $\triangle{ABP}$  from the Law of Sines, while the latter statement gives  $BP<CP$  in  $\triangle{BCP}$ . This implies  $AP<CP$ , contradicting the fact that  $AP=CP$ . Similarly, if we assume  $\angle{ABP}>\alpha$ , we can obtain  $AP>CP$ , contradicting the fact that  $AP=CP$ . Therefore,  $\angle{ABP}=\alpha$ , and  $AP=BP$ .

From  $AP=BP=CP$ , we can see that  $P$  is the circumcenter of  $\triangle{ABC}$  and the circumcenter of quadrilateral  $ABCD$ . Hence,  $m\angle{BPD}=2m\angle{BAD}=2(45^{\circ})=90^{\circ}$ , i.e.,  $\overline{PB} \perp \overline{PD}$ , as desired.

Second, we prove that if  $\overline{PB} \perp \overline{PD}$ , then  $\overline{AC} \perp \overline{BD}$ .

Let  $\angle{ABP}=\theta$ . We claim that  $\theta=\alpha$ . Assume that  $\theta<\alpha$ , which suggests that  $\angle{CBP}=\alpha+\beta-\theta$  because  $\angle{ABC}=\alpha+\beta$ . In  $\triangle{ABP}$ , we can see that  $AP<BP$  from the Law of Sines. Also, since  $\angle{BCP}<\angle{CBP}$ , we can see that  $BP<CP$  in  $\triangle{BCP}$ . From  $\triangle{ABD}$ , we have  $\angle{ADP}=180^{\circ}-45^{\circ}-\theta-90^{\circ}=45^{\circ}-\theta>45^{\circ}-\alpha=\angle{DAP}$ , leading to  $DP<AP$  in  $\triangle{ADP}$ . Thus, we have  $DP<AP<BP<CP$ . However, since  $\angle{CDP}=\angle{ADC}-\angle{ADP}=(180^{\circ}-\alpha-\beta)-(45^{\circ}-\theta)=135^{\circ}-\beta-(\alpha-\theta)<135^{\circ}-\beta=\angle{DCP}$ , we have  $CP<DP$  in  $\triangle{CPD}$ , which leads to a contradiction. Similarly, assuming that  $\theta>\alpha$  leads to  $DP>AP>BP>CP$  and  $CP>DP$ , a contradiction. Therefore,  $\angle{ABP}=\theta=\alpha$ .

It is straightforward from the above proof that  $AP=BP=CP=DP$  when  $\angle{ABP}=\alpha$ , so  $P$  is the circumcenter of quadrilateral  $ABCD$ . Thus,  $\angle{CAP}=\angle{ACP} \Rightarrow 45^{\circ}-2\alpha=135^{\circ}-2\beta \Rightarrow \beta=45^{\circ}+\alpha$ . Hence, we have  $\angle{ACD}=\beta=45^{\circ}+\alpha$ . Along with the fact that  $\angle{BDC}=\angle{BAC}=45^{\circ}-\alpha$ , it is clear from  $\triangle{CKD}$  that  $\angle{CKD}=90^{\circ}$ , i.e.,  $\overline{AC} \perp \overline{BD}$ , as desired.

This completes the proof that  $\overline{PB} \perp \overline{PD}$  if and only if  $\overline{AC} \perp \overline{BD}$ .</details>

I claim that the only ordered triples satisfying the problem are  $(a,b,c)=\boxed{(1,0,0),(2,0,1),(1,1,2)}$ , which clearly work.

First, we prove that there are no solutions with  $b\ge2$ , so for the sake of contradiction we assume  $b\ge2$ . Rearrange the given equation to  $2^a5^b=1+3^c$ . Consider the cases where  $a\ge2$ . Then, we have  $100=2^2 5^2\mid 2^a5^b$ . Therefore, when taking the equation  $2^a5^b=1+3^c$  modulo 100, we have
\[3^c\equiv -1\pmod{100}\]
By bashing out all of the powers of 3 mod 100, we find that  $3^c\equiv-1\pmod{100}$  is impossible. Therefore, we cannot have  $a\ge2$ .

Now consider the cases when  $a=0,1$ . We settle these cases together. Note that if  $b=2$ , then if  $a=1$ , then  $25(2)=1+3^c$  or  $3^c=49$ , and if  $a=0$ , then  $25(1)=1+3^c$  or  $3^c=24$ , both of which are impossible. Therefore,  $b\ge3$ , so  $125\mid 5^b$ . Taking  $2^a5^b=1+3^c$  mod 125, the LHS vanishes, so  $3^c\equiv-1\pmod{125}$ . By bashing out residues, this is equivalent to  $c\equiv50\pmod{100}$ .

Now consider  $2^a5^b=1+3^c$  mod 101. Because  $\phi(101)=100$ , where  $\phi(n)$  is Euler's totient function, by Euler's theorem, we have
\[2^a5^b\equiv1+3^c\equiv1+3^{c\bmod{100}}\equiv1+3^{50}\pmod{101}\]
However, residue bash shows that both the  $a=1$  case,  $2\cdot5^b\equiv1+3^{50}$ , and the  $a=0$  case,  $5^b\equiv 1+3^{50}$ , are impossible.

We must have  $b=1,0$ . We settle these cases separately.

If  $b=1$ , then our equation becomes  $2^a\cdot5=1+3^c$ . If  $a\ge2$ , then  $20\mid 2^a\cdot5$ , so mod 20, the LHS vanishes and we have  $3^c=-1\pmod{20}$ . However, this is also impossible. We must have  $a=1,0$ . If  $a=1$ , then  $2^a\cdot5=1+3^c$  becomes  $9=3^c$ , which has the solution  $c=2$ . This gives us our first ordered triple  $(a,b,c)=(1,1,2)$ . If  $a=0$ , then the equation becomes  $4=3^c$ , which is impossible. This exhausts all the cases for  $b=1$ .

If  $b=0$ , then our equation becomes  $2^a=1+3^c$ . If  $a\ge3$ , then  $8\mid2^a$ , so mod 8, the equation becomes  $3^c\equiv-1\pmod{8}$ . This one is easy to check by hand: the powers of 3 cycle 1, 3, 1, 3, \dots modulo 8, so it is impossible to have  $3^c\equiv-1\pmod{8}$ . Thus, we must have  $a=2,1,0$ . If  $a=2$ , then  $2^a=1+3^c$  becomes  $3=3^c$  which has the solution  $c=1$ , giving the second ordered triple  $(a,b,c)=(2,0,1)$ . If  $a=1$ , then the equation becomes  $1=3^c$ , which has the solution  $c=0$ , giving the third ordered triple  $(a,b,c)=(1,0,0)$ . If  $a=0$ , then the equation becomes  $0=3^c$ , which is impossible.

Having exhausted all nonnegative integer values of  $b$  through our casework, we are done.

We prove the only solutions are  $(a, b, c) = (1, 0, 0), (2, 0, 1), (1, 1, 2)$ .**Case 1**  $c$  is odd.

Consider  $3^c + 1 \pmod{5}$ . By Eulers Theorem, it suffices to consider  $c$  mod  $4 = \varphi(5)$ . 
If  $c = 1$  then  $3^c + 1 \equiv 4$ , but if  $c = 3$  then  $3^c + 1 \equiv 3$ . Therefore,  $3^c + 1$  is not divisible by  $5$  and so  $b = 0$ . Thus, our equation reduces to:
\[ 2^a - 3^b = 1 \]
By Mihailescus Theorem, there are no solutions to this for  $a, b > 1$ , and checking these cases manually produces  $(1, 0, 0)$  and  $(2, 0, 1)$ . **Case 2**  $c$  is even
Now consider  $3^c + 1 \pmod{4}$ . By Eulers Theorem, it suffices to consider  $c$  mod  $2$ . If  $c = 0$ , then  $3^c + 1 = 2$ , which is not divisible by  $4$ . Therefore,  $3^c + 1$  is not divisible by  $4$  in this case. This means that  $a \le 2$ . 

*Sub case 1:*  $a = 0$ .
The equation reduces to 
\[ 5^b - 3^c = 1\]
And by Mihailescus there are no solutions.

*Subcase 2:*  $a = 1$ . 
The equation reduces to:
\[ 2 \cdot 5^b = 3^c + 1 \]
Now let  $k = c/2$ . By LTE,  $b = \nu_5(3^c + 1) = \nu_5(9^k + 1) = \nu_5(k) + 1$ , so  $\nu_5(k) =  b - 1$ .

This means that  $k \ge 5^{b - 1}$ , so:
\[ 2 \cdot 5^b - 1 = 3^c = (3^k)^2 \ge (3^{2 \cdot 5^{b -1}}) \]
Then note that this equation has an equality case if  $b = 1$ , producing solution  $(1, 1, 2)$ . 

For  $b > 1$ , differentiating the LHS and RHS with respect to  $b$  shows that the derivative of the RHS is greater than that of the RHS, and as  $b = 1$  has equality, this means that the RHS is always more than the LHS. This implies there are no solutions for  $b >1$ .

A while back, I wrote the Diophantine Equations lesson for our new MathWOOT class, which discusses (among other things) the idea of reducing DEs modulo  $n.$  I noticed that many of the problems employing this idea required looking at two or three key moduli, and jokingly commented to one of my colleagues that it'd be funny to have a problem whose solution involved looking at an infinite number of moduli. Then I found this problem and the solution given in the official solutions doc. 

There are definitely cleaner solutions employing more machinery (and I hoped the other folks in the problem-selection pipeline would be able to think about this before putting it on the test) but I figured this would be a good fit for USAMTS as it's completely accessible to folks without any olympiad-level NT experience.

Comments on the official solution: If you have less experience with these types of problems, the moduli taken in the official solutions may look somewhat random. Here's some motivation for why we might look at these in first place.


- At the start of the solution, looking modulo  $3,$   $5,$  and small powers of  $2$  all get rid of one term of the equation, which allows us to say more about the possible values of some of our variables (especially when we specify down to particular values).
- Similarly, when we get to  $10 \cdot 5^{2d}-9 \cdot 3^{4e}=1,$  looking modulo  $9$  gets rid of one of the terms entirely, while being a modulus we haven't yet considered at this point.
- The motivation for looking at modulo  $7$  and  $13$  then comes from the fact that Fermat's Little Theorem allows us to eliminate one of our variables, since  $5^6 \equiv 1 \pmod{7}$  and  $3^{12} \equiv 1 \pmod{13}.$
- Finally, the motivation for looking modulo  $2^k$  comes from the Binomial Theorem: We know that  $5^{\text{big}}=(4+1)^{\text{big}}$  and  $3^{\text{big}}=(4-1)^{\text{big}},$  so both these powers will be very close to multiples of large powers of  $2.$

<details><summary>xooks</summary>We claim the answer is  $\boxed{(2,0,1), (1,0,0), (1,1,2)}.$ These work. We now proceed as follows.

We split this into  $2$  cases: 

Case  $1$ :  $b=0.$ Then,  $2^a\cdot 5^b-3^c=2^a-3^c=1.$  If  $c=0,$  then  $(a,b,c)=(1,0,0).$  If  $c\geq 1,$  then  $2^a=3^c+1\equiv 1\pmod{3},$  so  $a\equiv 0\pmod{2}.$ Now, let  $a=2x$  for some integer  $x.$  Then,  $3^c=2^a-1=2^{2x}-1=(2^x-1)(2^x+1).$  Since  $3$  is a prime, this means that we have \begin{align*} 3^y&=2^x-1  3^z&=2^x+1  \end{align*} for some nonnegative integers  $y$  and  $z.$  

As such,  $3^z-3^y=(2^x+1)-(2^x-1)=2>0,$  so  $z>y,$  and  $3^y(3^{z-y}-1)=2.$  Since  $z-y>0$  is an integer,  $3^{z-y}-1$  is an integer, so  $3^y\mid 2.$  Since  $y$  is a nonnegative integer,  $y=0,$  so  $2=3^y(3^{z-y}-1)=3^z-1,$  so  $z=1.$  Now,  $2^x=3^z-1=2,$  so  $x=1,$  and  $a=2x=2.$  Also,  $3^c=(2^x-1)(2^x+1)=3^y\cdot 3^z=3,$  so  $c=1,$  so  $(a,b,c)=(2,0,1).$ As such, the only solutions in this case are  $(1,0,0)$  and  $(2,0,1).$ Case  $2$ :  $b\geq 1.$ Now,  $3^c=2^a\cdot 5^b-1\equiv 4\pmod{5},$  so  $c\equiv 2\pmod{4}.$ Claim  $1$ :  $a=1.$ Proof:

For the sake of contradiction, assume that  $a\geq 2.$  Then,  $3^c=2^a\cdot 5^b-1\equiv 3\pmod{4},$  so  $c\equiv 1\pmod{2}.$  However,  $c\equiv 2\pmod{4},$  a contradiction, so  $a<2,$  and  $a=0$  or  $a=1.$  If  $a=0,$  then  $3^c=2^a\cdot 5^b-1=5^b-1\equiv 0\pmod{2},$  a contradiction, so  $a=1,$  as desired.

Thus,  $1=2^a\cdot 5^b-3^c=2\cdot 5^b-3^c.$ Claim  $2$ :  $b\leq 1.$ Proof:

Assume for the sake of contradiction that there exist nonnegative integers  $(b,c)$  such that  $b\geq 2$  and  $1=2\cdot 5^b-3^c.$  Then, there exists an ordered pair  $(b_1,c_1)$  of nonnegative integers such that  $b_1\geq 2,$   $1=2\cdot 5^{b_1}-3^{c_1},$  and  $c_1$  is minimized.

Then,  $3^{c_1}=2\cdot 5^{b_1}-1\equiv 24\pmod{25},$  so  $c_1\equiv 10\pmod{20}.$  As such,  $10\mid c_1,$  so  $c_1=10d$  for some nonnegative integer  $d.$  

Now,  $2\cdot 5^{b_1}=3^{c_1}+1=3^{10d}+1=(3^{2d}+1)(3^{8d}-3^{6d}+3^{4d}-3^{2d}+1).$  Since  $d$  is a nonnegative integer,  $3^{2d}+1$  and  $3^{8d}-3^{6d}+3^{4d}-3^{2d}+1$  are integers, so  $3^{2d}+1\mid 2\cdot 5^{b_1}.$ Since  $3^{2d}+1\equiv 0\pmod{2},$  and  $5$  is prime,  $3^{2d}+1=2\cdot 5^{f}$  for some nonnegative integer  $f,$  so  $1=2\cdot 5^f-3^{2d}.$  

Claim  $3$ :  $f<2.$ Assume for the sake of contradiction that  $f\geq 2.$  Then,  $(f,2d)$  is an ordered pair of nonnegative integers such that  $f\geq 2$  and  $1=2\cdot 5^f-3^{2d}.$  If  $d=0,$  then  $2=2\cdot 5^f,$  so  $f=0,$  but  $0<2,$  a contradiction. Thus,  $d>0,$  and  $2d<10d=c_1,$  so  $(b_1,c_1)$  is not an ordered pair of nonnegative integers with  $b_1\geq 2$  and  $1=2\cdot 5^{b_1}-3^{c_1}$  that minimizes  $c_1,$  a contradiction, as  $f<2,$  as desired.

Now,  $f=0$  or  $f=1.$  If  $f=0,$  then  $3^{2d}=2\cdot 5^f-1=1,$  so  $d=0,$  and  $c_1=0,$  so  $2\cdot 5^{b_1}=3^{c_1}+1=2,$  and  $b_1=0<2,$  but  $b_1\geq 2,$  a contradiction. Thus,  $f=1,$  so  $3^{2d}=2\cdot 5^f-1=9,$  so  $d=1,$  and  $c_1=10,$  and  $2\cdot 5^{b_1}=3^{c_1}+1=3^{10}+1=(3^5)^2+1=243^2+1=(240+3)^2+1=57600+1440+9+1=59050,$  so  $5^{b_1}=29525=25\cdot 1181,$  so  $5^{b_1-2}=1181.$  However, since  $b_1-2$  is an integer,  $1181$  is a power of  $5,$  a contradiction. Thus,  $b<2,$  and since  $b$  is an integer, so  $b\leq 1,$  as desired. 

Since  $b\leq 1$  and  $b\geq 1,$  we have  $b=1,$  so  $3^c=2\cdot 5^b-1=10-1=9,$  so  $c=2,$  so  $(a,b,c)=(1,1,2).$ As such, the only ordered pair in this case is  $(1,1,2).$ As such, we have exhausted all cases, and the only possible ordered pairs are  $(1,0,0),$   $(2,0,1),$   $(1,1,2),$  as desired.  $\Box$</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>We claim that the only solutions are \((1, 0, 0)\), \((2, 0, 1)\), and \((1, 1, 2)\). We will proceed with casework to verify this.

Case 1: \(a \geq b\)

The equation can be rewritten as \(10^b \cdot 2^{a-b} - 3^c = 1\). Note that \(a - b\) is a nonnegative integer, so \(2^{a-b}\) is a positive integer.

Subcase 1.1: \(b = 0\)

Our equation becomes \(2^a - 3^c = 1\).

For \(a = 0\), there is no solution.
For \(a = 1\), we get the solution \((1, 0, 0)\).
For \(a = 2\), we get the solution \((2, 0, 1)\).
For \(a \geq 3\), taking modulo 8, we get \(-3^c \equiv 1 \pmod{8}\), so \(3^c \equiv 7 \pmod{8}\). This has no solutions.

Subcase 1.2: \(b = 1\)

Our equation becomes \(5 \cdot 2^a - 3^c = 1\).

For \(a = 1\), we get the solution \((1, 1, 2)\).
For \(a = 2\), there is no solution.
For \(a \geq 3\), taking modulo 8, we get \(-3^c \equiv 1 \pmod{8}\), so \(3^c \equiv 7 \pmod{8}\). This has no solutions.

Subcase 1.3: \(b \geq 2\)

Our equation is \(10^b \cdot 2^{a-b} - 3^c = 1\). Taking modulo 100, we get \(-3^c \equiv 1 \pmod{100}\), so \(3^c \equiv 99 \pmod{100}\). This has no solutions.

Case 2: \(a < b\)

The equation can be rewritten as \(10^a \cdot 5^{b-a} - 3^c = 1\). Note that \(b - a\) is a positive integer, so \(5^{b-a}\) is a positive integer.

Subcase 2.1: \(a = 0\)

Our equation becomes \(5^b - 3^c = 1\). Since the left side must be even, there are no solutions.

Subcase 2.2: \(a = 1\)

Our equation becomes \(2 \cdot 5^b - 3^c = 1\).

Since \(b \geq 2\), we can take modulo 25 to get \(-3^c \equiv 1 \pmod{25}\), so \(3^c \equiv 24 \pmod{25}\). This implies that \(c\) can be written as \(c = 20n + 10\) where \(n\) is a nonnegative integer. Taking \(2 \cdot 5^b\) modulo \(3^{10} + 1\), we get:

\[2 \cdot 5^b \equiv 3^c + 1 \equiv 3^{20n + 10} + 1 \equiv 3^{10} \cdot 3^{20n} + 1 \equiv (-1)(1^n) + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{3^{10} + 1}\]

Hence, \(3^{10} + 1\) divides \(2 \cdot 5^b\). However, 1181, a prime, divides \(3^{10} + 1\), so 1181 divides \(2 \cdot 5^b\). This is a contradiction, so there are no solutions.

Subcase 2.3: \(a \geq 2\)

Our equation is \(10^a \cdot 5^{b-a} - 3^c = 1\). Taking modulo 100, we get \(-3^c \equiv 1 \pmod{100}\), so \(3^c \equiv 99 \pmod{100}\). This has no solutions.

Therefore, the only solutions are \((1, 0, 0)\), \((2, 0, 1)\), and \((1, 1, 2)\).</details>

My Solution.The only solutions are $$ (a, b, c)=\boxed{(1, 0, 0), (2, 0, 1), (1, 1, 2)}, $$ which we'll prove by using modular arithmetic and considering various cases on $b$ . First, suppose $b=0$ , so the equation becomes $$ 2^a-3^c=1\iff 2^a=3^c+1. $$ If $a=0$ , then there are no solutions for $c$ . If $a=1$ , then we have $c=0$ and the solution $(a, b, c)=(1, 0, 0)$ . If $a=2$ , then we have $c=1$ , giving $(a, b, c)=(2, 0, 1)$ . Now suppose $c\geq 3$ , so $2^3=8$ must divide $3^c+1$ and $$ 3^c+1\equiv 0\pmod 8\iff 3^c\equiv -1\pmod 8. $$ Since since the next power of $3$ is always $3$ times the previous and $3^2=9\equiv 1\pmod 8,$ the powers of $3$ alternate between $3^0=1$ and $3^1=3$ in modulo $8$ . Hence, no power of $3$ is ever $-1\pmod 8$ , so no such $c$ exist and there are no solutions when $b=0$ and $a\geq 3$ . Thus, we've found all solutions when $b=0$ . Now suppose $b\geq 1$ . Rearranging to get $2^a\cdot 5^b=3^c+1,$ we must have that $5$ divides $3^c+1$ , or $3^c\equiv -1\pmod 5$ . It is well known that if $k$ and $n$ are relatively prime, then $k^i\equiv k^j\pmod n$ if and only if $i\equiv j\pmod {\text{ord}_nk}.$ (This fact is also Theorem 8.2 from Elementary Number Theory by David M. Burton). Considering the powers of $3$ modulo $5$ , we have \begin{align*} 3^1\equiv& 3\pmod 5 3^2\equiv& 4\equiv -1\pmod 5 3^3\equiv& 2\pmod 5 3^4\equiv& 1\pmod 5 \end{align*} Hence $3$ has order $4$ , so $$ 3^c\equiv -1\equiv 3^2\pmod 5 $$ if and only if $c\equiv 2\pmod 4$ . In particular, $c$ is even, so $c=2\hat c$ for some nonnegative integer $\hat c$ . Then our original equation becomes $$ 2^a\cdot 5^b=3^{2\hat c}+1=9^{\hat c}+1. $$ Taking this modulo $4$ , we get $$ 2^a\cdot 5^b\equiv 9^{\hat c}+1\equiv1^{\hat c}+1\equiv 2\pmod 4. $$ Hence, the LHS is even but not a multiple of $4$ , so $a=1$ and our equation becomes $$ 2\cdot 5^b=9^{\hat c}+1. $$ If $b=1$ , then we get $\hat c=1$ , so $c=2$ , giving $(1, 1, 2).$ Otherwise, since we are in the $b\geq 1$ case, we must have $b\geq 2$ . Thus $5^2=25$ must divide $9^{\hat c}+1$ , so $9^{\hat c}\equiv -1\pmod {25}.$ We again list the powers of $9\pmod {25}$ : \begin{align*} 9^1\equiv& 9\pmod {25} 9^2\equiv& 6\pmod{25} 9^3\equiv& 4\pmod{25} 9^4\equiv& 11\pmod{25} 9^5\equiv& -1\pmod{25} 9^6\equiv& -9\pmod {25} 9^7\equiv& -6\pmod{25} 9^8\equiv& -4\pmod{25} 9^9\equiv& -11\pmod{25} 9^{10}\equiv& 1\pmod{25} \end{align*} In particular, the order of $9$ modulo $25$ is $10$ , and $9^5\equiv -1\pmod {25}$ . Thus $$ 9^{\hat c}\equiv -1\equiv 9^5\pmod {25}, $$ which is true if and only if $\hat c\equiv 5\pmod {10}.$ Therefore, $\hat c=10\bar c+5$ where $\bar c$ is a nonnegative integer. Then our equation becomes $$ 2\cdot 5^b=9^{\hat c}+1=9^{10\bar c+5}+1=\left(9^5\right)^{2\bar c+1}+1^{2\bar c+1}. $$ Before continuing, we'll prove a useful property. Suppose $p$ and $q$ are integers and $n$ is an odd integer, then $p+q\equiv 0\pmod{p+q}$ so $p\equiv -q\pmod{p+q}.$ Raising both sides to the odd power of $n$ , we get that $p^n\equiv q^n(-1)^n\equiv -q^n\pmod {p+q},$ so $p^n+q^n\equiv 0\pmod {p+q}$ and $(p+q)\mid \left (p^n+q^n\right).$ From our equation above, clearly $2\bar c+1$ is odd, so this implies that $$ \left(9^5+1\right)\mid \left(\left(9^5\right)^{2\bar c+1}+1^{2\bar c+1}\right)=\left(2\cdot 5^b\right) $$ However, $$ 9^5+1=59050=2\cdot 5^2\cdot 1181, $$ so this means that $1181$ must divide $2\cdot 5^b$ . Since neither $2$ nor $5$ divide $1181$ , there must be prime $p$ other than $2$ or $5$ that divides $1181$ , and thus $p\mid 2\cdot 5^b$ . This, however, is impossible since $p\not\in\{2, 5\},$ proving that there are no solutions when $b\geq 2$ . This completes the last sub-case of the last case in our solution. Therefore, we've found all solutions to the equations and proved that no others exist. $_\square$

*Case 2 :*  $a=1$ . The resultant equation is then,
