stem_md:
Let  $P(x)$  be a polynomial with integer coefficients that has at least one rational root. Let  $n$  be a positive integer.

Alan and Allan are playing a game. First, Alan writes down  $n$  integers at  $n$  different locations on a board. Then Allan may make moves of the following kind: choose a position that has integer  $a$  written, then choose a different position that has integer  $b$  written, then at the first position erase  $a$  and in its place write  $a+P(b)$ . After any nonnegative number of moves, Allan may choose to end the game. Once Allan ends the game, his score is the number of times the mode (most common element) of the integers on the board appears.

Find, in terms of  $P(x)$  and  $n$ , the maximum score Allan can guarantee.

*Henrick Rabinovitz*
solution_md:
Here is a write-up done with **pieater314159** and **numbersandnumbers**
SolutionThe answer is \[\begin{cases} 1 & P(x)=0 n-1 & P(x)=ax+b,\ \gcd(a,b)=1 \left\lceil \frac{n}{\gcd(a, b)} \right\rceil & P(x)=ax+b,\ \gcd(a,b)>1 1 & \deg P\geq 2. \end{cases}\] The problem is evident when $P$ is constant. -----**Proof for $\boldsymbol{\deg P\geq 2}$** We will show that we can find some positive integer $M$ for which $P$ has at least $n$ roots $r_1,\ldots,r_n$ modulo $M$ . Once we have shown this, Alan can pick one integer from each residue class $r_i$ , and as the integers will then be invariant modulo $M$ , they will always be distinct. To find such an $M$ , take a linear factor $ax+b$ of $P$ , and let $P(x) = (ax+b)^kQ(x)$ where $k$ is maximal. - If $Q$ is not constant, then we claim there exist infinitely many primes $p$ such that $P$ has at least two roots modulo $p$ . Indeed, by Schur's theorem there are infinitely many primes $p$ such that $Q$ has a root mod $p$ , and since $Q(-b/a) \neq 0$ , for all but finitely many such $p$ the value $-b/a$ is a root of $P$ that is not a root of $Q$ . We can then choose $M$ to be a product of many of these primes. - If $Q$ is constant, then $P(x) = c(ax+b)^k$ where $k\geq 2$ , in which case $P(x)$ will have at least $p$ roots modulo $p^2$ for all primes $p>\max(|a|,|b|)$ . So, taking $M=p^2$ for some large prime $p$ suffices. [/list] -----**Upper Bound for $\boldsymbol{\deg P = 1}$** Write $P(x) = c(ax + b)$ where $\gcd(a,b) = 1$ , $c > 0$ . [list] - If $c>1$ , then Allen's movement is invariant modulo $c$ , so Alan just needs to make the numbers as spread modulo $c$ as possible. - If $c=1$ and $a>0$ , then Alan can choose all the numbers not all equal and all greater than $k = \max(0, -bc)$ . Since $P(k) \geq 0$ , the numbers will always be greater than $k$ . Moreover, if Allen operates on $x$ and $y$ , then we have $x + P(y) \geq x + (y + cb) > y$ , so the two resulting integers are not equal. Thus, it is impossible to ever make the integers all equal. - If $c=1$ and $a<0$ , then Alan can pick some numbers strictly greater than the root of $P$ and some numbers strictly less than the root of $P$ . There is never a move that removes the last number strictly greater than the root of $P$ , and there is never a move that removes the last number strictly less than the root of $P$ , so there is always at least one pair of distinct numbers, giving an upper bound of $n - 1$ as well. [/list] -----**Construction for $\boldsymbol{\deg P=1}$** Write $P(x) = c(ax + b)$ where $\gcd(a,b) = 1$ , $c > 0$ , and $a$ , $b$ , and $c$ are integers. It suffices to consider $n\geq 3$ . Let the set of numbers be $x_1,\dots,x_n$ . The operation $(x,y) \mapsto (x+P(y),y)$ does not change the quantity $\gcd(P(x), P(y))$ . Thus, $v \coloneq \gcd(P(x_1), P(x_2), \ldots, P(x_n))$ is fixed throughout. We make the following key claim. **Claim.** Suppose the numbers on the board are $y_1,\ldots,y_m$ for $m \geq 3$ . Let $v=\gcd(P(y_1),\ldots,P(y_m))$ . If $y_1\equiv y_2\pmod v$ , then Allen can make (the numbers in the positions holding) $y_1$ and $y_2$ equal without changing any of $y_3,\ldots,y_m$ . *Proof.* Let $w=\gcd(P(y_3),\ldots,P(y_m))$ , so that $v=\gcd(P(y_1),P(y_2),w)$ . We first do the following two moves: [list] - Change $y_1$ to $y_1' \coloneq y_1 + \ell P(y_2)$ , where $\ell$ is to determined later. - Change $y_2$ to $y_2' \coloneq y_2 + kP(y_1')$ for some $k$ . As $k$ ranges through positive integers, the value of $y_2'\bmod \gcd(P(y_2),w)$ varies on an arithmetic progression of common difference $v$ (i.e., we can get anything $\equiv y_2\pmod v$ ). Thus, since $y_2\equiv y_1\pmod v$ , we may pick $k$ such that $y_2'\equiv y_1\pmod{\gcd(P(y_2),w)}$ , and thus, we have $\gcd(P(y_2'), P(y_2), w) = v$ . [/list] Now, we can turn $y_1' = y_1+\ell P(y_2)$ to $y_1 + \ell P(y_2) + e_2 P(y_2') + e_3P(y_3) +\dots + e_nP(y_n)$ for any positive integers $\ell$ , $e_2$ , $\dots$ , $e_n$ . Thus, by Bezout, we can add any sufficiently large multiple of $v$ to $y_1$ , and consequently we can make turn $y_1'$ to $y_1^*\equiv y_2'\pmod w$ . Finally, add a linear combination of $P(y_3),\dots,P(y_n)$ to $y_1^*$ and $y_2'$ to make them equal. $\blacksquare$ **Claim.** At most $c$ residue classes modulo $v$ are represented among the numbers on the board. *Proof.* Since $\gcd(a,b)=1$ , \begin{align*} v &=\gcd\big(c(ax_1+b),c(ax_2+b),\ldots,c(ax_n+b)\big) &=c\cdot\gcd(ax_1+b,ax_2+b,\ldots,ax_n+b) &=c\cdot\gcd\big(ax_1+b,a(x_2-x_1),\ldots,a(x_n-x_1)\big) &=c\cdot\gcd(ax_1+b,x_2-x_1,\ldots,x_n-x_1). \end{align*} So, $v$ divides $c(x_i-x_j)$ for each $i$ and $j$ , meaning that the $x_i$ all lie in the same residue class modulo $v/c$ . $\blacksquare$ Given these two claims, we now describe Allen's strategy. We first describe the strategy in the case where $c=1$ . By the second claim, all of the numbers on the board are equivalent modulo $v$ . Let $x_i$ denote the number in position $i$ ; $x_i$ can change over time. [list] - First, apply the first claim to the numbers $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ . After this, $x_1=x_2$ . - Now, apply the first claim to the numbers $(x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ ; after this $x_2=x_3$ . Every time something is added to $x_2$ , also add it to $x_1$ , so that $x_1=x_2$ at each step. So, at the end of this step, $x_1=x_2=x_3$ . - Repeat this process; we stop when $x_1=x_2=\cdots=x_{n-1}$ . So, when $c=1$ , we can make $n-1$ numbers equal. We now describe the approach when $c>1$ . We define an auxiliary list $L$ , which will always contain one of each distinct number. (For example, if the board consists of $[2,2,2,5,5]$ , then $L$ may contain the first $2$ and the second $5$ .) Note that we always have $v=\gcd(\{P(x)\colon x\in L\})$ . While $L$ has size at least $3$ and contains two distinct numbers $y_1$ and $y_2$ which are equivalent $\pmod v$ , use our claim with $(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)=L$ . Every time we replace $y_1$ with $y_1+P(y_i)$ for some $i$ , replace every number equal to $y_1$ with the same quantity, so that numbers equal to $y_1$ remain equal to $y_1$ ; do the same for $y_2$ . In this way, the number of distinct numbers on the board decreases. Once we can no longer do this anymore, we either have that $|L|=2$ or that $L$ contains at most one element in each residue class modulo $v$ . In the first case, some number occurs at least $\lceil n/2\rceil$ times, so we are done. In the second case, $|L|\leq c$ by Claim 2, so some number occurs at least $\lceil n/c\rceil$ times, and we are done.

candidates: ** 5 observation before going for solution****Case 1-** $ P(x) = 0$ In this case, the game is trivial, and Allan can guarantee a score of $1$ by simply not making any moves. This is because the polynomial $P(x) = 0$ has no roots $,$ so there are no moves that can be made to change the integers on the board.**Case 2-** $P(x) = ax + b, \gcd(a, b) = 1$ In this case, Allan can guarantee a score of $n-1$ by using the following strategy - Alan writes down n distinct integers at $n$ different locations on the board - Allan chooses a position with integer a and a different position with integer $b,$ and applies the move $a + P(b)$ to the first position - Allan repeats the previous step until all integers on the board are equal - Cuse the move $a + P(b)$ preserves the gcd of the integers on the board. Since $\gcd(a, b) = 1,$ the $\gcd$ of the integers on the board remains $1$ after each move. Therefore, Allan can keep applying this move until all integers are equal. [/list] The key insight here is that the move $a + P(b)$ is essentially adding a multiple of the $\gcd$ of $a, b$ to the first integer. Since the $\gcd = 1, \implies$ the move is essentially adding $1$ to the first integer, which preserves the gcd of the integers on the board.**Case 3-** $P(x) = ax + b, \gcd(a, b) > 1$ In this case, Allan can guarantee a score of $\lceil\frac{n}{\gcd(a, b)}\rceil$ by using a similar strategy to Case 2, but with some additional tricks. The key insight here is that the move $a + P(b)$ preserves the gcd of the integers on the board, but also increases the number of distinct residue classes modulo $\gcd(a, b).$ By carefully choosing the moves, Allan can ensure that the number of distinct residue classes modulo $\gcd(a, b)$ is at most $c,$ where $c $ is the number of distinct residue classes modulo $\gcd(a, b)$ that are represented among the integers on the board. Since $\gcd(a, b) > 1,$ the move $a + P(b)$ increases the number of distinct residue classes modulo $\gcd(a, b)$ by at least $1.$ Therefore, Allan can keep applying this move until the number of distinct residue classes modulo $\gcd(a, b)$ is at most $c.$ At this point, Allan can guarantee that at least $\lceil \frac{n}{\gcd(a, b)}\rceil$ integers on the board are equal.**Case 4-** $\mathrm{deg P}\geq 2$ In this case, Allan can guarantee a score of $1$ by using a different strategy. The key insight here is that there exists a positive integer $M$ such that P has at least n roots modulo $M$ . By choosing integers that are congruent to these roots $\text{modulo M},$ Allan can ensure that the integers on the board are always distinct. Cause the polynomial $P(x)$ has at least $n$ roots $\text{modulo M},\implies$ there are at least n distinct residue classes modulo M that are roots of P(x). By choosing integers that are congruent to these roots $\text{modulo M},$ Allan can ensure that the integers on the board are always distinct. **Solution-** $$ \textbf{Claim 1-}P(x) = 0 $$ $\textbf{Allan can guarantee a score of 1 by not making any moves.} $ $$ \textbf{Claim 2-} $$ $$ P(x) = ax + b, \gcd(a, b) = 1 \,\text{Allan can guarantee a score of } n-1 \text{ by using the following strategy-} $$ [list] - 1. Alan writes down distinct integers at $n$ different locations on the board. - 2. Allan chooses a position with integer $a$ and a different position with integer $ b, $ $\text{ and applies the move } a + P(b) \text{ to the first position.} $ - 3. $ \text{ Allan repeats the previous step until all integers on the board are equal.}$ \[P(x) = ax + b\] \[P(b) = ab + b = b(a + 1)\] Therefore $, $ the move \(a + P(b)\) is equivalent to adding \(b(a + 1)\) to the first integer. Since \(\gcd(a, b) = 1\) $,$ we know that \(a\) and \(b\) are coprime. Therefore, the move \(a + P(b)\) preserves the gcd of the integers on the board. Specifically, if the gcd of the integers on the board is \(d\) before the move, then the gcd after the move is also \(d\). Moreover, since \(a\) and \(b\) are coprime, we know that the move \(a + P(b)\) increases the value of the first integer by at least 1. Therefore, by repeatedly applying this move, Allan can ensure that all integers on the board are equal. $$ \textbf{Claim 3-} P(x) = ax + b, \gcd(a, b) > 1 \, $$ $\text{Allan can guarantee a score of } \lceil n/\gcd(a, b) \rceil \textbf{ by using a similar strategy to Case 2 ,but with some additional tricks.}$ The move \(a + P(b)\) still preserves the gcd of the integers on the board, but it also increases the number of distinct residue classes modulo \(\gcd(a, b)\). Specifically, if the gcd of the integers on the board is \(d\) before the move, then the gcd after the move is still \(d\), but the number of distinct residue classes modulo \(d\) increases by at least $1.$ Therefore, by carefully choosing the moves, Allan can ensure that the number of distinct residue classes modulo \(\gcd(a, b)\) is at most \(c\), where \(c\) is the number of distinct residue classes modulo \(\gcd(a, b)\) that are represented among the integers on the board. Moreover, since \(\gcd(a, b) > 1\), we know that the move \(a + P(b)\) increases the value of the first integer by at least \(\gcd(a, b)\). Therefore, by repeatedly applying this move, Allan can ensure that at least $\left(\lceil\frac{ n}{\gcd(a, b) }\rceil\right)$ integers on the board are equal. $$ \textbf{Claim 4:} \deg P \geq 2 \,\text{Allan can guarantee a score of 1 by using a different strategy.} $$ There exists a positive integer \(M\) such that \(P\) has at least \(n\) roots modulo \(M\). This is because the polynomial \(P(x)\) has degree at least 2, so it has at least one root modulo \(p\) for every prime \(p\). By choosing integers that are congruent to these roots modulo \(M\), Allan can ensure that the integers on the board are always distinct. Specifically, if the integers on the board are \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\), then Allan can choose integers \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\) such that \(y_i \equiv x_i \pmod{M}\) for all \(i\). Since \(P\) has at least \(n\) roots modulo \(M\), we know that there are at least \(n\) distinct residue classes modulo \(M\) that are roots of \(P(x)\). Therefore, by choosing integers that are congruent to these roots modulo \(M\), Allan can ensure that the integers on the board are always distinct.

Let  $P'$  be the intersection of lines  $OP$  and  $AB$ , and let  $Q'$  be the intersection of lines  $OQ$  and  $\overline{AC}$ ; in other words,  $P'$  and  $Q'$  are the images of  $P$  and  $Q$  under inversion about  $\omega$ . Therefore, line  $P'Q'$  is tangent to  $\omega$  at  $T$ .

Also, since  $A$ ,  $P$  and  $Q$  are collinear, it follows that  $(AOP'Q')$  is cyclic. By Simson's theorem, the feet from  $O$  onto sides  $\overline{AB}$ ,  $\overline{AC}$  and  $\overline{P'Q'}$  are collinear; in other words,  $T$  lies on the  $A$ -midline of  $\triangle ABC$ .**Claim:** We have  $\triangle TPQ \sim \triangle ACB$  (with similarity factor of  $\tfrac{1}{2}$ .)**Proof:** We have \[\angle TPQ = \angle TOQ' = 90^{\circ} - \angle OQ'P' = \angle P'AO - 90^{\circ} = \angle C,\]
and likewise for  $\angle TQP$  and  $\angle B$ .

If we define  $P_1$  and  $Q_1$  as the reflections of  $T$  across  $P$  and  $Q$ , respectively, we have that  $\triangle T Q_1 P_1$  and  $\triangle ABC$  are reflections (and in particular,  $\omega$  is the circumcircle of  $\triangle TQ_1 P_1$ ). From this, it follows by symmetry  $\angle PAT = \angle (P_1 Q_1, AT) = \angle (AT, BC)$ .

Now, we have
\[\angle BTD = \angle ATD - \angle C = \angle PAT + \angle (AT, BC) - \angle C = \angle PAT + \angle (AT, AC) = \angle PAT - \angle CAT = \angle CAP.\]

Let  $ABC$  be a triangle. Construct rectangles  $BA_1A_2C$ ,  $CB_1B_2A$ , and  $AC_1C_2B$  outside  $ABC$  such that  $\angle BCA_1=\angle CAB_1=\angle ABC_1$ . Let  $A_1B_2$  and  $A_2C_1$  intersect at  $A'$  and define  $B',C'$  similarly. Prove that line  $AA'$  bisects  $B'C'$ .

*Linus Tang*
solution_md:
Hyperbola solution by meLet $D, E, F$ be the centers of the three rectangles, so $\triangle BDC$ , $\triangle CEA$ , $\triangle AFB$ are similar isosceles triangles. Notice $EF\parallel B_1C_2$ and similar, so the problem is equivalent to $AA'$ is parallel to median of $\triangle DEF$ . Let $O$ , $G$ , $H$ be the circumcenter, centroid, and orthocenter. Recall that $AD$ , $BE$ , $CF$ concur at point $P$ on the **Kierpert's Hyperbola** of $\triangle ABC$ , which is the (rectangular) hyperbola $\mathcal H$ passing through $A$ , $B$ , $C$ , $H$ , $G$ . We have the following lemma. ----- **Lemma:** The perpendiculars from $A$ , $B$ , $C$ to $EF$ , $FD$ , $DE$ concur at point $T\in\mathcal H$ . Moreover, $O\in TP$ . *Proof.* The part that $O\in TP$ follows from Sondat's theorem. For the first part, note that $\mathcal H$ can be classified as the locus of point $U$ such that lines from $D$ , $E$ , $F$ parallel to $AU$ , $BU$ , $CU$ are concurrent. (This is also the conic used to prove Sondat's theorem). $\blacksquare$ ----- Now, let $X$ be on orthocenter of $\triangle BTC$ , so $X\in\mathcal H$ since $\mathcal H$ is rectangular. Note $BX\parallel DE$ and $CX\parallel DF$ . Pascal on $GXTPAH$ gives $D\in GX$ . Moreover, recall a well-known fact that $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DEF$ share the same centroid, so $DX$ bisects $EF$ . Finally, it suffices to show that $DX\parallel AA'$ . To that end, we let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ . Let $X'$ and $D'$ be the reflections of $X$ and $D$ across $M$ . Since lines $BX', DF, A_2C_1$ are equally spaced and lines $CX', DE, A_1B_2$ are equally spaced, we have that $D$ is the midpoint of $A'X'$ . Now, observe that - $X'D'\parallel DX$ - midpoint of $D'A$ lies on $DX$ (recall: $AFD'E$ is parallelogram) - midpoint of $A'X'$ is $D$ . These three items give that $AA'$ , $XD$ , $D'X'$ are parallel and equally spaced, so we are done.
Short synthetic solution by meqlLet $\omega_A$ be the circumcircle of $BA_1A_2C$ , and define $\omega_B$ and $\omega_C$ similarly. Let $R$ be the radical center of $\omega_A$ , $\omega_B$ , and $\omega_C$ . First, we claim that $AR\perp B'C'$ . Let $\omega_B$ and $\omega_C$ meet again at $X\neq A$ . Then $\angle AXB_1=\angle AXC_2=90^\circ$ , so $X$ is the foot from $A$ to $B_1C_2$ . But both $B',C'$ lie on $B_1C_2$ and $AX$ is the radical axis of $\omega_B, \omega_C$ , so $R$ lies on $AX$ , proving the claim. Note that the same logic works for $BR$ and $CR$ . [asy] size(7cm); defaultpen(fontsize(10pt)); import olympiad; import geometry; real t = 0.3; real t = 0.3; pair A = (1,4); pair B = (0,0); pair C = (4,0); pair A_1 = B + t*dir(-90)*(C-B); pair A_2 = C + t*dir(90)*(B-C); pair B_1 = C + t*dir(-90)*(A-C); pair B_2 = A + t*dir(90)*(C-A); pair C_1 = A + t*dir(-90)*(B-A); pair C_2 = B + t*dir(90)*(A-B); pair A_prime = extension(A_1,B_2,A_2,C_1); pair B_prime = extension(B_1,C_2,B_2,A_1); pair C_prime = extension(C_1,A_2,C_2,B_1); pair Y = extension(A,A+B_prime-C_prime,A_prime,B_prime); pair Z = extension(A,Y,A_prime,C_prime); pair R = extension(A,foot(A,B_1,C_2),B,foot(B,A_2,C_1)); fill(B--A_1--A_2--C--cycle, mediumgray); fill(C--B_1--B_2--A--cycle, mediumgray); fill(A--C_1--C_2--B--cycle, mediumgray); draw(A--B--C--cycle, linewidth(1)); draw(A_1--B_2, black); draw(B_1--C_2, black); draw(C_1--A_2, black); draw(Z--A, black, EndArrow(position=0.5)); draw(A--Y, black); draw(B_prime--C_prime, black, EndArrow(position=0.5)); draw(B--A_1--A_2--C--cycle, black); draw(C--B_1--B_2--A--cycle, black); draw(A--C_1--C_2--B--cycle, black); draw(A--R, gray); draw(B--R, gray); draw(C--R, gray); dot(" $A$ ", A, dir(101)); dot(" $B$ ", B, dir(-142)); dot(" $C$ ", C, dir(-27)); dot(" $A_1$ ", A_1, dir(-136)); dot(" $A_2$ ", A_2, dir(-45)); dot(" $B_1$ ", B_1, dir(-9)); dot(" $B_2$ ", B_2, dir(81)); dot(" $C_1$ ", C_1, dir(121)); dot(" $C_2$ ", C_2, dir(-149)); dot(" $A'$ ", A_prime, dir(-172)); dot(" $B'$ ", B_prime, dir(-53)); dot(" $C'$ ", C_prime, dir(66)); dot(" $Y$ ", Y, dir(-20)); dot(" $Z$ ", Z, dir(-143)); dot(" $R$ ", R, dir(45)); [/asy] Now let the line through $A$ parallel to $B'C'$ meet $A_1B_2$ and $A_2C_1$ at $Y,Z$ respectively. Then the problem is equivalent to showing that $A$ is the midpoint of $YZ$ . But note that $AB_2\perp AC$ , $B_2Y=A'B'\perp CR$ , and $AY\perp AR$ , so $\triangle AYB_2\sim \triangle ARC$ and $AY=AR\cdot\tfrac{AB_2}{AC}$ . Similarly, we get $AZ=AR\cdot\tfrac{AC_1}{AB}$ . But the angle conditions imply rectangles $CB_1B_2A$ and $AC_1C_2B$ are similar, so $\tfrac{AB_2}{AC}=\tfrac{AC_1}{AB}$ . Thus, $AY=AZ$ , so $A$ is the midpoint of $YZ$ , as desired.
RemarkThe second solution only requires that rectangles $CB_1B_2A$ and $AC_1C_2B$ are similar. Rectangle $BA_1A_2C$ can be arbitrarily chosen and the problem is still true.

Let  $ABC$  be a triangle, and let  $D$  be a point on the internal angle bisector of  $BAC$ . Let  $x$  be the ellipse with foci  $B$  and  $C$  passing through  $D$ ,  $y$  be the ellipse with foci  $A$  and  $C$  passing through  $D$ , and  $z$  be the ellipse with foci  $A$  and  $B$  passing through  $D$ . Ellipses  $x$  and  $z$  intersect at distinct points  $D$  and  $E$ , and ellipses  $x$  and  $y$  intersect at distinct points  $D$  and  $F$ . Prove that  $AD$  bisects angle  $EAF$ .

*Andrew Carratu*
solution_md:
Let  $A=(-a,0)$ ,  $B=(b,d)$ ,  $C=(c,e)$ , and  $D=(0,0)$ . Let  $p=-a=AD$ ,  $q=\sqrt{b^2+d^2}=BD$ , and  $r=\sqrt{c^2+e^2}=CD$ . We have  $AE+BE=p+q$  and  $BE+CE=q+r$ , so  $AE=(p+q-BE)$  and  $CE=(q+r-BE)$ . Therefore,  $(q+r)AE^2+(p-r)BE^2-(p+q)CE^2$  is constant and describes the equation of line  $DE$ . Therefore, if  $E=(x,y)$ , this is  $$ (q+r)(x+a)^2+(p-r)(x-b)^2-(p+q)(x-c)^2+(q+r)y^2+(p-r)(y-d)^2-(p+q)(y-e)^2 $$   so the equation of  $DE$  is   $$ x(aq+ar+br+cq+ac-ab)+y(ae-ad+dr+eq)=0. $$  The equation of the ellipse with foci  $B$  and  $C$  passing through  $D$  and  $E$  is
\begin{align*}
BE&=q+r-CE
BE^2&=(q+r)^2+CE^2-2(q+r)CE
(BE^2-CE^2-(q+r)^2)^2&=4(q+r)^2CE^2
(BE^2-CE^2)^2-2(q+r)^2(BE^2+CE^2)+(q+r)^4&=0
(-2bx+2cx-2dy+2ey+b^2-c^2+d^2-e^2)^2-2(q+r)^2(2x^2-2(b+c)x+2y^2-2(d+e)y+b^2+c^2+d^2+e^2)+(q+r)^4&=0
4x^2((c-b)^2-(q+r)^2)+4y^2((e-d)^2-(q+r)^2)+8xy(c-b)(e-d)+4x((c-b)(q^2-r^2)+(b+c)(q+r)^2)+4y((e-d)(q^2-r^2)+(d+e)(q+r)^2)&=0
(x(c-b)+y(e-d))^2-(q+r)^2(x^2+y^2)+2(q+r)(x(qc+rb)+y(qe+rd))&=0.
\end{align*}

Since  $D$  lies on the angle bisector,  $(a+b)e+(a+c)d=0$ , so  $a=-\frac{be+cd}{d+e}$ . Then, let  $m=aq+ar+br+cq+ac-ab$  and  $n=ae-ad+dr+eq$ . If  $x=Cn$  and  $y=-Cm$ , then we get
\begin{align*}
C((n(c-b)-m(e-d))^2-(q+r)^2(m^2+n^2))&=-2(q+r)(n(qc+rb)-m(qe+rd))
C((r(cd-be)+q(cd-be)-a(q+r)(e-d))^2-(q+r)^2(m^2+n^2))&=-2a(q+r)((e-d)(qc+rb)-(q+r+c-b)(qe+rd))
C(q+r)^2((cd-be-a(e-d))^2-m^2-n^2)&=-2a(q+r)(q(be-cd)+r(be-cd)-(q+r)(qe+rd))
C((cd-be-a(e-d))^2-m^2-n^2)&=2a(-be+cd+qe+rd).
\end{align*}

Therefore, if  $s=(cd-be-a(e-d))^2-m^2-n^2$  and  $t=-be+cd+qe+rd$ , then  $C=\frac{2at}s$ , so  $x=\frac{2atn}s$  and  $y=\frac{-2atm}s$ . The slope of  $AE$  is  $\frac{-2atm}{2atn+as}=\frac{-2tm}{2tn+s}$ . Then, we have
\begin{align*}
2tn+s&=2tn+(cd-be-a(e-d))^2-m^2-n^2
&=2tn+(t-n)^2-m^2-n^2
&=t^2-m^2.
\end{align*}

Therefore, the slope of  $AE$  is  $\frac{-2tm}{t^2-m^2}$ . Now, we have
\begin{align*}
m&=q(a+c)+r(a+b)+a(c-b)
&=q\frac{ce-be}{d+e}+r\frac{bd-cd}{d+e}+\frac{(b-c)(be+cd)}{d+e}
&=\frac{b-c}{d+e}(-qe+rd+be+cd).
\end{align*}
Then, if  $t'=be-cd+qe+rd$  and  $m'=\frac{c-b}{d+e}(qe-rd+be+cd)$ , the slope of  $AF$  is  $\frac{-2t'm'}{t'^2-m'^2}$ , so we need to show  $$ \frac{-2tm}{t^2-m^2}=-\frac{-2t'm'}{t'^2-m'^2} $$   or   $$ \frac tm-\frac mt=-\frac{t'}{m'}+\frac{m'}{t'}. $$   We claim  $\frac tm=-\frac{t'}{m'}$ , which implies the equality. This is equivalent to
\begin{align*}
(-be+cd+qe+rd)\frac{c-b}{d+e}(qe-rd+be+cd)&=-(be-cd+qe+rd)\frac{b-c}{d+e}(-qe+rd+be+cd)
(-be+cd+qe+rd)(qe-rd+be+cd)&=(be-cd+qe+rd)(-qe+rd+be+cd)
(qe+cd)^2-(be-rd)^2&=(rd+be)^2-(qe-cd)^2
(rd+be)^2+(rd-be)^2&=(qe+cd)^2+(qe-cd)^2
r^2d^2+b^2e^2&=q^2e^2+c^2d^2
d^2(c^2+e^2)+b^2e^2&=(b^2+d^2)e^2+c^2d^2.
\end{align*}

This is true, which implies that the slopes of  $AE$  and  $AF$  have quotient  $-1$ . Therefore,  $AE$  and  $AF$  are reflections over  $AD$ , so  $AD$  bisects  $EAF$ .

<details><summary>answer</summary>We claim that the answer is  $n-k+1$ .</details>
<details><summary>lower bound</summary>We use induction on  $k$ . For  $k=1$ , setting  $a_1,\ldots,a_n$  all distinct,  $f$  has at least  $n$  roots, so its degree is at least  $n$ .
Assume that the claim holds for  $k-1$ , and it does not for  $k$ . Let  $f$  be a polynomial satisfying the conditions with degree less than  $n-k+1$ .  Demonstrate  $f$  the following way:  $$ f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-k}x_1^ig_i(x_2,\ldots,x_n) $$  with each  $g_i$  a polynomial. Then there exists at least one  $g_i$  which is not identically zero. Let such  $i$  be  $t$ .
Assume that for all permutations  $b_1,\ldots,b_n$  of  $a_1,\ldots,a_n$  we have  $\forall{x\in\mathbb{R}},f(x,b_2,\ldots,b_k)=0$ .
Then  $g_t$  suffices the condition for  $k-1$ . By the induction hypothesis this is a contradiction.
Thus there exists some permutation such that  $\exists{x\in\mathbb{R}},f(x,b_2,\ldots,b_k)\neq0$ . If all  $a_i$  are distinct, this has  $n-k+1$  or more solutions, which is a contradiction.</details>
<details><summary>construction</summary>Let  $P(x)=(x-a_1)\cdots(x-a_n)=x^n-s_1x^{n-1}+s_2x^{n-2}-\cdots$ ,  $Q(x)=(x-b_1)\cdots(x-b_k)=x^k-t_1x^{k-1}+t_2x^{k-2}-\cdots$ .
We basically show that we can construct  $s_{n-k+1}$  only using numbers  $s_1$  to  $s_{n-k}$  and  $b_1$  to  $b_k$ . First we see that  $t_i$  is an  $i$ -degree polynomial in  $b_1,\ldots,b_k$ .
Set  $R(x)=x^{n-k}-c_1x^{n-k+1}+\cdots$  such that  $P(x)=Q(x)R(x)$ . Then we get the relations  $c_1+t_1=s_1, c_2+c_1t_1+t_2=s_2$  and such. Thus we can get  $c_i$  recursively, in the form of  $i$  or less degree polynomial in  $b_1,\ldots,b_k$ .
From the polynomial values  $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_{n-k+1}$  we get some polynomial  $g(b_1,\ldots,b_k)=s_{n-k+1}$  for all permutations, and we see its degree is no larger than  $n-k+1$ .
Furthermore, this function is not constant. For general values of  $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ , the function  $g(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$  yields the only possible value of  $s_{n-k+1}$ , given  $s_1$  through  $s_{n-k}$ , and  $Q(x)$ , a  $k$ -degree factor of  $P(x)$ . Adjusting  $x_i$ 's to some roots of unity can set  $P(x)=x^k+1$  or  $P(x)=x^k-1$ , in which  $g$  has a different value.
Set  $f=g-s_{n-k+1}$  and we are done.</details>

stem_md:
Over all complex-coefficient polynomials  $P(x)$  of degree  $n$ , what is the maximum number of complex numbers  $x$  with magnitude  $1$  such that  $P(x)$  is real?

*Aprameya Tripathy*
solution_md:
The answer is  $\boxed{2n}$ , achieved when  $P(x)=x^n$ ; its  $2n$  solutions are the  $2n^{\text{th}}$  roots of unity.
When  $P(\omega)$  is real where  $|\omega|=1$ , we have \[P(\omega)=\overline{P(\omega)}=P^*(\bar\omega)=P^*(\omega^{-1}),\]where  $P^*(x)$  is  $P(x)$  but all the coefficients are conjugated.
Multiply by  $\omega^n$  to get a degree  $2n$  polynomial in  $\omega$ , which has at most  $2n$  solutions.

Let  $ABCD$  be a convex quadrilateral with  $DA=AB=BC$ . Let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $\overline{AB}$ , and let  $P$  be a point in the plane with  $\angle PCA=\angle PDB=90^\circ$ . A circle centered at  $O$  is tangent to segments  $DA$ ,  $AB$ , and  $BC$ . Prove that  $M$ ,  $O$ , and  $P$  are collinear.

*Tiger Zhang and Calvin Wang*
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution 1</summary>Let  $K$  and  $L$  be the midpoints of  $\overline{PA}$  and  $\overline{PB}$ , respectively. By symmetry,  $\overline{AO}$  and  $\overline{BO}$  are the perpendicular bisectors of  $\overline{BD}$  and  $\overline{AC}$ . We also have  $KB=KD$  and  $LA=LC$ , so  $K$  lies on  $\overline{AO}$  and  $L$  lies on  $\overline{BO}$ . Thus,  $O$  is the centroid of  $PAB$ , which means  $M$ ,  $O$ , and  $P$  are collinear, as desired.  $\blacksquare$</details>

<details><summary>Solution 2</summary>Let  $\overline{PD}$  and  $\overline{PC}$  intersect  $\overline{AB}$  at  $X$  and  $Y$ , respectively. From  $\angle BDX=\angle ACY=90^\circ$ , we obtain that  $A$  is the circumcenter of  $BDX$  and  $B$  is the circumcenter of  $ACY$ . Thus, we have  $XA=AB=BY$ .

By symmetry,  $\overline{AO}$  and  $\overline{BO}$  are the perpendicular bisectors of  $\overline{BD}$  and  $\overline{AC}$ , so they are parallel to  $\overline{PX}$  and  $\overline{PY}$ , respectively. Thus,  $OAB$  and  $PXY$  are homothetic. Notice that a homothety at  $M$  with scale factor  $3$  sends  $A$  to  $X$  and  $B$  to  $Y$ , so it must send  $O$  to  $P$ . Therefore,  $M$ ,  $O$ , and  $P$  are collinear, as desired.  $\blacksquare$</details>

stem_md:
Let  $\triangle A_1A_2A_3$  be an equilateral triangle with isogonal conjugates  $P_1$  and  $P_2$  in its interior. Prove there exists a cyclic pentagon  $B_1B_2B_3Q_1Q_2$  such that  $A_iP_j=B_iQ_j$  for each  $i \in \{1,2,3\}$  and  $j \in \{1,2\}$ .

*Karn Chutinan*
solution_md:
Let  $P_1$  reflected over  $A_1A_2$  be  $R_3$ ,  $P_1$  reflected over  $A_2A_3$  be  $R_1$ , and  $P_1$  reflected over  $A_3A_1$  be  $R_2$ .
It is well-known that  $P_2$  is the circumcenter of  $R_1R_2R_3$ . This can be proven via angle chase to show  $A_1P_2$  bisects  $\angle R_2A_1R_3$  and then using  $A_1R_2=A_1P_1=A_1R_3$  to conclude that  $P_2R_2=P_2R_3$ . Let the circumradius be  $R$ .
Now place  $Q_1$  and  $Q_2$  such that  $|Q_1Q_2|=R$ . It remains to show that for each  $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ , in the triangle formed by the side lengths  $A_iP_1$ ,  $A_iP_2$  and  $R$ , the angle opposite  $R$  is the same.
But this is easy since this is precisely the triangle  $A_iR_{i+1}P_2$ , where the angle  $\angle P_2A_iR_{i+1}$  is equal to  $60^\circ$ .

candidates: Let  $x=Q_1Q_2$ . By the Law of Cosines, we need  $\frac{B_iQ_1^2+B_iQ_2^2-x^2}{2B_iQ_1B_iQ_2}=\frac{A_iP_1^2+A_iP_2^2-x^2}{2A_iP_1A_iP_2}$  to be constant for all  $i$ . This is equivalent to  $\sum_i (A_iP_1^2+A_iP_2^2)(A_{i+1}P_1A_{i+1}P_2-A_{i-1}P_1A_{i-1}P_2)=0$ . Let  $f_i=A_iP_1^2+A_iP_2^2$  and  $g_i=A_iP_1A_iP_2$ . Then, this is equivalent to  $g_1(f_3-f_2)+g_2(f_2-f_1)+g_3(f_1-f_3)=0$ . Now, use complex numbers. If  $p_1$  and  $q_1$  are isogonal conjugates in  $1$ ,  $\omega$ ,  $\omega^2$ , then  $p_1+p_2=-\overline{p_1p_2}$ . Then,  $f_1=(p_1-1)(\overline{p_1}-1)+(p_2-1)(\overline{p_2}-1)=p_1\overline{p_1}+p_2\overline{p_2}-p_1-p_2-\overline{p_1}-\overline{p_2}+2=p_1\overline{p_1}+p_2\overline{p_2}+p_1p_2+\overline{p_1p_2}$ . Then,  $f_2=p_1\overline{p_1}+p_2\overline{p_2}+\omega^2p_1p_2+\omega\overline{p_1p_2}$ , so  $f_1-f_2=(1-\omega^2)p_1p_2+(1-\omega)\overline{p_1p_2}$ . Also,  $g_1=(p_1-1)(p_2-1)=p_1p_2-p_1-p_2+1=p_1p_2+\overline{p_1p_2}+1$ , so since  $f_2-f_3=(\omega^2-\omega)p_1p_2+(\omega-\omega^2)\overline{p_1p_2}$ , we get  $g_1(f_2-f_3)=(\omega^2-\omega)p_1^2p_2^2+(\omega-\omega^2)\overline{p_1p_2}$ , so the cyclic sum adds to zero.

Let  $P_1'$  be the reflection of  $A_iA_{i+1}$ . Then  $R = P_1'P_2$  is constant regardless of  $i$  and 
\[
\angle P_1'A_iP_2 = \angle P_1A_iA_{i+1} + \angle P_2A_iA_{i+1} = 60^\circ.
\]
As such, taking the circle with chord  $Q_1Q_2$  of length  $R$  suffices and allows for placing  $B_i$ .

stem_md:
Find the maximum positive integer  $n$  for which there exist distinct points  $A_1$ ,  $A_2$ ,  $\dots$ ,  $A_{2025}$ ,  $B_1$ ,  $B_2$ ,  $\dots$ ,  $B_n$  in the plane such that for  $i=1,2,\dots,n$ , the multisets  $\{B_iA_1,B_iA_2,\dots,B_iA_{2025}\}$  are the same.

*Tiger Zhang*
solution_md: We claim  $n=\boxed{4050}$ . The construction is a regular  $2025$ -gon for  $A_i$ , then pick  $B_i$  to be a point inside the polygon, its  $2024$  other rotations with angle  $\frac{2\pi k}{2025}$ , and its reflections about the  $2025$  axes of symmetry. Suppose  $n\geq4051$ . Let  $A_i=(x_i,y_i)$ . If  $B_i=(x,y)$ , then  $\sum_{i=1}^{4050}(x-x_i)^2+(y-y_i)^2$  is constant, which describes a circle, so all the  $B_i$  lie on a circle. Then, if  $A_j$  is not the center of the circle, there are three  $B_i$  with the same distance to  $A_j$ , contradicting the fact that they all lie on a circle.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/USA Contests/MOP Contests/ELMO Shortlist/2025 ELMO  Shortlist/3600597.json

candidates: My problem! Let $N=2025$ . The answer is $2N=4050$ . The construction for $n=2N$ is as follows. Let $A_1A_2 \dotsm A_N$ be a regular $N$ -gon with center $O$ , and let $P$ be an arbitrary point. Consider the $2N$ rigid transformations that send $A_1A_2 \dotsm A_N$ to itself (the $N$ rotations by a multiple of $\tfrac{\tau}{N}$ around $O$ and the $N$ reflections over the lines of symmetry of $A_1A_2 \dotsm A_N$ ). Let $B_1$ , $B_2$ , $\dots$ , $B_{2N}$ be the images of $P$ under these $2N$ transformations. Notice that $\{B_iA_1,B_iA_2,\dots,B_iA_N\}=\{PA_1,PA_2,\dots,PA_N\}$ for any index $i$ . Furthermore, almost all choices of $P$ in the plane ensure $B_1$ , $B_2$ , $\dots$ , $B_{2N}$ are distinct, as desired. We now prove $n \le 2N$ . Let $P$ be any point in $\{B_1,\dots,B_n\}$ . The main claim is the following. **Claim:** $P$ lies on a fixed (possibly degenerate) circle. *Proof:* Suppose $\{PA_1,\dots,PA_N\}=\{d_1,\dots,d_N\}$ , let $P=(x,y)$ , and let $A_i=(x_i,y_i)$ for all indices $i$ . We have \begin{align*} d_1^2+\dots+d_N^2 &= PA_1^2+\dots+PA_N^2 &= (x-x_1)^2+\dots+(x-x_N)^2+(y-y_1)^2+\dots+(y-y_N)^2. \end{align*} Upon expanding, this is the equation of a circle, so $P$ must lie on a fixed circle. $\square$ Call this fixed circle $\omega$ . Consider any $A_i$ not coinciding with the center of $\omega$ . Notice that $P$ must lie on one of the circles centered at $A_i$ with radius $d_1$ , $\dots$ , $d_N$ . Since each of these circles intersects $\omega$ at most twice, there are at most $2N$ choices for $P$ , so $n \le 2N$ and we are done. $\blacksquare$

The answer is  $4050$ , with  $A$  being a regular  $2025$ -gon. Take a point not on any of the lines of symmetry of  $A$ , and consider its reflections about the lines of symmetry. There will be  $4050$  in total, choosing these as  $B_i$  works. $\sum |B_iA_k|^2$  is constant for all  $B_i$ . This is in fact (by expanding coordinates) the locus of a circle.
Now take  $A_m$  to be a point that's not the center of this circle. For each of the  $\leq2025$  possible values of  $|A_mB_i|$ , there are at most two possible points on the circle making  $A_mB_i$  equal to that, giving the  $4050$  bound.

stem_md:
Let  $A_1A_2\dots A_{2n}$  be a cyclic polygon, and let  $k\le n$  be a positive integer. Suppose that for all  $1\le i\le 2n$ ,  $\angle A_i A_{i-1}A_{i+k}\le \pi/2$ . Prove that
\[\min(\angle A_1 A_{2n}A_{n+1},\angle A_1A_2A_{n+1})+\cdots+\min(\angle A_n A_{n-1}A_{2n},\angle A_nA_{n+1}A_{2n})\ge \frac {\pi k}2.\]
(Indices are taken mod  $2n$ .)

*Rohan Bodke*
solution_md:
"ill let somebody else post the one liner" ahh The problem statement translates as follows:
We choose points $A_1, \ldots, A_{2n}$ on a circle, labelled in clockwise order. Points are not necessarily distinct. For each $i$ , point $A_{i+k}$ (indices taken modulo $2n$ ) is at most $180^{\circ}$ clockwise of $A_i$ (call this the semicircle condition). We wish to show that the sum of the minor arcs $A_1 A_{n+1}$ , $A_2 A_{n+2}$ , etc sum up to at least $k \cdot (180^{\circ})$ (call this the sum condition). We allow $k=0$ .
We basically use induction, but the order of logic is so convoluted that it makes more sense to just avoid using that word. Clearly, the problem is true when $k = 0$ . Now, suppose FTSOC that there exists a pair of integers $(n,k)$ with $k \leq n$ for which we can find a set of points $A_1, \ldots, A_{2n}$ on a circle meeting the semicircle condition but failing the sum condition. Choose $n$ to be minimal, and then choose points $A_1, \ldots, A_{2n}$ to minimize the sum of the minor arcs. We must have $k < n$ then, since if $k = n$ the inequality is clearly true. We also must have $k > 0$ for the reasons established before. **Claim:** Under these assumptions, there cannot exist an index $i$ for which $A_i$ and $A_{i+n}$ are antipodal.**Proof:** We can delete $A_i$ and $A_{i+n}$ . Relabel the remaining $2n-2$ points in clockwise order; then, analyzing the semicircle and sum condition for $n \to n-1$ and $k \to k-1$ , these new $2n-2$ points satisfy the semicircle condition but fail the sum condition. This is a contradiction, so in our supposed set $A_1, \ldots, A_{2n}$ , no two points $A_i$ and $A_{i+n}$ are antipodal. We now split into cases: - **Case 1:** There exists an index $i$ for which points $A_i$ and $A_{i+n}$ (indices taken modulo $2n$ ) coincide. Then, consider the set of (at least) $n+1$ points that coincide at that common point $P$ . The sum of the minor arcs is precisely equal to the sum of the distances from the other points to this common point $P$ . We can slide $P$ along the circle, sweeping up other points into the mega-point $P$ as we move along. Due to linearity, moving $P$ in one direction will make the sum of the minor arcs non-increasing. Eventually, $P$ will reach an extreme value where sliding $P$ any further will break the semicircle condition. Because our mega point contains one point in each of $\{P_1, P_{n+1} \}$ , $\{ P_2, P_{n+2} \}$ , $\ldots$ , two points $A_i$ and $A_{i+n}$ must be antipodal, contradiction. - **Case 2:** For all indices $i$ , points $A_i$ and $A_{i+n}$ do not coincide. **Claim:** We can make local modifications such that each point $A_i$ must be antipodal from some point in the circle $A_j$ .**Proof:** Indeed, for any set of points $A_i$ (possibly a single point) that all coincide at a common point $P$ , we can slide the mega-point $P$ along the circle, sweeping up other points as we move along, making sure that we always slide $P$ in a direction that makes the sum of the minor arcs non-increasing. (This could mean changing directions throughout the process). We stop the process only when $P$ is antipodal from another point—note that, as a corollary, the semicircle condition is maintained (because if the semicircle condition is broken, the moment it happens, $P$ will be antipodal from another point). Then, we pick another set of coinciding points and repeat. When we can't make any moves, it must be because every point is antipodal from another one. Now, we claim that after these local modifications, two points $A_i$ and $A_{i+n}$ must be antipodal. We define a particular sequence of pairs $(i,j)$ for which $A_i$ and $A_j$ are antipodal for every pair in the sequence. Let $A_x$ and $A_y$ be a pair of antipodal points. Our sequence will begin with $(x,y)$ and end with $(y,x)$ : [list] - Begin the sequence with the pair $(x,y)$ . - Add $(x+1,y)$ , $(x,y+1)$ and $(x+1,y+1)$ as suitable to meet the above conditions. For any consecutive pairs $(i,j)$ and $(k,\ell)$ in the sequence, $j-i$ and $\ell-k$ differ by $1$ . Since this difference goes from $y-x$ to $x-y + 2n$ , at some point the difference must be exactly $n$ . So some points $A_i$ and $A_{i+n}$ are antipodal, contradiction.

Let  $H$  be the orthocenter of an acute triangle  $ABC$ . solution_md:
Let  $H_B$  and  $H_C$  be the feet from  $B$  and  $C$  to  $\overline{AC}$  and  $\overline{AB}$ . Now, invert at  $H$  and refer to points' images by their new names, except for  $H$  which we will refer to by its original name. <details><summary>New locations</summary>

- In  $\triangle ABC$ ,  $H$  is the incenter,
- Points  $H_B$  and  $H_C$  are the  $B$  and  $C$  excenters in the (inverted) diagram, respectively; the circle with diameter  $\overline{BC}$  *in the original diagram* inverts to  $(H_B H_C)$ .
- Points  $D$  and  $E$  become points on  $(AHB H_C)$  and  $(AHC H_B)$ , respectively, such that  $\angle DHE = 90^{\circ}$  and  $(DHE)$  passes through the reflection  $H'$  of  $H$  across line  $H_B H_C$ .
- We wish to show that the antipode  $X$  of  $H'$  in  $(DH'HE)$  lies on  $(H_B H_C)$ .
</details>
Let  $X'$  be the antipode of  $H$  in  $(DH'HE)$ . Then, since  $H$  and  $H'$  are reflections across  $\overline{H_B H_C}$ , it follows that  $X$  and  $X'$  are also reflections across  $\overline{PQ}$ . It would suffice to show that  $X'$  lies on  $(H_B H_C)$ . We have  $\angle H_C D H = \angle HDX' = 90^{\circ}$ , so  $H_C$ ,  $D$  and  $X'$  are collinear—similarly,  $H_B$ ,  $E$  and  $X'$  are collinear. We now have
\[\angle H_C X' H_B = \angle DX'E = 180^{\circ} - \angle DHE = 90^{\circ}. \]

\]

\]

stem_md:
Some positive integers, not necessarily distinct, are written on a board. Prove that Elmo can write additional positive integers on the board so that


- he writes no number more than twice
- the square of the sum of the resulting numbers on the board is equal to the sum of the cubes of the numbers.

*Seongjin Shim*
solution_md:
Here's a solution that writes  $O(n^4)$  numbers.

Claim 1: there exists a tesseract of cells such that each horizontal cube slice is a Latin cube, and each 1D vertical column contains each integer at most twice, except for the first column, which contains every number on the board and at most two of each additional number.

Proof: fix  $N$  to be chosen later. Start with the latin cube that you build recursively by taking  $8$  copies of the cube half the size, and shifting the ones with even sum of coordinates by half of  $N$ , and constructed such that the three edges coming from some vertex are exactly  $1,2,\dots,N$  in order. Notice that this has the property that along the diagonal from that vertex, each box which shares that diagonal and the original vertex contains exactly two distinct labels, one of which is  $1$ . To construct the tesseract, make its first slice the cyclic permutation of that cube starting with  $N$ , then the next row the same but starting with  $N-1$ , and so on down to  $1$ . This should make the first column  $N,N-1,\dots,1$  in order.

Next to turn this into our desired tesseract, we make a series of swaps as follows. WLOG the numbers on the board are in nondecreasing order, then in layer  $i$  of the tesseract, pick the (hollow) cube which shares a vertex and diagonal as described above that also contains the  $i$ th number on the board. Then swap the cells labeled  $1$  and those labeled with the  $i$ th number on the board. This preserves the latin cubeness and makes the first column correct. Additionally, notice that as  $i$  increases, the swapped cube gets further from the first column, so by picking  $N$  large enough we can force this to never roll over. In particular this means no cell from another column is swapped twice, which proves the claim.

Claim 2: Given an  $n$ -dimensional latin square of size  $N$ , turn the square into a list of numbers by replacing cell  $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$  with  $Na_1+N^2a_2+\dots+N^na_n$  plus its label. Then for  $1\le i\le n$ , the sum of the  $i$ th powers of this list is exactly  $\tfrac1N$  the sum of the  $i$ th powers of  $1,\dots,N^{n+1}$ .

Proof: induct. The idea is that removing the term  $N^na_n$  from the sum, we get exactly the integers  $1,\dots,N^n$ . This follows from a much easier induction. Then we may write the sum of the  $i$ th powers as  $b_1^i+b_2^i+\dots+(N^n+b_{N^{n-1}+1})^i+\dots+((N-1)N^n+b_{N^n})^i$  for some permutation  $b_i$  of  $1,\dots,N^n$ . Thus distributing this, we get the sum of  $i$ th powers of  $1,\dots,N^n$  and sum of  $\le i-1$ th powers of groups of numbers which must be lists generated by  $n-1$ -dimensional latin squares. By inductive hypothesis, these are all equal. Thus the sum of the  $i$ th powers are equal for all  $n$ -dimensional latin squares. The average is  $\tfrac1N$  times the sum of the  $i$ th powers of  $1,\dots,N^{n+1}$ , finishing. TLDR this is the same idea as 2024 TSTST 3.

To solve the problem, turn every slice from our Claim 1 tesseract into a list of numbers as in Claim 2. Then each slice's sum is  $\tfrac1N$  times the sum from  $1$  to  $N^4$ , and each slice's sum of cubes is  $\tfrac1N$  times the sum of cubes of  $1$  to  $N^4$ . Thus if we combine these lists, we get a list whose sum and sum of cubes are the same as  $1,\dots,N^4$ , so in particular the sum of cubes is equal to the square of sum. By Claim 1, if we remove the initial numbers on the board, which end up unchanged when creating the lists, no number appears more than twice, as desired.

candidates: Recall the following identity:   $$ x^3-(x-y)^3-(x-2y)^3+(x+3y)^3-(x-4y)^3+(x-5y)^3+(x-6y)^3-(x-7y)^3-(x-8y)^3+(x-9y)^3+(x-10y)^3-(x-11y)^3+(x-12y)^3-(x-13y)^3-(x-14y)^3+(x-15y)^3=0. $$  Now, consider the multiset of integers from  $1$  to  $N$ , where  $N$  is a large integer we choose later. For every integer originally on the board multiple times, let  $x$  be that integer, and pick a sufficiently large common difference  $y$ . Then, use the identity to increase the number of occurrences of  $x$  by  $1$  while keeping all other numbers having at most two occurrences.

We prove the stronger statement that starting from any positive integers  $a\equiv b\pmod 6$ , Elmo can write positive integers  $n_1$  to  $n_m$ , no number appearing thrice, such that \[a+n_1^3+n_2^3+\dots+n_m^3=(b+n_1+n_2+\dots+n_m)^2.\]

Step 1: Write some numbers until  $48\mid a$  and  $48\mid b$ . This is possible by writing  $2\pmod{48}$  numbers until  $48\mid a-b$ , then writing  $1\pmod{48}$  numbers until  $48\mid a$ . Now replace  $a$  and  $b$  with these new values.

Step 2: Let  $b=2t-2$ . Write  $1,2,\dots,X-t$  and  $X$ , for some large enough  $X=4Y$  to be determined later. The current value of the LHS is \[a+(1^3+2^3+\cdots+(X-t)^3)+X^3\] and the current value of the RHS is \[(b+(1+2+\cdots+(X-t))+X)^2.\] The difference is
\begin{align*}
D&=a+(1^3+2^3+\cdots+(X-t)^3)+X^3-(b+(1+2+\cdots+(X-t))+X)^2
&=a+\left(\frac{(X-t)(X-t+1)}{2}\right)^2+X^3-(b+X)^2-2(b+X)\frac{(X-t)(X-t+1)}{2}-\left(\frac{(X-t)(X-t+1)}{2}\right)^2
&=a+X^3-(b+X)^2-(-bt+bt^2+(b-t-2bt+t^2)X+(1+b-2t)X^2+X^3)
&=a-b^2+bt-bt^2-(3b-t-2bt+t^2)X-(2+b-2t)X^2
&=-3(t^2-3t+2)X+(a+b(-b+t-t^2)).
\end{align*}

Step 3: We replace  $Y-2,Y-1,Y+1,Y+2$  with  $Y-t,Y-(t-3),Y+(t-3),Y+t$ . This keeps the sum the same but increases the sum of cubes (and therefore  $D$ ) by \[(Y-t)^3+(Y-(t-3))^3+(Y+(t-3))^3+(Y+t)^3-(Y-2)^3-(Y-1)^3-(Y+1)^3-(Y+2)^3=3(t^2-3t+2)X.\]

Step 4: We can replace  $n+1,n+4,n+6,n+7$  with  $n+2,n+3,n+5,n+8$ . This keeps the sum the same but increases the sum of cubes (and therefore  $D$ ) by \[(n+2)^3+(n+3)^3+(n+5)^3+(n+8)^3-(n+1)^3-(n+4)^3-(n+6)^3-(n+7)^3=48.\]
Doing the reverse replacement decreases  $D$  by  $48$ . So doing the appropriate replacement  $\left|\frac{a+b(-b+t-t^2)}{48}\right|$  times changes  $D$  by  $-a-b(-b+t-t^2)$ .

Combining all these steps results in  $D=0$ , which is exactly what we wanted. We only need to make sure that this results in no number appearing thrice by choosing  $X$  large enough. Step 1 writes a set of numbers independent of  $a,b,X$ , then step 2 writes each number only once. In step 3, the only edits are made at a small distance away from  $Y=\frac X4$ , and in step 4, the only edits are made in a small region independent of  $X$ , at any point. Thus by making  $X$  large, steps 1, 3 and 4 can be independent of each other, and on top of step 2, this makes sure each number is written  $0$ ,  $1$  or  $2$  times.

stem_md:
Let  $S$  be the set of edges in an  $m \times n$  rectangular grid. What is the fewest number of rectangles such that the union of their perimeters is  $S$ ?

*Benny Wang*
solution_md: The answer is  $\boxed{\left\lceil \frac{m+1}{2} \right\rceil + \left\lceil \frac{n+1}{2} \right\rceil - 1}$ . This is achievable by having  $\left\lceil \frac{m+1}{2} \right\rceil$  rectangles covering the entire length of the  $m+1$  horizontal gridlines,  $\left\lceil \frac{n+1}{2} \right\rceil$  rectangles covering the entirety of the  $n+1$  vertical gridlines, with the overlap coming from the largest rectangle in the grid. To prove this, consider the set of  $2n + 2m$  line segments formed by all the segments either connecting a point on the exterior of the rectangle to a point on the interior, or a segment connecting a corner to the point directly clockwise from it. Note that a given rectangle can cover at maximum  $4$  of these  $2m + 2n$  segments, so we need at least  $\left\lceil \frac{m+n}{2} \right\rceil$  rectangles to cover these points. This is sufficient if at least one of  $m, n$  is odd, so we assume  $m, n$  even. If  $\left\lceil \frac{m+n}{2} \right\rceil$  rectangles sufficed, there must be a way to partition the  $2m + 2n$  points into groups of  $4$  such that each group of  $4$  lies entirely on a rectangle. Consider the segments on the perimeter. To contain  $4$  segments, each partition containing a segment on the perimeter must contain exactly  $2$  or  $4$  perimeter segments. In either case, we are left with numbers of vertical and horizontal segments that are not multiples of  $4$ . Since we cannot create a group of  $4$  segments on a rectangle by including both vertical and horizontal segments from this set, we need at least  $\left\lceil \frac{m+n}{2} \right\rceil$  rectangles if  $m, n$  even, so we are done.  $\blacksquare$

Color the first and last edges purple. Similarly for the horizontal lines, color the first and last edges pink. Finally, on the four lines forming perimeter, color the first edge clockwise orange. There are $2m-2$ purple, $2n-2$ pink, and $4$ orange edges. We show that each rectangle can cover at most $4$ colored edges. If the rectangle touches neither the left nor the right perimeter of the grid, it could only have purple edges. It has $4$ purple edges iff it spans the entire height of the grid. Vice versa for pink. Now consider rectangles that share both horizontal and vertical perimeter with the grid outline, which means it contains a corner, and hence an orange edge. If it contains no other corner, it covers $1$ orange, $1$ purple and $1$ pink edge, total of $3$ . If it contains one other corner, then it covers $2$ orange edges, and: $2$ purple edges if the corners are vertically adjacent, or $2$ pink edges if the corners are horizontally adjacent. Either way, $4$ total edges are covered. And if it contains all corners, then it covers $4$ orange edges. In all cases, $\leq4$ colored edges are covered. Therefore, $\left\lceil\frac{(2m-2)+(2n-2)+4}4\right\rceil$ rectangles are required. This coincides with our answer, except for the case where $m,n$ are both even, where we need to show $1$ more rectangle is needed. For the case that both $m,n$ are even, every rectangle must cover exactly $4$ unique colored edges for equality to hold, since $2m-2+2n-2+4$ is divisible by $4$ . The number of purple edges is $2$ mod $4$ , which means that a rectangle must cover some number of purple edges that is neither $0$ or $4$ . This is only possible with the corner rectangle that covers $2$ orange and $2$ purple edges, which contains two vertically adjacent corners of the grid. Similarly for pink, the rectangle must contain two horizontally adjacent corners of the grid. But this forces the chosen rectangles to overlap, and thus share an orange edge, so equality cannot occur. We conclude that $1+\left\lceil\frac{(2m-2)+(2n-2)+4}4\right\rceil$ rectangles are required when both $m,n$ are even, which coincides with the construction of $1+\left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor$ .

stem_md:
Let  $n$  and  $k$  be fixed positive integers. Let  $T$  be the set of all infinite tuples  $A = (a_0, a_1, ...)$  of integers with  $0 \leq a_i \leq k$  for each  $i$ , finitely many nonzero  $a_i$ , and \[ \sum_{i=0}^\infty 2^i a_i = n. \]
Compute \[ \sum_{A \in T} \prod_{i=0}^\infty \binom{k}{a_i}. \]

*Oron Wang*
solution_md: Sketch of a double-counting solution: consider the strip  $$ X=\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\times\{1,2,\ldots,k\}. $$  Let  $S\subset P(X)$  be the set of all finite subsets  $Y\subset X$  such that  $\sum_{(i,j)\in Y}2^i=n$ . By summing over columns, we obtain that  $$ |S|=\sum_{A \in T} \prod_{i=0}^\infty \binom{k}{a_i}. $$  On the other hand, since each nonnegative integer has a unique binary representation, it follows that  $|S|$  equals number of ways to express  $n$  as the sum of tuples of  $k$  non-negative integers, which is  $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$ .

Let  $\omega_1$  and  $\omega_2$  be circles intersecting at  $A$  and  $B$ . Let  $\ell$  be the common tangent of both circles closer to  $A$ . The line through  $A$  tangent to  $\omega_1$  intersects  $\omega_2$  at  $A$  and  $C$ . Prove that there exists a circle tangent to  $\omega_1,\omega_2,$  and the lines through  $A$  and  $C$  parallel to  $\ell$ .

*Michael Zhao*
solution_md: Let $\ell$ tangent to $\omega_1, \omega_2$ at $T_1, T_2$ , respectively. Denote $\ell_A$ and $\ell_C$ as lines parallel to $\ell$ through $A$ and $C$ , respectively. First, we introduce the following claim. [rule]**Claim : **For any point $P$ on $AC$ , $4$ points $PT_1 \cap \omega_1, \ell_C = P_1, P_C$ and $PT_2 \cap \omega_2, \ell_A = P_2, P_A$ are concyclic on $\Omega_P$ .**Proof :** Let $PA \cap \ell$ at $R$ . We just do power bash $$ PT_1 \cdot PP_1 = PA^2, \frac{PR}{PC} = \frac{PT_1}{PP_C} $$ $$ PT_2 \cdot PP_2 = PC \cdot PA, \frac{PR}{PA} = \frac{PT_2}{PP_A} $$ Combining $2$ equations gives $$ \frac{PA}{PC} = \frac{PT_1 \cdot PP_A}{PT_2 \cdot PP_C} \rightarrow PP_C \cdot PP_1 = PP_2 \cdot PP_A $$ as desired. $\blacksquare$ [rule] Now, assume that there exist a point $Z$ on $AC$ such that $Z_1Z_2$ pass through insimilicenter of $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ . Hence, there exist a circle $\Omega$ that is tangent to $\omega_1, \omega_2$ at $Z_1, Z_2$ , respectively. By radical axis, the tangent to $\Omega$ at $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ intersect on a point distinct from $A$ on $AB$ . However, by converse of shooting lemma, there exist $2$ circles $\Omega_A$ , that is tangent to $\ell_A$ at $Z_A$ and tangent to $\omega_2$ at $Z_2$ and $\Omega_C$ that is tangent to $\ell_C$ at $Z_C$ and $\omega_1$ at $Z_1$ . Assume that $\Omega_A$ and $\Omega_C$ are distinct. By radical axis on $\Omega_P, \Omega_A, \Omega_C$ , $BD$ is the radical axis of $\Omega_A, \Omega_C$ . By radical axis on $\Omega_A, \Omega, \Omega_C$ , the tangent to $\Omega$ at $Z_1, Z_2$ intersect on $BD$ . Hence, contradiction. Thus, $\Omega_A = \Omega_C$ . This immediately implies the desired result. $\blacksquare$

The length of the common tangent of these two circles is $c$ . Therefore, it suffices to show that the product of the radii is $\frac14c^2$ . By the Law of Sines, the radius of the first circle is $\frac{c(s-b)}{2a\sin B}$ , and the radius of the second circle is $\frac1{2(s-b)}ac\sin B$ . The product is $\frac14c^2$ .

<details><summary>coord bash</summary>Set up the problem with  $O=(0,0)$  as the origin. $\omega_1$  has center  $O_1=(-1,a)$  and radius  $a$ , so its equation is \[(x+1)^2+(y-a)^2=a^2\]which can be simplified to \[(x+1)^2+y^2-2ay=0.\]Similarly  $\omega_2$  has center  $O_2=(1,b)$  and radius  $b$ , so its equation is \[(x-1)^2+y^2-2by=0.\]
The radical axis can be computed by subtracting the equations and we get \[x=\frac{a-b}{2}y.\]Substituting this back and solving for  $y$  gives us the quadratic \[\left(\left(\tfrac{a-b}{2}\right)^2+1\right)y^2-(a+b)y+1=0.\]Solving and taking the solution with the smaller  $y$  coordinate, gets us \[A\left(\frac{a-b}{q},\frac{2}{q}\right)\]where  $q=a+b+2\sqrt{ab-1}$ .

The set of points  $P$  on the tangent to  $\omega_1$  at  $A$  is given by solving  $\overrightarrow{PA}\cdot\overrightarrow{AO_1}$ . This gives \[\left(a-\frac{a-b}{q}\right)\left(\frac{a-b}{q}+1\right)+\left(y-\frac{2}{q}\right)\left(\frac{2}{q}-a\right)=0.\]Multiply out by  $q^2$  and simplify to get \[x(a-b+q)+y(2-aq)-a-b+q=0.\]Rearrange to get  $(a-b+q)(x-1)$  on the LHS: \[(a-b+q)(x-1)=y(aq-2)+2(b-q)\]Substitute this into the equation for  $\omega_2$  (multiplied by  $(a-b+q)^2$ ) to get
\[\left((aq-2)^2+(a-b+q)^2\right)y^2+\left(4(aq-2)(b-q)-2b(a-b+q)^2\right)y+\text{const.}=0.\]This simplifies as follows (calculations omitted):
\[(aq-2)^2+(a-b+q)^2=(aq)^2\]\[4(aq-2)(b-q)-2b(a-b+q)^2=-4q(aq+ab-2)\]and therefore by Vieta, the sum of  $y$  coordinates of the two intersections of tangents is \[\frac{4q(aq+ab-2)}{(aq)^2}=\frac{4(aq+ab-2)}{a^2q}.\]Knowing that one of the intersections is  $A$  and has  $y$  coordinate  $\frac{2}{q}$  we can calculate the other as \[\frac{4(aq+ab-2)}{a^2q}-\frac{2}{q}=\frac{2(2aq+2ab-a^2-4)}{a^2q}.\]
The circle we're looking for therefore will have its center at  $y$  coordinate as the average of these two, which is  $\frac{2(aq+ab-2)}{a^2q}$  and its radius will be half the distance between the two lines at  $r=\frac{2(aq+ab-a^2-2)}{a^2q}$ .

Now consider the circles  $\Omega_1$  centered at  $O_1$  with radius  $a+r$  and  $\Omega_2$  centered at  $O_2$  with radius  $b-r$ , we want to show that they intersect on the line  $y=\frac{2(aq+ab-2)}{a^2q}=r+\frac{2}{q}$ .

We can proceed to calculate the radical axis as before by subtracting the two equations:
\[(x+1)^2+(y-a)^2-(x-1)^2-(y-b)^2=(a+r)^2-(b-r)^2\]which simplifies to \[2x+(b-a)y=(a+b)r.\]Sub  $y=r+\frac 2q$  to get
\[x=ar+\frac{a-b}{q}.\]It remains to verify that the point \[O_x\left(ar+\frac{a-b}{q},r+\frac{2}{q}\right)\]lies on one of the circles (we check  $\Omega_1$ ):
\begin{align*}
(x+1)^2+(y-a)^2&=\left(ar+\frac{a-b}{q}+1\right)^2+\left(r+\frac{2}{q}-a\right)^2
&=(ar)^2+2ar\left(\frac{a-b}{q}+1\right)+\left(\frac{a-b}{q}+1\right)^2+r^2+2r\left(\frac{2}{q}-a\right)+\left(\frac{2}{q}-a\right)^2
&=r^2+r\left(2a\left(\frac{a-b}{q}+1\right)+a^2r+2\left(\frac{2}{q}-a\right)\right)+\left(\left(\frac{a-b}{q}+1\right)^2+\left(\frac{2}{q}-a\right)^2\right)
&=a^2r^2+2r\left(\frac{a^2-ab+aq+aq+ab-a^2-2+2-aq}{q}\right)+a^2
&=a^2r^2+2ar+a^2
&=(a+r)^2.
\end{align*}Therefore  $O_x$  is the center of the desired circle and we are done.

stem_md:
Each cell in an infinite grid is colored gray, pink, or green. Call a sub-rectangle of grid cells *indecisive* if, within the rectangle, no color appears more frequently than the other two colors. Could there exist an integer  $n$  and a coloring of the grid so that every subrectangle with both side lengths at least  $n$  is indecisive?

*Benny Wang*
solution_md: Take odd $m$ coprime to $3$ . Then for an $m \times m$ square, note that its impossible for all colors to appear the same number of times. Note that the least appearing color appears an odd number of times, and that the two colors appearing most appear with a parity.**Claim:** Any two adjacent $m \times m$ squares have the same two colors with maximal parity. *Proof:* If this wasn't the case, then the single color that appears maximally twice over the two squares would be maximal over the $m \times 2m$ . $\blacksquare$ Thus, it follows that for a large $(N_1m + a) \times (N_2m + b)$ rectangle with $0 \le a, b < m$ , the two colors that appear the most appear at least $(N_1-1)(N_2-1)$ times more than the color that appears the least in the $N_1m \times N_2m$ subgrid made of $m \times m$ subrectangles of a fixed parity $\pmod{m}$ . There are then at most $ab + a(N_2+m)m + b(N_1+m)m$ remaining cells. If we take $\min(N_1, N_2) > 1434m^2$ then it follows that this fact can't change in this are rectangle. Thus, for sufficiently large rectangles, the two colors that appear the most are always the same, regardless of which rectangle is chosen. Now, for large odd $T$ , take a $T \times T$ and $T \times (T + 1)$ square. Since the two maximal colors appear the same number of times in both, they must appear the same number of times in the $1 \times T$ slice, and similarly in every $T \times 1$ slice. Shifting this slice by $1$ implies that the coloring is periodic mod $T$ . Taking two values of $T$ as $t, t+2$ gives that this coloring is periodic mod $\gcd(t, t+2) = \gcd(t, 2) = 1$ which implies the coloring is monochromatic, which is evidently impossible.

stem_md:
Tacocat the cat, who can write lowercase English letters as well as paw prints  $\star$ , wishes to identify palindromes! Let  $S=\{a,b,\dots,z\}$  be the set of English letters, and define  $T=S\cup \{\star\}$ .

Tacocat has a list of words  $(w_1, u_1)$ ,  $\dots$ ,  $(w_n, u_n)$ , made up of characters in  $T$ . A human gives Tacocat a string  $s$  of letters in  $S$ , to which Tacocat prepends two paw prints to the left of the string, creating  $s'$ . Then, Tacocat repeatedly does the following until none of  $w_1$ ,  $\dots$ ,  $w_n$  is a substring of  $s'$ :

- For the smallest  $i$  such that  $w_i$  is a substring of  $s'$ , the first instance of  $w_i$  is replaced by  $u_i$ .

Can Tacocat choose words  $w_i$  and  $u_i$ , and a word  $W$ , consisting of letters in  $T$ , so that the process terminates for all  $s$ , and the final word will be  $W$  if and only if the original string  $s$  was a palindrome?

*Karn Chutinan*
solution_md:
Best problem on the shortlist by far.

The answer is yes: first let two paw prints denote the single character  $\bullet$ . This problem is stronger than the original.

Now take the following dictionary (in order, with pairs on the same level arranged arbitrarily):


- $\bullet\bullet\bullet\,\bullet\to\emptyset$
- $a\bullet\bullet\,\bullet\to\bullet\bullet\bullet\,a$  for any letter  $a$
- $a\bullet b\to b\,a\,\bullet$  for any two (not necessarily distinct) letters  $a,b$
- $a\,a\bullet\bullet\to\emptyset$  for any letter  $a$
- $a\,b\bullet\bullet\to a\bullet\bullet\bullet b$  for distinct letters  $a,b$
- $\bullet\,a\bullet\bullet\to\bullet$  for any letter  $a$
- $a\,\bullet\to a\bullet\bullet$  for any letter  $a$
- $\bullet\,a\to\bullet\,a\,\bullet$  for any letter  $a$

and  $W=\bullet$ . We claim this works.

We show this by induction. For  $s$  of length  $0$  this is trivial. For  $s$  of length  $1$  then we must do steps  $8,7,6$  in order, giving the desired result.

Now suppose  $s$  has length  $\ge 2$ . We do step  $8$  first, then repeat step  $3$  until the  $\bullet$  reaches the right. Doing this also takes the first letter of  $s$  and brings it to the back, right before the  $\bullet$ . Then step  $7$  runs. If the first and last letters of  $s$  were the same, then step  $4$  runs, reducing to the same problem but with the first and last letters of  $s$  cut off. By inductive hypothesis, this reaches  $W$  iff this is a palindrome, which happens iff  $s$  was a palindrome.

If the first and last letters were different,  $s$  was not a palindrome, and step  $5$  runs, then step  $2$  runs repeatedly, taking the  $\bullet\bullet\bullet$  string backwards until it reaches the front. Then step  $1$  runs, removing all  $\bullet$ s from the string, and it terminates at a string other than  $W$ , as desired.

Consider the process. The string starts out beginning with two paw prints, so then after one operation, the string begins  $\star\star\ell_1\star$ , where  $\ell_1$  is the first letter of  $s$ . Then, on successive moves, the substring  $\star\star\ell_1\star$  moves across the string, eventually reaching the end. Then, the string ends  $\ell_n\star\star\ell_1\star$ , where  $\ell_2$  is the last letter of  $s$ . If the first and last letters of  $s$  are not equal, then  $s$  is not a palindrome, so the string ends in  $\star\star\star\star\star$  after one more operation, which turns the entire string into  $\star\star\star\star\star$ . Otherwise, if the first and last letters of  $s$  are equal, then those two letters are deleted, so the string now ends in  $\star\star\star$ . Then, this substring moves back across the string to get back to the beginning, and  $\star\star\star$  is replaced with  $\star\star$ . Then, the entire process starts again.

If the string is not a palindrome, then the string becomes a sequence of five paw prints. Otherwise, the string is either  $\star\star$  or  $\star\star\ell$ . In the second case, the string becomes  $\star\star\ell\star$ , which then becomes  $\star\star$ . Therefore, the final word is  $\star\star$  if and only if  $s$  is a palindrome.

The first step is to functionally extend our alphabet. We define special characters 
\[
	 \ell \equiv \star\ \star\ S\ \star
\]
for a unique string  $S$  of length  $\ge 2$ . Note that if all of our  $u_i$  create special characters, and we deal with the initially starting  $\star \star$ , then we never interpret a special character when one shouldn't exist. Also index the alphabet  $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_{26}$ .

We define special characters  $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \omega_1, \dots, \omega_{26}, \gamma, \Omega, \delta, \varepsilon$  as well.

As such, we define our last rule to replace  $\star \star$  with  $\alpha_0$  for special character  $\alpha_0$ . Now add the rule  $\alpha_0 \ell_i \to \alpha_1 \omega_i \gamma \ell_i$  for each letter  $\ell_i$ . The idea now is that  $\omega_i$  is a packet of information which deletes itself with the last element of the string.

For each  $i$  and  $j$ , add the rules  $\gamma \ell_i \to \ell_i \gamma, \omega_i \ell_j \to \ell_j \omega_i$  for each letter  $\ell_i$  first, which means  $\gamma$  moves to the end of the string with priority higher than  $\ell_i$ .

Now, we add rules  $\ell_i \omega_i \gamma \to \Omega$  and  $\ell_i \Omega \to \Omega \ell_i$  which means that if the packet  $\omega_i$  is same as the last character  $\ell_i$ , we delete both and send  $\Omega$  back to the front. We then add rule  $\alpha_1\Omega \to \alpha_0$  to indicate reading in the next character. 

Finally, for  $i \ne j$ , we add rules  $\ell_i \omega_j \gamma \to \delta, \ell_i \delta \to \delta, \alpha_1 \delta \to \delta, \delta \to ilostthegame$  with the highest priority which means the program turns into  $ilostthegame$ . 

We now consider termination logic. For odd length initial strings, we add the rule  $\alpha_1 \omega_i \gamma \to \epsilon$  with lower priority than  $\gamma$  moving. For even length initial strings, we add the rule  $\alpha_1 \to \epsilon$  with even lower priority than that. Finally, we add  $\epsilon \to popop$  with penultimate priority.

This means that all palindromes terminate into  $popop$ , and all those which aren't palindromes turn into  $ilostthegame$ .

We show it can be done with only one pawprint. Consider the following operations written as  $w_i\to u_i$  and in increasing order of  $i$ :
\begin{align*}
\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{o}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{o}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}&\to\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{o}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{o}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\tag{ $\alpha\in S$ }
\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\beta}&\to\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\beta}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\tag{ $\alpha,\beta\in S$ }
\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}&\to\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\tag{ $\alpha\in S$ }
\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\beta}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}&\to\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star} \mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{o}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{o}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\tag{ $\alpha\neq\beta\in S$ }
\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}&\to\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}\tag{ $\alpha\in S$ }
\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}&\to\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}
\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}&\to\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\tag{ $\alpha\in S$ }
\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}&\to\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\tag{ $\alpha\in S$ }
\end{align*}

This outlines the following process:


- If there's only one  $\star$ :
[list]
- If there's a letter  $\alpha$  to the right of the  $\star$ , then it will be encapsulated as  $\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}$ .
- Otherwise, the operations will terminate.
[/list]
- If there's two  $\star$ :
[list]
- If the two  $\star$  are adjacent:
[list]
- If there is a character to the left, shift  $\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}$  to the left.
- If there is no character to the left, reduce it to a single  $\star$ .
[/list]
- If there's a single character  $\alpha$ :
[list]
- If there's still a character  $\beta$  to the right, shift the entire  $\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}$  to the right of  $\beta$ .
- If there's no more character to the right:
[list]
- If there's no character to the left, reduce the entire string to  $\star$ .
- If the character to the left is the same as  $\alpha$ , then reduce it to  $\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}$ .
- If the character to the left is not the same as  $\alpha$ , then create  $\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{o}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{o}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}$ .
[/list]
[/list]
- If  $\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{o}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{o}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}$  is present, delete the character to its left.
[/list]


At any point in time, there's at least one  $\star$ . A single  $\star$  can only appear at the very left of the string; if it's alone then the process stops and otherwise it will encapsulate the character to its right as  $\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}$ .

If there's two  $\star$ , and there's exactly one character in between, it will be transported all the way to the right (unless that's all that's left, in which case it will be converted to  $\star$ ). There, a decision will be made: if the rightmost character of the unencapsulated string is the same as the character inside the capsule  $\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\alpha}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}$ , then it will be accepted, making it  $\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}$ . This will get transported all the way to the left, be converted to a single  $\star$ , restarting the process on a shorter string. Otherwise, it will get changed to  $\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{o}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{o}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}$ , which will devour the rest of the string. $W=\star$  is the result if the initial string was a palindrome, and  $\texttt{XooX}=\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{o}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{o}\mathmakebox[0.67em][c]{\star}$  otherwise.

This works as a palindrome check because it's equivalent to checking if the leftmost and rightmost letters are the same, if yes then delete and repeat, else return false.

stem_md:
Let  $n$  be a positive integer. Alexandre fills each cell of an  $n \times n$  grid with an integer between  $1$  and  $n$  inclusive such that no two cells which contain the same number share a row or column. He places a token on the top left cell. He may move the token between two orthogonally adjacent cells if and only if the numbers on the cells differ by  $1$ . Find all  $n$  for which is it possible for Alexandre to fill the grid in a way such that the token can be moved to any cell of the grid.

*Benny Wang*
solution_md:
The answer is  $\boxed{n=1\text{ and all even }n}$ . $n=1$  vacuously works, and all other odd  $n$  fail because in two rows, there are  $2n+1$  odd numbers, which can’t all lie on the same checkerboard color, and it’s impossible to get between two odd numbers on different colors.

Now it remains to show all even  $n$  work. Label the cells  $(0,0)$  at the bottom left through  $(n-1,n-1)$  at the top right, and fill in with the numbers  $0$  to  $n-1$  instead. Let cell  $(i,j)$  in row  $i$  column  $j$  have the number  $i+j(-1)^i\pmod n$ .

It is easy to see that there are no repeats within each row (fixed value of  $i$ ). As for the column (fixed value of  $j$ ), if two numbers are equal, then they have to have the same parity, so their two  $i$ 's must have the same parity. But this means  $(-1)^i$  must be equal, so their  $i$ 's are in fact equal. In conclusion, we have constructed a Latin Square.

For  $n=8$ , we get \[
\left(
\begin{array}{cccccccc}
 7 & 6 & 5 & 4 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 0 
 6 & 7 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 
 5 & 4 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 7 & 6 
 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 
 3 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 7 & 6 & 5 & 4 
 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 0 & 1 
 1 & 0 & 7 & 6 & 5 & 4 & 3 & 2 
 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 
\end{array}
\right)
\]Thanks Mathematica!

We want to show that all cells are connected (in terms of token adjacency).

Rows  $0$  and  $n-1$  are made of the numbers  $0$  to  $n-1$  in order, so each row is connected. Color them green.
Now for every  $k$  from  $1$  to  $\frac n2-1$ , consider rows  $2k$  and  $2k-1$ .
In row  $2k-1$ , take the numbers  $0$  and to the left, and in row  $2k$ , take the numbers  $n-1$  and to the left. Within the row they are connected as they each differ by  $1$ , and the leftmost numbers belong to the first column so they are connected. Color these  $n$  numbers red.
Take the rest of the  $n$  numbers and color them blue. Similarly they differ by  $1$  in the row so they're connected in the row, and then by considering the two numbers in column  $n-1$  which are  $(2k-1)-(-1)=2k>0$  and  $(2k)+(-1)=2k-1>0$ , we see they differ by  $1$  so they are also connected.
This forms the following diagram:
\[
\left(
\begin{array}{cccccccc}
 \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}7 & \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}6 & \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}5 & \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}4 & \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}3 & \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}2 & \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}1 & \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}0 
 \textcolor{red}6 & \textcolor{red}7 & \textcolor{blue}0 & \textcolor{blue}1 & \textcolor{blue}2 & \textcolor{blue}3 & \textcolor{blue}4 & \textcolor{blue}5 
 \textcolor{red}5 & \textcolor{red}4 & \textcolor{red}3 & \textcolor{red}2 & \textcolor{red}1 & \textcolor{red}0 & \textcolor{blue}7 & \textcolor{blue}6 
 \textcolor{red}4 & \textcolor{red}5 & \textcolor{red}6 & \textcolor{red}7 & \textcolor{blue}0 & \textcolor{blue}1 & \textcolor{blue}2 & \textcolor{blue}3 
 \textcolor{red}3 & \textcolor{red}2 & \textcolor{red}1 & \textcolor{red}0 & \textcolor{blue}7 & \textcolor{blue}6 & \textcolor{blue}5 & \textcolor{blue}4 
 \textcolor{red}2 & \textcolor{red}3 & \textcolor{red}4 & \textcolor{red}5 & \textcolor{red}6 & \textcolor{red}7 & \textcolor{blue}0 & \textcolor{blue}1 
 \textcolor{red}1 & \textcolor{red}0 & \textcolor{blue}7 & \textcolor{blue}6 & \textcolor{blue}5 & \textcolor{blue}4 & \textcolor{blue}3 & \textcolor{blue}2 
 \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}0 & \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}1 & \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}2 & \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}3 & \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}4 & \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}5 & \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}6 & \textcolor[rgb]{0.1,0.4,0.1}7 
\end{array}
\right)
\]Now we consider column  $\frac n2$ . Every blue region intersects it, and it counts up by  $1$  from  $\frac n2$  at the bottom to  $\frac n2-1$  at the top, therefore it is connected in two segments. Therefore, each blue region is either connected to the top or the bottom green region.
And in a similar way consider column  $0$ . Every red region intersects it and it counts up by  $1$  from  $0$  to  $n-1$ . Therefore, every red region is connected to both the top and bottom green region.
This completes the proof.

The answer is  $\boxed{n=1\text{ and all even }n}$ . Construction for  $n=1,2$  is obvious.

Odd  $n\ge 3$  don't work by checkerboard coloring (parity of checkerboard must match parity of number).

Even  $n\ge 4$  do work by the following construction:
[pywindow]
n = input("Value of n (must be even): ")
n = int(n)
assert n % 2 == 0
assert n >= 2

def goodPrint(arr):
    print(" ".join("%2d" % x for x in arr))

print()
for i in range(1,n+1):
    if i % 2 == 1:
        goodPrint(range(i,n+1)+range(1,i))
    else:
        goodPrint(range(i,0,-1)+range(n,i,-1))
[/pywindow]
First, note that the left column is connected. For now, only consider the top half of the grid. Consider the two "components" of each row (besides the top). The left component is always connected to the left column, and the right component for odd rows connects to the right component of the previous row, while the right component for even rows connects to the left component of the previous row.

Similarly, the bottom half of the grid is also connected. Now obviously the top half and bottom half are connected (by the left column), done.  $\blacksquare$
